entries.example: f(x) = k*x^2 for 0 <= x <= 2. Normalise: integral_0^2 k*x^2 dx = 8k/3 = 1, so k = 3/8. Then P(0.5 < X < 1.5) = 13/32 ~ 0.406.
entries.fact: A continuous RV takes uncountably many values. P(X = c) = 0 for every single point c — probabilities only live on intervals. PDF axioms: f(x) >= 0 and the integral over all x equals 1. A PDF is a density, not a probability, so f(x) CAN exceed 1.
entries.formula: P(a <= X <= b) = integral_a^b f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a). If a PDF does not integrate to 1, normalise first.
entries.subject: Probability & Stats

entries.fact: CDF F(x) = P(X <= x) = integral_{-inf}^x f(t) dt. Reverse it: f(x) = F'(x). For continuous X, F is continuous and non-decreasing, F(-inf) = 0, F(inf) = 1. A jump in a CDF means a discrete mass point — it is not purely continuous.
entries.formula: Median: solve F(m) = 1/2. Mode: where f is tallest. E[g(X)] = integral g(x) f(x) dx (LOTUS). Var(X) = E[X^2] - mu^2.
entries.subject: Probability & Stats

entries.fact: Continuous Uniform[a, b]: every point in [a, b] equally likely. CDF has three pieces: 0 for x < a, (x-a)/(b-a) for a <= x <= b, 1 for x > b. Single points have probability zero, so P(X <= 3) = P(X < 3).
entries.subject: Probability & Stats

entries.example: X ~ Exponential(lambda = 0.5). By memoryless, P(X > 6 | X > 2) = P(X > 4) = e^{-0.5*4} = e^{-2} ~ 0.135.
entries.fact: Exponential(lambda) is the continuous version of Geometric. It is the ONLY continuous distribution with the memoryless property: past waiting buys you nothing. GATE uses rate lambda (mean 1/lambda); some textbooks use mean theta instead — read the question's definition first.
entries.formula: f(x) = lambda*e^{-lambda*x}, x >= 0. F(x) = 1 - e^{-lambda*x}. E[X] = 1/lambda. Var(X) = 1/lambda^2. P(X > s+t | X > s) = P(X > t). Median = ln 2 / lambda ~ 0.693/lambda, below the mean (right-skewed).
entries.subject: Probability & Stats

entries.fact: Normal X ~ N(mu, sigma^2) is a symmetric bell curve with mean = median = mode = mu. Always standardise first: Z = (X - mu)/sigma ~ N(0,1), then read the table. GATE writes N(10, 4) — the 4 is the VARIANCE, sigma = 2, not 4. 68-95-99.7 rule: within 1/2/3 sigma of mu.
entries.formula: f(x) = 1/(sigma*sqrt(2*pi)) * e^{-(x-mu)^2/(2*sigma^2)}. P(a < X < b) = Phi((b-mu)/sigma) - Phi((a-mu)/sigma). Phi(1) ~ 0.8413, Phi(2) ~ 0.9772, Phi(1.96) ~ 0.975. Phi(-z) = 1 - Phi(z). P(|Z| < z) = 2*Phi(z) - 1.
entries.subject: Probability & Stats

entries.fact: A linear combination of independent normals is normal. Means add or subtract; variances ALWAYS add, never subtract. Sum of n iid N(mu, sigma^2) is N(n*mu, n*sigma^2) — mean scales by n, variance by n, SD by sqrt(n).
entries.formula: aX + bY ~ N(a*mu_x + b*mu_y, a^2*sigma_x^2 + b^2*sigma_y^2) for independent X, Y. E[X - Y] = mu_x - mu_y, Var(X - Y) = sigma_x^2 + sigma_y^2.
entries.subject: Probability & Stats

entries.fact: Chi-squared with n degrees of freedom is the sum of n squared iid standard normals: Z1^2 + ... + Zn^2. Always >= 0, right-skewed, NOT symmetric — do not import bell-curve instincts. Chi-squared(1) = Z^2; chi-squared(2) is Exponential(1/2). Sampling link: (n-1)S^2/sigma^2 ~ chi-squared(n-1).
entries.formula: E[chi^2] = n. Var(chi^2) = 2n. Mode = n - 2 (for n >= 2). E[X^2] = Var + (E[X])^2 = 2n + n^2. Independent chi-squares add: df adds.
entries.subject: Probability & Stats

entries.example: Joint PDF f(x,y) = 2 on the triangle 0 < y < x < 1. f_X(x) = integral_0^x 2 dy = 2x. So f_{Y|X}(y|x) = 2/(2x) = 1/x on 0 < y < x — y's ceiling is x, not 1.
entries.fact: Conditional PDF = joint divided by the marginal of the GIVEN variable. It must integrate to 1 over x for the fixed y — if it does not, you divided by the wrong marginal. The support can shrink after conditioning. If X, Y are independent, conditioning does nothing: f_{X|Y}(x|y) = f_X(x).
entries.formula: f_{X|Y}(x|y) = f_{X,Y}(x,y) / f_Y(y). P(X in A | Y = y) = integral_A f_{X|Y}(x|y) dx. Law of total expectation: E[X] = E[E[X|Y]].
entries.subject: Probability & Stats

entries.fact: Joint = both happen at once. Marginal = sum (discrete) or integrate (continuous) out the other variable — you 'forget' that column. Marginal limits follow the region, not the rectangle: on 0 <= x < y <= 1, f_X(x) integrates y from x to 1, not 0 to 1. Draw the region first.
entries.formula: Discrete: P_X(x) = sum_y P(x, y). Continuous: f_X(x) = integral f_{X,Y}(x, y) dy. Independent continuous variables: joint = product of marginals.
entries.subject: Probability & Stats

entries.example: A test is 95% accurate both ways, but only 1% have the disease. P(disease | +) = (0.95*0.01)/(0.95*0.01 + 0.05*0.99) = 0.0095/0.059 ~ 0.161. The base rate dominates — a positive test is still usually a false positive.
entries.fact: Conditional = zoom in on the given slice, then renormalise so it sums to 1. P(A|B) is NOT P(B|A) — Bayes' theorem exists precisely because they differ. Law of total probability needs a partition that is mutually exclusive AND exhaustive; a missing case corrupts the whole answer. Parse the English first: 'given that' = condition, 'both/and' = joint, 'overall/regardless' = marginal or total probability.
entries.formula: P(X=x | Y=y) = P(X=x, Y=y) / P(Y=y), needs P(Y=y) > 0. Bayes: P(B_i|A) = P(A|B_i)*P(B_i) / sum_j P(A|B_j)*P(B_j). Law of total probability: P(A) = sum_i P(A|B_i)*P(B_i).
entries.subject: Probability & Stats

entries.fact: Independent means P(x,y) = P_X(x)*P_Y(y) for EVERY x, y — equivalently, conditioning changes nothing. Independent implies Cov = 0, but the converse is FALSE in general: zero covariance does not imply independence (the one exception is jointly Gaussian variables).
entries.formula: Cov(X,Y) = E[XY] - E[X]*E[Y]. Independent: E[XY] = E[X]*E[Y] and Var(X+Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y). Var(X - Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) for independent X, Y — the minus does NOT carry inside. General: Var(aX + bY) = a^2*Var(X) + b^2*Var(Y) + 2ab*Cov(X,Y).
entries.subject: Probability & Stats

entries.example: Data 7, 3, 9, 3, 12, 5. Sorted: 3, 3, 5, 7, 9, 12. Mean = 39/6 = 6.5. Median = (5+7)/2 = 6. Mode = 3. For median 24 and mean 27 (moderately skewed), mode ~ 3*24 - 2*27 = 18.
entries.fact: Mean = share everything out flat. Median = the middle value AFTER SORTING (odd n: middle value; even n: average of the two middle values). Mode = most frequent value — it may not exist (all distinct) or there may be several (bimodal). Mean is dragged by outliers, median is not. Empirical relation (moderately skewed, unimodal only — an approximation, not a theorem): mode = 3*median - 2*mean.
entries.formula: Mean x-bar = (sum x_i)/n. Weighted mean = sum w_i*x_i / sum w_i. Empirical: mean - mode = 3*(mean - median).
entries.subject: Probability & Stats

entries.example: Observations 4, 8, 6, 10, 12. Mean = 8, sum of squared deviations = 40. Sample variance = 40/4 = 10. Population variance = 40/5 = 8. If SD = 4 and x -> 3 - 2x, new SD = |-2|*4 = 8 — the +3 shift does nothing.
entries.fact: Variance = E[(X-mu)^2] = E[X^2] - mu^2 — the formula never changes. SD = sqrt(variance), always >= 0. Sample variance divides by (n-1); population variance divides by n — if GATE says 'sample', the denominator is n-1. A shift (+b) never changes spread; scaling multiplies SD by |a| and variance by a^2.
entries.formula: Var(X) = E[X^2] - mu^2. E[aX+b] = a*E[X] + b. Var(aX+b) = a^2*Var(X). SD(aX+b) = |a|*SD(X). Var(X+Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) + 2*Cov(X,Y).
entries.subject: Probability & Stats

entries.example: X takes -1, 0, 1 with equal probability; Y = X^2. Cov = 0, so rho = 0 — yet Y is a perfect function of X. Correlation only sees straight lines. Exam scores mean 70, SD 8: by Chebyshev (k=2), at least 1 - 1/4 = 75% score between 54 and 86.
entries.fact: Correlation is covariance squashed into [-1, 1] — a score for 'how close is this to a perfect straight line?'. Correlation is unitless; covariance has units (units of X times units of Y), so covariance's magnitude alone is meaningless. Independent implies rho = 0, but rho = 0 only kills LINEAR dependence. If X is constant (sigma = 0), rho is undefined, not zero.
entries.formula: Cov(X,Y) = E[XY] - E[X]*E[Y]. rho = Cov(X,Y)/(sigma_x*sigma_y), -1 <= rho <= 1. rho = +1 or -1 iff Y = aX + b exactly. Cov(aX+b, cY+d) = a*c*Cov(X,Y). Chebyshev: P(|X-mu| >= k*sigma) <= 1/k^2.
entries.subject: Probability & Stats

entries.fact: A discrete RV takes values in a countable set. PMF axioms: p(x) >= 0 and sum p(x_i) = 1 over the whole support — always add first, three of four options in a GATE question are usually fakes. The CDF jumps by p(x_i) at each mass point and is flat between them. For discrete RVs, P(X <= 3) and P(X < 3) differ exactly by p(3) — read the inequality carefully. Never integrate a PMF; never treat a staircase CDF as continuous.
entries.formula: E[X] = sum x_i*p(x_i). E[g(X)] = sum g(x_i)*p(x_i) (LOTUS — no need to find g(X)'s distribution). Var(X) = E[X^2] - mu^2. Linearity: E[aX + bY + c] = a*E[X] + b*E[Y] + c, no independence needed. Var(aX+b) = a^2*Var(X).
entries.subject: Probability & Stats

entries.example: A fair die rolled 4 times; X = number of sixes ~ Binomial(4, 1/6). P(X=2) = C(4,2)*(1/6)^2*(5/6)^2 = 25/216 ~ 0.116. E[X] = 4/6 = 2/3. Calls Poisson(2)/hour: P(exactly 2) = e^{-2}*2^2/2! = 2*e^{-2} ~ 0.271.
entries.fact: Binomial = sum of n iid Bernoulli(p) — spot 'n identical yes/no trials' and it is binomial instantly. Poisson = binomial limit (n large, p small, np = lambda); mean = variance = lambda is the giveaway. Sums of independent Poissons stay Poisson (lambdas add); sums of binomials need the SAME p. Geometric has two conventions: trials-to-first-success {1,2,...} (GATE usually means this, E = 1/p) vs failures-before-first {0,1,2,...} — check the support first.
entries.formula: Bernoulli(p): E = p, Var = p(1-p). Binomial(n,p): P(X=k) = C(n,k)*p^k*(1-p)^{n-k}, E = np, Var = np(1-p). Geometric(p): P(X=k) = (1-p)^{k-1}*p, E = 1/p, Var = (1-p)/p^2. Poisson(lambda): P(X=k) = e^{-lambda}*lambda^k/k!, E = lambda, Var = lambda. Discrete Uniform{1..n}: E = (n+1)/2, Var = (n^2-1)/12.
entries.subject: Probability & Stats
entries.topic: Bernoulli, Binomial, Geometric, Poisson, Discrete Uniform

entries.example: X ~ Geometric(p = 0.3), trials to first success. P(X > 4 | X > 2) = P(X > 2) = (1-0.3)^2 = 0.49. A fair coin tossed until the first head: E[X] = 1/0.5 = 2 tosses; P(first head on 3rd toss) = (1/2)^3 = 1/8.
entries.fact: Geometric is the ONLY discrete distribution with the memoryless property: past failures buy you nothing. Continuous twin: Exponential. Mode of a discrete RV = the value with the largest p(x).
entries.formula: P(X > m+n | X > m) = P(X > n). For the trials convention, P(X > k) = (1-p)^k. E[X] = 1/p.
entries.subject: Probability & Stats

entries.fact: 'At least one' shortcut: P(X >= 1) = 1 - P(X=0) = 1 - (1-p)^n. Never sum the whole PMF for this. Mode (most likely k) = floor((n+1)p); if (n+1)p is an integer, k and k-1 are both modes. Normal approximation (large n, p not near 0/1): Binomial ~ N(np, npq) with continuity correction +/-0.5. If success probability changes trial to trial, X is a sum of non-identical Bernoullis — E[X] still sums by linearity, but no binomial PMF applies.
entries.formula: P(X=k) = C(n,k)*p^k*(1-p)^{n-k}. E[X] = np. Var(X) = np(1-p). E[X^2] = npq + n^2*p^2.
entries.subject: Probability & Stats

entries.fact: Two different 'uniform variance' formulas — swapping them is the most common 1-mark loss here. Continuous Uniform[a,b]: (b-a)^2/12. Discrete Uniform{1..n}: (n^2-1)/12. Bernoulli variance p(1-p) is maximised at p = 1/2, max 0.25. Discrete inequalities bite (P(X<=3) != P(X<3) for Binomial); continuous ones do not (single points are zero).
entries.formula: Continuous Uniform: E = (a+b)/2, Var = (b-a)^2/12. Discrete Uniform{1..n}: E = (n+1)/2, Var = (n^2-1)/12. Bernoulli(p): E = p, Var = p(1-p) <= 1/4.
entries.subject: Probability & Stats
entries.topic: Uniform vs Bernoulli — the two variance traps

entries.example: lim(x->0) (sin 3x - 3x)/x^3 = -9/2 (series: sin 3x = 3x - (3x)^3/6 + ...). lim(x->inf) x*[ln(x+1) - ln x] = 1. lim(x->0+) x^x = 1 (x ln x -> 0).
entries.fact: L'Hopital applies ONLY to 0/0 or infinity/infinity forms — check the form first, then differentiate top and bottom separately (NOT the quotient rule). One-sided limits must both agree for the two-sided limit to exist. Squeeze theorem kills things like x*sin(1/x) as x -> 0.
entries.formula: lim(x->0) sin x / x = 1. lim(x->0) (1-cos x)/x^2 = 1/2. lim(x->0) (e^x-1)/x = 1. lim(x->0) ln(1+x)/x = 1. lim(x->inf) (1+1/x)^x = e. Conversions: 0*inf -> inf/inf or 0/0; 1^inf / 0^0 / inf^0 -> take ln.
entries.subject: Calculus & Optimization

entries.example: f(x) = (x^3-8)/(x-2) for x != 2, f(2) = 6. Limit at 2 is 12, but f(2) = 6, so it is discontinuous at 2 — removable. f continuous on [0,1] with f(0) = -2, f(1) = 3 guarantees at least one root in (0,1) by IVT.
entries.fact: f is continuous at a iff lim(x->a-) f = lim(x->a+) f = f(a) — all three must exist AND match. Discontinuity types: removable (hole), jump (one-sided limits differ), essential/infinite (blows up), oscillatory (sin(1/x) at 0). IVT: continuous on [a,b] with f(a)*f(b) < 0 guarantees at least one root in (a,b). Continuous on a closed interval is bounded and attains its max/min (Extreme Value Theorem).
entries.formula: Continuity at a: LHL = RHL = f(a). IVT: f(a)*f(b) < 0 => exists c in (a,b) with f(c) = 0.
entries.subject: Calculus & Optimization

entries.example: f(x) = x^2*sin(1/x), f(0)=0: continuous at 0 (squeeze) and differentiable at 0 with f'(0)=0. |x-1| + |x-2| is differentiable everywhere except x=1 and x=2 (kinks). MVT on sqrt(x) over [1,4]: f'(c) = 1/3, c = 9/4.
entries.fact: Differentiable at a implies continuous at a. The converse is FALSE — |x| at 0 is the classic counterexample. Check left and right derivatives separately for piecewise/absolute-value functions. Differentiable does NOT mean continuously differentiable: x^2*sin(1/x) is differentiable at 0 with derivative 0, but f' is discontinuous there.
entries.formula: f'(a) = lim(h->0) [f(a+h) - f(a)]/h. Rolle: f continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), f(a) = f(b) => some c in (a,b) with f'(c) = 0. MVT: f'(c) = [f(b)-f(a)]/(b-a). Taylor: e^x = 1+x+x^2/2!+...; sin x = x-x^3/3!+...; cos x = 1-x^2/2!+...; ln(1+x) = x-x^2/2+x^3/3-... (|x|<1).
entries.subject: Calculus & Optimization

entries.example: f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 + 1. f'(x) = 3x(x-2); f''(x) = 6x-6. Local max at x=0, f(0)=1; local min at x=2, f(2)=-3. g(x) = (x-1)^4: second derivative test is inconclusive at x=1 (g''(1)=0); first derivative test confirms global minimum 0 at x=1.
entries.fact: Fermat: if f has a local max/min at interior point c and f'(c) exists, then f'(c) = 0 — necessary, NOT sufficient. Critical points = f'(c) = 0 OR f'(c) undefined (cusps, kinks) — plus endpoints on a closed interval. First derivative test: f' changes + to - => local max; - to + => local min; no sign change => neither (x^3 at 0). Second derivative test: f''(c) > 0 => local min, < 0 => local max, = 0 => INCONCLUSIVE (x^4 min, -x^4 max, x^3 neither all have f'(0)=f''(0)=0).
entries.formula: First derivative test: sign change of f' across c decides. Second derivative test: f'(c)=0 and f''(c)>0 => min; f''(c)<0 => max; f''(c)=0 => inconclusive, go back to the first derivative test.
entries.subject: Calculus & Optimization

entries.example: f(x) = |x^2 - 4| on [-3, 3]. Candidates: kinks at x = +/-2 (f=0), f(0)=4, endpoints f(+/-3)=5. Global max 5 at x=-3 and x=3 — endpoints win. h(x) = x + 1/x, x > 0: h'(x) = 1 - 1/x^2 = 0 => x=1, minimum value 2. Two positive numbers summing to 10 minimise sum of squares at (5, 5): minimum 50.
entries.fact: Global max/min on [a,b]: evaluate f at every critical point inside (a,b) AND at a and b. The largest/smallest value wins — never skip the endpoints; on a closed interval the global extremum is very often at an endpoint. Local max can sit below a local min elsewhere — 'local' means in a neighbourhood only. Domain first: x + 1/x has a clean minimum 2 on x > 0, but on R minus {0} there is no global min at all. Applied setup: use the constraint to eliminate the second variable, then differentiate.
entries.formula: Global on [a,b]: compare f(critical points) and f(a), f(b). AM-GM shortcut: x + 1/x >= 2*sqrt(x*1/x) = 2 for x > 0.
entries.subject: Calculus & Optimization

entries.example: Air (density 1.225 kg/m3) speeds up from 50 m/s below a wing to 70 m/s above it at the same height. Pressure drop = 0.5 x 1.225 x (70^2 - 50^2) = 0.5 x 1.225 x 2400 = 1470 Pa, so the upper surface pressure is 1470 Pa lower than the lower surface.
entries.fact: Along a streamline in steady, incompressible, inviscid flow, the sum of static pressure, dynamic pressure and elevation pressure is constant. Faster flow therefore means lower static pressure, which is the basic explanation for the pressure difference that produces lift on a wing.
entries.formula: p + (1/2) rho V^2 + rho g h = constant; dynamic pressure q = (1/2) rho V^2
entries.subject: Aerodynamics

entries.example: For rho = 1.225 kg/m3, V = 60 m/s, wing area S = 20 m2 and CL = 0.5: L = 0.5 x 1.225 x 60^2 x 20 x 0.5 = 22,050 N.
entries.fact: Lift is proportional to dynamic pressure, wing area and the lift coefficient. The lift coefficient depends mainly on angle of attack, airfoil shape and Mach and Reynolds numbers, and it rises roughly linearly with angle of attack until stall.
entries.formula: L = (1/2) rho V^2 S CL
entries.subject: Aerodynamics

entries.example: With CD0 = 0.02, CL = 0.5, Oswald efficiency e = 0.8 and aspect ratio AR = 8: CD = 0.02 + 0.5^2 / (pi x 0.8 x 8) = 0.02 + 0.0124 = 0.0324.
entries.fact: Total drag coefficient is the sum of parasite (zero-lift) drag and lift-induced drag. Induced drag falls as aspect ratio rises, which is why gliders have long slender wings, while parasite drag dominates at high speed.
entries.formula: CD = CD0 + CL^2 / (pi e AR); D = (1/2) rho V^2 S CD
entries.subject: Aerodynamics

entries.example: At angle of attack 5 degrees = 0.0873 rad, Cl = 2 pi x 0.0873 = 0.55 for a thin symmetric airfoil at zero camber offset.
entries.fact: Thin airfoil theory predicts that a thin symmetric airfoil has a lift slope of 2 pi per radian (about 0.11 per degree) and zero lift at zero angle of attack. Camber shifts the zero-lift angle to a negative value but does not change the slope much.
entries.formula: Cl = 2 pi (alpha - alpha0); lift slope dCl/dalpha = 2 pi per radian
entries.subject: Aerodynamics

entries.example: A jet exhausts 100 kg/s at 600 m/s while flying at 200 m/s, with no pressure thrust: F = 100 x (600 - 200) = 40,000 N.
entries.fact: Thrust is the rate of change of momentum of the air and fuel passing through the engine, plus any pressure thrust at the nozzle exit. Increasing exhaust velocity or mass flow increases thrust, and thrust falls as flight speed approaches exhaust speed.
entries.formula: F = mdot_e Ve - mdot_0 V0 + (pe - p0) Ae
entries.subject: Propulsion
entries.topic: Thrust equation for a jet engine

entries.example: At about 11,000 m altitude the speed of sound is about 295 m/s, so an aircraft flying at 250 m/s has M = 250 / 295 = 0.85, in the high-subsonic / transonic range.
entries.fact: Mach number is flight speed divided by the local speed of sound, which depends on temperature. Flow is subsonic below M = 1, transonic near M = 1, supersonic above it, and hypersonic above about M = 5.
entries.formula: M = V / a; a = sqrt(gamma R T), with gamma = 1.4 for air
entries.subject: Aerodynamics
entries.topic: Mach number and speed of sound

entries.example: With V = 240 m/s, thrust specific fuel consumption cT = 0.6 per hour = 1.667 x 10^-4 per second, L/D = 15 and Wi/Wf = 1.25: R = (240 / 1.667 x 10^-4) x 15 x ln(1.25) = about 4.82 x 10^6 m, about 4,820 km.
entries.fact: The Breguet range equation gives the cruise range of a jet aircraft assuming constant speed, lift-to-drag ratio and specific fuel consumption. Range improves with higher L/D, lower fuel consumption, and a larger fraction of the takeoff weight carried as fuel.
entries.formula: R = (V / cT) (L / D) ln(Wi / Wf), where Wi is initial weight and Wf is final weight
entries.subject: Flight Mechanics

entries.example: For R = 0.1 Pa/(m3/s)^2 and airflow Q = 20 m3/s: pressure drop = 0.1 x 20^2 = 40 Pa.
entries.fact: Atkinson's square law states that the frictional pressure drop in a mine airway is proportional to the square of the airflow quantity. The resistance R depends on airway length, perimeter, area and roughness, so doubling the airflow quadruples the pressure drop and greatly increases fan power.
entries.formula: Delta p = R Q^2; R = K L per / A^3, where K is the friction factor, L length, per perimeter and A area
entries.subject: Mine Ventilation
entries.topic: Atkinson's square law for mine ventilation

entries.example: A fan delivering 10 m3/s at 1000 rpm is sped up to 1200 rpm (ratio 1.2): new flow = 12 m3/s, new pressure = 500 x 1.2^2 = 720 Pa, and new power = 10 kW x 1.2^3 = 17.28 kW.
entries.fact: The fan laws predict how a fan performs when its speed changes at constant air density. Flow varies directly with speed, pressure with the square of speed, and power with the cube of speed, so a small speed increase costs a disproportionately large power increase.
entries.subject: Mine Ventilation

entries.example: With cohesion c = 5 MPa, normal stress 10 MPa and friction angle phi = 30 degrees (tan phi = 0.577): shear strength = 5 + 10 x 0.577 = 10.77 MPa.
entries.fact: The Mohr-Coulomb criterion states that a rock or soil fails in shear when the shear stress on a plane reaches the cohesion plus the normal stress times tan phi. Cohesion is the shear strength at zero normal stress and phi is the angle of internal friction.
entries.formula: tau = c + sigma_n tan(phi)
entries.subject: Rock Mechanics

entries.example: A 500 kN load fails a 54 mm diameter core (area 2290 mm2): UCS = 500,000 / 2290 = 218 N/mm2 = 218 MPa, a strong rock.
entries.fact: Uniaxial compressive strength (UCS) is the maximum axial compressive stress a rock specimen carries before failure, with no lateral confinement. It is a basic index of rock strength used in pillar design, tunnel support and rock classification.
entries.formula: sigma_c = P_max / A, where P_max is the peak axial load and A is the cross-sectional area
entries.subject: Rock Mechanics

entries.example: In 100 cm of core run, pieces longer than 10 cm total 75 cm: RQD = (75 / 100) x 100 = 75%, which is good quality rock.
entries.fact: Rock Quality Designation (RQD) is the percentage of a core run made up of sound core pieces longer than 10 cm. It is a simple index of rock mass quality: below 25% is very poor, 50-75% is fair, 75-90% is good and above 90% is excellent.
entries.formula: RQD (%) = (sum of lengths of core pieces > 10 cm / total core run length) x 100
entries.subject: Rock Mechanics

entries.example: A blast uses 120 kg of explosive to break 300 m3 of rock: powder factor = 120 / 300 = 0.4 kg/m3.
entries.fact: Powder factor is the mass of explosive used per unit volume (or per tonne) of rock broken. It measures blasting efficiency: too low a factor gives poor fragmentation and boulders, too high wastes explosive, increases vibration and flyrock, and raises cost.
entries.formula: Powder factor = mass of explosive / volume of rock broken (kg/m3)
entries.subject: Mining Methods

entries.example: Feed 1000 t at 1% Cu contains 10 t of copper. Concentrate 25 t at 32% Cu contains 8 t of copper: recovery = (8 / 10) x 100 = 80%.
entries.fact: Recovery is the fraction of the valuable metal in the feed that reports to the concentrate. Grade is the metal content of a stream. A plant trades off grade against recovery: pushing for a higher grade usually drops recovery, and vice versa.
entries.formula: Recovery (%) = (mass of concentrate x grade of concentrate) / (mass of feed x grade of feed) x 100
entries.subject: Mineral Processing
entries.topic: Metal recovery and grade in mineral processing

entries.example: With friction stress sigma0 = 50 MPa, Hall-Petch constant k = 0.15 MPa m^1/2 and grain size d = 25 micrometres (2.5 x 10^-5 m): d^-1/2 = 200 m^-1/2, so sigma_y = 50 + 0.15 x 200 = 80 MPa.
entries.fact: The Hall-Petch relation states that yield strength rises as grain size falls, because grain boundaries block dislocation motion. It holds over the usual micrometre range but breaks down at very fine nanometre grain sizes, where the inverse Hall-Petch effect can appear.
entries.formula: sigma_y = sigma0 + k d^-1/2
entries.subject: Mechanical Metallurgy

entries.example: For steel with Young's modulus E = 200 GPa, a strain of 0.001 gives stress = 200 x 10^9 x 0.001 = 200 x 10^6 Pa = 200 MPa, within the elastic range.
entries.fact: Hooke's law states that in the elastic region stress is proportional to strain, with Young's modulus as the constant. Beyond the yield point the material deforms plastically and does not return to its original shape when unloaded.
entries.formula: sigma = E epsilon
entries.subject: Mechanical Metallurgy

entries.example: For D = 1 x 10^-10 m2/s and a concentration drop of 100 mol/m3 over 0.001 m (gradient 1 x 10^5 mol/m4): flux magnitude = 1 x 10^-10 x 1 x 10^5 = 1 x 10^-5 mol/m2 s, from high to low concentration.
entries.fact: Fick's first law states that diffusive flux is proportional to the concentration gradient, flowing from high to low concentration. Fick's second law describes how concentration changes with time and is the basis for carburising, homogenisation and other diffusion-controlled treatments.
entries.formula: J = -D (dC/dx); dC/dt = D (d2C/dx2)
entries.subject: Physical Metallurgy

entries.example: For a binary alloy (C = 2) with two phases present (P = 2) at constant pressure: F = 2 - 2 + 1 = 1, so one variable, such as temperature or composition, can change independently.
entries.fact: The Gibbs phase rule gives the number of degrees of freedom of a system at equilibrium from the number of components and phases. At constant pressure the 2 is replaced by 1, which is the usual form for metallurgical phase diagrams.
entries.formula: F = C - P + 2; at constant pressure F = C - P + 1
entries.subject: Physical Metallurgy

entries.example: An alloy of overall composition 0.5% C lies between liquid of 0.2% C and solid of 0.8% C: fraction solid = (0.5 - 0.2) / (0.8 - 0.2) = 0.5, so the alloy is 50% solid and 50% liquid.
entries.fact: The lever rule gives the weight fractions of two phases in a two-phase field of a binary phase diagram. The fraction of a phase is the length of the opposite lever arm divided by the total tie-line length.
entries.formula: Fraction of solid = (C0 - CL) / (CS - CL); fraction of liquid = (CS - C0) / (CS - CL)
entries.subject: Physical Metallurgy

entries.example: For a reaction with delta H = -500 kJ/mol and delta S = -0.1 kJ/mol K at 1000 K: delta G = -500 - 1000 x (-0.1) = -400 kJ/mol, so the reaction is spontaneous at that temperature.
entries.fact: Gibbs free energy decides whether a reaction can proceed: a negative change means it is spontaneous. Ellingham diagrams plot delta G against temperature for oxide formation, and the slope is minus delta S, so they show which metal can reduce another oxide at a given temperature.
entries.formula: delta G = delta H - T delta S; delta G = -R T ln K
entries.subject: Thermodynamics
entries.topic: Gibbs free energy and Ellingham diagrams

entries.example: A steel with 0.77 wt% C cooled slowly through 727 C transforms completely to pearlite, a lamellar mixture of ferrite and cementite, with no proeutectoid ferrite or cementite.
entries.fact: The eutectoid point of the iron-carbon diagram is 0.77 wt% carbon at 727 C, where austenite transforms on cooling to pearlite (ferrite plus cementite). Steels below this carbon content are hypoeutectoid and above it are hypereutectoid.
entries.formula: Eutectoid: austenite (0.77 wt% C) -> ferrite + cementite (pearlite) at 727 C
entries.subject: Physical Metallurgy

entries.example: A ship displaces 1000 m3 of seawater (density 1025 kg/m3): buoyant force = 1025 x 9.81 x 1000 = 10.06 x 10^6 N, equal to the weight of 1025 tonnes of seawater.
entries.fact: Archimedes' principle states that the buoyant force on a floating body equals the weight of the fluid it displaces. A ship floats when this force equals its weight, and the displaced volume determines its draft for a given hull form.
entries.formula: Fb = rho g V, where V is the submerged (displaced) volume
entries.subject: Naval Architecture

entries.example: With KM = 8.0 m and KG = 6.5 m: GM = 8.0 - 6.5 = 1.5 m, positive, so the ship is initially stable.
entries.fact: Metacentric height GM is the distance between the centre of gravity G and the metacentre M. Positive GM means the ship rights itself after a small heel; negative GM means it is unstable. BM = I/V shows that a wide waterplane gives a large BM and hence more stability.
entries.formula: GM = KM - KG = BM - BG; BM = I / V, where I is the waterplane second moment of area and V is displaced volume
entries.subject: Naval Architecture

entries.example: With GM = 1.5 m and heel angle 10 degrees: GZ = 1.5 x sin(10 degrees) = 1.5 x 0.174 = 0.26 m. For a ship weighing 98.1 MN, the righting moment is 98.1 x 0.26 = 25.5 MN m.
entries.fact: The righting arm GZ is the horizontal distance between the lines of action of weight and buoyancy when heeled. At small angles GZ is approximately GM times sin theta, and the righting moment is displacement weight times GZ.
entries.formula: GZ = GM sin(theta) for small angles; righting moment = Delta x GZ, where Delta is displacement weight
entries.subject: Naval Architecture

entries.example: A ship 100 m long at 10 m/s: Fn = 10 / sqrt(9.81 x 100) = 10 / 31.3 = 0.32, a typical Froude number for a fast displacement ship.
entries.fact: Froude number is the ratio of inertial to gravitational forces and governs wave-making resistance. Ships with the same Froude number have similar wave patterns, which is the basis of model testing: a model is run at the same Froude number as the full-scale ship.
entries.formula: Fn = V / sqrt(g L), where L is waterline length
entries.subject: Hydrodynamics

entries.example: With frictional coefficient Cf = 0.002, wetted area S = 1000 m2 and speed V = 8 m/s in seawater: Rf = 0.5 x 1025 x 8^2 x 1000 x 0.002 = 65,600 N = 65.6 kN.
entries.fact: Total ship resistance is the sum of frictional resistance, wave-making (residuary) resistance, air resistance and appendage resistance. Frictional resistance depends on wetted area and speed squared and usually dominates at low speed, while wave resistance grows rapidly at high Froude number.
entries.formula: Rt = Rf + Rw + Ra + Rapp; Rf = (1/2) rho V^2 S Cf
entries.subject: Hydrodynamics

entries.example: With advance speed Va = 7.5 m/s, propeller speed n = 2 rev/s and diameter D = 5 m: J = 7.5 / (2 x 5) = 0.75.
entries.fact: Advance coefficient J is the non-dimensional speed at which a propeller works and is the main parameter of propeller open-water curves. Thrust and torque coefficients and efficiency are plotted against J, and efficiency peaks at a particular J for a given propeller.
entries.formula: J = Va / (n D); KT = T / (rho n^2 D^4); KQ = Q / (rho n^2 D^5)
entries.subject: Marine Engineering

entries.example: A hull with displaced volume 5000 m3, length 100 m, beam 20 m and draft 5 m: Cb = 5000 / (100 x 20 x 5) = 0.50, a moderately fine hull form.
entries.fact: Block coefficient is the ratio of displaced volume to the volume of the enclosing rectangular block L x B x T. Fine fast ships have Cb near 0.5-0.6, while full slow cargo ships and tankers have Cb near 0.8-0.85.
entries.formula: Cb = displaced volume / (L B T)
entries.subject: Naval Architecture

entries.example: For k = 0.5 Darcy, A = 10 cm2, pressure drop 2 atm, viscosity 2 cP and length 10 cm: q = 0.5 x 10 x 2 / (2 x 10) = 0.5 cm3/s.
entries.fact: Darcy's law states that flow rate through a porous medium is proportional to permeability, area and pressure gradient, and inversely proportional to viscosity. It is the foundation of reservoir engineering; it applies to laminar single-phase flow and is extended for radial flow around wells.
entries.formula: q = (k A / mu) (Delta p / L); in differential form q = -(k A / mu) dp/dx
entries.subject: Reservoir Engineering
entries.topic: Darcy's law for flow in porous media

entries.example: A rock sample has bulk volume 100 cm3 and pore volume 25 cm3: porosity = (25 / 100) x 100 = 25%.
entries.fact: Porosity is the fraction of a rock's bulk volume occupied by pores. Effective porosity counts only interconnected pores that can hold and transmit fluids; isolated pores do not contribute to flow. Typical sandstone reservoirs have 10-30% porosity.
entries.formula: phi = (Vp / Vb) x 100%, where Vp is pore volume and Vb is bulk volume
entries.subject: Reservoir Engineering

entries.example: For area A = 100 acres, thickness h = 10 ft, porosity 0.20, water saturation 0.25 and formation volume factor Bo = 1.25: N = 7758 x 100 x 10 x 0.20 x 0.75 / 1.25 = 930,960 STB.
entries.fact: The volumetric method estimates original oil in place from reservoir area, thickness, porosity, water saturation and the oil formation volume factor, which converts reservoir barrels to stock-tank barrels. It is the starting point for reserves estimation before production data exist.
entries.formula: N (STB) = 7758 A h phi (1 - Sw) / Bo, with A in acres and h in feet
entries.subject: Reservoir Engineering

entries.example: Mud of 12 lb/gal at 10,000 ft depth: pressure = 0.052 x 12 x 10,000 = 6240 psi.
entries.fact: Hydrostatic pressure in a wellbore increases linearly with depth and mud density. Drilling mud must balance formation pore pressure: too low risks a kick or blowout, too high risks fracturing the formation and losing circulation.
entries.formula: p = rho g h; in oilfield units p (psi) = 0.052 x mud weight (lb/gal) x depth (ft)
entries.subject: Drilling

entries.example: A well produces 500 STB/day with reservoir pressure 3000 psi and flowing bottom-hole pressure 2500 psi: J = 500 / (3000 - 2500) = 1.0 STB/day/psi.
entries.fact: Productivity index is the production rate per unit pressure drawdown and measures how easily a well produces. A higher index means a more productive well; it falls as permeability, thickness or pressure support fall, and it is the basis of inflow performance curves.
entries.formula: J = q / (pr - pwf), where pr is reservoir pressure and pwf is flowing bottom-hole pressure
entries.subject: Production Engineering

entries.example: One mole of gas at 300 K in 0.024 m3 with Z = 0.9: p = 0.9 x 1 x 8.314 x 300 / 0.024 = 93,500 Pa, about 0.94 bar.
entries.fact: Real gases deviate from ideal behaviour at high pressure, and the compressibility factor Z corrects the ideal gas law. Z is near 1 at low pressure and is obtained from charts or equations of state using reduced pressure and temperature.
entries.formula: p V = Z n R T
entries.subject: Reservoir Engineering
entries.topic: Real gas law and compressibility factor

entries.example: Original oil in place is 1,000,000 STB and 300,000 STB have been produced: recovery factor = (300,000 / 1,000,000) x 100 = 30%.
entries.fact: Recovery factor is the fraction of original oil in place that is ultimately produced. Primary recovery by natural pressure typically recovers 10-25%, secondary water or gas flooding adds more, and enhanced oil recovery methods such as chemical or thermal flooding can raise it further.
entries.formula: Recovery factor (%) = (cumulative oil produced / original oil in place) x 100
entries.subject: Production Engineering

entries.example: For a 1 km sight, the combined curvature and refraction correction is 0.0673 x 1^2 = 0.067 m, so the observed staff reading must be reduced by about 6.7 cm.
entries.fact: Levelling must correct for the Earth's curvature, which makes a level line fall below a horizontal line, and for atmospheric refraction, which bends the line of sight downward. Refraction partly cancels curvature, leaving a combined correction proportional to the square of the sight distance.
entries.formula: Combined correction = -0.0673 D^2 metres, where D is distance in km; curvature alone = 0.0785 D^2, refraction = -0.0112 D^2
entries.subject: Surveying
entries.topic: Curvature and refraction correction in levelling

entries.example: A slope distance of 100 m measured at a vertical angle of 10 degrees gives horizontal distance = 100 x cos(10 degrees) = 98.48 m.
entries.fact: EDM measures the slope distance between instrument and reflector. The horizontal distance is the slope distance times the cosine of the vertical angle, and the vertical difference is the slope distance times the sine of the vertical angle.
entries.formula: Horizontal distance = S cos(theta); vertical difference = S sin(theta), where S is slope distance and theta is vertical angle
entries.subject: Surveying
entries.topic: EDM slope distance to horizontal distance

entries.example: On a 1:50,000 map, 1 cm represents 50,000 cm = 500 m on the ground, so a 4 cm line on the map is 2 km on the ground.
entries.fact: Map scale is the ratio of a distance on the map to the corresponding distance on the ground. A representative fraction of 1:50,000 means one unit on the map equals 50,000 of the same units on the ground; large-scale maps show small areas in more detail.
entries.formula: Scale = map distance / ground distance; representative fraction = 1 : (ground distance / map distance)
entries.subject: Surveying

entries.example: With near-infrared reflectance 0.6 and red reflectance 0.2: NDVI = (0.6 - 0.2) / (0.6 + 0.2) = 0.5, indicating healthy green vegetation.
entries.fact: NDVI is the standard vegetation index from remote sensing: healthy vegetation reflects strongly in near-infrared and absorbs red light, giving a high positive value, while bare soil, water and clouds give values near zero or negative. It ranges from -1 to +1.
entries.formula: NDVI = (NIR - Red) / (NIR + Red)
entries.subject: Remote Sensing

entries.example: A camera with focal length 150 mm flown 1500 m above ground gives photo scale = 0.15 / 1500 = 1:10,000.
entries.fact: The scale of a vertical aerial photograph is focal length divided by flying height above ground. A larger scale (smaller denominator) shows more detail but covers less ground per photograph.
entries.formula: Photo scale = f / H, where f is focal length and H is flying height above ground
entries.subject: Photogrammetry
entries.topic: Scale of a vertical aerial photograph

entries.example: A traverse closes with sum of latitude errors 0.4 m and sum of departure errors 0.3 m: linear misclosure = sqrt(0.4^2 + 0.3^2) = 0.5 m.
entries.fact: In a closed traverse the sums of latitudes and departures should each be zero. Any residual is the closing error, and the Bowditch rule distributes it among the legs in proportion to their lengths.
entries.formula: Linear misclosure = sqrt((sum of latitudes)^2 + (sum of departures)^2); Bowditch correction is proportional to leg length
entries.subject: Surveying
entries.topic: Traverse closing error and Bowditch rule

entries.example: Longitude 78 degrees E lies in UTM zone = floor((78 + 180) / 6) + 1 = 44, so it is in UTM Zone 44N.
entries.fact: UTM divides the Earth into 60 zones, each 6 degrees of longitude wide, with a transverse Mercator projection per zone. Within a zone, positions are given in eastings and northings in metres, which makes distance and area calculations simple.
entries.formula: UTM zone number = floor((longitude + 180) / 6) + 1; each zone is 6 degrees wide
entries.subject: Geomatics

entries.example: A plate moving at 5 cm/year travels 50 km in one million years, so in 10 million years it moves about 500 km.
entries.fact: Plate tectonics states that the Earth's lithosphere is divided into plates that move over the asthenosphere at a few centimetres per year. Divergent boundaries create new crust, convergent boundaries destroy it or build mountains, and transform boundaries slide past each other.
entries.formula: Distance moved = plate velocity x time; typical plate speeds are 2-10 cm/year
entries.subject: Geology

entries.example: For shear modulus 30 GPa and density 2700 kg/m3: Vs = sqrt(30 x 10^9 / 2700) = 3333 m/s. P-waves are faster than this in the same rock.
entries.fact: P-waves are compressional waves that travel through solids and fluids, while S-waves are shear waves that travel only through solids. P-waves always arrive first at a seismograph, and the P-S time difference is used to locate an earthquake's epicentre.
entries.formula: Vp = sqrt((K + 4 mu/3) / rho); Vs = sqrt(mu / rho); Vp > Vs
entries.subject: Seismology

entries.example: A ray enters a faster layer (V1 = 2000 m/s, V2 = 4000 m/s) at 30 degrees: sin(i2) = (4000/2000) x sin(30 degrees) = 1.0, so i2 = 90 degrees and 30 degrees is the critical angle.
entries.fact: Snell's law relates the angles of a seismic ray to the velocities on either side of an interface. When a ray goes from a slow to a fast layer at the critical angle it is refracted along the interface, producing head waves used in seismic refraction surveys.
entries.formula: sin(i1) / V1 = sin(i2) / V2; critical angle ic = arcsin(V1 / V2) when V2 > V1
entries.subject: Geophysics
entries.topic: Snell's law and critical angle in seismic refraction

entries.example: A buried slab 100 m thick with density contrast 2.0 g/cm3 gives a Bouguer anomaly of 0.0419 x 2.0 x 100 = 8.38 mGal.
entries.fact: A gravity anomaly is the difference between observed gravity and the theoretical gravity for the location, after latitude, elevation and terrain corrections. Dense rocks give positive anomalies and low-density bodies give negative ones, so gravity surveys map buried structures.
entries.formula: Bouguer slab anomaly Delta g = 2 pi G rho h = 0.0419 rho h mGal, with rho in g/cm3 and h in metres
entries.subject: Geophysics

entries.example: Quartz (hardness 7) scratches glass and a steel nail (about 5.5) but is scratched by topaz (8), so an unknown mineral that scratches quartz but not topaz has hardness between 7 and 8.
entries.fact: Mohs hardness scale ranks minerals from 1 (talc) to 10 (diamond) by scratch resistance: a harder mineral scratches a softer one. It is a relative, ordinal scale, not a linear measure of hardness, and is a standard field test for mineral identification.
entries.formula: Mohs scale: 1 talc, 2 gypsum, 3 calcite, 4 fluorite, 5 apatite, 6 orthoclase, 7 quartz, 8 topaz, 9 corundum, 10 diamond
entries.subject: Mineralogy

entries.example: Weathering of granite produces sand and clay; burial and compaction turn the sand into sandstone, and heating and pressure can turn that sandstone into quartzite, a metamorphic rock.
entries.fact: The rock cycle describes how igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks transform into each other through melting, cooling, weathering, erosion, deposition, compaction, cementation, heat and pressure. Any rock type can become any other given the right process.
entries.formula: Igneous rock --weathering/erosion--> sediment --compaction/cementation--> sedimentary rock --heat/pressure--> metamorphic rock --melting--> magma --cooling--> igneous rock
entries.subject: Geology

entries.example: For a magnitude 6 earthquake: log10 E = 4.8 + 1.5 x 6 = 13.8, so E = 10^13.8 = 6.3 x 10^13 joules.
entries.fact: Earthquake magnitude is a logarithmic measure of energy released: each whole magnitude step increases wave amplitude about 10 times and energy about 32 times. The Gutenberg-Richter law states that the number of earthquakes falls by about a factor of 10 for each unit increase in magnitude.
entries.formula: log10 E = 4.8 + 1.5 M (E in joules); log10 N = a - b M, with b about 1
entries.subject: Seismology

entries.example: In a graph A connected to B and C, and B and C both connected to goal D: BFS visits A, B, C, D and finds D at depth 2. DFS visits A, B, D and also reaches D, but it may first explore a long deep branch before finding the shallowest goal.
entries.fact: Uninformed search explores a state space using only the problem definition, with no heuristic estimate of distance to the goal. Breadth-first search (BFS) expands nodes level by level using a queue and is complete and optimal when all step costs are equal. Depth-first search (DFS) expands the deepest node first using a stack, uses little memory, but is neither complete in infinite spaces nor optimal.
entries.formula: BFS time and space: O(b^d), where b is the branching factor and d is the depth of the shallowest goal. DFS space: O(b*m), where m is the maximum depth explored.
entries.subject: Artificial Intelligence

entries.example: From start S, S to A costs 1 and S to B costs 4; A to G costs 5 and B to G costs 1, with h(A) = 5 and h(B) = 1. Then f(A) = 1 + 5 = 6 and f(B) = 4 + 1 = 5, so A* expands B first and finds the optimal path S-B-G with total cost 5, rather than S-A-G with cost 6.
entries.fact: Informed search uses a heuristic function to guide exploration toward the goal. A* search expands the node with the lowest f(n) = g(n) + h(n), where g(n) is the cost from the start to n and h(n) is the estimated cost from n to the goal. A* is complete and optimal if the heuristic is admissible, meaning it never overestimates the true cost to the goal.
entries.formula: f(n) = g(n) + h(n). Admissible heuristic: 0 <= h(n) <= h*(n), where h*(n) is the true cheapest cost from n to the goal.
entries.subject: Artificial Intelligence

entries.example: On a grid with moves up, down, left and right, the goal is at (3, 4) and the agent is at (0, 0). The Manhattan distance heuristic is |3 - 0| + |4 - 0| = 7, which equals the true cost of 7 steps, so it is admissible and exact here.
entries.fact: A heuristic function h(n) estimates the cost of the cheapest path from node n to a goal. An admissible heuristic never overestimates the true cost, which is required for A* optimality. A consistent (monotone) heuristic also satisfies h(n) <= c(n, a, n') + h(n') for every action a from n to n', which guarantees that f values never decrease along a path.
entries.formula: Admissible: h(n) <= h*(n). Consistent: h(n) <= c(n, a, n') + h(n'). Manhattan distance: h = |x1 - x2| + |y1 - y2|.
entries.subject: Artificial Intelligence

entries.example: Root MAX has MIN children A and B. A has leaves 3 and 5, so A = min(3, 5) = 3 and alpha becomes 3. B's first leaf is 2, which is already <= alpha = 3, so B's second leaf (9) is pruned and B = 2. The root value is max(3, 2) = 3.
entries.fact: Minimax chooses the move that maximises the player's minimum guaranteed outcome in a two-player zero-sum game, assuming the opponent also plays optimally. MAX nodes take the maximum of their children and MIN nodes take the minimum. Alpha-beta pruning skips branches that cannot affect the final decision: a MAX node prunes when a child value is at most beta, and a MIN node prunes when a child value is at least alpha.
entries.formula: Minimax: V(s) = max_a min_b V(result(s, a, b)) for a MAX node, and the minimum over opponent moves at a MIN node. Prune a MIN branch when value <= alpha; prune a MAX branch when value >= beta.
entries.subject: Artificial Intelligence

entries.example: Knowledge base: Rain -> WetRoad, and Rain is true. By modus ponens, WetRoad is true. If instead Rain were false, Rain -> WetRoad would still be true as an implication, but WetRoad could not be inferred from it alone.
entries.fact: Knowledge representation stores facts about the world in a formal language so an agent can reason with them. In propositional logic, statements are built from atomic propositions with connectives such as NOT, AND, OR, implication and biconditional. A sentence is entailed by a knowledge base if it is true in every model in which the knowledge base is true, and modus ponens lets us infer Q from P and P implies Q.
entries.formula: Modus ponens: from P and (P -> Q), infer Q. Implication truth table: P -> Q is false only when P is true and Q is false.
entries.subject: Artificial Intelligence

entries.example: Given forall x (Human(x) -> Mortal(x)) and Human(Socrates), universal instantiation gives Human(Socrates) -> Mortal(Socrates), and modus ponens then gives Mortal(Socrates).
entries.fact: First-order logic extends propositional logic with objects, predicates, functions and quantifiers, so it can express general rules about many individuals at once. The universal quantifier (for all x) states that a property holds for every object, and the existential quantifier (there exists x) states that it holds for at least one object. Variables can be instantiated to specific constants to derive concrete facts.
entries.formula: Universal instantiation: from forall x P(x), infer P(a) for any constant a. Example rule: forall x (Human(x) -> Mortal(x)).
entries.subject: Artificial Intelligence

entries.example: Let A -> B with P(A) = 0.5, P(B | A) = 0.8 and P(B | not A) = 0.2. Then P(A and B) = 0.5 * 0.8 = 0.4, and by total probability P(B) = 0.5 * 0.8 + 0.5 * 0.2 = 0.5.
entries.fact: A Bayesian network is a directed acyclic graph in which nodes are random variables and edges represent direct dependencies, with each node carrying a conditional probability table given its parents. The joint distribution factorises as the product of each variable's probability given its parents, which encodes conditional independence: a variable is independent of its non-descendants given its parents.
entries.formula: P(X1, ..., Xn) = product over i of P(Xi | Parents(Xi)). Bayes' rule: P(A | B) = P(B | A) * P(A) / P(B).
entries.subject: Artificial Intelligence

entries.example: In state s, action a gives reward 5 for sure and moves to state s' with V*(s') = 10, with discount gamma = 0.9. Then Q*(s, a) = 5 + 0.9 * 10 = 14.
entries.fact: A Markov decision process (MDP) models sequential decision making with states, actions, transition probabilities and rewards, under the Markov property that the future depends only on the current state and action. The goal is a policy maximising expected discounted return. The optimal value function satisfies the Bellman optimality equation, which relates the value of a state to the best immediate reward plus the discounted value of the next state.
entries.formula: V*(s) = max_a sum over s' of P(s' | s, a) * [R(s, a, s') + gamma * V*(s')]. Q*(s, a) = sum over s' of P(s' | s, a) * [R(s, a, s') + gamma * max_a' Q*(s', a')]. Discount factor: 0 <= gamma < 1.
entries.subject: Artificial Intelligence

entries.example: With Q(s, a) = 1, learning rate alpha = 0.5, reward r = 10, gamma = 0.9 and max_a' Q(s', a') = 2, the target is 10 + 0.9 * 2 = 11.8, so the new Q(s, a) = 1 + 0.5 * (11.8 - 1) = 6.4.
entries.fact: In reinforcement learning an agent learns a policy by trial and error, receiving rewards from the environment and aiming to maximise cumulative discounted reward. Q-learning is a model-free, off-policy method that learns the action-value function Q(s, a) directly from experience. It updates Q toward the target reward plus the discounted best Q of the next state, balancing exploration of new actions with exploitation of known good ones.
entries.formula: Q(s, a) <- Q(s, a) + alpha * [r + gamma * max_a' Q(s', a') - Q(s, a)], where alpha is the learning rate and gamma is the discount factor.
entries.subject: Artificial Intelligence

entries.example: The sentence 'the cat sat' tokenizes into ['the', 'cat', 'sat'] and has two bigrams: ('the', 'cat') and ('cat', 'sat'). If 'cat' occurs 3 times in a corpus and 'cat sat' occurs 2 times, then P(sat | cat) = 2 / 3, about 0.67.
entries.fact: Natural language processing starts by turning raw text into units a model can use. Tokenization splits text into tokens such as words or subwords, and normalisation steps like lowercasing may follow. An n-gram model predicts a word from the previous n - 1 words, estimating the probability by counting how often that word sequence occurs in a corpus.
entries.formula: Bigram probability: P(w_n | w_{n-1}) = Count(w_{n-1}, w_n) / Count(w_{n-1}). General n-gram: P(w_n | w_{n-n+1}, ..., w_{n-1}) = Count(w_{n-n+1}, ..., w_n) / Count(w_{n-n+1}, ..., w_{n-1}).
entries.subject: Artificial Intelligence

entries.example: For a fair die, the true mean is (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6) / 6 = 3.5. Averaging 6000 rolls, the sample mean will typically be very close to 3.5, for example 3.48, whereas the average of only 6 rolls could easily be far from 3.5.
entries.fact: The law of large numbers says that the sample mean of independent, identically distributed random variables converges to the true population mean as the sample size grows. The weak law states convergence in probability, while the strong law states convergence with probability 1. It is the theoretical basis for estimating probabilities and means from large samples.
entries.formula: Sample mean: Xbar_n = (1/n) * sum_{i=1 to n} X_i. Weak law: for any epsilon > 0, P(|Xbar_n - mu| > epsilon) -> 0 as n -> infinity, where mu = E[X_i].
entries.subject: Probability & Stats

entries.example: If a population has mean mu = 50 and standard deviation sigma = 10, the mean of n = 100 observations is approximately N(50, 1), since sigma / sqrt(n) = 10 / 10 = 1. So about 95% of such sample means lie roughly between 48 and 52.
entries.fact: The central limit theorem says that the sum or average of many independent, identically distributed random variables is approximately normally distributed, regardless of the shape of the original distribution, provided the mean and variance are finite. The approximation improves as the sample size grows, which is why normal-based confidence intervals and tests are so widely used.
entries.formula: Z_n = (Xbar_n - mu) / (sigma / sqrt(n)) converges in distribution to N(0, 1). Approximately: Xbar_n ~ N(mu, sigma^2 / n), and S_n ~ N(n*mu, n*sigma^2).
entries.subject: Probability & Stats

entries.example: For X Bernoulli(p), M_X(t) = (1 - p) + p * e^t. Differentiating gives M_X'(t) = p * e^t, so M_X'(0) = p, which is E[X] = p. For p = 0.3, the mean is 0.3.
entries.fact: The moment-generating function (MGF) of a random variable X is the expected value of e^(tX), when it exists in a neighbourhood of zero. Differentiating the MGF k times and evaluating at t = 0 gives the k-th moment E[X^k]. The MGF uniquely determines the distribution, and the MGF of a sum of independent variables is the product of their MGFs.
entries.formula: M_X(t) = E[e^{tX}]. Moments: M_X^{(k)}(0) = E[X^k]. Sum of independent variables: M_{X+Y}(t) = M_X(t) * M_Y(t).
entries.subject: Probability & Stats

entries.example: Roll a fair die and let Y be whether the result is even. Given Y = even, the possible values are 2, 4 and 6, each equally likely, so E[X | even] = (2 + 4 + 6) / 3 = 4, which is higher than the unconditional mean 3.5.
entries.fact: The conditional expectation E[X | Y] is the expected value of X given the information in Y; for discrete Y it is the average of X weighted by the conditional distribution P(X | Y = y). It is itself a random variable that depends on Y. The law of total expectation says that averaging the conditional expectation over Y recovers the unconditional expectation E[X].
entries.formula: E[X | Y = y] = sum_x x * P(X = x | Y = y). Law of total expectation: E[X] = E[E[X | Y]].
entries.subject: Probability & Stats

entries.example: If Var(X) = 4, Var(Y) = 9 and Cov(X, Y) = 2, the covariance matrix is [[4, 2], [2, 9]] and the correlation is 2 / (2 * 3) = 1/3, about 0.33, so X and Y are positively but only weakly linearly related.
entries.fact: The covariance matrix of a random vector collects the variances of each component on its diagonal and the covariances between pairs off the diagonal; it is symmetric and positive semidefinite. A multivariate normal distribution is fully determined by its mean vector mu and covariance matrix Sigma, and every linear combination of its components is normally distributed.
entries.formula: Cov(X, Y) = E[(X - E[X])(Y - E[Y])] = E[XY] - E[X]E[Y]. Correlation: rho = Cov(X, Y) / (sigma_X * sigma_Y). Multivariate normal density: f(x) = (1 / sqrt((2*pi)^k * det(Sigma))) * exp(-(1/2) * (x - mu)^T * Sigma^{-1} * (x - mu)).
entries.subject: Probability & Stats

entries.example: For Integral of x * e^x dx, take u = x and dv = e^x dx, so du = dx and v = e^x. Then the integral is x*e^x - Integral of e^x dx = x*e^x - e^x + C = (x - 1)*e^x + C. From 0 to 1 this equals 0 - (-1) = 1.
entries.fact: Integration by parts comes from the product rule for differentiation and is used when an integrand is a product of two functions, one easy to differentiate and the other easy to integrate. Choose u to differentiate and dv to integrate, then apply the formula. The LIATE guideline (logarithmic, inverse trigonometric, algebraic, trigonometric, exponential) often helps in choosing u.
entries.formula: Integral of u dv = u*v - Integral of v du. Definite form: Integral from a to b of u dv = [u*v] from a to b - Integral from a to b of v du.
entries.subject: Calculus & Optimization

entries.example: Integral from 0 to 2 of (x + 1) dx = [x^2/2 + x] from 0 to 2 = (2 + 2) - 0 = 4. Splitting at 1 gives Integral from 0 to 1 plus Integral from 1 to 2, which is 1.5 + 2.5 = 4, as expected.
entries.fact: A definite integral gives the signed area under a curve between two limits. Reversing the limits changes the sign, the integral over a zero-width interval is zero, and integrals add over adjacent intervals. Integrals are linear: the integral of a sum is the sum of the integrals, and constants factor out. The fundamental theorem of calculus evaluates a definite integral from an antiderivative.
entries.formula: Integral from a to b of f(x) dx = - Integral from b to a of f(x) dx. Integral from a to b of f(x) dx = Integral from a to c of f(x) dx + Integral from c to b of f(x) dx. Fundamental theorem: Integral from a to b of f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a), where F' = f.
entries.subject: Calculus & Optimization

entries.example: For f(x, y) = x^2 * y, the partial derivatives are df/dx = 2xy and df/dy = x^2, so at (2, 3) they are 12 and 4. With x = t and y = t^2, f = t^4, and the chain rule gives df/dt = 2xy * 1 + x^2 * 2t = 2t^3 + 2t^3 = 4t^3, matching the direct derivative of t^4.
entries.fact: A partial derivative measures how a multivariable function changes when one variable changes while the others are held fixed. The gradient collects all the partial derivatives into a vector. The multivariable chain rule adds the contributions through each intermediate variable: if z = f(x, y) and x and y depend on t, then dz/dt is the sum of the partial derivative with respect to each variable times that variable's rate of change.
entries.formula: Partial derivative: df/dx = limit as h -> 0 of [f(x + h, y) - f(x, y)] / h. Chain rule: dz/dt = (df/dx)(dx/dt) + (df/dy)(dy/dt). Gradient: grad f = (df/dx, df/dy).
entries.subject: Calculus & Optimization

entries.example: Maximise f(x, y) = xy subject to x + y = 10. The Lagrangian is L = xy - lambda * (x + y - 10). Setting partial derivatives to zero gives y = lambda and x = lambda, so x = y, and with x + y = 10, x = y = 5 and the maximum is 25.
entries.fact: Lagrange multipliers find the maximum or minimum of a function subject to an equality constraint. At a constrained extremum, the gradient of the objective function is parallel to the gradient of the constraint function, so their difference is zero for some multiplier lambda. Solving the resulting system together with the constraint gives the candidate points, which are then compared by evaluating the objective.
entries.formula: Lagrangian: L(x, y, lambda) = f(x, y) - lambda * (g(x, y) - c). Conditions: grad f = lambda * grad g, and g(x, y) = c.
entries.subject: Calculus & Optimization

entries.example: For f(x) = x^2, f'(x) = 2x. Starting at x_0 = 4 with learning rate eta = 0.1, the first update is x_1 = 4 - 0.1 * 8 = 3.2, and the function value falls from 16 to 10.24, moving toward the minimum at x = 0.
entries.fact: Gradient descent is an iterative optimisation method that moves a point in the direction of steepest decrease of a function, which is the negative gradient. The step size, or learning rate, controls how far each step goes: too large a step can overshoot or diverge, while too small a step converges slowly. It stops when the gradient is near zero or the change in the function value becomes negligible.
entries.formula: Update rule: x_{t+1} = x_t - eta * grad f(x_t), where eta > 0 is the learning rate. For a single variable: x_{t+1} = x_t - eta * f'(x_t).
entries.subject: Calculus & Optimization

entries.example: For f(n) = 2n + 10, with c = 3 and n0 = 10, 2n + 10 <= 3n for all n >= 10, so f(n) = O(n). An algorithm doing 2n + 10 steps on n = 1000 takes about 2010 steps, growing linearly with n.
entries.fact: Big-O notation describes the upper bound on the growth rate of an algorithm's running time or space use as the input size n grows. We say f(n) = O(g(n)) if there exist positive constants c and n0 such that f(n) <= c*g(n) for all n >= n0. It lets us compare algorithms by their scaling behaviour, ignoring constant factors and lower-order terms.
entries.formula: f(n) = O(g(n)) if there exist c > 0 and n0 such that 0 <= f(n) <= c*g(n) for all n >= n0. Common orders: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n^2) < O(2^n).
entries.subject: Algorithms

entries.example: Sorting n = 1,000,000 items: merge sort needs roughly n log2 n = 1,000,000 x 20 = 20,000,000 comparisons, while bubble sort in the worst case needs about n^2 / 2 = 500,000,000,000 comparisons.
entries.fact: Any comparison-based sorting algorithm needs Omega(n log n) comparisons in the worst case, because there are n! possible orders and each comparison gives one bit of information. Merge sort and heap sort achieve O(n log n) in the worst case, quicksort averages O(n log n) but degrades to O(n^2) in the worst case, and bubble sort and insertion sort are O(n^2) in the worst case.
entries.formula: Lower bound: Omega(n log n) comparisons. Merge sort / heap sort: O(n log n) worst case. Quicksort: O(n log n) average, O(n^2) worst case. Bubble / insertion sort: O(n^2) worst case, O(n) best case for insertion sort on sorted input.
entries.subject: Algorithms

entries.example: Insert 10, 5, 15, 3, 7 in that order. Searching for 7 visits 10, then 5, then 7: 3 comparisons. The tree height is 3, so search costs O(log n) here.
entries.fact: A binary search tree is a binary tree in which every node's left subtree holds only keys smaller than the node's key and its right subtree holds only keys larger than it. Search, insert and delete therefore follow one path from the root, taking time proportional to the height h of the tree. A balanced tree has h = O(log n), while a degenerate tree has h = O(n).
entries.formula: Search / insert / delete time: O(h), where h is the height. Balanced tree: h = O(log n), so operations are O(log n). Inorder traversal visits keys in sorted order.
entries.subject: Data Structures

entries.example: An NFA with 3 states can convert to a DFA with at most 2^3 = 8 states, one for each subset of NFA states, including the empty subset. The DFA accepts exactly the same strings as the NFA.
entries.fact: A deterministic finite automaton (DFA) has exactly one transition per symbol from each state, while a nondeterministic finite automaton (NFA) may have zero, one or several transitions per symbol and may use epsilon transitions. Every NFA can be converted to an equivalent DFA by the subset construction, and both recognise exactly the regular languages.
entries.formula: DFA is a 5-tuple (Q, Sigma, delta, q0, F). Subset construction: an NFA with n states converts to a DFA with at most 2^n states. A language is regular if and only if some DFA recognises it.
entries.subject: Theory of Computation

entries.example: With memory access time ma = 100 ns, page-fault time = 8 ms = 8,000,000 ns and fault rate p = 0.001, EAT = 0.999 x 100 + 0.001 x 8,000,000 = 99.9 + 8000 = 8099.9 ns, about 8.1 microseconds.
entries.fact: Paging divides physical memory into fixed-size frames and logical memory into pages of the same size, so a process's pages can be placed in any free frames. A page table maps each page number to a frame number, and the offset within the page is unchanged. If a page is not in memory, a page fault loads it from disk, which is far slower than a memory access.
entries.formula: Logical address = page number p + offset d; physical address = frame number f + offset d. Effective access time EAT = (1 - p) x ma + p x page-fault time, where p is the page-fault rate and ma is the memory access time.
entries.subject: Operating Systems

entries.example: In StudentCourse(StudentID, CourseID, CourseName), with key (StudentID, CourseID), CourseName depends only on CourseID, a partial dependency, so the table is in 1NF but not 2NF. Moving CourseName to a Course(CourseID, CourseName) table fixes it.
entries.fact: Normal forms are progressive rules for relational schemas that reduce redundancy and prevent insert, update and delete anomalies. First normal form (1NF) requires atomic values in every cell. Second normal form (2NF) removes partial dependencies on part of a composite key. Third normal form (3NF) removes transitive dependencies, and Boyce-Codd normal form (BCNF) is stricter: every determinant must be a superkey.
entries.formula: 1NF: all values atomic, no repeating groups. 2NF: in 1NF and every non-prime attribute depends on the whole primary key. 3NF: in 2NF and no non-prime attribute depends on another non-prime attribute. BCNF: for every non-trivial functional dependency X -> Y, X is a superkey.
entries.subject: DBMS

entries.example: Sending an email uses SMTP at the Application layer, TCP at the Transport layer (port 25 or 587), IP at the Internet layer to route packets to the mail server, and Ethernet or Wi-Fi at the Link layer to reach the next hop.
entries.fact: The OSI model has seven layers: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation and Application. The TCP/IP model used on the Internet has four layers: Link, Internet, Transport and Application. IP routes packets between networks at the Internet layer, TCP gives reliable ordered delivery at the Transport layer, and UDP gives fast unreliable delivery.
entries.formula: OSI (7 layers): Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application. TCP/IP (4 layers): Link, Internet, Transport, Application. TCP: reliable, connection-oriented, ordered. UDP: connectionless, no retransmission, low overhead.
entries.subject: Computer Networks

entries.example: For a = b + c * 2, the lexer produces tokens [a, =, b, +, c, *, 2]. The parser respects precedence, so it groups c * 2 first: a = b + (c * 2). With b = 1 and c = 3, the result is a = 1 + 6 = 7.
entries.fact: A compiler translates source code in six phases: lexical analysis turns characters into tokens, syntax analysis builds a parse tree from the grammar, semantic analysis checks types and scopes, intermediate code generation produces a machine-independent form, code optimisation improves it, and code generation emits target machine code. A symbol table is maintained across the phases.
entries.formula: Source code -> lexical analysis (tokens) -> syntax analysis (parse tree) -> semantic analysis -> intermediate code -> optimisation -> target code. Example tokenisation: a = b + c * 2 becomes identifiers a, b, c, operators =, +, *, and number 2.
entries.subject: Compiler Design

entries.example: For A = [[4, 1], [2, 3]], det(A - lambda I) = (4 - lambda)(3 - lambda) - 2 = lambda^2 - 7 lambda + 10 = 0, so lambda = 5 or lambda = 2. The eigenvalues are 5 and 2; their sum 7 equals the trace and their product 10 equals the determinant.
entries.fact: For a square matrix A, a non-zero vector v is an eigenvector with eigenvalue lambda if A v = lambda v, so A only scales v. Eigenvalues are the roots of the characteristic equation det(A - lambda I) = 0. They determine stability, principal components and many other properties, and a matrix is singular if and only if 0 is one of its eigenvalues.
entries.formula: A v = lambda v, v != 0. Characteristic equation: det(A - lambda I) = 0. For a 2x2 matrix [[a, b], [c, d]], det(A - lambda I) = (a - lambda)(d - lambda) - bc = 0. Trace = sum of eigenvalues; determinant = product of eigenvalues.
entries.subject: Linear Algebra

entries.fact: A square matrix A has an inverse A^-1 with A A^-1 = A^-1 A = I exactly when its determinant is non-zero. For a 2x2 matrix the inverse is found by swapping the diagonal entries, negating the off-diagonal entries and dividing by the determinant. Solving A x = b is then x = A^-1 b.
entries.formula: For A = [[a, b], [c, d]], det(A) = ad - bc. If det(A) != 0, A^-1 = (1 / (ad - bc)) x [[d, -b], [-c, a]].
entries.subject: Linear Algebra

entries.example: Approximate sin(0.1) using sin x approx x - x^3/6: 0.1 - 0.001/6 = 0.1 - 0.0001667 = 0.0998333. The true value sin(0.1) = 0.0998334, so the error is about 0.0000001.
entries.fact: A Taylor series represents a smooth function as an infinite sum of powers of (x - a), using the function's derivatives at a. The Maclaurin series is the case a = 0. Truncating the series gives a polynomial approximation whose error is controlled by the next term when x is close to a.
entries.subject: Calculus

entries.example: Integral from 0 to 1 of x^2 dx = [x^3/3] from 0 to 1 = 1/3 - 0 = 1/3, about 0.3333. This is the area under y = x^2 between x = 0 and x = 1.
entries.fact: The fundamental theorem of calculus links differentiation and integration. If F is an antiderivative of f, the definite integral of f from a to b is F(b) - F(a). Equivalently, differentiating the integral of f from a fixed point to x recovers f(x). It turns area and accumulation problems into antiderivative problems.
entries.formula: If F'(x) = f(x), then integral from a to b of f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a). Also, d/dx [integral from a to x of f(t) dt] = f(x). Power rule: integral of x^n dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + C for n != -1.
entries.subject: Calculus

entries.example: A disease affects 1% of people. A test is 99% sensitive and 95% specific. P(disease | positive) = 0.99 x 0.01 / (0.99 x 0.01 + 0.05 x 0.99) = 0.0099 / 0.0594 = 0.1667, about 16.7%, despite the test's high accuracy.
entries.fact: Bayes theorem updates the probability of a hypothesis after seeing evidence, combining the prior probability with the likelihood of the evidence. It follows directly from the definition of conditional probability, P(A|B) = P(A and B) / P(B). It is the basis of Bayesian inference and of many classifiers and diagnostic calculations.
entries.formula: P(A|B) = P(B|A) x P(A) / P(B), where P(B) = P(B|A) x P(A) + P(B|not A) x P(not A). P(A) is the prior, P(B|A) the likelihood, P(A|B) the posterior.
entries.subject: Probability & Statistics

entries.example: Solve dy/dx + 2y = 4. Here P = 2, so mu = e^(2x). Then d/dx (e^(2x) y) = 4 e^(2x), so e^(2x) y = 2 e^(2x) + C, giving y = 2 + C e^(-2x). Check: y' + 2y = -2C e^(-2x) + 4 + 2C e^(-2x) = 4.
entries.fact: A first-order linear ordinary differential equation has the form dy/dx + P(x) y = Q(x). It is solved with an integrating factor mu(x) = exp(integral of P(x) dx), which turns the left side into the derivative of mu(x) y. Integrating then gives the general solution, and an initial condition fixes the constant.
entries.formula: dy/dx + P(x) y = Q(x). Integrating factor: mu(x) = exp(integral P(x) dx). Solution: y = (1 / mu(x)) x [integral mu(x) Q(x) dx + C].
entries.subject: Differential Equations

entries.example: Find sqrt(2), so f(x) = x^2 - 2 and f'(x) = 2x. From x0 = 1.5, x1 = 1.5 - (1.5^2 - 2) / (2 x 1.5) = 1.5 - 0.25/3 = 1.4167. The true sqrt(2) is 1.4142, so one step already gives about 3 correct digits.
entries.fact: The Newton-Raphson method finds a root of f(x) = 0 by repeatedly following the tangent line at the current guess to its x-intercept. Near a simple root it converges quadratically, roughly doubling the number of correct digits per iteration, provided the starting guess is close enough and f'(x) is not zero.
entries.formula: x(n+1) = x(n) - f(x(n)) / f'(x(n)), with f'(x(n)) != 0. Stop when |x(n+1) - x(n)| is below the tolerance. Convergence is quadratic near a simple root.
entries.subject: Numerical Methods

entries.example: Approximate the integral from 0 to 1 of x^2 dx with n = 2, h = 0.5: (0.5/2) x [f(0) + 2 f(0.5) + f(1)] = 0.25 x [0 + 2 x 0.25 + 1] = 0.25 x 1.5 = 0.375. The exact value is 1/3 = 0.3333, so the error is 0.0417.
entries.fact: The trapezoidal rule approximates a definite integral by dividing the interval into n equal subintervals and replacing the curve on each subinterval by a straight line, forming a trapezium. Its error decreases as 1/n^2, so doubling n roughly quarters the error. It is exact for linear functions.
entries.formula: Integral from a to b of f(x) dx approx (h/2) x [f(x0) + 2 f(x1) + 2 f(x2) + ... + 2 f(x(n-1)) + f(xn)], where h = (b - a)/n and xi = a + i h. Error is O(h^2).
entries.subject: Numerical Methods

entries.example: For X ~ N(mu = 100, sigma = 15), the value x = 115 has z = (115 - 100)/15 = 1, so it is one standard deviation above the mean. About 68.27% of values lie between 85 and 115.
entries.fact: The normal distribution is the bell-shaped distribution defined by its mean mu and standard deviation sigma. About 68.27% of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean, 95.45% within two, and 99.73% within three. Standardising a value gives its z-score, which measures how many standard deviations it is from the mean.
entries.formula: Probability density: f(x) = (1 / (sigma x sqrt(2 pi))) x exp(-(x - mu)^2 / (2 sigma^2)). z-score: z = (x - mu) / sigma. Empirical rule: P(mu - sigma < X < mu + sigma) = 0.6827; P(mu - 2 sigma < X < mu + 2 sigma) = 0.9545.
entries.subject: Probability

entries.example: A population has sigma = 20. For a sample of n = 100, the standard error of the sample mean is SE = 20 / sqrt(100) = 20/10 = 2. So sample means typically fall within about 2 of mu, and about 95% fall within about 1.96 x 2 = 3.92 of mu.
entries.fact: The central limit theorem says that the mean of a large random sample is approximately normally distributed, whatever the shape of the population, provided the population variance is finite. The sampling distribution of the sample mean has mean mu and standard deviation sigma / sqrt(n), called the standard error, which shrinks as n grows.
entries.formula: For a sample of size n from a population with mean mu and standard deviation sigma, the sample mean X-bar is approximately N(mu, sigma^2 / n). Standard error of the mean: SE = sigma / sqrt(n). A common rule of thumb is n >= 30 for the approximation to be reasonable.
entries.subject: Sampling

entries.example: For data 2, 4, 6 from a normal distribution with unknown mean mu, the log-likelihood is maximised at mu-hat = (2 + 4 + 6)/3 = 4. So the MLE of the mean is 4, the sample mean.
entries.fact: Maximum likelihood estimation picks the parameter values that make the observed data most probable. The likelihood is the joint density of the data viewed as a function of the parameters, and it is usually maximised by maximising the log-likelihood and setting its derivative to zero. MLEs are consistent and asymptotically efficient under regular conditions.
entries.formula: Likelihood: L(theta) = product over i of f(xi; theta). Log-likelihood: l(theta) = log L(theta). MLE: theta-hat = argmax L(theta), found by solving d l(theta) / d theta = 0. For a normal sample, the MLE of mu is the sample mean x-bar.
entries.subject: Statistical Inference

entries.example: A sample of n = 100 has mean 50 and sigma = 10. The standard error is 10/sqrt(100) = 1, so a 95% confidence interval is 50 +/- 1.96 x 1 = (48.04, 51.96).
entries.fact: A confidence interval gives a range of plausible values for a population parameter, computed from a sample. A 95% confidence interval means that if the sampling were repeated many times, about 95% of the intervals so constructed would contain the true parameter. Wider intervals come from smaller samples, larger variability or higher confidence levels.
entries.formula: For a large sample with known sigma: x-bar +/- z(alpha/2) x sigma / sqrt(n). For 95% confidence, z = 1.96; for 90%, z = 1.645; for 99%, z = 2.576. With sigma unknown and a small sample, use t(alpha/2, n-1) x s / sqrt(n).
entries.subject: Statistical Inference

entries.example: A test gives p = 0.03 with alpha = 0.05. Since 0.03 < 0.05, reject H0 at the 5% level. If instead p had been 0.20, we would fail to reject H0, which is not proof that H0 is true.
entries.fact: In hypothesis testing, the null hypothesis H0 is a default claim and the alternative H1 is what the test looks for evidence against. The p-value is the probability of getting a test statistic at least as extreme as the observed one, assuming H0 is true. If p is smaller than the chosen significance level alpha, usually 0.05, H0 is rejected. A p-value is not the probability that H0 is true.
entries.formula: p-value = P(test statistic at least as extreme as observed | H0 true). Decision: reject H0 if p < alpha; otherwise fail to reject H0. Type I error rate = alpha = P(reject H0 | H0 true).
entries.subject: Hypothesis Testing

entries.fact: Simple linear regression fits a straight line to the relationship between a predictor x and a response y by least squares, minimising the sum of squared residuals. The slope measures the average change in y per unit change in x, and the intercept is the predicted y when x is zero. The fitted values and residuals are used to judge the fit.
entries.formula: Model: y = beta0 + beta1 x + epsilon. Least-squares slope: beta1-hat = Cov(x, y) / Var(x) = sum((xi - x-bar)(yi - y-bar)) / sum((xi - x-bar)^2). Intercept: beta0-hat = y-bar - beta1-hat x-bar. Fitted value: y-hat = beta0-hat + beta1-hat x.
entries.subject: Regression

entries.example: With k = 3 groups, MS_between = 120 and MS_within = 30, F = 120/30 = 4.0, with degrees of freedom (2, 27) if N = 30. A large F like this suggests the group means differ more than chance alone would explain.
entries.fact: One-way analysis of variance tests whether the means of three or more independent groups are all equal. It splits the total variation into variation between group means and variation within groups. If the between-group variation is large relative to the within-group variation, the F statistic is large and the null hypothesis of equal means is rejected.
entries.formula: F = MS_between / MS_within, where MS_between = SS_between / (k - 1) and MS_within = SS_within / (N - k), with k groups and N total observations. SS_between = sum n_i (x-bar_i - x-bar)^2; SS_within = sum sum (x_ij - x-bar_i)^2. Under H0, F follows an F distribution with (k - 1, N - k) degrees of freedom.
entries.subject: Hypothesis Testing

entries.example: A mass m = 1 kg on a spring with k = 100 N/m has omega = sqrt(100/1) = 10 rad/s and period T = 2 pi sqrt(1/100) = 2 pi x 0.1 = 0.628 s. Its frequency is f = 1/0.628 = 1.59 Hz.
entries.fact: Simple harmonic motion is periodic motion in which the restoring force is proportional to the displacement from equilibrium and opposite in direction, as in a mass on a spring or a simple pendulum for small angles. The displacement is sinusoidal, and the period depends only on the mass and the spring constant, not on the amplitude.
entries.formula: F = -k x; acceleration a = -(k/m) x. Displacement: x(t) = A cos(omega t + phi), with angular frequency omega = sqrt(k/m). Period: T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k); frequency f = 1/T = (1 / 2 pi) sqrt(k/m).
entries.subject: Mechanics

entries.example: A net force of 6 N acts on a mass of 2 kg, so a = F/m = 6/2 = 3 m/s^2. Starting from rest, after 4 s its speed is v = u + a t = 0 + 3 x 4 = 12 m/s.
