entries.fact: Newton's second law states that the net force on an object equals the rate of change of its momentum, which for constant mass is mass times acceleration. It is a vector law, so it holds separately in each direction. It explains why a larger force or a smaller mass gives a larger acceleration.
entries.formula: F = dp/dt = m a (for constant mass m). Weight: W = m g, with g = 9.8 m/s^2 near the Earth's surface. Work-energy theorem: net work = change in kinetic energy = (1/2) m v^2 - (1/2) m u^2.
entries.subject: Mechanics

entries.example: In vacuum with no charges or currents, rho = 0 and J = 0, so div E = 0, div B = 0, curl E = -dB/dt and curl B = mu0 epsilon0 dE/dt. These combine to give wave equations for E and B with wave speed c = 1/sqrt(mu0 epsilon0) = 3.00 x 10^8 m/s.
entries.fact: Maxwell's equations are four coupled equations that describe all classical electric and magnetic fields. Gauss's law says charges produce electric fields, Gauss's law for magnetism says there are no magnetic monopoles, Faraday's law says a changing magnetic field creates an electric field, and the Ampere-Maxwell law says currents and changing electric fields create magnetic fields. Together they predict electromagnetic waves travelling at the speed of light.
entries.formula: Differential form in vacuum: div E = rho / epsilon0; div B = 0; curl E = -dB/dt; curl B = mu0 J + mu0 epsilon0 dE/dt. Speed of light: c = 1 / sqrt(mu0 epsilon0) = 3.00 x 10^8 m/s.
entries.subject: Electromagnetism

entries.example: For a free particle with V = 0, a plane-wave solution psi = A exp(i(kx - omega t)) satisfies the equation with E = (h-bar^2 k^2) / (2m) = p^2 / 2m, where p = h-bar k. For p = 1.055 x 10^-24 kg m/s, E = (1.055 x 10^-24)^2 / (2 x 9.11 x 10^-31) = 6.11 x 10^-19 J, about 3.8 eV for an electron.
entries.fact: The Schrodinger equation governs how the wavefunction psi of a quantum system evolves in time. The Hamiltonian operator H is the total-energy operator, kinetic plus potential energy. For a time-independent potential, stationary states have definite energy E and satisfy the time-independent equation H psi = E psi, and the probability density is |psi|^2.
entries.formula: Time-dependent: i h-bar d psi / dt = H psi, with H = -(h-bar^2 / 2m) d^2/dx^2 + V(x) in one dimension. Time-independent: H psi = E psi. Probability density: P(x) = |psi(x)|^2. Reduced Planck constant: h-bar = h / 2 pi = 1.055 x 10^-34 J s.
entries.subject: Quantum Mechanics

entries.example: A metal has work function phi = 2.0 eV. Light with photon energy h nu = 3.0 eV gives K_max = 3.0 - 2.0 = 1.0 eV. The stopping potential is V0 = K_max / e = 1.0 V. Light with photon energy below 2.0 eV ejects no electrons at all.
entries.fact: In the photoelectric effect, light of frequency above a threshold ejects electrons from a metal, with each photon giving its energy to one electron. Einstein explained it by treating light as photons of energy h nu. The maximum kinetic energy of the ejected electrons depends only on the photon frequency, not on the light intensity, which only changes how many electrons are ejected.
entries.formula: Photon energy: E = h nu = h c / lambda. Einstein equation: K_max = h nu - phi, where phi is the work function. Threshold frequency: nu0 = phi / h; no emission occurs for nu < nu0. Stopping potential: e V0 = K_max.
entries.subject: Quantum Mechanics

entries.example: An electron (m = 9.11 x 10^-31 kg) moving at v = 1.0 x 10^6 m/s has momentum p = 9.11 x 10^-25 kg m/s, so lambda = 6.626 x 10^-34 / 9.11 x 10^-25 = 7.27 x 10^-10 m, about 0.73 nm, comparable to atomic spacings.
entries.fact: De Broglie proposed that every moving particle has a wavelength inversely proportional to its momentum, so matter shows wave behaviour at small scales. The Heisenberg uncertainty principle sets a fundamental limit: position and momentum cannot both be known arbitrarily precisely at the same time, because measuring one disturbs the other.
entries.formula: de Broglie wavelength: lambda = h / p = h / (m v). Uncertainty principle: delta x x delta p >= h-bar / 2, where h = 6.626 x 10^-34 J s and h-bar = h / 2 pi.
entries.subject: Quantum Mechanics
entries.topic: de Broglie wavelength and uncertainty principle

entries.example: A Carnot engine works between Th = 600 K and Tc = 300 K. Its efficiency is eta = 1 - 300/600 = 1 - 0.5 = 0.50, or 50%. If it absorbs Qh = 1000 J, it does W = 500 J of work and rejects Qc = 500 J.
entries.fact: The Carnot cycle is a reversible cycle between a hot reservoir at Th and a cold reservoir at Tc, and it is the most efficient heat engine possible between those temperatures. Its efficiency depends only on the two absolute temperatures, not on the working fluid or the engine design. No real engine can exceed it, by the second law of thermodynamics.
entries.formula: Efficiency: eta = W / Qh = 1 - Qc / Qh = 1 - Tc / Th, with Th and Tc in kelvin. Carnot cycle: two isothermal and two adiabatic reversible processes. Coefficient of performance of a Carnot refrigerator: COP = Tc / (Th - Tc).
entries.subject: Thermodynamics & Statistical Physics

entries.example: A 12 V battery drives a 4 ohm resistor, so I = V/R = 12/4 = 3 A. The power dissipated is P = V I = 12 x 3 = 36 W, also I^2 R = 9 x 4 = 36 W.
entries.fact: Ohm's law states that the current through a conductor is proportional to the voltage across it, with resistance as the constant of proportionality, for materials that obey it at fixed temperature. The electrical power dissipated as heat in a resistor is the product of voltage and current, and resistors in series add while resistors in parallel combine by reciprocals.
entries.formula: V = I R. Power: P = V I = I^2 R = V^2 / R. Series: R_total = R1 + R2 + ... . Parallel: 1 / R_total = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ... .
entries.subject: Electronics

entries.example: In a university database, Student(roll_no, name) and Course(course_id, title) are entity sets, and 'Enrolls' is a many-to-many relationship between them. It becomes a table Enrolls(roll_no, course_id, grade) whose primary key is (roll_no, course_id), with roll_no and course_id as foreign keys.
entries.fact: The ER model describes data as entities (real-world objects), attributes (their properties) and relationships between entities. Each entity set has a key attribute that uniquely identifies its entities, and relationships have a cardinality such as one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many. An ER diagram is converted into relational tables by creating one table per entity set and using foreign keys for relationships.
entries.formula: Entity set -> table; key attribute -> primary key; many-to-many relationship -> separate table with the keys of both entity sets as a composite primary key; one-to-many relationship -> foreign key on the 'many' side.
entries.subject: Database Management & Warehousing

entries.example: Student(roll_no, name, email, dept_id) has primary key roll_no, unique key email, and dept_id is a foreign key referring to Department(dept_id). A row with dept_id = 99 is rejected if no department with dept_id 99 exists.
entries.fact: In the relational model, data is stored in tables (relations) of rows (tuples) and columns (attributes), and each cell holds a single atomic value. A superkey is a set of attributes that uniquely identifies each row; a candidate key is a minimal superkey, and one candidate key is chosen as the primary key. A foreign key is an attribute in one table that refers to the primary key of another table, enforcing referential integrity.
entries.formula: Primary key: unique and NOT NULL for every row. Foreign key: every value must either match a primary key value in the referenced table or be NULL. Candidate key: minimal superkey (no attribute can be removed without losing uniqueness).
entries.subject: Database Management & Warehousing

entries.example: For Student(roll_no, name, age), the query 'names of students older than 20' is pi_name(sigma_age > 20(Student)). On rows (1, Ana, 21), (2, Ben, 19), (3, Cara, 22), selection keeps Ana and Cara, and projection gives {Ana, Cara}.
entries.fact: Relational algebra is a procedural query language whose operators take relations as input and produce a relation as output. The basic operators are selection (sigma, filters rows), projection (pi, keeps chosen columns), union, set difference, Cartesian product and rename. The join combines two relations on a matching condition and is the most used operator in practice.
entries.formula: Selection: sigma_condition(R) keeps rows satisfying the condition. Projection: pi_attributes(R) keeps only listed columns, removing duplicates. Natural join: R natural-join S matches rows on common attributes. Theta join: R join_condition S.
entries.subject: Database Management & Warehousing

entries.example: Students: (1, Ana), (2, Ben), (3, Cara). Enrollments: (1, CS101), (1, MA101), (2, CS101). SELECT name FROM Students INNER JOIN Enrollments ON Students.id = Enrollments.student_id returns 3 rows: Ana, Ana, Ben. Cara has no enrollment, so she is excluded; a LEFT JOIN would return 4 rows with NULL for Cara.
entries.fact: SQL is the standard language for relational databases: DDL statements such as CREATE TABLE define schema, while DML statements such as SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE manipulate data. A join combines rows from two tables on a related column. INNER JOIN returns only matching rows, LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table with NULLs where there is no match, and the WHERE and GROUP BY clauses filter and aggregate rows.
entries.formula: SELECT columns FROM A INNER JOIN B ON A.key = B.key; LEFT JOIN keeps every row of A. Aggregate: SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM Employee GROUP BY dept HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;
entries.subject: Database Management & Warehousing

entries.example: For R(A, B, C) with FDs A -> B and B -> C: A+ starts as {A}, A -> B adds B, then B -> C adds C, so A+ = {A, B, C}. Hence A is a candidate key, and by transitivity A -> C also holds.
entries.fact: A functional dependency X -> Y means that any two rows agreeing on the attributes X must also agree on Y, so X determines Y. Armstrong's axioms (reflexivity, augmentation, transitivity) let us derive all implied dependencies, and the closure X+ is the set of all attributes functionally determined by X. A dependency is trivial if Y is a subset of X. Closures are used to find candidate keys and to test normal forms.
entries.formula: Armstrong's axioms: Reflexivity: if Y is a subset of X then X -> Y. Augmentation: if X -> Y then XZ -> YZ. Transitivity: if X -> Y and Y -> Z then X -> Z. Closure: X+ is computed by repeatedly adding Y for every X -> Y until no change.
entries.subject: Database Management & Warehousing

entries.example: Order(order_id, item, qty, customer_name) with composite key (order_id, item) violates 2NF because customer_name depends only on order_id, a part of the key. Split it into Order(order_id, customer_name) and OrderItem(order_id, item, qty), and both tables are in 2NF.
entries.fact: A relation is in first normal form (1NF) if every attribute holds only atomic (indivisible) values, with no repeating groups or multi-valued attributes. A relation is in second normal form (2NF) if it is in 1NF and every non-prime attribute is fully functionally dependent on each candidate key, meaning no partial dependency on only part of a composite key exists. Normalization removes redundancy and the update, insertion and deletion anomalies it causes.
entries.formula: 1NF: all attribute values are atomic. 2NF: in 1NF and no partial dependency, i.e. no non-prime attribute A such that part of a candidate key K' -> A where K' is a proper subset of a candidate key K.
entries.subject: Database Management & Warehousing

entries.topic: Third normal form (3NF) and Boyce-Codd normal form (BCNF)
entries.fact: A relation is in third normal form (3NF) if it is in 2NF and no non-prime attribute is transitively dependent on any candidate key. BCNF is stricter: for every non-trivial functional dependency X -> Y, X must be a superkey, with no exception for prime attributes. Every BCNF relation is in 3NF, but a 3NF relation can fail BCNF when a non-superkey determines a prime attribute. Decomposing into BCNF can lose a functional dependency, unlike 3NF decomposition.
entries.formula: 3NF rule: for every non-trivial FD X -> Y, X is a superkey OR every attribute of Y not in X is prime. BCNF rule: for every non-trivial FD X -> Y, X is a superkey (no prime-attribute exception). Classical 3NF wording: in 2NF and no transitive dependency of a non-prime attribute on any candidate key.
entries.example: Student(roll_no, dept, dept_head) with roll_no -> dept and dept -> dept_head has the transitive dependency roll_no -> dept -> dept_head, so it violates 3NF; split into Student(roll_no, dept) and Dept(dept, dept_head). Separately, Enroll(student, course, instructor) with FDs {student, course} -> instructor and instructor -> course has candidate keys {student, course} and {student, instructor}: instructor -> course violates BCNF because instructor is not a superkey, but it passes 3NF because course is prime, so this relation is in 3NF but not in BCNF.
entries.subject: Database Management & Warehousing

entries.example: Account balance is 1000. T1 withdraws 100 (reads 1000, writes 900) and T2 deposits 200 (reads 1000, writes 1200) concurrently without locking. Whichever writes last wins, so the final balance is 900 or 1200 instead of the correct 1100: one update is lost. Two-phase locking prevents this by serializing the two transactions.
entries.fact: A transaction is a unit of work that must satisfy ACID: Atomicity (all operations or none), Consistency (the database moves from one valid state to another), Isolation (concurrent transactions behave as if run one after another) and Durability (committed changes survive crashes). Concurrency control, usually two-phase locking, prevents lost updates, dirty reads and other anomalies, and a schedule is serializable if its result equals some serial execution of the same transactions.
entries.formula: ACID: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability. Two-phase locking: a transaction acquires all locks before releasing any (growing phase, then shrinking phase). Serializable schedule: equivalent to some serial schedule; conflict-serializable if its precedence graph is acyclic.
entries.subject: Database Management & Warehousing

entries.example: With fanout F = 100 and 1,000,000 records, the B+ tree height is log_100(1,000,000) = 3, so a lookup touches only about 3 disk pages instead of scanning 1,000,000 rows. A range query such as marks BETWEEN 80 AND 90 finds the first leaf and then follows leaf links to collect all matching rows in order.
entries.fact: An index is an auxiliary structure that lets the database find rows by a key without scanning the whole table. A B+ tree is the standard index structure: a balanced multi-way tree in which internal nodes hold only separator keys for routing, all data pointers live in the leaf nodes, and leaves are linked in sorted order. Its high fanout keeps the tree shallow (typically 3-4 levels), so search, insert and delete cost O(log n) disk accesses, and range scans walk the linked leaves in order.
entries.formula: Search/insert/delete cost: O(log_F N), where F is the fanout (children per node) and N is the number of records. Height is about log_F(N); range query with k results costs O(log_F N + k).
entries.subject: Database Management & Warehousing

entries.example: A Sales fact table has measures amount and quantity, with dimensions Time, Product and Store. Monthly sales of 100 in January, 150 in February and 200 in March roll up to Q1 sales of 100 + 150 + 200 = 450. Drilling down from Q1 back to months recovers the three monthly figures.
entries.fact: A data warehouse is a subject-oriented, integrated, time-variant and non-volatile store built for analysis rather than day-to-day transactions. A star schema models it with one central fact table holding numeric measures and foreign keys, surrounded by dimension tables (such as time, product and store) that describe the context. OLAP operations analyse this cube: roll-up aggregates to coarser levels, drill-down goes to finer detail, slice and dice select subsets, and pivot rotates the view.
entries.formula: Star schema: fact table (foreign keys to dimensions + numeric measures) at the centre, dimension tables around it. OLAP: roll-up (aggregate up a hierarchy, e.g. month -> quarter), drill-down (quarter -> month), slice (fix one dimension value), dice (select a sub-cube).
entries.subject: Database Management & Warehousing
entries.topic: Data warehousing, star schema and OLAP

entries.example: Points (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 6) lie exactly on y = 2x, so the fitted line has slope w1 = 2 and intercept w0 = 0, with MSE = 0. Predicting at x = 4 gives y_hat = 2 * 4 = 8.
entries.fact: Linear regression fits a straight line (or hyperplane) to numeric data by modelling the target as a weighted sum of the features plus an intercept. It is trained by minimising the mean squared error between predictions and true values, which has a closed-form least-squares solution. The fitted coefficients show how much the prediction changes when one feature increases by one unit, holding the others fixed.
entries.formula: Model: y_hat = w0 + w1*x1 + ... + wn*xn. Cost (MSE): J(w) = (1/n) * sum_i (y_i - y_hat_i)^2. Closed-form solution: w = (X^T X)^-1 X^T y.
entries.subject: Machine Learning

entries.example: With w.x + b = 2, sigma(2) = 1 / (1 + e^-2) = 1 / 1.1353 = 0.881, so the model predicts class 1 with probability 0.881. With z = 0, sigma(0) = 0.5, exactly on the decision boundary.
entries.fact: Logistic regression is a classification algorithm, not a regressor: it passes a linear score through the sigmoid function to output the probability that an example belongs to the positive class. It is trained by minimising log loss (binary cross-entropy), which heavily penalises confident wrong predictions. The model is linear in the log-odds, and the usual decision rule is to predict class 1 when the probability exceeds 0.5.
entries.formula: Sigmoid: sigma(z) = 1 / (1 + e^-z), where z = w.x + b. Model: P(y = 1 | x) = sigma(w.x + b). Log-odds: ln(p / (1 - p)) = w.x + b. Log loss: L = -(1/n) * sum_i [y_i ln p_i + (1 - y_i) ln(1 - p_i)].
entries.subject: Machine Learning

entries.example: A model with Bias^2 = 0.04, Variance = 0.09 and irreducible noise sigma^2 = 0.01 has expected test error 0.04 + 0.09 + 0.01 = 0.14. Fitting a degree-15 polynomial to 20 noisy points drives training error near zero but inflates variance, so test error rises; adding an L2 penalty lambda * sum w_j^2 shrinks the wild coefficients and lowers test error.
entries.fact: Overfitting is when a model memorises training noise and performs much worse on unseen data, while underfitting is when a model is too simple to capture the pattern at all. The bias-variance tradeoff explains this: expected test error splits into squared bias (error from wrong assumptions), variance (error from sensitivity to the training sample) and irreducible noise. Simpler models have high bias and low variance; complex models have low bias and high variance. Regularization controls overfitting by penalising large weights: L2 (ridge) shrinks all weights, while L1 (lasso) can drive some to exactly zero.
entries.formula: Expected test error: E[(y - y_hat)^2] = Bias^2 + Variance + sigma^2 (irreducible noise), where Bias = E[y_hat] - f(x) and Variance = E[(y_hat - E[y_hat])^2]. Ridge (L2): cost + lambda * sum_j w_j^2. Lasso (L1): cost + lambda * sum_j |w_j|.
entries.subject: Machine Learning

entries.example: With 100 samples and 5-fold cross-validation, each round trains on 80 samples and tests on 20. If the five test accuracies are 0.82, 0.85, 0.80, 0.84 and 0.83, the cross-validated accuracy is (0.82 + 0.85 + 0.80 + 0.84 + 0.83) / 5 = 4.14 / 5 = 0.828.
entries.fact: Cross-validation estimates how well a model generalises by repeatedly training on one part of the data and testing on a held-out part. In k-fold cross-validation the data is split into k equal folds; each fold serves once as the test set while the other k-1 folds train the model, and the k test scores are averaged. Leave-one-out cross-validation is the extreme case with k equal to the number of samples. It gives a more reliable estimate than a single train-test split and is the standard way to choose hyperparameters.
entries.formula: k-fold CV error: CV = (1/k) * sum_j Error_j, where Error_j is the test error on fold j. Each fold is the test set exactly once; training uses the other k - 1 folds. Leave-one-out: k = n.
entries.subject: Machine Learning

entries.example: On the classic Play Tennis data, 14 examples have 9 Yes and 5 No, so entropy H = -(9/14) log2(9/14) - (5/14) log2(5/14) = 0.940 bits. Splitting on Outlook separates the data into purer groups and lowers the weighted entropy, giving a positive information gain, so Outlook is chosen as the root split.
entries.fact: A decision tree predicts by asking a sequence of yes/no questions about the features, splitting the data at each node until the leaves are nearly pure in one class (or one value, for regression). At each node it picks the split that most reduces impurity, measured by Gini impurity or entropy, and the gain from a split is the impurity drop. Trees are easy to interpret and need no feature scaling, but a deep tree overfits, so pruning or a depth limit is used.
entries.formula: Gini impurity: Gini = 1 - sum_k p_k^2. Entropy: H = -sum_k p_k log2(p_k), where p_k is the fraction of class k in the node. Information gain: IG = I(parent) - sum_v (|S_v| / |S|) * I(S_v).
entries.subject: Machine Learning

entries.example: Training points: A(1, 1) class 0, B(2, 2) class 0, C(5, 5) class 1. Query point (2, 3): distances are d(A) = sqrt(5) = 2.24, d(B) = 1, d(C) = sqrt(13) = 3.61. With k = 3 the neighbours vote 0, 0, 1, so the prediction is class 0.
entries.fact: k-NN is a lazy, non-parametric classifier: it stores the whole training set and only works at prediction time. For a new point it finds the k training points closest to it (usually by Euclidean distance) and predicts the majority class among them, or the average target for regression. It makes no assumption about the shape of the decision boundary, but it needs feature scaling, slows down on large datasets, and suffers in very high dimensions.
entries.formula: Euclidean distance: d(x, q) = sqrt(sum_j (x_j - q_j)^2). Prediction: majority vote of the k nearest neighbours' labels (classification) or their mean (regression).
entries.subject: Machine Learning

entries.example: If a trained SVM has weight vector w = (3, 4), then ||w|| = 5 and the margin width is 2 / 5 = 0.4. The support vectors are the training points lying exactly on w.x + b = 1 or w.x + b = -1; only these points determine the boundary, and removing any other point leaves it unchanged.
entries.fact: An SVM is a classifier that finds the hyperplane separating two classes with the largest possible margin, the gap between the hyperplane and the nearest training points, called support vectors. Maximising the margin improves generalisation. For data that is not linearly separable, the kernel trick maps points into a higher-dimensional space (for example with an RBF kernel) where a linear separator exists, and a soft margin with slack variables allows a few misclassifications in exchange for a wider margin.
entries.formula: Hyperplane: w.x + b = 0. Margin width: 2 / ||w||. Hard-margin SVM: minimise (1/2)||w||^2 subject to y_i (w.x_i + b) >= 1 for all i. RBF kernel: K(x, z) = exp(-gamma ||x - z||^2).
entries.subject: Machine Learning

entries.example: Points (1, 1), (2, 1), (8, 8), (9, 8) with k = 2 and initial centroids (1, 1) and (8, 8): cluster 1 = {(1, 1), (2, 1)} with new centroid (1.5, 1), cluster 2 = {(8, 8), (9, 8)} with new centroid (8.5, 8). WCSS = 0.25 + 0.25 + 0.25 + 0.25 = 1.0, and the next assignment step changes nothing, so it has converged.
entries.fact: k-means is an unsupervised algorithm that partitions data into k clusters by minimising the within-cluster sum of squared distances to the cluster centroids. It alternates two steps: assign each point to its nearest centroid, then recompute each centroid as the mean of its assigned points, repeating until the assignments stop changing. The result depends on the initial centroids and on the choice of k, often picked with the elbow method, and features should be scaled first.
entries.formula: Objective (WCSS): J = sum_{j=1..k} sum_{x in C_j} ||x - mu_j||^2, where mu_j is the centroid of cluster C_j. Centroid update: mu_j = (1 / |C_j|) * sum_{x in C_j} x.
entries.subject: Machine Learning

entries.example: Minimise f(w) = (w - 3)^2, whose gradient is 2(w - 3). Starting at w0 = 0 with learning rate alpha = 0.1: w1 = 0 - 0.1 * 2 * (0 - 3) = 0.6, then w2 = 0.6 - 0.1 * 2 * (0.6 - 3) = 1.08. The iterates move toward the minimum at w = 3.
entries.fact: Gradient descent is the workhorse optimiser of machine learning: it minimises a cost function by repeatedly stepping in the direction of steepest decrease, which is the negative gradient. The learning rate controls the step size: too small and training crawls, too large and it overshoots or diverges. Batch gradient descent uses the whole dataset per step, stochastic gradient descent uses one example, and mini-batch gradient descent uses a small batch, which is the usual compromise.
entries.formula: Update rule: w := w - alpha * (dJ/dw), where alpha is the learning rate and dJ/dw is the gradient of the cost J at w. For linear regression, dJ/dw_j = (1/n) * sum_i (y_hat_i - y_i) * x_ij (up to a constant factor of 2, depending on the MSE convention).
entries.subject: Machine Learning

entries.example: A random forest of 100 trees classifies a loan application: 62 trees vote 'approve' and 38 vote 'reject', so the ensemble predicts 'approve' by majority vote. In AdaBoost, a weak learner with error err = 0.2 gets weight alpha = (1/2) ln(0.8 / 0.2) = (1/2) ln(4) = 0.693, so it counts more than a learner with error 0.4.
entries.fact: Ensemble methods combine many weak learners into one stronger model. Bagging (bootstrap aggregating) trains each learner on a bootstrap sample of the data and averages or majority-votes their predictions, which reduces variance; a random forest is bagging plus random feature subsets at each split. Boosting trains learners sequentially, each new one focusing on the examples the previous ones got wrong, which reduces bias; AdaBoost reweights misclassified examples and gradient boosting fits each new tree to the residual errors of the ensemble so far.
entries.formula: Bagging prediction: average (regression) or majority vote (classification) over B bootstrap-trained models. AdaBoost: final prediction H(x) = sign(sum_t alpha_t * h_t(x)), with learner weight alpha_t = (1/2) ln((1 - err_t) / err_t). Gradient boosting: F_m(x) = F_{m-1}(x) + nu * h_m(x), where h_m fits the negative gradient (residuals) and nu is the learning rate.
entries.subject: Machine Learning

entries.example: A 12 V battery is connected across a 4 ohm resistor. Current I = V / R = 12 / 4 = 3 A, and power dissipated P = V * I = 12 * 3 = 36 W.
entries.fact: Ohm's law states that the voltage across a resistor is directly proportional to the current through it, provided the temperature and other physical conditions remain constant. The constant of proportionality is the resistance. It applies to linear, ohmic resistors in DC and, in phasor form, to AC circuits.
entries.formula: V = I * R, I = V / R, R = V / I, where V is voltage in volts, I is current in amperes and R is resistance in ohms. Power dissipated: P = V * I = I^2 * R = V^2 / R.
entries.subject: Electric Circuits

entries.example: A 12 V source drives 2 ohm and 4 ohm resistors in series. By KVL, loop current I = 12 / (2 + 4) = 2 A. Voltage across the 2 ohm resistor is 4 V and across the 4 ohm resistor is 8 V, and 4 + 8 = 12 V, satisfying KVL.
entries.fact: Kirchhoff's current law states that the algebraic sum of currents entering a node is zero, which is conservation of charge. Kirchhoff's voltage law states that the algebraic sum of voltages around any closed loop is zero, which is conservation of energy. Together they are the basis for nodal and mesh analysis of any circuit.
entries.formula: KCL: sum of currents entering a node = sum of currents leaving the node, or Sigma I = 0 at a node. KVL: Sigma V = 0 around a closed loop, or sum of voltage rises = sum of voltage drops.
entries.subject: Electric Circuits
entries.topic: Kirchhoff's current law (KCL) and voltage law (KVL)

entries.example: For f = 50 Hz, N = 100 turns and Phi_m = 0.02 Wb, E = 4.44 * 50 * 100 * 0.02 = 444 V RMS.
entries.fact: When a sinusoidal flux links a transformer winding, Faraday's law gives an induced EMF whose RMS value depends on frequency, turns and maximum flux. The factor 4.44 comes from the sinusoidal form factor 1.11 multiplied by 4. It applies to both primary and secondary windings, which share the same core flux.
entries.formula: E = 4.44 * f * N * Phi_m, where E is RMS induced EMF in volts, f is supply frequency in Hz, N is number of turns and Phi_m is maximum core flux in webers. E1 = 4.44 * f * N1 * Phi_m and E2 = 4.44 * f * N2 * Phi_m, so E2 / E1 = N2 / N1.
entries.subject: Electrical Machines

entries.example: A balanced load has VL = 400 V, IL = 10 A and cos(phi) = 0.8. Real power P = 1.732 * 400 * 10 * 0.8 = 5542 W (about 5.54 kW) and apparent power S = 1.732 * 400 * 10 = 6928 VA.
entries.fact: Power factor is the cosine of the angle between voltage and current in an AC circuit, and it equals real power divided by apparent power. A low power factor means more current is needed for the same useful power. For a balanced three-phase load, power is expressed with line voltage and line current and the factor sqrt(3).
entries.formula: Power factor = cos(phi) = P / S, where P is real power in watts and S is apparent power in volt-amperes. Single-phase: P = V * I * cos(phi), S = V * I, Q = V * I * sin(phi). Balanced three-phase: P = sqrt(3) * VL * IL * cos(phi), S = sqrt(3) * VL * IL, Q = sqrt(3) * VL * IL * sin(phi), S^2 = P^2 + Q^2.
entries.subject: Power Systems

entries.example: For G(s) = 1 / (s + 2), the DC gain is G(0) = 1 / 2 = 0.5. A unit step input therefore settles to a steady-state output of 0.5.
entries.fact: The transfer function is the Laplace transform of the output divided by the Laplace transform of the input, with all initial conditions zero. It completely describes a linear time-invariant system in the s-domain. Its poles determine stability and its value at s = 0 gives the DC gain.
entries.formula: G(s) = Y(s) / X(s), where Y(s) is the Laplace transform of the output and X(s) is the Laplace transform of the input. DC gain = G(0). For a first-order system G(s) = K / (tau * s + 1), the pole is at s = -1 / tau.
entries.subject: Control Systems
entries.topic: Transfer function of a linear system

entries.example: A coil has N = 200 turns, Phi_m = 0.01 Wb and f = 50 Hz. Peak EMF Em = 2 * pi * 50 * 200 * 0.01 = 628.3 V, so RMS EMF E = 628.3 / 1.414 = 444.3 V.
entries.fact: Faraday's law states that a changing magnetic flux linking a coil induces an EMF in the coil. The minus sign in the law is Lenz's law: the induced EMF opposes the change in flux that produced it. This is the operating principle of transformers, generators and inductors.
entries.formula: e = -N * dPhi/dt, where e is induced EMF in volts, N is number of turns and Phi is magnetic flux in webers. For sinusoidal flux Phi = Phi_m * sin(2 * pi * f * t), peak EMF Em = 2 * pi * f * N * Phi_m and RMS EMF E = Em / sqrt(2) = 4.44 * f * N * Phi_m.
entries.subject: Electromagnetic Fields

entries.example: A sine wave has peak voltage Vm = 10 V. Its RMS value is Vrms = 10 / 1.414 = 7.07 V. Across a 10 ohm resistor it delivers P = 7.07^2 / 10 = 5 W.
entries.fact: The RMS (root mean square) value of an AC signal is the equivalent DC value that would deliver the same average power to a resistor. For a sinusoid it is the peak value divided by sqrt(2). Household mains are quoted in RMS, so 230 V RMS in India corresponds to a peak of about 325 V.
entries.formula: Vrms = Vm / sqrt(2) = 0.707 * Vm, where Vm is the peak voltage. Similarly Irms = Im / sqrt(2). Average power in a resistor: P = Vrms * Irms = Vrms^2 / R.
entries.subject: Signals & Systems
entries.topic: RMS value of a sinusoidal signal

entries.example: A 20 V source is connected to a 4 ohm resistor. Current I = 20 / 4 = 5 A and power P = 20 * 5 = 100 W.
entries.fact: Ohm's law relates voltage, current and resistance in a linear resistor, and it is the starting point for network analysis. In a network it is applied branch by branch, together with KCL and KVL, to find unknown voltages and currents. Series resistors add directly, while parallel resistors combine by reciprocal addition.
entries.formula: V = I * R. Resistors in series: R_eq = R1 + R2 + ... Resistors in parallel: 1 / R_eq = 1 / R1 + 1 / R2 + ... Power: P = V * I = I^2 * R.
entries.subject: Networks

entries.fact: The Shockley diode equation models the exponential current-voltage characteristic of a p-n junction diode. A small increase in forward voltage causes a large increase in current because voltage appears in the exponent. In reverse bias the current saturates at about minus the reverse saturation current.
entries.formula: I = Is * (exp(V / (n * VT)) - 1), where I is diode current, Is is reverse saturation current, V is diode voltage, n is ideality factor (about 1) and VT = k * T / q is thermal voltage, about 26 mV at room temperature (300 K).
entries.subject: Electronic Devices

entries.example: With Rf = 90 k ohm and R1 = 10 k ohm, gain Av = 1 + 90 / 10 = 10. An input Vin = 0.5 V gives Vout = 10 * 0.5 = 5 V.
entries.fact: An ideal op-amp with negative feedback has virtually no input current and virtually no voltage difference between its two inputs. In the non-inverting configuration the input goes to the positive terminal, so the output is in phase with the input. The gain is set only by the two feedback resistors, not by the op-amp itself.
entries.formula: Gain Av = Vout / Vin = 1 + Rf / R1, where Rf is the feedback resistor and R1 is the resistor to ground. For an inverting amplifier, Av = -Rf / R1.
entries.subject: Analog Circuits

entries.example: Take A = 1, B = 0. Left side of the first law: (1 + 0)' = 1' = 0. Right side: 1' * 0' = 0 * 1 = 0. Both sides agree.
entries.fact: Boolean algebra is the mathematics of digital logic, with variables taking only 0 or 1. De Morgan's laws show how to convert between AND and OR forms using complements, which is essential for simplifying logic and implementing circuits with only NAND or only NOR gates. They are used in almost every digital design and GATE question on logic minimisation.
entries.formula: De Morgan's laws: (A + B)' = A' * B' and (A * B)' = A' + B', where + is OR, * is AND and ' is NOT. Basic identities: A + 0 = A, A * 1 = A, A + A' = 1, A * A' = 0.
entries.subject: Digital Circuits
entries.topic: Boolean algebra and De Morgan's laws

entries.example: An audio signal has fm = 20 kHz, so the Nyquist rate is 2 * 20 = 40 kHz. A CD samples at 44.1 kHz, which is above 40 kHz and therefore avoids aliasing for 20 kHz audio.
entries.fact: The Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem states that a band-limited signal can be perfectly reconstructed from its samples if the sampling rate is at least twice its highest frequency. Sampling slower than this causes aliasing, where high frequencies falsely appear as low frequencies. The minimum rate is called the Nyquist rate.
entries.formula: fs >= 2 * fm, where fs is sampling frequency and fm is the highest frequency in the signal. Nyquist rate = 2 * fm. Nyquist frequency = fs / 2. Sampling period Ts = 1 / fs.
entries.subject: Signals & Systems

entries.example: With Am = 2 V, Ac = 10 V and fm = 5 kHz, mu = 2 / 10 = 0.2 (20 percent modulation) and bandwidth BW = 2 * 5 = 10 kHz.
entries.fact: In amplitude modulation the message signal varies the amplitude of a high-frequency carrier. The modulation index measures how deeply the carrier is modulated, and it must not exceed 1 or the envelope distorts on demodulation. An AM signal occupies twice the message bandwidth, one sideband on each side of the carrier.
entries.formula: Modulation index mu = Am / Ac = (Amax - Amin) / (Amax + Amin), where Am is message amplitude, Ac is carrier amplitude, and Amax and Amin are the maximum and minimum envelope amplitudes. Bandwidth BW = 2 * fm, where fm is the highest message frequency. AM wave: s(t) = Ac * (1 + mu * cos(2 * pi * fm * t)) * cos(2 * pi * fc * t).
entries.subject: Communication
entries.topic: Amplitude modulation: modulation index and bandwidth

entries.example: For G(s) = 10 / (s * (s + 2)), the system is type 1 because of the 1 / s term. Kp is infinite, so the steady-state error to a unit step input is 0.
entries.fact: Steady-state error is the difference between the desired output and the actual output after transients have died out. A system with at least one integrator (type 1 or higher) tracks a step input with zero steady-state error in unity feedback. A type 0 system has a finite step error determined by its position error constant Kp.
entries.formula: For unity feedback, step-input steady-state error e_ss = 1 / (1 + Kp), where Kp = limit as s -> 0 of G(s). For a type 1 or higher system, Kp is infinite, so e_ss = 0 for a step input.
entries.subject: Control Systems
entries.topic: Steady-state error of a unity-feedback system

entries.example: With R1 = 100 ohm, R2 = 200 ohm and R3 = 150 ohm at balance, the unknown resistance R4 = R2 * R3 / R1 = 200 * 150 / 100 = 300 ohm.
entries.fact: A Wheatstone bridge has four resistors in a diamond, with a supply across one diagonal and a galvanometer across the other. It is balanced when no current flows through the galvanometer, which happens when the two voltage dividers give equal midpoint voltages. At balance an unknown resistance can be found accurately from the three known resistances.
entries.formula: Balance condition: R1 / R2 = R3 / R4, where R1, R2, R3 and R4 are the four arm resistances. Unknown resistance Rx = R2 * R3 / R1 (with the labelling R1 / R2 = R3 / Rx). At balance the galvanometer current is zero.
entries.subject: Measurements

entries.example: A 10-bit ADC with Vref = 5 V has 2^10 = 1024 levels and LSB = 5 / 1024 = 0.00488 V, about 4.88 mV per count.
entries.fact: An N-bit ADC divides its full-scale input range into 2^N discrete levels. The resolution, or one LSB step, is the smallest change in input voltage that changes the output code by one count. More bits give a smaller step and smaller quantisation error, at the cost of slower or more expensive conversion.
entries.formula: Number of levels = 2^N. LSB step = Vref / 2^N (for a unipolar range 0 to Vref), where N is the number of bits and Vref is the reference voltage. Maximum quantisation error is about plus or minus LSB / 2.
entries.subject: Instrumentation
entries.topic: ADC resolution and LSB step size

entries.example: A 120 ohm gauge with GF = 2 is strained by epsilon = 0.001 (1000 microstrain). Delta R = 2 * 120 * 0.001 = 0.24 ohm, so the resistance becomes 120.24 ohm.
entries.fact: A strain gauge is a resistive transducer whose resistance changes when it is stretched or compressed. The gauge factor relates the fractional change in resistance to the mechanical strain, and for common metallic foil gauges it is about 2. Because the resistance change is tiny, strain gauges are usually read with a Wheatstone bridge.
entries.formula: Gauge factor GF = (Delta R / R) / (Delta L / L) = (Delta R / R) / epsilon, where epsilon = Delta L / L is strain (dimensionless). Change in resistance: Delta R = GF * R * epsilon. Typical GF is about 2 for metallic gauges.
entries.subject: Instrumentation

entries.example: A voltmeter reads 10.2 V for a true voltage of 10.0 V. Absolute error = 0.2 V and percentage error = (0.2 / 10.0) * 100 = 2 percent.
entries.fact: Absolute error is the difference between the measured value and the true value, while relative error expresses that difference as a fraction of the true value. Percentage error is the relative error multiplied by 100 and is the usual way to report accuracy. Systematic errors repeat in the same direction, while random errors vary unpredictably.
entries.formula: Absolute error = measured value - true value. Relative error = absolute error / true value. Percentage error = (absolute error / true value) * 100 percent.
entries.subject: Measurements
entries.topic: Measurement error: absolute, relative and percentage error

entries.example: With Kp = 2 and an instantaneous error e = 0.5, the proportional term alone contributes Kp * e = 2 * 0.5 = 1 unit to the control output at that instant.
entries.fact: A PID controller combines proportional, integral and derivative action on the error between setpoint and measured output. The proportional term reacts to the present error, the integral term removes steady-state error by acting on past error, and the derivative term damps overshoot by acting on the rate of change of error. It is the most widely used controller in industry.
entries.formula: u(t) = Kp * e(t) + Ki * integral of e(t) dt + Kd * de(t)/dt, where u(t) is the control output, e(t) is the error, and Kp, Ki and Kd are the proportional, integral and derivative gains. In the s-domain: U(s)/E(s) = Kp + Ki/s + Kd * s.
entries.subject: Control Systems

entries.example: A vibration signal has fm = 3 kHz, so the minimum sampling rate is 2 * 3 = 6 kHz. Sampling at 10 kHz satisfies the theorem with margin.
entries.fact: To digitise an analogue signal without losing information, it must be sampled at least twice as fast as its highest frequency component. Sampling slower causes aliasing, in which higher frequencies appear as lower ones in the sampled data. Practical data-acquisition systems therefore use an anti-aliasing filter before the ADC and sample above the Nyquist rate.
entries.formula: fs >= 2 * fm, where fs is sampling frequency and fm is the highest frequency in the signal. Nyquist rate = 2 * fm. Nyquist frequency = fs / 2.
entries.subject: Signals & Systems
entries.topic: Nyquist sampling theorem for data acquisition

entries.example: A current of 2 A flows through a 0.1 ohm shunt resistor. The voltage across the shunt is V = 2 * 0.1 = 0.2 V, which a voltmeter can measure to infer the current.
entries.fact: Ohm's law is the basic relation used to size shunts, series resistors and loads in measurement circuits. A current is often measured as the voltage drop across a known shunt resistor, and a voltage is scaled down with a resistive divider. The law holds for linear resistors at constant temperature.
entries.formula: V = I * R, I = V / R, R = V / I. Voltage divider: Vout = Vin * R2 / (R1 + R2). Power: P = V * I = I^2 * R.
entries.subject: Electrical Circuits

entries.example: If the R-R interval is 0.8 s, heart rate = 60 / 0.8 = 75 bpm, which is within the normal resting range of 60 to 100 bpm.
entries.fact: An ECG records the electrical activity of the heart: the P wave is atrial depolarisation, the QRS complex is ventricular depolarisation, and the T wave is ventricular repolarisation. The PR interval measures conduction from atria to ventricles through the AV node. Heart rate is found from the time between successive R peaks.
entries.formula: Heart rate (bpm) = 60 / R-R interval in seconds. Normal resting heart rate: 60 to 100 bpm. Normal PR interval: 120 to 200 ms (0.12 to 0.20 s). Normal QRS duration: less than 120 ms, typically 80 to 100 ms.
entries.subject: Biomedical Signals

entries.example: With epsilon = 10000 L/(mol cm), c = 2e-5 mol/L and l = 1 cm, A = 10000 * 0.00002 * 1 = 0.2. Transmittance T = 10^-0.2 = 0.63, so about 63 percent of the light is transmitted.
entries.fact: The Beer-Lambert law describes how light is absorbed as it passes through a solution or tissue. Absorbance grows linearly with both the concentration of the absorbing substance and the path length of light through it. It is the basis of pulse oximetry and many spectroscopic measurements of blood and tissue.
entries.formula: A = epsilon * c * l, where A is absorbance (dimensionless), epsilon is molar absorptivity in L/(mol cm), c is concentration in mol/L and l is path length in cm. Absorbance is also A = log10(I0 / I) = -log10(T), where I0 is incident intensity, I is transmitted intensity and T is transmittance.
entries.subject: Medical Imaging

entries.example: A soft tissue sample has Young's modulus E = 0.5 MPa and is strained by epsilon = 0.1 (10 percent). Stress sigma = 0.5 * 0.1 = 0.05 MPa, which is 50 kPa.
entries.fact: Stress is force per unit area and strain is the fractional change in length of a tissue under load. In the linear elastic region they are related by Young's modulus, but most soft tissues are viscoelastic and non-linear, so the modulus is quoted for a small strain range. This relation underlies biomechanical modelling of skin, tendon, blood vessels and other tissues.
entries.formula: Stress sigma = F / A, where F is force and A is cross-sectional area. Strain epsilon = Delta L / L. Hooke's law in the linear region: sigma = E * epsilon, where E is Young's modulus. Stiffness increases with E.
entries.subject: Biomechanics

entries.example: A neuron at -70 mV receives a stimulus that depolarises it by 15 mV to -55 mV. It reaches threshold, so an action potential fires and the membrane potential rises toward about +30 mV.
entries.fact: A resting neuron or muscle cell sits at about -70 mV inside relative to outside, maintained mainly by the sodium-potassium pump and potassium leak channels. If a stimulus depolarises the membrane to the threshold of about -55 mV, voltage-gated sodium channels open and the membrane rapidly depolarises toward about +30 mV. Repolarisation follows as potassium channels open, restoring the resting potential.
entries.formula: Resting membrane potential is about -70 mV. Threshold potential is about -55 mV. Peak of the action potential is about +30 mV. Depolarisation needed to reach threshold from rest: (-55) - (-70) = +15 mV.
entries.subject: Physiology

entries.example: At f = 5 MHz in soft tissue, lambda = 1540 / 5000000 = 0.000308 m, about 0.31 mm. This short wavelength is why 5 MHz ultrasound gives fine image detail.
entries.fact: Medical ultrasound sends high-frequency sound pulses into tissue and forms an image from their echoes. The speed of sound in soft tissue is about 1540 m/s, and higher frequency gives shorter wavelength and finer resolution but shallower penetration. Depth is found from the echo return time, halved because the pulse travels out and back.
entries.formula: Wave speed c = f * lambda, where f is frequency and lambda is wavelength. In soft tissue c is about 1540 m/s. Depth d = c * t / 2, where t is the echo return time. Wavelength lambda = c / f.
entries.subject: Medical Imaging
entries.topic: Ultrasound imaging: speed, wavelength and depth

entries.example: Titanium has E = 110 GPa. Under a strain epsilon = 0.001, the stress is sigma = 110e9 * 0.001 = 110e6 Pa = 110 MPa.
entries.fact: Young's modulus measures how stiff a biomaterial is: a high modulus means little strain for a given stress. Implant materials must be chosen so their stiffness is compatible with surrounding tissue, since a large stiffness mismatch can cause stress shielding and bone loss around an implant. Metals are far stiffer than bone, while polymers and hydrogels are much closer to soft tissue.
entries.formula: E = sigma / epsilon, where E is Young's modulus, sigma is stress and epsilon is strain. Stress sigma = E * epsilon. Typical values: titanium about 110 GPa, cortical bone about 18 GPa, soft tissue well below 1 MPa.
entries.subject: Biomaterials

entries.example: With HR = 70 bpm and SV = 70 mL per beat, CO = 70 * 70 = 4900 mL/min = 4.9 L/min, close to the normal resting value of about 5 L/min.
entries.fact: Cardiac output is the volume of blood the heart pumps per minute, and it is the product of heart rate and stroke volume. At rest it is about 5 L/min in a typical adult, and it rises several-fold during exercise as both heart rate and stroke volume increase. It is a central measure of cardiovascular function.
entries.formula: Cardiac output CO = HR * SV, where HR is heart rate in beats per minute and SV is stroke volume in mL per beat. CO is usually expressed in L/min.
entries.subject: Physiology

entries.example: For u = (3, 4) and v = (1, 2): u . v = 3*1 + 4*2 = 3 + 8 = 11. ||u|| = sqrt(9 + 16) = 5, ||v|| = sqrt(1 + 4) = sqrt(5) = 2.236. So cos(theta) = 11 / (5 * 2.236) = 11 / 11.18 = 0.984, so the angle between them is about 10.3 degrees.
entries.fact: A vector is an ordered list of numbers that represents a point or a direction in space. Vectors can be added component-wise and scaled by a scalar, and the dot product measures how much two vectors point in the same direction. The length (norm) of a vector generalises Pythagoras' theorem to n dimensions, and two non-zero vectors are orthogonal when their dot product is zero.
entries.formula: u . v = u1*v1 + u2*v2 + ... + un*vn; ||u|| = sqrt(u . u); cos(theta) = (u . v) / (||u|| * ||v||)
entries.subject: Linear Algebra

entries.fact: A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers, and matrix multiplication composes linear transformations: the (i, j) entry of AB is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B. Multiplication is associative and distributive but generally not commutative. The transpose flips rows and columns, and a square matrix A is invertible when there is a matrix A^-1 with A * A^-1 = I, which happens exactly when det(A) is non-zero.
entries.formula: (AB)[i][j] = sum over k of A[i][k] * B[k][j]; (AB)^T = B^T * A^T; A * A^-1 = A^-1 * A = I; for 2x2 [[a, b], [c, d]], inverse = (1 / (ad - bc)) * [[d, -b], [-c, a]]
entries.subject: Linear Algebra

entries.example: Vectors (1, 2) and (2, 4) are linearly dependent because (2, 4) = 2 * (1, 2), so 2*(1, 2) - 1*(2, 4) = (0, 0) with non-zero coefficients. In contrast, (1, 0) and (0, 1) are independent: c1*(1, 0) + c2*(0, 1) = (0, 0) forces c1 = 0 and c2 = 0.
entries.fact: A set of vectors is linearly independent when the only way to combine them to get the zero vector is to use all zero coefficients; otherwise the set is linearly dependent, meaning at least one vector is a combination of the others. The span of a set is all vectors obtainable as linear combinations of it. A basis is a linearly independent set that spans the whole space, and every basis of R^n has exactly n vectors.
entries.formula: c1*v1 + c2*v2 + ... + ck*vk = 0 implies c1 = c2 = ... = ck = 0 (independence); span(v1, ..., vk) = {a1*v1 + ... + ak*vk}
entries.subject: Linear Algebra

entries.example: A = [[1, 2], [2, 4]]. Row 2 is 2 times row 1, so rank(A) = 1. By rank-nullity, nullity = 2 - 1 = 1. Ax = 0 gives x + 2y = 0, so x = -2y and the null space is all multiples of (-2, 1). The column space is the span of (1, 2).
entries.fact: The rank of a matrix is the number of linearly independent rows or columns, equivalently the dimension of its column space. The null space is the set of all vectors x with Ax = 0, and its dimension is the nullity. The rank-nullity theorem links them: for an m x n matrix, rank + nullity = n. The column space is the span of the columns, and Ax = b has a solution exactly when b lies in the column space.
entries.formula: rank(A) + nullity(A) = n (number of columns); null space = {x : Ax = 0}; column space = span of the columns of A
entries.subject: Linear Algebra
entries.topic: Rank, null space and column space

entries.fact: The determinant is a single number assigned to a square matrix that measures how the matrix scales volumes: it is zero exactly when the matrix is singular (not invertible), and non-zero exactly when it is invertible. Swapping two rows flips the sign of the determinant, multiplying a row by a scalar multiplies the determinant by that scalar, and the determinant of a product is the product of the determinants. For a triangular matrix the determinant is the product of the diagonal entries.
entries.formula: det([[a, b], [c, d]]) = ad - bc; det(AB) = det(A) * det(B); det(A^T) = det(A); det of a triangular matrix = product of diagonal entries
entries.subject: Linear Algebra

entries.example: A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]]. det(A - lambda*I) = (2 - lambda)^2 - 1 = lambda^2 - 4*lambda + 3 = (lambda - 1)(lambda - 3), so eigenvalues are 1 and 3. For lambda = 3, (A - 3I)v = 0 gives -x + y = 0, so v = (1, 1) is an eigenvector. Check: A*(1, 1) = (3, 3) = 3*(1, 1). Trace 4 = 1 + 3 and det 3 = 1 * 3, as expected.
entries.fact: An eigenvector of a square matrix A is a non-zero vector v whose direction is unchanged by A; A only stretches it by a scalar factor lambda, the eigenvalue. Eigenvalues are found by solving the characteristic equation det(A - lambda*I) = 0. The trace of A equals the sum of its eigenvalues and the determinant equals their product, and eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent.
entries.formula: Av = lambda*v; det(A - lambda*I) = 0 (characteristic equation); trace(A) = sum of eigenvalues; det(A) = product of eigenvalues
entries.subject: Linear Algebra

entries.fact: A square n x n matrix A is diagonalizable when it can be written as A = P D P^-1, where D is diagonal and P is invertible. This is possible exactly when A has n linearly independent eigenvectors; the columns of P are those eigenvectors and the diagonal entries of D are the matching eigenvalues. Diagonalization makes matrix powers easy, since A^k = P D^k P^-1, and D^k just raises each diagonal entry to the power k. A matrix with n distinct eigenvalues is always diagonalizable, as are all real symmetric matrices.
entries.formula: A = P D P^-1, where columns of P are eigenvectors and D = diag(lambda1, ..., lambdan); A^k = P D^k P^-1
entries.subject: Linear Algebra

entries.example: A = [[3, 2], [2, 3]]. A^T A = [[13, 12], [12, 13]]. Its characteristic equation is lambda^2 - 26*lambda + 25 = (lambda - 25)(lambda - 1) = 0, so eigenvalues are 25 and 1. The singular values are sqrt(25) = 5 and sqrt(1) = 1. Both are non-zero, so rank(A) = 2, and the Frobenius norm is sqrt(25 + 1) = sqrt(26).
entries.fact: Every real matrix A, square or rectangular, can be factored as A = U Sigma V^T, where U and V are orthogonal matrices and Sigma is a diagonal matrix of non-negative singular values in decreasing order. The singular values are the square roots of the eigenvalues of A^T A, the columns of V are eigenvectors of A^T A, and the columns of U are eigenvectors of A A^T. The number of non-zero singular values equals the rank of A, and keeping only the largest k singular values gives the best rank-k approximation of A, which is the basis of PCA and data compression.
entries.formula: A = U Sigma V^T; sigma_i = sqrt(lambda_i(A^T A)), where lambda_i are eigenvalues of A^T A; rank(A) = number of non-zero singular values
entries.subject: Linear Algebra

entries.fact: Two vectors are orthogonal when their dot product is zero, and an orthonormal set is an orthogonal set in which every vector has unit length. The Gram-Schmidt process turns any linearly independent set into an orthogonal (or, after normalising, orthonormal) basis for the same span, by keeping the first vector and subtracting from each later vector its projections onto all previously built orthogonal vectors. Orthonormal bases make projections and least-squares problems simple, because coordinates are just dot products.
entries.formula: proj_u(v) = ((v . u) / (u . u)) * u; u1 = v1; u_i = v_i - sum over j < i of proj_{u_j}(v_i); e_i = u_i / ||u_i||
entries.subject: Linear Algebra

entries.example: Q(x, y) = 3x^2 + 4xy + 5y^2 has A = [[3, 2], [2, 5]], since 2*b = 4 gives b = 2. At (1, 1), Q = 3 + 4 + 5 = 12. Leading minors: 3 > 0 and det(A) = 3*5 - 2*2 = 11 > 0, so A is positive definite. Its eigenvalues are 4 + sqrt(5) = 6.236 and 4 - sqrt(5) = 1.764, both positive, confirming it.
entries.fact: A quadratic form is a homogeneous degree-two polynomial that can always be written as Q(x) = x^T A x, where A is a symmetric matrix; the off-diagonal entries of A are half the coefficients of the cross terms. A symmetric matrix (and its form) is positive definite when Q(x) > 0 for every non-zero x, which happens exactly when all its eigenvalues are positive, and equivalently when all leading principal minors are positive. Positive definite forms have a unique minimum at the origin, which is why they appear in optimisation and in covariance matrices.
entries.formula: Q(x) = x^T A x; for 2 variables, Q(x, y) = a*x^2 + 2*b*x*y + c*y^2 with A = [[a, b], [b, c]]; positive definite iff all eigenvalues > 0 iff all leading principal minors > 0
entries.subject: Linear Algebra

entries.example: Searching a sorted array of n = 1,000,000 elements by binary search takes about log2(1,000,000) = 19.93, about 20 comparisons, while linear search takes up to 1,000,000 comparisons in the worst case. Summing 1 to n with a single loop does n additions, so it is O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
entries.fact: Big-O notation describes how an algorithm's running time or memory use grows as the input size n grows, ignoring constant factors and lower-order terms. Common growth rates, from fastest to slowest, are O(1) constant, O(log n) logarithmic, O(n) linear, O(n log n), O(n^2) quadratic, and O(2^n) exponential. Time complexity counts the dominant operations and space complexity counts the extra memory used; the worst case is the usual measure quoted, and Big-O gives an upper bound on that growth.
entries.formula: T(n) = O(f(n)) means T(n) <= c * f(n) for all large n and some constant c; binary search: O(log n); linear search: O(n); sorting by comparison: Omega(n log n) lower bound
entries.subject: Programming/DSA
entries.topic: Time and space complexity and Big-O notation

entries.example: Binary search for 23 in [2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 56, 72, 91]: mid index (0 + 9) / 2 = 4 gives 16 < 23, so search right; mid (5 + 9) / 2 = 7 gives 56 > 23, so search left; mid (5 + 6) / 2 = 5 gives 23, found in 3 comparisons. Accessing index 2 of [10, 20, 30, 40] returns 30 in O(1).
entries.fact: An array stores a fixed-size sequence of elements of the same type in contiguous memory, so the element at index i is found by direct address arithmetic in O(1) time. Searching an unsorted array takes O(n) time, while binary search on a sorted array takes O(log n). Inserting or deleting in the middle costs O(n) because the elements after the position must be shifted, which is the main weakness of arrays compared with linked lists.
entries.formula: address of a[i] = base address + i * element size; binary search: mid = (low + high) / 2, compare a[mid] with target, halve the interval each step; time O(log n)
entries.subject: Programming/DSA

entries.example: List 10 -> 20 -> 30. To insert 15 after 10: create node 15, set its next pointer to 20, then set 10's next pointer to 15, giving 10 -> 15 -> 20 -> 30. No elements are shifted; only two pointers change. Reaching the 3rd element still needs 3 steps from the head.
entries.fact: A linked list is a chain of nodes, each holding data and a pointer to the next node (and, in a doubly linked list, to the previous node as well). Unlike arrays, nodes need not be contiguous, so inserting or deleting at a known position costs O(1) by rewiring pointers. The trade-off is that reaching the i-th element requires walking from the head, so access and search cost O(n), and each node carries extra pointer memory.
entries.formula: Access/search: O(n); insert/delete at head or at a known node: O(1); insert/delete at position i: O(n) to reach it, then O(1) to rewire; node = {data, next}
entries.subject: Programming/DSA

entries.example: Push 1, 2, 3 onto a stack, then pop three times: the pops return 3, then 2, then 1 (LIFO). Enqueue 1, 2, 3 into a queue, then dequeue three times: the dequeues return 1, then 2, then 3 (FIFO). Checking '(()())' with a stack: each '(' is pushed and each ')' pops one, ending with an empty stack, so the parentheses are balanced.
entries.fact: A stack is a last-in, first-out (LIFO) structure with push to add to the top and pop to remove from the top, both O(1); it is used for function calls, undo, expression evaluation and checking balanced parentheses. A queue is a first-in, first-out (FIFO) structure with enqueue at the rear and dequeue from the front, both O(1) in a linked or circular-array implementation; it is used for breadth-first search, scheduling and buffering. A deque allows insertion and deletion at both ends.
entries.formula: Stack: push(x), pop() returns the most recently pushed item, peek() returns the top; Queue: enqueue(x) at rear, dequeue() returns the oldest item; all four operations O(1)
entries.subject: Programming/DSA

entries.example: Insert 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80 into an empty BST. The inorder traversal is 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, in sorted order. Searching for 60: compare with 50 (go right), then 70 (go left), then find 60, taking 3 comparisons.
entries.fact: A tree is a hierarchical structure of nodes connected by edges, with one root and no cycles; a binary tree gives each node at most two children. In a binary search tree (BST), every node's left subtree holds smaller keys and its right subtree holds larger keys, so search, insert and delete take O(log n) on average in a balanced tree but degrade to O(n) if the tree becomes skewed like a linked list. An inorder traversal of a BST visits keys in sorted order, and the height of a balanced tree with n nodes is about log2(n).
entries.formula: BST property: keys in left subtree < node key < keys in right subtree; search/insert/delete: O(log n) average, O(n) worst case; inorder traversal visits keys in ascending order; height of balanced tree = O(log n)
entries.subject: Programming/DSA

entries.example: Min-heap array [10, 15, 20, 30, 40] is valid: 10 is the parent of 15 and 20, and 15 is the parent of 30 and 40. Insert 5: append it to get [10, 15, 20, 30, 40, 5], swap 5 with its parent 20, then swap 5 with 10, giving [5, 15, 10, 30, 40, 20] with 5 at the root.
entries.fact: A heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array that satisfies the heap property: in a min-heap every parent is smaller than or equal to its children, so the minimum is always at the root, while a max-heap keeps the maximum at the root. Insert and extract-min (or extract-max) both take O(log n) by bubbling an element up or sifting it down, and building a heap from n elements takes O(n). A heap implements a priority queue, and heapsort sorts in O(n log n) time with O(1) extra space.
entries.formula: 0-indexed array: parent(i) = (i - 1) / 2, left child(i) = 2i + 1, right child(i) = 2i + 2; insert: O(log n); extract-min/max: O(log n); build heap: O(n); heapsort: O(n log n)
entries.subject: Programming/DSA

entries.example: With table size m = 7 and h(k) = k mod 7, keys 10, 17 and 24 all hash to 3, since 10 mod 7 = 3, 17 mod 7 = 3 and 24 mod 7 = 3, so they collide and share bucket 3 as a chain [10, 17, 24]. With n = 3 items in m = 7 buckets, the load factor is 3 / 7 = 0.43.
entries.fact: A hash table stores key-value pairs by passing each key through a hash function that maps it to a bucket index, giving average O(1) time for insert, search and delete. Different keys can collide in the same bucket; collisions are handled by chaining (a list per bucket) or open addressing (probing for another slot). Performance depends on the load factor, the number of items divided by the number of buckets: a high load factor means more collisions, so tables resize and rehash when it grows too large. In the worst case, with all keys colliding, operations degrade to O(n).
entries.formula: index = hash(key) mod m, where m is the table size; load factor alpha = n / m; average insert/search/delete: O(1); worst case: O(n)
entries.subject: Programming/DSA

entries.example: Mergesort on [38, 27, 43, 3, 9, 82, 10] splits it down to single elements and merges sorted halves back up. One merge step combines the sorted halves [27, 38] and [3, 43] by comparing heads: 3 < 27, then 27 < 43, then 38 < 43, giving [3, 27, 38, 43]. The final sorted array is [3, 9, 10, 27, 38, 43, 82].
entries.fact: Sorting arranges elements in order, and the classic comparison sorts differ in cost and stability. Bubble, selection and insertion sort all take O(n^2) time in the worst case, though insertion sort is O(n) on nearly sorted input. Mergesort always takes O(n log n) time but needs O(n) extra space, while quicksort averages O(n log n) with O(log n) stack space but degrades to O(n^2) on already sorted input with a bad pivot. A stable sort preserves the relative order of equal elements; mergesort is stable and standard quicksort is not.
entries.formula: Bubble/selection/insertion sort: O(n^2) worst case; mergesort: T(n) = 2*T(n/2) + O(n), O(n log n) time, O(n) space; quicksort: O(n log n) average, O(n^2) worst case
entries.subject: Programming/DSA

entries.example: Graph with edges 1-2, 1-3, 2-4, 3-4. BFS from 1: visit 1, then its neighbours 2 and 3, then 4, giving order 1, 2, 3, 4; vertex 4 is at distance 2. DFS from 1 (neighbours in order 2 then 3): go 1 -> 2 -> 4, backtrack, then 3, giving order 1, 2, 4, 3.
entries.fact: A graph is a set of vertices connected by edges, stored as an adjacency list or an adjacency matrix. Breadth-first search (BFS) explores level by level using a queue, visiting vertices in order of increasing distance from the start, so it finds shortest paths in an unweighted graph. Depth-first search (DFS) goes as deep as possible first, using a stack or recursion, and is used for cycle detection, topological sorting and connected components. Both visit every vertex and edge once, taking O(V + E) time with an adjacency list.
entries.formula: BFS and DFS: O(V + E) time with an adjacency list, O(V^2) with an adjacency matrix; BFS distance from start = number of edges on the shortest path (unweighted graph)
entries.subject: Programming/DSA

entries.example: Fibonacci with a table: fib(0) = 0, fib(1) = 1, fib(2) = 1 + 0 = 1, fib(3) = 1 + 1 = 2, fib(4) = 2 + 1 = 3, fib(5) = 3 + 2 = 5. Each value is computed once from the previous two, so fib(5) = 5 in 5 steps, instead of the naive recursion which recomputes fib(3) twice, fib(2) three times, and so on.
entries.fact: Dynamic programming solves a problem by breaking it into overlapping subproblems, solving each subproblem once, and storing its result for reuse, either top-down with memoisation or bottom-up with a table. It applies when the problem has optimal substructure, meaning an optimal solution is built from optimal solutions of smaller subproblems, and overlapping subproblems, meaning the same subproblems recur. Classic examples are Fibonacci numbers, 0/1 knapsack, longest common subsequence and shortest paths in DAGs. Memoisation turns the naive exponential Fibonacci recursion into linear time.
entries.formula: Fibonacci: fib(0) = 0, fib(1) = 1, fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2); with memoisation/tabulation: O(n) time, O(n) space (O(1) space with two variables); naive recursion: O(2^n) time
entries.subject: Programming/DSA

entries.example: A soil column has K = 1 x 10^-5 m/s, area A = 2 m2 and hydraulic gradient 0.05. Q = 1 x 10^-5 x 2 x 0.05 = 1 x 10^-6 m3/s, which is 0.086 m3/day.
entries.fact: Darcy's law describes laminar flow of water through a saturated porous medium such as soil. Discharge is proportional to the hydraulic conductivity, the cross-sectional area, and the hydraulic gradient. It is the foundation of groundwater flow, drainage design, and seepage calculations in agricultural engineering.
entries.formula: Q = K * A * (dh/dl);  v = K * i, where Q is discharge, K is hydraulic conductivity, A is cross-sectional area, dh/dl is the hydraulic gradient, v is Darcy velocity, and i is the gradient.
entries.subject: Soil & Water

entries.example: 100 mm of water is applied and 65 mm is stored in the root zone. Ea = (65/100) x 100 = 65%.
entries.fact: Irrigation efficiency measures how much of the water applied to a field is actually stored in the root zone and used by the crop. Application efficiency is the ratio of water stored in the root zone to water applied. Low efficiency means losses to runoff, deep percolation, and evaporation.
entries.formula: Application efficiency Ea = (water stored in root zone / water applied) x 100%. Overall project efficiency = conveyance efficiency x application efficiency.
entries.subject: Soil & Water

entries.example: Field capacity is 30%, wilting point is 15%, and root depth is 0.6 m (600 mm). Available water = (0.30 - 0.15) x 600 = 90 mm.
entries.fact: Available water is the water held in soil between field capacity and permanent wilting point that plants can extract. Field capacity is the water remaining after free drainage, and wilting point is the moisture at which plants can no longer extract water and wilt permanently. It depends on soil texture: clay holds more than sand.
entries.formula: Available water depth = (field capacity - wilting point) x root-zone depth, with moisture contents as fractions by volume.
entries.subject: Soil & Water

entries.fact: Manning's equation is the standard empirical formula for velocity in open channels such as irrigation canals, under steady uniform flow. Velocity increases with hydraulic radius and channel slope and decreases with roughness. The roughness coefficient n is taken from standard tables for the channel material.
entries.formula: V = (1/n) x R^(2/3) x S^(1/2);  Q = A x V;  R = A/P, where V is mean velocity, n is Manning's roughness, R is hydraulic radius, S is slope, A is flow area and P is wetted perimeter (SI units).
entries.subject: Soil & Water

entries.example: Bulk density is 1.32 g/cm3 and particle density is 2.65 g/cm3. Porosity = 1 - (1.32/2.65) = 1 - 0.498 = 0.50, or about 50%.
entries.fact: Bulk density is the mass of dry soil per unit total volume, including pore space, while particle density is the mass per unit volume of the solid particles only (about 2.65 g/cm3 for most mineral soils). Porosity is the fraction of soil volume occupied by pores, which hold air and water. Compaction raises bulk density and lowers porosity.
entries.formula: Porosity n = 1 - (bulk density / particle density). Bulk density = mass of dry soil / total volume.
entries.subject: Soil & Water

entries.example: If Kc = 1.1 and ETo = 5 mm/day, ETc = 1.1 x 5 = 5.5 mm/day. Over 10 days the crop needs 55 mm of water.
entries.fact: Crop water requirement is the depth of water needed to meet the evapotranspiration of a crop, and it is estimated from reference evapotranspiration and a crop coefficient that varies with growth stage. Reference evapotranspiration ETo is the demand of a well-watered reference grass surface. Irrigation requirement is crop water requirement minus effective rainfall.
entries.formula: ETc = Kc x ETo, where ETc is crop evapotranspiration, Kc is the crop coefficient and ETo is reference evapotranspiration. Irrigation requirement = ETc - effective rainfall.
entries.subject: Soil & Water

entries.example: If Vmax = 100 micromol/min, Km = 2 mM and [S] = 2 mM, v = (100 x 2)/(2 + 2) = 50 micromol/min, exactly half of Vmax.
entries.fact: Michaelis-Menten kinetics describes the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction as a function of substrate concentration. At low substrate the rate rises almost linearly, and at high substrate it approaches a maximum rate Vmax when the enzyme is saturated. Km is the substrate concentration at half Vmax and measures affinity: a low Km means high affinity.
entries.formula: v = (Vmax x [S]) / (Km + [S]), where v is reaction rate, Vmax is maximum rate, [S] is substrate concentration and Km is the Michaelis constant.
entries.subject: Biochemistry

entries.example: If mu_max = 0.8 per hour, Ks = 0.5 g/L and S = 1.5 g/L, mu = (0.8 x 1.5)/(0.5 + 1.5) = 0.6 per hour. Doubling time = ln 2 / 0.6 = 1.16 hours.
entries.fact: Monod kinetics is the microbial-growth analogue of Michaelis-Menten kinetics: the specific growth rate of a culture depends on the concentration of the limiting substrate. Growth is slow when substrate is scarce and approaches a maximum rate mu_max when substrate is plentiful. Ks is the substrate concentration at half the maximum growth rate.
entries.formula: mu = (mu_max x S) / (Ks + S), where mu is specific growth rate, mu_max is maximum specific growth rate, S is limiting substrate concentration and Ks is the half-saturation constant.
entries.subject: Bioprocess Engineering

entries.example: Starting with 10 copies and running 30 cycles, N = 10 x 2^30 = about 1.07 x 10^10 copies.
entries.fact: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplifies a specific DNA segment through repeated cycles of denaturation, annealing of primers, and extension by a heat-stable DNA polymerase such as Taq. In ideal conditions the number of copies doubles each cycle, so amplification is exponential. After n cycles, one starting molecule yields about 2^n copies.
entries.formula: N = N0 x 2^n, where N is the final copy number, N0 is the initial copy number and n is the number of cycles.
entries.subject: Molecular Biology

entries.example: A coding sequence of 900 nucleotides contains 900/3 = 300 codons, so it encodes a protein of about 300 amino acids (before the stop codon).
entries.fact: The central dogma states that genetic information flows from DNA to RNA to protein: DNA is transcribed into messenger RNA, which is translated into protein on ribosomes. DNA replication copies the genome before cell division. In retroviruses, reverse transcriptase can copy RNA back into DNA, an exception to the usual flow.
entries.formula: DNA --transcription--> RNA --translation--> Protein. One codon (3 bases) codes for one amino acid.
entries.subject: Molecular Biology

entries.example: With X0 = 1 g/L, mu = 0.5 per hour and t = 4 hours, X = 1 x e^2 = 7.39 g/L. The doubling time is ln 2 / 0.5 = 1.39 hours.
entries.fact: In the exponential (log) phase, a microbial population grows at a constant specific growth rate, with cell number or biomass increasing exponentially with time. The doubling time is the time for the population to double and is inversely related to the specific growth rate. This phase ends when a nutrient is exhausted or waste accumulates.
entries.formula: X = X0 x e^(mu x t);  doubling time td = ln 2 / mu, where X is biomass, X0 is initial biomass, mu is specific growth rate and t is time.
entries.subject: Bioprocess Engineering

entries.example: If 20 g of glucose is consumed and 10 g of dry cells are produced, Yx/s = 10/20 = 0.5 g cells per g glucose.
entries.fact: A yield coefficient relates the amount of biomass or product formed to the amount of substrate consumed in a fermentation. The biomass yield Yx/s is the mass of cells produced per mass of substrate used. It is used in mass balances to size media, estimate substrate demand, and compare strains and processes.
entries.formula: Yx/s = (change in biomass) / (change in substrate consumed);  Yp/s = (change in product) / (change in substrate consumed).
entries.subject: Bioprocess Engineering

entries.example: For Ea = 50 kJ/mol, warming from 300 K to 310 K gives ln(k2/k1) = -(50000/8.314) x (1/310 - 1/300) = 0.65, so k2/k1 = e^0.65 = about 1.9. The rate nearly doubles.
entries.fact: The Arrhenius equation relates the rate constant of a reaction to temperature and activation energy. A higher temperature increases the fraction of molecules with enough energy to overcome the activation barrier, so the rate rises exponentially. The activation energy Ea is the minimum energy reacting molecules must have.
entries.formula: k = A x e^(-Ea / (R x T));  ln(k2/k1) = -(Ea/R) x (1/T2 - 1/T1), where k is the rate constant, A is the pre-exponential factor, Ea is activation energy, R is the gas constant and T is absolute temperature.
entries.subject: Physical Chemistry

entries.example: If epsilon = 10,000 L/(mol cm), c = 2 x 10^-5 mol/L and l = 1 cm, A = 10,000 x 2 x 10^-5 x 1 = 0.20.
entries.fact: The Beer-Lambert law relates the absorbance of a solution to the concentration of the absorbing species and the path length of light through it. Absorbance is proportional to concentration, which is why UV-visible spectroscopy is used for quantitative analysis. The law holds for dilute solutions with monochromatic light.
entries.formula: A = epsilon x c x l, where A is absorbance, epsilon is molar absorptivity, c is concentration and l is path length. Transmittance T = 10^(-A).
entries.subject: Spectroscopy

entries.fact: The Nernst equation gives the electrode or cell potential under non-standard conditions, correcting the standard potential for the concentrations of reactants and products. As the reaction proceeds and the reaction quotient changes, the cell potential falls, reaching zero at equilibrium. At 25 C the factor 2.303 RT/F is 0.0592 V.
entries.formula: E = E0 - (RT/(nF)) x ln Q;  at 25 C, E = E0 - (0.0592/n) x log10 Q, where E0 is standard potential, n is electrons transferred, F is Faraday's constant and Q is the reaction quotient.
entries.subject: Physical Chemistry

entries.example: If Delta H = -100 kJ/mol, Delta S = -0.20 kJ/(mol K) and T = 298 K, Delta G = -100 - 298 x (-0.20) = -100 + 59.6 = -40.4 kJ/mol, so the process is spontaneous.
entries.fact: Gibbs free energy determines whether a process is spontaneous at constant temperature and pressure: a negative change in Gibbs energy means the process is spontaneous, zero means equilibrium, and positive means non-spontaneous. Enthalpy favours exothermic processes, while entropy favours disorder; temperature decides which dominates.
entries.formula: Delta G = Delta H - T x Delta S;  Delta G0 = -R x T x ln K, where Delta G is Gibbs energy change, Delta H is enthalpy change, Delta S is entropy change, T is absolute temperature and K is the equilibrium constant.
entries.subject: Physical Chemistry

entries.example: For acetic acid, pKa = 4.76. If [acetate]/[acetic acid] = 10, pH = 4.76 + log10(10) = 4.76 + 1 = 5.76.
entries.fact: The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation gives the pH of a buffer made of a weak acid and its conjugate base. When the acid and base concentrations are equal, pH equals pKa. A buffer resists pH change because added acid or base is consumed by the conjugate pair, and it works best within about one pH unit of pKa.
entries.formula: pH = pKa + log10([A-] / [HA]), where pKa is the acid dissociation constant, [A-] is conjugate base concentration and [HA] is weak acid concentration.
entries.subject: Physical Chemistry

entries.example: For 1 mol at 273 K and 1 atm, V = nRT/P = (1 x 0.0821 x 273)/1 = 22.4 L.
entries.fact: The ideal gas law combines Boyle's, Charles's and Avogadro's laws into one relation between pressure, volume, temperature and amount of gas. It assumes gas molecules have negligible volume and no intermolecular forces, which is a good approximation for most gases at ordinary temperature and pressure. One mole of an ideal gas occupies about 22.4 L at 0 C and 1 atm.
entries.formula: P x V = n x R x T, where P is pressure, V is volume, n is moles, R is the gas constant (0.0821 L atm/(mol K) or 8.314 J/(mol K)) and T is absolute temperature.
entries.subject: Physical Chemistry

entries.example: With lambda = 0.154 nm, d = 0.20 nm and n = 1, sin(theta) = 0.154/(2 x 0.20) = 0.385, so theta = about 22.6 degrees.
entries.fact: Bragg's law explains diffraction of X-rays by crystal planes: rays reflected from successive planes interfere constructively only when their path difference is a whole number of wavelengths.
