entries.example: A 4-bit ripple counter uses 4 T flip-flops in series and counts 0 to 15 before wrapping. A D flip-flop with D = ~Q toggles every clock, acting as a divide-by-2 counter.
entries.subject: Digital Logic

entries.fact: Integers are stored in binary, usually two's complement, where negating means inverting bits and adding 1; this makes subtraction an addition. Fixed-point numbers place the binary point at a fixed position, while floating point stores a sign, exponent and mantissa. IEEE 754 single precision uses 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits (bias 127) and 23 mantissa bits with an implicit leading 1.
entries.formula: IEEE 754 single: value = (-1)^sign * (1.mantissa) * 2^(exponent - 127); two's complement of x = ~x + 1; range of n-bit signed two's complement: -2^(n-1) to 2^(n-1) - 1
entries.example: 0x3F800000 is IEEE 754 single precision for 1.0: sign 0, exponent 01111111 = 127 (so 2^0), mantissa all zero, giving 1.0 * 2^0 = 1. Adding 1.0 + 2^-25 in single precision rounds back to 1.0.
entries.subject: Digital Logic

entries.topic: Machine instructions, addressing modes, ALU, datapath and control unit
entries.fact: An instruction encodes an opcode and operands; addressing modes specify where operands live: immediate (value in the instruction), direct, register, register-indirect, indexed and relative. The datapath (registers, ALU, buses) executes operations while the control unit generates the signals that steer it. A hardwired control unit is fast but inflexible, while microprogrammed control stores control signals as microinstructions.
entries.formula: Effective address (indexed) = base register + offset; number of addressable locations with n address bits = 2^n; CPI = total clock cycles / instruction count
entries.example: In 'ADD R1, [R2+8]', the operand address is the contents of R2 plus offset 8 (indexed addressing). A load instruction typically takes more cycles than an ALU instruction because it must access memory.
entries.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture

entries.fact: Pipelining overlaps the fetch, decode, execute, memory and write-back stages of successive instructions so throughput approaches one instruction per cycle. Hazards stall or corrupt this flow: structural hazards (resource conflicts), data hazards (an instruction needs a result not yet produced) and control hazards (branches change the flow). Data hazards are reduced by forwarding and by compiler reordering; control hazards by branch prediction or delayed branches.
entries.formula: Speedup = (time without pipeline) / (time with pipeline); ideal CPI with a k-stage pipeline approaches 1; average CPI = 1 + stall cycles per instruction
entries.example: In 'ADD R1,R2,R3' followed by 'SUB R4,R1,R5', the SUB reads R1 before the ADD writes it (RAW hazard). Forwarding the ALU result directly to the SUB avoids a stall.
entries.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture

entries.topic: Memory hierarchy: cache, main memory and secondary storage
entries.fact: Memory is organized as a hierarchy: small fast registers and cache at the top, then main memory, then large slow secondary storage. Caches exploit temporal locality (recently used data is reused) and spatial locality (nearby data is used next). A cache is characterized by block size, mapping (direct-mapped, set-associative, fully associative), replacement policy and write policy (write-through vs write-back).
entries.formula: AMAT = hit time + miss rate * miss penalty; miss rate = misses / accesses; number of cache blocks = cache size / block size
entries.example: A 32 KB direct-mapped cache with 64-byte blocks has 512 blocks. For a 32-bit address, the offset is 6 bits, the index 9 bits and the tag 17 bits. Sequential array access has a low miss rate because of spatial locality.
entries.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture

entries.topic: I/O interface: interrupt and DMA mode
entries.fact: Programmed I/O makes the CPU poll device status, wasting cycles. Interrupt-driven I/O lets the device signal the CPU when it is ready, and the CPU suspends the current task to run an interrupt service routine. Direct memory access (DMA) goes further: a DMA controller moves blocks of data between device and memory without the CPU, which is only interrupted when the transfer completes.
entries.formula: CPU time with DMA is roughly one interrupt per block instead of one per word; interrupt overhead is dominated by context save/restore time
entries.example: Reading a 1 MB disk block by programmed I/O would need about 262,144 CPU-mediated word transfers; with DMA the CPU is interrupted once, when the whole block is in memory.
entries.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture

entries.fact: C is a procedural language with manual memory control: stack allocation for locals, heap via malloc/free, and pointers that expose raw addresses. Recursion solves a problem by calling the same function on smaller inputs; every recursive function needs a base case and progress toward it, or it recurses forever. Each call gets its own stack frame holding parameters and locals, so deep recursion can overflow the stack.
entries.formula: Recursive structure: f(n) = base case for n = 0, else combine(f(n-1)); stack depth of naive Fibonacci recursion is O(n), number of calls O(2^n)
entries.example: factorial(5) = 5 * factorial(4) = ... = 120, with base case factorial(0) = 1. Binary search implemented recursively halves the array each call, giving O(log n) depth.
entries.subject: Data Structures

entries.topic: Arrays, stacks, queues and linked lists
entries.fact: An array gives O(1) access by index but fixed size and O(n) insertion in the middle. A stack is LIFO (push/pop at one end) and a queue is FIFO (enqueue at the rear, dequeue at the front); both are O(1) per operation. A linked list stores nodes with data and a next pointer, so insertion and deletion are O(1) once the position is found, at the cost of O(n) search and extra pointer memory.
entries.formula: Array element address = base + index * element size; stack operations are O(1); linked list insertion/deletion at a known node is O(1)
entries.example: Function call/return uses a stack; breadth-first search uses a queue. Reversing a linked list in place takes O(n) time and O(1) extra space by flipping each next pointer.
entries.subject: Data Structures

entries.fact: A binary heap is a complete binary tree satisfying the heap property: in a min-heap every parent is smaller than its children, so the minimum sits at the root. Insertion adds at the end and bubbles up; extraction removes the root, moves the last element up and sifts it down. Both operations cost O(log n), and building a heap from n elements costs O(n). A priority queue is the abstract type a heap implements.
entries.formula: For a node at index i (0-based): parent = (i-1)/2, children = 2i+1 and 2i+2; insert and extract-min are O(log n); heapify is O(n)
entries.example: Inserting 3, 1, 4 into a min-heap leaves 1 at the root. Heap sort repeatedly extracts the minimum to sort n elements in O(n log n) time with O(1) extra space.
entries.subject: Data Structures

entries.fact: A tree is a hierarchical structure with a root and parent-child links; a binary tree has at most two children per node. The standard traversals are inorder (left, root, right), preorder (root, left, right) and postorder (left, right, root), plus level order (breadth-first). Inorder traversal of a binary search tree visits keys in sorted order. A full binary tree of height h has at most 2^h - 1 nodes.
entries.formula: Maximum nodes at level l = 2^l; height of a balanced binary tree with n nodes is O(log n); inorder of a BST yields sorted order
entries.example: For a tree with root 4, left child 2 (children 1, 3) and right child 6 (children 5, 7), inorder gives 1 2 3 4 5 6 7, preorder gives 4 2 1 3 6 5 7.
entries.subject: Data Structures

entries.fact: Linear search scans all n elements (O(n)); binary search halves a sorted array each step (O(log n)). Comparison-based sorting has an Omega(n log n) lower bound; merge sort and heap sort achieve O(n log n) worst case, quicksort averages O(n log n) but degrades to O(n^2) on bad pivots, and counting sort beats the bound for small integer keys in O(n + k). Sorting is stable if equal keys keep their relative order.
entries.formula: Binary search: O(log n); merge sort: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) = O(n log n); quicksort average O(n log n), worst O(n^2); comparison sort lower bound Omega(n log n)
entries.example: Sorting [5,2,9,1] by merge sort splits to [5,2] and [9,1], sorts to [2,5] and [1,9], then merges to [1,2,5,9]. Binary search finds 9 in [1,2,5,9] in 3 probes at most.
entries.subject: Algorithms

entries.fact: A hash function maps keys to table slots so average lookup, insertion and deletion cost O(1). Collisions are resolved by chaining (linked lists per slot) or open addressing (linear probing, quadratic probing, double hashing). The load factor alpha = n/m governs performance; chaining keeps average search at O(1 + alpha), and rehashing into a bigger table keeps alpha bounded. A good hash function spreads keys uniformly and is cheap to compute.
entries.formula: Load factor alpha = n / m; expected successful search with chaining = 1 + alpha/2; with linear probing about (1/2)(1 + 1/(1-alpha))
entries.example: With h(k) = k mod 7, keys 10, 17, 24 all hash to slot 3 and chain there. Doubling the table when alpha exceeds about 0.7 keeps operations near O(1).
entries.subject: Algorithms

entries.fact: A greedy algorithm makes the locally best choice at each step and never revisits it, which is correct only when the problem has the greedy-choice property and optimal substructure. Classic successes include activity selection, Huffman coding, and Prim's and Kruskal's minimum spanning tree algorithms. Greedy fails where a locally good choice blocks the global optimum, as in the general 0/1 knapsack.
entries.formula: Huffman coding gives optimal prefix codes; activity selection by earliest finish time is optimal; fractional knapsack by value/weight ratio is optimal
entries.example: For activities (1,4), (3,5), (0,6), (5,7), picking by earliest finish gives (1,4) then (5,7): 2 activities, optimal. For coins 1, 3, 4 and amount 6, greedy gives 4+1+1 (3 coins) but 3+3 (2 coins) is better, so greedy fails.
entries.subject: Algorithms

entries.fact: Dynamic programming solves problems with overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure by storing subproblem results (memoization or tabulation) instead of recomputing them. The method is: define the subproblem, write its recurrence, compute bottom-up or with memoization, and reconstruct the solution if needed. Classic examples are Fibonacci, longest common subsequence, 0/1 knapsack, matrix chain multiplication and edit distance.
entries.formula: LCS: L(i,j) = L(i-1,j-1)+1 if x_i = y_j, else max(L(i-1,j), L(i,j-1)); 0/1 knapsack: K(i,w) = max(K(i-1,w), K(i-1,w-w_i)+v_i)
entries.example: LCS of 'ABCBDAB' and 'BDCABA' has length 4 ('BCBA'). Edit distance between 'kitten' and 'sitting' is 3 (substitute k->s, e->i, insert g).
entries.subject: Algorithms

entries.topic: Divide and conquer and the Master theorem
entries.fact: Divide and conquer splits a problem into smaller subproblems, solves them recursively and combines the results; merge sort, quicksort and binary search follow this pattern. The Master theorem solves recurrences of the form T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n) by comparing f(n) with n^(log_b a): if f(n) is polynomially smaller, the leaves dominate; if it matches, an extra log factor appears; if it is polynomially larger and regular, the root dominates.
entries.formula: T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n). Case 1: f(n) = O(n^(log_b a - e)) => T(n) = Theta(n^(log_b a)). Case 2: f(n) = Theta(n^(log_b a) log^k n) => T(n) = Theta(n^(log_b a) log^(k+1) n). Case 3: f(n) = Omega(n^(log_b a + e)) with regularity => T(n) = Theta(f(n))
entries.example: Merge sort: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n is Case 2 with log_2 2 = 1, giving Theta(n log n). Binary search: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1 is Case 2 with log_2 1 = 0, giving Theta(log n).
entries.subject: Algorithms

entries.fact: Breadth-first search (BFS) explores level by level using a queue and finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs; depth-first search (DFS) goes deep first using a stack or recursion. Both run in O(V + E) on adjacency lists. DFS classifies edges as tree, back, forward or cross edges, and a back edge reveals a cycle in a directed graph. BFS on a tree visits nodes level by level.
entries.formula: BFS and DFS time: O(V + E) with adjacency lists, O(V^2) with adjacency matrix; BFS distance from source s to v is the fewest edges
entries.example: In a graph s-a, s-b, a-c, DFS from s may visit s, a, c, b, while BFS visits s, a, b, c. DFS finishing times give a topological order of a DAG when reversed.
entries.subject: Algorithms

entries.topic: Minimum spanning trees and shortest paths
entries.fact: A minimum spanning tree (MST) connects all vertices with minimum total edge weight; Kruskal's algorithm adds the cheapest edge that avoids a cycle (using union-find), and Prim's grows the tree from a starting vertex by the cheapest crossing edge. Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths from a source in graphs with non-negative weights using a priority queue in O((V+E) log V). Bellman-Ford handles negative weights in O(VE) and detects negative cycles; Floyd-Warshall computes all-pairs shortest paths in O(V^3).
entries.formula: Dijkstra: dist[v] = min(dist[v], dist[u] + w(u,v)) for non-negative weights; Bellman-Ford relaxes all edges V-1 times; Floyd-Warshall: D_k[i][j] = min(D_{k-1}[i][j], D_{k-1}[i][k] + D_{k-1}[k][j])
entries.example: On a triangle with edges AB=1, BC=2, AC=4, Kruskal picks AB and BC for an MST of weight 3. Dijkstra from A gives dist(B)=1, dist(C)=3 via B, not the direct edge of 4.
entries.subject: Algorithms

entries.topic: Regular expressions, regular languages and the pumping lemma
entries.fact: Regular languages are exactly those recognized by finite automata and described by regular expressions, and they are closed under union, concatenation, star, complement and intersection. The pumping lemma for regular languages says any long enough string in a regular language can be split as xyz with |xy| <= p, |y| > 0, and xy^i z in the language for all i >= 0. It is used to prove non-regularity by contradiction.
entries.formula: Pumping lemma: for regular L there is a pumping length p such that any s in L with |s| >= p splits as xyz, |xy| <= p, |y| > 0, and xy^i z in L for all i >= 0
entries.example: L = {a^n b^n : n >= 0} is not regular: take s = a^p b^p; pumping y (which lies within the a's) changes the count of a's but not b's, leaving the language. In contrast, (0+1)*01 is regular.
entries.subject: Theory of Computation

entries.fact: A context-free grammar (CFG) generates a language by rewriting a start symbol with productions A -> alpha; the language is the set of terminal strings derivable. A pushdown automaton (PDA) is a finite automaton with a stack, and PDAs recognize exactly the context-free languages. A grammar is ambiguous if some string has two different parse trees; ambiguity matters because parsers must choose one derivation. The pumping lemma for CFLs is used to prove languages non-context-free.
entries.formula: CFL pumping lemma: any long string s in L splits as uvwxy with |vwx| <= p, |vx| > 0, and u v^i w x^i y in L for all i >= 0
entries.example: S -> aSb | epsilon generates {a^n b^n}. The language {a^n b^n c^n} is not context-free (pumping breaks the equal counts), though it is context-sensitive.
entries.subject: Theory of Computation

entries.fact: A Turing machine has a finite control and an unbounded tape; it defines the recursively enumerable languages, and a language is decidable (recursive) if some machine halts with the right answer on every input. The halting problem (does machine M halt on input w?) is undecidable, proved by diagonalization. Undecidability spreads by reduction: if a decidable problem could solve the halting problem, it too is undecidable. Rice's theorem says every non-trivial property of the language of a Turing machine is undecidable.
entries.formula: Halting problem is undecidable; Rice's theorem: any non-trivial semantic property of recursively enumerable languages is undecidable
entries.example: There is no algorithm that decides whether an arbitrary program prints 'hello'. If such a checker existed, it could be adapted to decide halting, a contradiction.
entries.subject: Theory of Computation

entries.fact: Lexical analysis converts source text into tokens (identifiers, keywords, literals, operators) using regular expressions and finite automata, discarding whitespace and comments. Parsing builds a syntax tree from tokens according to a grammar: top-down (recursive descent, LL) parsers expand from the start symbol, while bottom-up (LR, SLR, LALR) parsers shift tokens and reduce by productions. LL(1) parsing uses a single lookahead token; LR parsers handle a larger class of grammars and detect errors as soon as possible.
entries.formula: FIRST(A) = terminals that can begin strings derived from A; FOLLOW(A) = terminals that can follow A; LL(1) table entry M[A, a] uses FIRST and FOLLOW
entries.example: For E -> E + T | T and T -> id, the input 'id + id' parses to a tree with + at the root. Left recursion (E -> E + T) must be removed before recursive-descent parsing.
entries.subject: Compiler Design

entries.topic: Syntax-directed translation, intermediate code and runtime environments
entries.fact: Syntax-directed translation attaches semantic actions or attributes to grammar productions; synthesized attributes flow up the parse tree (e.g. a value) and inherited attributes flow down (e.g. a symbol table entry). Intermediate code such as three-address code (t1 = a + b) is machine-independent and eases optimization and retargeting. The runtime environment manages activation records on a stack: parameters, return address, saved registers and locals, with static and dynamic links for nested scopes.
entries.formula: Three-address code: at most one operator per instruction, e.g. t1 = b * c; t2 = a + t1; activation record size = parameters + locals + saved state + return address
entries.example: The expression a + b * c translates to t1 = b * c; t2 = a + t1. In a recursive call, a fresh activation record is pushed so each call has its own locals.
entries.subject: Compiler Design

entries.topic: Local optimisation and data flow analysis
entries.fact: Local optimization improves code within basic blocks: constant folding evaluates constant expressions at compile time, common subexpression elimination reuses an already computed value, and dead-code elimination removes code whose results are never used. Data flow analysis computes facts over the control-flow graph: liveness analysis finds variables live at each point (used later without redefinition), and constant propagation tracks variables holding known constants. These analyses are solved as iterative equations over the CFG until a fixed point.
entries.formula: Liveness: LiveOut[B] = union over successors S of (uses(S) union (LiveOut[S] - defs(S))); available expressions and reaching definitions use similar forward equations
entries.example: In 'x = 2 * 3; y = x + 1;', constant folding gives x = 6 and then y = 7. In 'a = b + c; d = b + c;', the second b + c is a common subexpression and can reuse the first result.
entries.subject: Compiler Design

entries.topic: Processes, threads, IPC, concurrency and synchronization
entries.fact: A process is a running program with its own address space; a thread is a lighter unit sharing the process's memory, so threads switch cheaply but must synchronize. Processes communicate via pipes, message queues, shared memory and signals. A race condition occurs when the result depends on the timing of unsynchronized accesses, so critical sections are protected with mutexes, semaphores or monitors. A semaphore's wait (P) decrements and blocks at zero; signal (V) increments and wakes a waiter.
entries.formula: Semaphore: wait(S): if S > 0 then S = S - 1 else block; signal(S): S = S + 1 and wake a waiter; mutual exclusion requires at most one thread in a critical section
entries.example: The producer-consumer problem uses an empty-slot semaphore, a full-slot semaphore and a mutex around the buffer. Two threads incrementing a shared counter without a lock can lose an update.
entries.subject: Operating Systems

entries.fact: Deadlock is when a set of processes each waits forever for a resource held by another process in the set. Coffman gave four necessary conditions: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Deadlock can be prevented by breaking one condition (e.g. ordering all resource requests), avoided with the Banker's algorithm (grant only if the state stays safe), detected and recovered from, or simply ignored (the ostrich approach used by most general-purpose OSes).
entries.formula: Banker's algorithm: a state is safe if there is an order in which all processes can finish with available plus releasable resources; need = max - allocation
entries.example: Process P1 holds the printer and wants the scanner while P2 holds the scanner and wants the printer: circular wait, deadlock. Forcing all processes to request resources in increasing numeric order prevents this cycle.
entries.subject: Operating Systems

entries.fact: CPU scheduling picks which ready process runs next. FCFS is simple but suffers the convoy effect; shortest-job-first is optimal for average waiting time but needs burst estimates; round robin gives each process a time quantum for fairness; priority scheduling can starve low-priority processes unless aging is used. I/O (disk) scheduling orders requests to reduce seek time: FCFS, SSTF (nearest track first), SCAN (elevator) and C-SCAN (one-direction sweep) are the standard policies.
entries.formula: Turnaround time = completion time - arrival time; waiting time = turnaround time - burst time; SSTF picks the request with the smallest seek from the current head position
entries.example: Jobs with bursts 5, 3, 8 arriving together: SJF order 3, 5, 8 gives average waiting (0 + 3 + 8)/3 = 3.67, better than FCFS (0 + 5 + 8)/3 = 4.33. With disk requests at tracks 10, 50, 90 and head at 40, SSTF serves 50 first.
entries.subject: Operating Systems

entries.fact: Virtual memory lets each process use a large logical address space backed partly by disk; pages are mapped to frames through page tables, and the TLB caches recent translations. On a page fault the OS loads the missing page, evicting a victim chosen by a replacement policy: FIFO, LRU (least recently used) or optimal (evict the page used farthest in the future). Thrashing occurs when the system spends more time paging than executing, and the working-set model keeps a process's active pages resident to prevent it.
entries.formula: Effective access time = (1 - p) * memory access time + p * page fault service time, where p is the page fault rate; Belady's anomaly: FIFO can fault more with more frames
entries.example: Reference string 1,2,3,4,1,2,5 with 3 frames: FIFO faults 9 times, LRU faults 8 times, optimal faults 7 times. A page fault rate of 0.001 with 10 ms disk service adds about 10 microseconds per access on average.
entries.subject: Operating Systems

entries.fact: A file system maps names to data on disk: a directory maps file names to inodes (Unix) or file control blocks, which store metadata and pointers to data blocks. Allocation methods include contiguous (fast sequential access but fragmentation), linked (no external fragmentation but slow random access) and indexed (an index block lists all data blocks, as in Unix inodes). Free space is tracked by a bitmap or a free list, and journaling records changes before applying them so a crash can be recovered.
entries.formula: Disk blocks for a file of size S with block size B: ceil(S / B) data blocks; Unix inode typically has 12 direct pointers plus single, double and triple indirect pointers
entries.example: A 5000-byte file with 1024-byte blocks needs 5 data blocks. Deleting a file frees its blocks in the bitmap and removes the directory entry, but the data lingers until overwritten.
entries.subject: Operating Systems

entries.fact: The ER model designs a database with entities (objects), attributes (properties) and relationships (associations), with keys identifying entities and cardinality (1:1, 1:N, M:N) describing relationships. The relational model stores data as tables: each row is a tuple, each column an attribute, and a primary key uniquely identifies rows while a foreign key references another table's primary key. Integrity constraints enforce entity integrity (primary keys never null), referential integrity (foreign keys must match or be null) and domain constraints.
entries.formula: Relational schema: R(A1, A2, ..., An) with primary key underlined; a foreign key in R referencing S must equal an existing primary key value in S or be NULL
entries.example: Student(roll_no, name) with roll_no as primary key, and Enrolment(roll_no, course_id) where roll_no is a foreign key to Student. A many-to-many relationship between students and courses becomes the Enrolment table.
entries.subject: DBMS

entries.topic: Relational algebra, tuple calculus and SQL
entries.fact: Relational algebra is the procedural query language behind SQL: selection (sigma) filters rows, projection (pi) picks columns, and join combines tables on matching values; set operations union, intersection and difference apply to union-compatible relations. Tuple relational calculus is the declarative counterpart: queries state what tuples satisfy a predicate. SQL implements these with SELECT-FROM-WHERE, joins, GROUP BY with aggregates, nested subqueries, and data definition statements (CREATE, ALTER, DROP).
entries.formula: Selection: sigma_condition(R); projection: pi_attributes(R); natural join: R ⋈ S; SQL: SELECT A FROM R WHERE cond GROUP BY A HAVING count(*) > 1
entries.example: SELECT name FROM Student WHERE dept = 'CS' is pi_name(sigma_dept='CS'(Student)). An inner join of Student and Enrolment on roll_no lists each student's courses.
entries.subject: DBMS

entries.topic: File organization and indexing: B and B+ trees
entries.fact: An index speeds up lookups by mapping key values to record locations; a primary index is built on the ordering key, a secondary index on other attributes. B and B+ trees are balanced multi-way search trees designed for disk: each node holds many keys, so height stays small and lookups cost O(log n) disk accesses. In a B+ tree all data pointers live in leaf nodes linked in key order, so range scans are fast and internal nodes hold only keys for routing.
entries.formula: A B+ tree of order m with n keys has height O(log_m n); a node holds at most m-1 keys and m children; search cost is O(log_m n) node accesses
entries.example: A B+ tree of order 4 indexing 1,000,000 keys has height about log_4(1,000,000) = 10 at worst, but with nodes nearly full it is typically 3-4 levels, so a lookup needs only 3-4 disk reads.
entries.subject: DBMS

entries.fact: A transaction is an atomic unit of work satisfying ACID: atomicity (all or nothing), consistency, isolation and durability. Concurrent transactions can lose updates, read uncommitted data or read inconsistently, so schedules must be serializable. Two-phase locking (2PL) guarantees conflict serializability: a transaction acquires all locks before releasing any. Timestamp ordering and optimistic concurrency control are alternatives; deadlocks between transactions are handled by detection or timeout.
entries.formula: Strict 2PL: growing phase (acquire locks) then shrinking phase (release locks), with exclusive locks held until commit; a schedule is conflict-serializable iff its precedence graph is acyclic
entries.example: Two transactions each read a balance of 100, add 50 and write back 150: without locking the final balance is 150 instead of 200 (lost update). 2PL forces one to wait for the other's lock.
entries.subject: DBMS

entries.topic: Data link layer: switching, framing, MAC, Ethernet and bridging
entries.fact: Packet switching forwards each packet independently, circuit switching reserves a dedicated path, and virtual-circuit switching sets up a path first but shares links. The data link layer frames bits into packets, and medium access control (MAC) decides who transmits on a shared medium: ALOHA and CSMA use contention with backoff, while token passing and polling schedule access. Ethernet uses CSMA/CD on a shared medium (and full-duplex switching today), and bridges/switches forward frames by MAC address, learning addresses from source fields.
entries.formula: Pure ALOHA max efficiency is 1/(2e) = about 18%, slotted ALOHA 1/e = about 37%; Ethernet minimum frame is 64 bytes; binary exponential backoff waits a random 0 to 2^k - 1 slot times after k collisions
entries.example: Two stations transmitting at once on classic Ethernet detect the collision, jam, and back off for a random number of slot times. A switch learns that host A is on port 1 from the source MAC of A's frame and forwards frames for A only there.
entries.subject: Computer Networks

entries.fact: Error detection adds redundant bits so corrupted frames can be spotted: a parity bit catches any odd number of bit errors, checksums catch most errors cheaply, and cyclic redundancy checks (CRC) treat data as a polynomial and append the remainder of division by a generator polynomial. Hamming codes add enough parity bits to both detect and correct single-bit errors. The Hamming distance between codewords sets how many errors can be detected or corrected.
entries.formula: CRC: append remainder of data(x) * x^r divided by generator G(x); Hamming code needs r parity bits with 2^r >= m + r + 1 for m data bits; to correct t errors need Hamming distance >= 2t + 1
entries.example: For 4 data bits, 3 parity bits suffice (2^3 = 8 >= 4 + 3 + 1), giving the (7,4) Hamming code. Ethernet uses CRC-32, which detects all burst errors up to 32 bits long.
entries.subject: Computer Networks

entries.topic: Routing protocols: shortest path, flooding, distance vector and link state
entries.fact: Routing chooses paths through the network. Flooding sends every packet on every link (simple but wasteful) and is used for link-state advertisement. Distance vector protocols (e.g. RIP) have each router share its vector of distances with neighbours and update by the Bellman-Ford equation, but they converge slowly and can count to infinity. Link-state protocols (e.g. OSPF) flood link costs so every router builds the same topology map and runs Dijkstra locally, converging fast. Shortest path is the core computation in both.
entries.formula: Distance vector update: D_x(y) = min over neighbours v of (cost(x,v) + D_v(y)); link-state routers run Dijkstra on the flooded topology
entries.example: In RIP, if the link to a network fails, routers may keep advertising increasing hop counts (count to infinity) until the 16-hop limit marks it unreachable. OSPF routers instead flood the failure and recompute with Dijkstra.
entries.subject: Computer Networks

entries.fact: An IPv4 address is 32 bits, written as four decimal octets, split into a network part and a host part. CIDR notation a.b.c.d/n says the first n bits are the network prefix, allowing variable-size subnets; the network address has host bits zero and the broadcast address has them all one. A datagram larger than a link's MTU is fragmented: each fragment carries the same identification, an offset in units of 8 bytes, and a more-fragments flag, and the destination reassembles them.
entries.formula: Hosts in a /n network = 2^(32-n) - 2 (excluding network and broadcast); fragment offset counts 8-byte units; MTU of Ethernet is 1500 bytes
entries.example: 192.168.1.0/24 has 254 usable hosts (192.168.1.1 to 192.168.1.254), broadcast 192.168.1.255. A 4000-byte datagram over a 1500-byte MTU link splits into fragments of 1480, 1480 and 1040 bytes of data.
entries.subject: Computer Networks

entries.fact: ARP maps an IP address to a MAC address on a LAN by broadcasting 'who has this IP?' and caching the reply. DHCP automates host configuration: a new host broadcasts a discover message and a server offers an IP address, subnet mask, gateway and DNS server, leased for a limited time. ICMP carries error and control messages such as destination unreachable and echo (ping). NAT lets many private-address hosts share one public address by rewriting source addresses and ports in a translation table.
entries.formula: ARP cache maps IP -> MAC with a timeout; DHCP lease renewal happens at half the lease time; NAT table entry maps (private IP, private port) to (public IP, public port)
entries.example: A laptop joining a Wi-Fi network gets 192.168.1.5 from DHCP, then ARPs for the gateway 192.168.1.1 to learn its MAC. Its packets leave the home router with the router's single public IP via NAT.
entries.subject: Computer Networks

entries.topic: Transport layer: TCP, UDP, flow control and congestion control
entries.fact: UDP is connectionless and unreliable: it adds only ports and a checksum to IP, suiting DNS and streaming. TCP is connection-oriented and reliable: a three-way handshake opens a connection, sequence numbers and ACKs detect loss, and retransmission recovers it. Flow control uses a sliding window so a fast sender does not overwhelm a slow receiver, while congestion control (slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit) probes the network's capacity and backs off on loss. Sockets are the programming interface to both.
entries.formula: Slow start: cwnd doubles each RTT until ssthresh, then grows by about 1 segment per RTT; on loss, ssthresh = cwnd/2; effective window = min(receiver window, congestion window)
entries.example: A TCP sender starts with cwnd = 1 segment, doubling to 2, 4, 8 per RTT in slow start. Three duplicate ACKs trigger fast retransmit of the missing segment without waiting for a timeout.
entries.subject: Computer Networks

entries.topic: Application layer protocols: DNS, SMTP, HTTP, FTP, Email
entries.fact: DNS translates hostnames to IP addresses through a hierarchy of root, TLD and authoritative servers, with caching at each level. SMTP sends email between mail servers (port 25), while users fetch mail with POP3 or IMAP. HTTP is the Web's request-response protocol: methods like GET and POST, status codes (200 OK, 404 not found), and persistent connections in HTTP/1.1. FTP transfers files over separate control and data connections.
entries.formula: DNS resolution is recursive from the client to its resolver, then iterative across root, TLD and authoritative servers; HTTP status classes: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error
entries.example: Resolving www.example.com queries the root for .com, then the .com server for example.com, then its authoritative server for the A record. An HTTP GET returning 404 means the server understood the request but found no such resource.
entries.subject: Computer Networks

entries.topic: Functions of several variables: partial derivatives, maxima, minima and Lagrange multipliers
entries.fact: For f(x,y), the partial derivatives f_x and f_y measure change along each axis, and the gradient points in the direction of steepest increase. The total derivative combines them: df = f_x dx + f_y dy. A critical point has zero gradient; the second derivative test uses the Hessian determinant D = f_xx f_yy - f_xy^2 to classify it as a max, min or saddle point. Lagrange multipliers handle constrained extrema by solving grad f = lambda grad g.
entries.formula: df = f_x dx + f_y dy; D = f_xx f_yy - (f_xy)^2: D > 0 and f_xx > 0 gives local min, D > 0 and f_xx < 0 gives local max, D < 0 gives saddle point; constrained: grad f = lambda grad g
entries.example: Maximizing f = xy subject to x + y = 10: grad f = (y, x) = lambda (1, 1) gives x = y = 5, so the maximum is 25. For f = x^2 + y^2, the origin has D = 4 > 0 and f_xx = 2 > 0, a local minimum.
entries.subject: Calculus

entries.topic: Double and triple integrals and their applications
entries.fact: A double integral over a region gives volume under a surface or area when the integrand is 1; a triple integral gives volume or mass of a solid. Changing to polar coordinates (x = r cos theta, y = r sin theta) introduces the Jacobian r, and cylindrical or spherical coordinates simplify symmetric solids. Fubini's theorem lets iterated integrals be computed in either order when the function is continuous.
entries.formula: Area = double integral of dA; volume = double integral of f(x,y) dA; polar: dA = r dr dtheta; triple integral in spherical coordinates: dV = rho^2 sin(phi) d rho d phi d theta
entries.example: The area of a circle of radius a is the integral over r from 0 to a and theta from 0 to 2 pi of r dr dtheta = pi a^2. The volume of a sphere of radius a is (4/3) pi a^3 by a triple integral.
entries.subject: Calculus

entries.topic: Vector calculus: gradient, divergence, curl and integral theorems
entries.fact: The gradient of a scalar field is a vector pointing in the direction of greatest increase; the divergence of a vector field measures net outflow per unit volume; the curl measures local rotation. Green's theorem relates a line integral around a closed curve to a double integral over the enclosed region. Stokes' theorem generalizes this to surfaces, and Gauss's divergence theorem relates flux through a closed surface to the volume integral of divergence.
entries.formula: Green: line integral of (P dx + Q dy) = double integral of (dQ/dx - dP/dy) dA; Stokes: line integral of F . dr = surface integral of (curl F) . n dS; Gauss: surface integral of F . n dS = triple integral of div F dV
entries.example: For F = (x, y, 0), div F = 2, so the flux through a sphere of radius a is 2 times its volume, (8/3) pi a^3. For F = (-y, x, 0), curl F = (0,0,2), giving circulation 2 pi a^2 around a circle of radius a.
entries.subject: Calculus

entries.topic: Vector spaces, linear transformations, rank and nullity
entries.fact: A vector space is a set closed under addition and scalar multiplication; a basis is a linearly independent spanning set, and its size is the dimension. A linear transformation T is determined by its action on a basis and is represented by a matrix once bases are fixed. The rank-nullity theorem says rank(T) + nullity(T) = dim(domain), and a system Ax = b is consistent exactly when b lies in the column space of A.
entries.formula: rank(T) + nullity(T) = dim(V); rank(A) = number of pivots in row echelon form; Ax = b is consistent iff rank(A) = rank([A|b])
entries.example: T: R^3 -> R^2 defined by T(x,y,z) = (x + y, y + z) has rank 2 and nullity 1 (kernel spanned by (1,-1,1)). The system x + y = 1, 2x + 2y = 3 is inconsistent since rank(A) = 1 but rank([A|b]) = 2.
entries.subject: Linear Algebra

entries.topic: Diagonalization, characteristic polynomial, minimal polynomial and Cayley-Hamilton theorem
entries.fact: A matrix is diagonalizable if it has a basis of eigenvectors, equivalently if its minimal polynomial has distinct linear factors; symmetric matrices are always diagonalizable. The characteristic polynomial p(lambda) = det(A - lambda I) has the eigenvalues as roots, and the Cayley-Hamilton theorem says every matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation, p(A) = 0. The minimal polynomial is the smallest-degree monic polynomial annihilating A and divides the characteristic polynomial.
entries.formula: Cayley-Hamilton: p(A) = 0 where p(lambda) = det(A - lambda I); A is diagonalizable iff its minimal polynomial splits into distinct linear factors; A = PDP^-1 with D diagonal
entries.example: For A = [[2,1],[1,2]], p(lambda) = (lambda-3)(lambda-1), so A^2 - 4A + 3I = 0, and A^2 = 4A - 3I without multiplying matrices. The matrix [[1,1],[0,1]] has minimal polynomial (lambda-1)^2 and is not diagonalizable.
entries.subject: Linear Algebra

entries.topic: Inner product spaces, Gram-Schmidt and special matrices
entries.fact: An inner product space has an inner product generalizing the dot product, giving lengths and orthogonality. The Gram-Schmidt process turns a basis into an orthonormal one by subtracting projections onto earlier vectors. Symmetric and Hermitian matrices have real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors; normal matrices are unitarily diagonalizable; orthogonal and unitary matrices preserve lengths and have orthonormal columns.
entries.formula: Gram-Schmidt: u1 = v1, u_k = v_k - sum_{i<k} proj_{u_i}(v_k); proj_u(v) = (<v,u>/<u,u>) u; unitary: U*U = I; Hermitian: A* = A
entries.example: Applying Gram-Schmidt to (1,1,0) and (1,0,1) gives orthonormal vectors (1/sqrt2, 1/sqrt2, 0) and (1/sqrt6, -1/sqrt6, 2/sqrt6). The rotation matrix [[cos t, -sin t],[sin t, cos t]] is orthogonal with determinant 1.
entries.subject: Linear Algebra

entries.topic: Jordan canonical form and bilinear and quadratic forms
entries.fact: Every square matrix over the complex numbers is similar to a Jordan canonical form: a block diagonal matrix whose blocks have an eigenvalue on the diagonal and 1s just above it. The number and sizes of Jordan blocks for an eigenvalue are fixed by the dimensions of kernels of powers of (A - lambda I). A bilinear form is linear in each argument; a quadratic form Q(x) = x^T A x with symmetric A is classified by its eigenvalues as positive definite, negative definite, indefinite or semidefinite, and can be diagonalized by an orthogonal change of variables.
entries.formula: Jordan block J = lambda I + N with N nilpotent having 1s on the superdiagonal; quadratic form Q(x) = x^T A x; Sylvester's law of inertia: the numbers of positive, negative and zero eigenvalues are invariant under congruence
entries.example: The matrix [[2,1],[0,2]] is a single Jordan block for eigenvalue 2 and is not diagonalizable. The form 2x^2 + 2xy + 2y^2 has matrix [[2,1],[1,2]] with eigenvalues 3 and 1, so it is positive definite.
entries.subject: Linear Algebra

entries.topic: Metric spaces: connectedness, compactness and completeness
entries.fact: A metric space has a distance function satisfying non-negativity, symmetry and the triangle inequality. A set is compact if every open cover has a finite subcover; in R^n this is equivalent to being closed and bounded (Heine-Borel). A sequence is Cauchy if its terms get arbitrarily close to each other, and a space is complete if every Cauchy sequence converges inside it. A connected set cannot be split into two disjoint non-empty open pieces.
entries.formula: Heine-Borel: in R^n, compact iff closed and bounded; R is complete but (0,1) and Q are not; continuous image of a compact set is compact
entries.example: The closed interval [0,1] is compact, so a continuous function on it attains its maximum. The sequence 1, 1.4, 1.41, 1.414, ... is Cauchy in Q but converges to sqrt(2), which is not in Q, showing Q is incomplete.
entries.subject: Real Analysis

entries.topic: Sequences and series of functions and uniform convergence
entries.fact: A sequence of functions can converge pointwise (at each x separately) or uniformly (the worst-case error over all x goes to zero). Uniform convergence preserves continuity, and lets limits pass through integrals and (with uniformly convergent derivatives) through differentiation. The Weierstrass M-test proves uniform convergence by dominating terms with a convergent numeric series. The contraction mapping principle says a contraction on a complete metric space has a unique fixed point, found by iteration.
entries.formula: M-test: if |f_n(x)| <= M_n for all x and sum M_n converges, then sum f_n converges uniformly; contraction: d(Tx, Ty) <= k d(x,y) with k < 1 implies a unique fixed point
entries.example: f_n(x) = x^n on [0,1] converges pointwise to 0 for x < 1 and 1 at x = 1, so the limit is discontinuous and convergence is not uniform. The Weierstrass approximation theorem says every continuous function on [a,b] is a uniform limit of polynomials.
entries.subject: Real Analysis

entries.fact: Lebesgue measure extends length to a large class of sets, including all intervals and countable sets (which have measure zero). A function is measurable if preimages of intervals are measurable sets, and the Lebesgue integral is built by partitioning the range rather than the domain, so it handles many more functions than the Riemann integral. The monotone convergence theorem, Fatou's lemma and the dominated convergence theorem justify passing limits through integrals under mild conditions.
entries.formula: Monotone convergence: if 0 <= f_n increasing to f, then integral f_n -> integral f; dominated convergence: if f_n -> f pointwise and |f_n| <= g integrable, then integral f_n -> integral f; Fatou: integral liminf f_n <= liminf integral f_n
entries.example: The Dirichlet function (1 on rationals, 0 on irrationals) is not Riemann integrable but is Lebesgue integrable with integral 0, since the rationals have measure zero. Dominated convergence justifies differentiating under the integral sign for e^{-tx} type integrands.
entries.subject: Real Analysis

entries.topic: Differentiation of several variables, inverse and implicit function theorems
entries.fact: A function of several variables is differentiable at a point if it is well approximated by a linear map, its derivative matrix being the Jacobian. The inverse function theorem says that if the Jacobian determinant is non-zero at a point, the function is locally invertible with a differentiable inverse. The implicit function theorem says an equation F(x,y) = 0 with F_y != 0 locally defines y as a differentiable function of x, with dy/dx = -F_x / F_y.
entries.formula: Implicit differentiation: dy/dx = -F_x / F_y when F(x,y) = 0 and F_y != 0; inverse function theorem needs det(J) != 0 at the point
entries.example: The circle x^2 + y^2 = 1 near (0,1) defines y = sqrt(1 - x^2), and dy/dx = -x/y = 0 at x = 0. The polar map (r, theta) -> (r cos theta, r sin theta) has Jacobian determinant r, so it is locally invertible where r != 0.
entries.subject: Real Analysis

entries.topic: Analytic functions, Cauchy-Riemann equations and harmonic functions
entries.fact: A complex function f(z) = u + iv is differentiable at z0 if the limit of the difference quotient exists independent of direction; it is analytic if differentiable in a neighbourhood. Differentiability is equivalent to the Cauchy-Riemann equations u_x = v_y and u_y = -v_x (with continuous partials). The real and imaginary parts of an analytic function are harmonic (their Laplacian is zero) and are conjugate to each other.
entries.formula: Cauchy-Riemann: du/dx = dv/dy and du/dy = -dv/dx; f'(z) = u_x + i v_x; Laplace: u_xx + u_yy = 0 for analytic f
entries.example: f(z) = z^2 = (x^2 - y^2) + i(2xy) satisfies u_x = 2x = v_y and u_y = -2y = -v_x, so it is analytic everywhere with f'(z) = 2z. The function f(z) = conjugate(z) fails Cauchy-Riemann everywhere and is nowhere differentiable.
entries.subject: Complex Analysis

entries.topic: Cauchy's integral theorem and formula, Liouville's theorem and maximum modulus principle
entries.fact: Cauchy's integral theorem says the integral of an analytic function around a closed contour is zero. Cauchy's integral formula recovers values inside a contour from boundary values: f(a) = (1/2 pi i) times the integral of f(z)/(z-a) dz. From this follow Liouville's theorem (a bounded entire function is constant), the maximum modulus principle (a non-constant analytic function attains no maximum inside a domain), and Morera's theorem (vanishing integrals over all closed contours imply analyticity).
entries.formula: Cauchy integral formula: f(a) = (1/(2 pi i)) integral_C f(z)/(z - a) dz; f^(n)(a) = (n!/(2 pi i)) integral_C f(z)/(z - a)^(n+1) dz; Liouville: bounded entire f is constant
entries.example: The integral of 1/z around the unit circle is 2 pi i, showing 1/z is not analytic inside (it has a pole at 0). Liouville's theorem gives a one-line proof of the fundamental theorem of algebra.
entries.subject: Complex Analysis

entries.topic: Taylor and Laurent series, singularities and the residue theorem
entries.fact: An analytic function expands as a Taylor series inside its disk of convergence; near an isolated singularity it expands as a Laurent series with negative powers. Singularities are removable, poles (of some finite order) or essential. The residue at a pole is the coefficient of (z-a)^-1, and the residue theorem says the integral around a closed contour equals 2 pi i times the sum of residues inside, which evaluates many real integrals.
entries.formula: Residue theorem: integral_C f(z) dz = 2 pi i * sum of residues inside C; for a simple pole, Res(f, a) = lim_{z->a} (z-a) f(z); radius of convergence reaches the nearest singularity
entries.example: The integral from -infinity to infinity of dx/(1 + x^2) equals pi: close the contour in the upper half-plane, where the only pole is at i with residue 1/(2i), giving 2 pi i * 1/(2i) = pi.
entries.subject: Complex Analysis

entries.topic: Conformal mappings, Mobius transformations, Rouche's theorem and Schwarz lemma
entries.fact: A conformal map is an analytic function with non-zero derivative, preserving angles and local shape. Mobius transformations (az+b)/(cz+d) map circles and lines to circles and lines and are determined by the images of three points. Rouche's theorem counts zeros inside a contour by comparing a function with a dominant term on the boundary. The Schwarz lemma bounds analytic maps of the unit disk fixing the origin: |f(z)| <= |z|.
entries.formula: Mobius: w = (a z + b)/(c z + d), ad - bc != 0; Rouche: if |f| > |g| on C then f and f+g have the same number of zeros inside C; Schwarz: |f(z)| <= |z| and |f'(0)| <= 1
entries.example: The map w = (z - i)/(z + i) sends the upper half-plane onto the unit disk. Rouche's theorem shows z^5 + 3z + 1 has exactly one zero inside |z| < 1, since |3z| = 3 dominates |z^5 + 1| <= 2 on |z| = 1.
entries.subject: Complex Analysis

entries.topic: Higher order linear ODEs with constant coefficients
entries.fact: A linear ODE of order n with constant coefficients is solved by its characteristic equation: distinct real roots give exponentials, repeated roots give exponentials times polynomials, and complex roots give exponentially modulated sines and cosines. The general solution is the complementary function plus a particular integral, found by undetermined coefficients or variation of parameters. Existence and uniqueness hold when the coefficients and forcing term are continuous.
entries.formula: For a y'' + b y' + c y = 0, characteristic a r^2 + b r + c = 0; roots r1 != r2 give y = C1 e^{r1 x} + C2 e^{r2 x}; repeated root r gives (C1 + C2 x) e^{r x}
entries.example: y'' - 3y' + 2y = 0 has characteristic r^2 - 3r + 2 = (r-1)(r-2), so y = C1 e^x + C2 e^{2x}. For y'' + y = 0 the roots are +-i, giving y = C1 cos x + C2 sin x.
entries.subject: Differential Equations

entries.topic: Second order ODEs with variable coefficients, Cauchy-Euler equation and Laplace transforms
entries.fact: The Cauchy-Euler equation a x^2 y'' + b x y' + c y = 0 becomes constant-coefficient under x = e^t, with trial solutions y = x^m. Laplace transforms turn differential equations into algebraic ones: the transform of y' is sY(s) - y(0), so initial conditions enter directly, and the solution follows by partial fractions and inverse transforms. This is especially handy for equations with discontinuous forcing or impulses.
entries.formula: Cauchy-Euler: try y = x^m, giving a m(m-1) + b m + c = 0; Laplace: L{y'} = sY(s) - y(0), L{y''} = s^2 Y(s) - s y(0) - y'(0); L{1} = 1/s, L{e^{at}} = 1/(s-a)
entries.example: x^2 y'' - 2y = 0 gives m(m-1) - 2 = 0, so m = 2 or -1 and y = C1 x^2 + C2/x. Solving y' + y = 0 with y(0) = 1 by Laplace gives (s+1)Y = 1, so Y = 1/(s+1) and y = e^{-t}.
entries.subject: Differential Equations

entries.topic: Series solutions, Legendre and Bessel functions
entries.fact: Near an ordinary point, an ODE has power-series solutions found by substituting y = sum a_n x^n and matching coefficients. At a regular singular point the Frobenius method uses y = x^r sum a_n x^n, with r from the indicial equation. Legendre's equation produces Legendre polynomials P_n(x), orthogonal on [-1,1]; Bessel's equation produces Bessel functions J_n(x), orthogonal with a weight on [0,1] and central to circular and cylindrical problems.
entries.formula: Legendre: (1-x^2) y'' - 2x y' + n(n+1) y = 0; integral_{-1}^{1} P_m P_n dx = 0 for m != n, = 2/(2n+1) for m = n; Bessel: x^2 y'' + x y' + (x^2 - n^2) y = 0
entries.example: P_0 = 1, P_1 = x, P_2 = (3x^2 - 1)/2. The Frobenius method on Bessel's equation of order 0 gives J_0(x) = 1 - x^2/4 + x^4/64 - ...
entries.subject: Differential Equations

entries.topic: Systems of linear ODEs and Sturm-Liouville eigenvalue problems
entries.fact: A system x' = Ax of first-order linear ODEs is solved by the matrix exponential; eigenvalues of A give exponential modes, and the solution is a combination of them. Sturm's oscillation and separation theorems describe how zeros of solutions interlace. A Sturm-Liouville problem (p y')' + (lambda w - q) y = 0 with boundary conditions has real eigenvalues lambda_n increasing to infinity and eigenfunctions orthogonal with weight w, forming a basis for expansions.
entries.formula: System solution: x(t) = e^{At} x(0); Sturm-Liouville: (p(x) y')' + (lambda w(x) - q(x)) y = 0; orthogonality: integral w y_m y_n dx = 0 for m != n
entries.example: The system x' = y, y' = -x has eigenvalues +-i and solutions x = A cos t + B sin t. The problem y'' + lambda y = 0 with y(0) = y(pi) = 0 has eigenvalues lambda_n = n^2 and eigenfunctions sin(nx).
entries.subject: Differential Equations

entries.fact: A planar autonomous system x' = f(x,y), y' = g(x,y) has stationary points where f = g = 0. Linearized stability examines the Jacobian at the point: eigenvalues with negative real parts give asymptotic stability, positive real parts give instability, and a zero or purely imaginary pair is inconclusive by linearization. Lyapunov functions give a direct method: if a positive definite function decreases along trajectories, the equilibrium is stable.
entries.formula: Linearized system: u' = J u where J is the Jacobian at the equilibrium; trace-determinant test: stable node/spiral when trace < 0 and det > 0; Lyapunov: V > 0 and dV/dt < 0 implies asymptotic stability
entries.example: For the pendulum linearized at the bottom, the Jacobian has eigenvalues +-i sqrt(g/l), a centre; at the top the eigenvalues are real of opposite sign, a saddle and unstable. The damped oscillator x'' + 2x' + x = 0 has eigenvalues -1 (repeated), a stable node.
entries.subject: Differential Equations

entries.topic: Partial differential equations: classification and separation of variables
entries.fact: Second-order PDEs in two variables are classified by the discriminant B^2 - AC: elliptic (Laplace, steady state), parabolic (heat, diffusion) or hyperbolic (wave, propagation). The method of characteristics solves first-order linear and quasilinear PDEs by reducing them to ODEs along characteristic curves. Separation of variables writes u(x,t) = X(x)T(t), turning a PDE into ODEs whose solutions superpose to satisfy boundary conditions, as in Laplace's equation in Cartesian and polar coordinates and the heat and wave equations in one space variable.
entries.formula: Classification: B^2 - AC < 0 elliptic, = 0 parabolic, > 0 hyperbolic; Laplace: u_xx + u_yy = 0; heat: u_t = k u_xx; wave: u_tt = c^2 u_xx
entries.example: The heat equation u_t = u_xx on 0 < x < pi with u = 0 at both ends separates to modes sin(nx) e^{-n^2 t}. Laplace's equation in a disk gives solutions r^n cos(n theta) and r^n sin(n theta).
entries.subject: Differential Equations

entries.topic: Wave and heat equations: d'Alembert formula and Cauchy problems
entries.fact: The wave equation's Cauchy problem has d'Alembert's explicit solution: the initial displacement splits into left- and right-moving waves, and the initial velocity contributes an integral over the interval between the wave fronts. The domain of dependence of a point (x,t) is the interval [x-ct, x+ct] on the initial line, expressing finite propagation speed. The heat equation's Cauchy problem is solved by convolution with the Gaussian heat kernel, which instantly smooths and spreads data.
entries.formula: d'Alembert: u(x,t) = (1/2)[g(x-ct) + g(x+ct)] + (1/(2c)) integral_{x-ct}^{x+ct} h(s) ds for u_tt = c^2 u_xx, u(x,0) = g(x), u_t(x,0) = h(x)
entries.example: For a plucked string with u(x,0) = sin x and u_t(x,0) = 0, d'Alembert gives u(x,t) = (1/2)[sin(x-ct) + sin(x+ct)] = sin x cos ct, a standing wave.
entries.subject: Differential Equations

entries.topic: Numerical solution of linear systems: direct and iterative methods
entries.fact: Direct methods finish in a fixed number of steps: Gaussian elimination reduces a system to triangular form, LU decomposition reuses the factorization for many right-hand sides, and Cholesky factorization applies to symmetric positive definite matrices. Iterative methods (Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel) start from a guess and refine it; they converge for strictly diagonally dominant matrices, with Gauss-Seidel usually faster since it uses updated values immediately.
entries.formula: Jacobi: x_i^(k+1) = (b_i - sum_{j != i} a_ij x_j^(k)) / a_ii; Gauss-Seidel uses x_j^(k+1) for j < i; strict diagonal dominance: |a_ii| > sum_{j != i} |a_ij| guarantees convergence
entries.example: For 4x + y = 9 and x + 3y = 8, Jacobi from (0,0) gives (2.25, 2.67), then (1.58, 1.92), converging to (2, 2). Gaussian elimination on the same system gives x = 2, y = 2 directly.
entries.subject: Numerical Methods

entries.topic: Numerical solution of nonlinear equations: bisection, secant and fixed point iteration
entries.fact: The bisection method halves a bracketing interval each step and always converges, but slowly (linearly). The secant method replaces the derivative in Newton's method by a finite difference and converges superlinearly, while fixed point iteration x = g(x) converges when |g'(x)| < 1 near the root. These methods trade reliability (bisection) against speed (secant, Newton).
entries.formula: Bisection: error after n steps <= (b - a)/2^n; secant: x_{n+1} = x_n - f(x_n)(x_n - x_{n-1})/(f(x_n) - f(x_{n-1})); fixed point converges if |g'(x)| < 1
entries.example: Solving x^2 - 2 = 0 on [1,2] by bisection: after 10 steps the interval width is 1/1024, so sqrt(2) is pinned to about 3 decimal places. Fixed point iteration x = (x + 2/x)/2 is Newton's method for this equation.
entries.subject: Numerical Methods

entries.topic: Interpolation: Lagrange and Newton forms and error
entries.fact: Given n+1 points, there is a unique interpolating polynomial of degree at most n. Lagrange's form builds it as a sum of basis polynomials, each 1 at one node and 0 at the others. Newton's form uses divided differences, which makes adding a new point cheap. The interpolation error at x is f^(n+1)(xi)/(n+1)! times the product of (x - x_i), so error grows with the spacing and the size of the next derivative.
entries.formula: Lagrange: P(x) = sum y_i l_i(x), l_i(x) = product_{j != i} (x - x_j)/(x_i - x_j); error: f(x) - P(x) = f^(n+1)(xi)/(n+1)! * product (x - x_i)
entries.example: Interpolating (0,1), (1,2), (2,5) gives P(x) = x^2 + 1: at x = 1.5 it predicts 3.25. Adding the point (3,10) to Newton's form needs only one new divided difference.
entries.subject: Numerical Methods

entries.topic: Numerical differentiation and integration: Simpson's rule and Newton-Cotes formulas
entries.fact: Numerical differentiation approximates derivatives by difference quotients; the central difference is second-order accurate. Numerical integration replaces the integrand by an interpolating polynomial: the trapezoidal rule uses linear pieces (error O(h^2)), Simpson's rule uses parabolas (error O(h^4)) and needs an even number of intervals, and composite rules split the range into many small panels. Newton-Cotes formulas are this family with equally spaced nodes.
entries.formula: Trapezoidal: integral = (h/2)[f0 + 2f1 + ... + 2f_{n-1} + fn]; Simpson: integral = (h/3)[f0 + 4f1 + 2f2 + 4f3 + ... + fn] with n even; central difference: f'(x) = (f(x+h) - f(x-h))/(2h) + O(h^2)
entries.example: Simpson's rule with h = 0.5 on the integral of x^2 from 0 to 1 gives (0.5/3)[0 + 4(0.25) + 1] = 1/3 exactly, since Simpson is exact for cubics. The trapezoidal rule on the same integral gives 0.375.
entries.subject: Numerical Methods

entries.topic: Numerical solution of ODE initial value problems: Euler and Runge-Kutta methods
entries.fact: Euler's method advances the solution by the tangent slope: y_{n+1} = y_n + h f(x_n, y_n); its local error is O(h^2) and global error O(h), so it needs small steps. Second-order Runge-Kutta (RK2, e.g. Heun's method) averages the slopes at the start and a predicted end of the step, giving global error O(h^2). Smaller step size or higher order both improve accuracy, at the cost of more function evaluations.
entries.formula: Euler: y_{n+1} = y_n + h f(x_n, y_n); Heun (RK2): y_{n+1} = y_n + (h/2)[f(x_n, y_n) + f(x_{n+1}, y_n + h f(x_n, y_n))]; Euler global error O(h), RK2 global error O(h^2)
entries.example: For y' = y with y(0) = 1 and h = 0.1, Euler gives y(0.1) = 1.1 (true e^0.1 = 1.1052); Heun gives 1.105, much closer. Halving h roughly halves Euler's error but quarters RK2's.
entries.subject: Numerical Methods

entries.topic: Axiomatic probability, conditional probability and Bayes theorem
entries.fact: Kolmogorov's axioms define probability: P(A) >= 0 for every event, P(sample space) = 1, and probabilities add over disjoint events. From these follow the addition rule, the complement rule and monotonicity. Events A and B are independent if P(A and B) = P(A) P(B). Conditional probability P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B) updates beliefs with evidence, and Bayes' theorem reverses the conditioning.
entries.formula: P(A union B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B); P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B); Bayes: P(A|B) = P(B|A) P(A) / P(B); independence: P(A and B) = P(A) P(B)
entries.example: Drawing two cards without replacement: P(two aces) = (4/52)(3/51) = 1/221. If a test has 1% false positives and a disease affects 0.1% of people, a positive result still leaves the disease unlikely by Bayes' theorem.
entries.subject: Probability

entries.topic: Random variables, distributions, expectation and moment generating functions
entries.fact: A random variable has a distribution function F(x) = P(X <= x); discrete variables use a probability mass function and continuous ones a density, with the density integrating to 1. Expectation E(X) is the long-run average, variance measures spread, and moments E(X^k) summarize shape. The moment generating function M(t) = E(e^{tX}) generates moments by differentiation and identifies distributions; the quantile function inverts F. A function of a random variable gets its distribution by transformation or the Jacobian method.
entries.formula: E(X) = sum x p(x) or integral x f(x) dx; Var(X) = E(X^2) - (E X)^2; MGF: M(t) = E(e^{tX}), E(X^k) = M^(k)(0); E(aX + b) = a E(X) + b
entries.example: For a fair die, E(X) = 3.5 and Var(X) = 35/12. For X uniform on (0,1), E(X) = 1/2 and the MGF is (e^t - 1)/t. If Y = 2X + 1, then E(Y) = 2 E(X) + 1 and Var(Y) = 4 Var(X).
entries.subject: Probability

entries.fact: Markov's inequality bounds the tail of a non-negative random variable using only its mean: P(X >= a) <= E(X)/a. Chebyshev's inequality uses the variance: P(|X - mu| >= k sigma) <= 1/k^2, so most mass lies within a few standard deviations of the mean. Jensen's inequality says a convex function of an average is at most the average of the function: E(phi(X)) >= phi(E(X)), with the reverse for concave functions.
entries.formula: Markov: P(X >= a) <= E(X)/a for X >= 0, a > 0; Chebyshev: P(|X - mu| >= k sigma) <= 1/k^2; Jensen: E(phi(X)) >= phi(E X) for convex phi
entries.example: A variable with mean 10 and standard deviation 2 lies in [4, 16] with probability at least 1 - 1/9 = 89% by Chebyshev (k = 3). Jensen gives E(1/X) >= 1/E(X) for positive X, so the harmonic mean is below the arithmetic mean.
entries.subject: Probability

entries.fact: The Bernoulli(p) distribution is a single 0/1 trial; the binomial(n,p) counts successes in n independent trials; the geometric(p) counts trials until the first success and is memoryless; the negative binomial counts trials until the r-th success; the hypergeometric counts successes in draws without replacement from a finite population; the discrete uniform gives equal probability to each of n values; the Poisson(lambda) models rare events in a fixed interval.
entries.formula: Binomial: P(X=k) = C(n,k) p^k (1-p)^(n-k), mean np, variance np(1-p); Geometric: P(X=k) = (1-p)^(k-1) p, mean 1/p; Poisson: P(X=k) = e^-lambda lambda^k/k!, mean = variance = lambda; Hypergeometric: P(X=k) = C(K,k) C(N-K,n-k)/C(N,n)
entries.example: The number of heads in 10 fair coin tosses is Binomial(10, 0.5) with mean 5. Calls arriving at 3 per minute follow Poisson(3): the chance of no calls in a minute is e^-3 = 5%. Drawing 5 cards, the number of aces is hypergeometric, not binomial.
entries.subject: Probability

entries.fact: The continuous uniform(a,b) spreads mass evenly over an interval; the exponential(lambda) models waiting times and is memoryless; the gamma(alpha, beta) generalizes the exponential to the waiting time for alpha events; the beta(a,b) lives on (0,1) and models proportions; the Weibull models lifetimes with a changing hazard rate; the normal(mu, sigma^2) is the bell curve that the central limit theorem produces. Many of these are special cases of each other.
entries.formula: Exponential pdf: lambda e^{-lambda x}, mean 1/lambda, memoryless P(X > s+t | X > s) = P(X > t); Gamma mean = alpha/beta; Beta mean = a/(a+b); Weibull pdf: (k/lambda)(x/lambda)^(k-1) e^{-(x/lambda)^k}
entries.example: If buses arrive as a Poisson process at 6 per hour, the waiting time is Exponential(6 per hour) with mean 10 minutes. The sum of two independent Exponential(lambda) variables is Gamma(2, lambda). A proportion with a Beta(2,2) prior is symmetric around 0.5.
entries.subject: Probability

entries.fact: Two random variables have a joint distribution (joint pmf or pdf) from which marginal distributions follow by summing or integrating out the other variable, and conditional distributions by dividing by the marginal. The conditional expectation E(Y|X) is itself a random variable, and the law of total expectation says E(Y) = E(E(Y|X)). Covariance and correlation measure linear association; the joint moment generating function extends the one-variable version; independent variables factor their joint distribution into the product of marginals.
entries.formula: f_{X,Y}(x,y) = f_X(x) f_Y(y) if independent; E(Y) = E(E(Y|X)); Cov(X,Y) = E(XY) - E(X)E(Y); correlation rho = Cov(X,Y)/(sigma_X sigma_Y); Var(X+Y) = Var X + Var Y + 2 Cov(X,Y)
entries.example: Rolling two dice, the sum S and the first die X have E(S|X = 4) = 4 + 3.5 = 7.5. For a bivariate normal with correlation rho, the conditional mean of Y given X = x is mu_Y + rho (sigma_Y/sigma_X)(x - mu_X).
entries.subject: Probability

entries.fact: Order statistics X_(1) <= X_(2) <= ... <= X_(n) are the sorted values of a sample; the minimum and maximum are the extremes. Their distributions follow from the original CDF: the CDF of the maximum is F(x)^n and of the minimum is 1 - (1-F(x))^n. Joint densities of order statistics involve multinomial-type counting of how many observations fall in each interval, and they are the basis of rank-based tests and quantile estimation.
entries.example: For 5 independent Uniform(0,1) draws, the maximum has CDF x^5 and mean 5/6, while the median (3rd order statistic) has mean 1/2. The sample range X_(n) - X_(1) measures spread without assuming a distribution.
entries.subject: Probability

entries.fact: The multinomial distribution generalizes the binomial to k categories with probabilities p_1,...,p_k over n trials; its counts have means n p_i and covariances -n p_i p_j between different categories. The bivariate normal is determined by two means, two variances and a correlation rho; its marginals are normal, its conditionals are normal with a linear regression mean, and zero correlation is equivalent to independence for it (unlike in general).
entries.formula: Multinomial: P(X1=x1,...,Xk=xk) = n!/(x1! ... xk!) p1^x1 ... pk^xk; Cov(Xi, Xj) = -n pi pj; bivariate normal conditional mean: E(Y|X=x) = mu_Y + rho (sigma_Y/sigma_X)(x - mu_X)
entries.example: Rolling a die 60 times, the counts of the six faces are Multinomial(60, 1/6 each). For a bivariate normal with rho = 0.6, sigma_X = sigma_Y = 1, observing X = 1 shifts the mean of Y to 0.6.
entries.subject: Probability

entries.topic: Sampling distributions: chi-square, t and F
entries.fact: The chi-square distribution with nu degrees of freedom is the sum of squares of nu independent standard normals, and it describes the sampling distribution of the sample variance of normal data. The t distribution is a standard normal divided by the square root of an independent chi-square over its degrees of freedom, used for inference about a mean with unknown variance. The F distribution is the ratio of two independent chi-squares each divided by its degrees of freedom, used to compare variances and in ANOVA.
entries.formula: If Z_i are iid N(0,1), sum Z_i^2 is chi-square(nu); (n-1) S^2 / sigma^2 is chi-square(n-1); T = Z / sqrt(V/nu) is t(nu); F = (U/nu1)/(V/nu2) with U, V independent chi-squares
entries.example: With a sample of 10 from a normal population, the 95% confidence interval for the mean uses t_9 (critical value 2.262) rather than the normal 1.96, because sigma is estimated. The ratio of two sample variances follows an F distribution under equal population variances.
entries.subject: Sampling

entries.topic: Modes of convergence, laws of large numbers and the delta method
entries.fact: Convergence in probability means P(|X_n - X| > e) -> 0; almost sure convergence means X_n -> X with probability 1; convergence in distribution means CDFs converge at continuity points; convergence in r-th mean means E|X_n - X|^r -> 0. Almost sure implies in probability implies in distribution; r-th mean implies in probability. Slutsky's lemma lets limits be combined, Borel-Cantelli links summable tail probabilities to finitely-many occurrences, and the weak and strong laws of large numbers make sample averages converge to the mean. The delta method propagates asymptotic normality through a smooth function.
entries.formula: WLLN: Xbar -> mu in probability; SLLN: Xbar -> mu almost surely; delta method: if sqrt(n)(T_n - theta) -> N(0, sigma^2), then sqrt(n)(g(T_n) - g(theta)) -> N(0, (g'(theta))^2 sigma^2)
entries.example: For iid data with mean mu, the sample mean converges to mu by the laws of large numbers. If the sample proportion p-hat has asymptotic variance p(1-p)/n, the delta method gives log(p-hat) an asymptotic variance of (1-p)/(n p).
entries.subject: Probability

entries.fact: A Markov chain is a sequence where the future depends on the present only, described by transition probabilities P_ij. States are classified as transient or recurrent, and recurrent states split into positive recurrent and null recurrent; a state is periodic if returns are possible only at multiples of some period d > 1. An irreducible aperiodic positive recurrent chain has a unique stationary distribution pi with pi = pi P, and n-step transition probabilities converge to it. Finite irreducible chains are always positive recurrent.
entries.formula: Chapman-Kolmogorov: P^(m+n) = P^(m) P^(n); stationary distribution: pi = pi P with sum pi_i = 1; mean recurrence time of state i is 1/pi_i
entries.example: A two-state weather chain with P(sunny->rainy) = 0.3 and P(rainy->sunny) = 0.4 has stationary distribution pi_sunny = 0.4/0.7 = 4/7, pi_rainy = 3/7. A simple symmetric random walk on the integers is null recurrent.
entries.subject: Stochastic Processes

entries.fact: A Poisson process counts events occurring at constant rate lambda with independent increments: the count in any interval is Poisson(lambda * length) and inter-arrival times are independent exponentials. Birth-and-death processes generalize this with state-dependent birth rates lambda_n and death rates mu_n, covering queues (M/M/1) and population models. A pure-birth process has only births (e.g. the Yule process) and a pure-death process only deaths; the stationary distribution of a birth-death process follows from detailed balance when it exists.
entries.formula: Poisson process: P(N(t) = k) = e^{-lambda t} (lambda t)^k / k!; inter-arrival times iid Exponential(lambda); birth-death stationary: pi_n = pi_0 * product_{i=0}^{n-1} (lambda_i / mu_{i+1})
entries.example: Calls arriving at 5 per hour form a Poisson process: the chance of exactly 3 calls in the next hour is e^-5 5^3/6 = 14%. An M/M/1 queue with arrival rate 2 and service rate 3 per hour has stationary probabilities pi_n = (1/3)(2/3)^n.
entries.subject: Stochastic Processes

entries.fact: Brownian motion (the Wiener process) is a continuous-time process starting at 0 with independent, stationary, normally distributed increments: B(t) - B(s) is Normal(0, t - s). Its paths are continuous everywhere but differentiable nowhere, and it is the scaling limit of random walks (Donsker's theorem). It is the basic building block of stochastic calculus and diffusion models in finance and physics.
entries.formula: B(t) - B(s) ~ N(0, t - s) for t > s; Cov(B(s), B(t)) = min(s, t); Var(B(t)) = t
entries.example: A particle's position after t seconds of Brownian motion with diffusion coefficient D has variance 2Dt, so typical displacement grows like sqrt(t), not t. Simulating it means adding N(0, dt) steps.
entries.subject: Stochastic Processes

entries.topic: Sufficiency, minimal sufficiency, completeness and Basu's theorem
entries.fact: A statistic is sufficient if it captures all information about the parameter, so the conditional distribution of the data given the statistic does not depend on the parameter. The factorization theorem identifies sufficient statistics from the likelihood: f(x; theta) = g(T(x); theta) h(x). A minimal sufficient statistic is a coarsest sufficient one. A statistic is complete if no non-zero function of it has zero expectation for all theta; exponential families are complete under mild conditions. Basu's theorem says a complete sufficient statistic is independent of every ancillary statistic (one whose distribution is free of theta).
entries.formula: Factorization: f(x; theta) = g(T(x); theta) h(x) iff T is sufficient; Basu: complete sufficient T is independent of any ancillary statistic
entries.example: For a sample from N(mu, 1), the sample mean is sufficient and complete for mu, while the sample variance is ancillary for mu. For Uniform(0, theta), the maximum is sufficient and complete.
entries.subject: Statistical Inference

entries.topic: Unbiased estimation, UMVUE, Rao-Blackwell and Cramer-Rao inequality
entries.fact: An estimator is unbiased if its expectation equals the parameter. The Rao-Blackwell theorem improves any unbiased estimator by conditioning on a sufficient statistic, never increasing variance. The Lehmann-Scheffe theorem says conditioning an unbiased estimator on a complete sufficient statistic gives the unique uniformly minimum variance unbiased estimator (UMVUE). The Cramer-Rao inequality lower-bounds the variance of any unbiased estimator by the reciprocal of the Fisher information, so an estimator attaining it is efficient.
entries.formula: Cramer-Rao: Var(T) >= 1 / I(theta) for unbiased T, where I(theta) = E[(d/d theta log f(X; theta))^2]; Rao-Blackwell: Var(E(T|S)) <= Var(T) for sufficient S
entries.example: For a sample from N(mu, sigma^2) with sigma known, the sample mean attains the Cramer-Rao bound  sigma^2/n and is the UMVUE. For Poisson(lambda), the sample mean is the UMVUE of lambda.
entries.subject: Statistical Inference

entries.topic: Method of moments estimators and consistency
entries.fact: The method of moments estimates parameters by equating sample moments to population moments and solving; it is simple and often gives a starting value for maximum likelihood. An estimator is consistent if it converges in probability to the true parameter as the sample size grows; the sample mean and sample variance are consistent for their targets under mild conditions. Consistency is a minimal requirement: an inconsistent estimator stays wrong even with infinite data.
entries.formula: Method of moments: set (1/n) sum X_i^k = E_theta(X^k) for k = 1, 2, ... and solve for theta; consistent: T_n -> theta in probability as n -> infinity
entries.example: For Gamma(alpha, beta) data, equating the sample mean to alpha/beta and the sample variance to alpha/beta^2 gives moment estimators of both parameters. The sample proportion is consistent for a population proportion by the weak law of large numbers.
entries.subject: Statistical Inference

entries.topic: Interval estimation with pivotal quantities and coverage probability
entries.fact: A confidence interval is built by inverting a pivotal quantity: a function of data and parameter whose distribution does not depend on the parameter. The classic pivot (Xbar - mu)/(S/sqrt(n)) follows a t distribution, giving the usual interval for a normal mean. Coverage probability is the long-run fraction of intervals that contain the true parameter; a 95% interval covers the truth in 95% of repeated samples, not with 95% probability for one realized interval.
entries.formula: 95% CI for a normal mean: Xbar +- t_{n-1, 0.975} * S/sqrt(n); pivot: (Xbar - mu)/(sigma/sqrt(n)) ~ N(0,1) when sigma is known
entries.example: With n = 16, Xbar = 10 and S = 4, the 95% CI for mu is 10 +- 2.131 * 4/4 = (7.87, 12.13). A pivotal quantity for an exponential scale parameter uses the ratio Xbar/theta.
entries.subject: Statistical Inference

entries.topic: Neyman-Pearson lemma, most powerful and uniformly most powerful tests
entries.fact: For testing a simple null against a simple alternative, the Neyman-Pearson lemma says the most powerful test of a given size rejects for large values of the likelihood ratio. When the family has monotone likelihood ratio (MLR), the same one-sided test is uniformly most powerful (UMP) for all alternatives on one side. Unbiasedness adds the requirement that power is at least the size under the alternative, giving uniformly most powerful unbiased (UMPU) tests; one-parameter exponential families admit UMPU tests for two-sided hypotheses.
entries.formula: Neyman-Pearson: reject when f1(x)/f0(x) > k, with k chosen so size = alpha; MLR: the likelihood ratio is monotone in a statistic T(x)
entries.example: Testing mu = 0 against mu > 0 for N(mu, 1) data, the UMP test rejects when Xbar is large: Xbar > 1.645/sqrt(n) at size 5%. The Karlin-Rubin theorem extends this to all MLR families.
entries.subject: Hypothesis Testing

entries.topic: Likelihood ratio tests and large sample tests
entries.fact: The likelihood ratio test compares the maximized likelihood under the null to the unrestricted maximum: lambda = L(theta_hat_0)/L(theta_hat). Wilks' theorem says -2 log lambda is asymptotically chi-square with degrees of freedom equal to the number of constraints, giving large-sample tests and confidence regions. The Wald test uses the estimate and its standard error, and the score test uses the score at the null; all three agree asymptotically.
