entries.example: A 1 uC point charge at 1 m in air: E = 9 x 10^9 x 1e-6 / 1^2 = 9000 V/m radially outward. At 2 m the field is 2250 V/m, one quarter as large.
entries.fact: Gauss law says the total electric flux through any closed surface equals the charge enclosed divided by epsilon_0. By symmetry it gives the field directly: a point charge gives E falling as 1/r^2, an infinite line charge gives E falling as 1/r, and an infinite plane sheet gives a constant field. Electric field is the negative gradient of potential, and potential is found by integrating the field. A dielectric reduces the field by its relative permittivity.
entries.formula: Integral form: integral_S D . dS = Q_enclosed; E = Q / (4 pi epsilon r^2) for a point charge; E = lambda / (2 pi epsilon r) for a line charge; E = sigma / (2 epsilon) for a plane sheet; E = -grad V.
entries.subject: Electromagnetic Fields
entries.topic: Gauss law and electric field of charge distributions

entries.example: A wire carrying 10 A produces B = (4 pi x 10^-7 x 10) / (2 pi x 0.1) = 2 x 10^-5 T = 20 uT at 0.1 m, directed tangentially around the wire.
entries.fact: Biot-Savart law gives the magnetic field of a current element: dB is proportional to I dl cross r-hat over r^2. Ampere law in integral form says the line integral of B around a closed path equals mu_0 times the current enclosed. For a long straight wire this gives B = mu_0 I / (2 pi r), circling the wire by the right-hand rule. The curl form, curl B = mu_0 J, is one of Maxwell equations.
entries.formula: dB = (mu_0 / 4 pi) I dl x r-hat / r^2; integral_C B . dl = mu_0 I_enclosed; long wire: B = mu_0 I / (2 pi r); curl B = mu_0 J.
entries.subject: Electromagnetic Fields

entries.example: A coil with N = 100 turns carrying 2 A has MMF = 200 ampere-turns. If the core reluctance is 1 x 10^6 A-turns/Wb, flux Phi = 200 / 1e6 = 0.2 mWb. Two coils of 4 mH and 9 mH with k = 0.5 have M = 0.5 x sqrt(36) = 3 mH.
entries.fact: A magnetic circuit obeys the same form as an electric circuit: magnetomotive force (MMF = N I) drives flux Phi through a reluctance R = l / (mu A), just as voltage drives current through resistance. Self-inductance is L = N Phi / I, the flux linkage per ampere; a changing current induces v = L di/dt. Two coupled coils have mutual inductance M = k sqrt(L1 L2), with coupling coefficient k between 0 and 1, and the induced voltage in one coil is M times the rate of change of current in the other.
entries.formula: MMF = N I; reluctance R = l / (mu A); Phi = MMF / R; L = N Phi / I; v = L di/dt; M = k sqrt(L1 L2); v2 = M di1/dt.
entries.subject: Electromagnetic Fields
entries.topic: Magnetic circuits, reluctance, self and mutual inductance

entries.example: x(t) = e^{-2t} u(t) has X(omega) = 1/(2 + j omega). Its magnitude is 1/sqrt(4 + omega^2), falling to half its DC value when omega = 2 sqrt(3) rad/s.
entries.fact: The Fourier transform decomposes a non-periodic signal into its frequency components; the inverse transform rebuilds the time signal from them. It turns convolution into multiplication and differentiation into multiplication by j omega, which is why it solves linear systems and differential equations so cleanly. The transform of a rectangular pulse is a sinc, and of an exponential e^{-a t} u(t) is 1/(a + j omega). Parseval theorem says total energy is the same in time and frequency.
entries.formula: X(omega) = integral_{-inf}^{inf} x(t) e^{-j omega t} dt; x(t) = (1/2 pi) integral X(omega) e^{j omega t} d omega; convolution: x * h <-> X(omega) H(omega); energy: integral |x(t)|^2 dt = (1/2 pi) integral |X(omega)|^2 d omega.
entries.subject: Signals & Systems

entries.example: Solve y' + 2y = 0, y(0) = 3: s Y(s) - 3 + 2 Y(s) = 0, so Y(s) = 3/(s + 2), and y(t) = 3 e^{-2t}. The single pole at s = -2 is in the left half-plane, so the response decays.
entries.fact: The Laplace transform turns a linear differential equation with initial conditions into an algebraic equation in s, which is why it is the standard tool for transient analysis and control. Differentiation becomes multiplication by s (minus the initial value), integration becomes division by s, and a time delay becomes multiplication by e^{-sT}. The transfer function of a system is the Laplace transform of its impulse response, and poles of the transfer function decide stability: all poles in the left half-plane means stable.
entries.formula: X(s) = integral_0^{inf} x(t) e^{-s t} dt; L{dx/dt} = s X(s) - x(0); L{1} = 1/s; L{e^{-a t}} = 1/(s + a); L{sin omega t} = omega / (s^2 + omega^2); transfer function H(s) = Y(s)/X(s).
entries.subject: Signals & Systems
entries.topic: Laplace transform and solving differential equations

entries.example: x[n] = (0.5)^n u[n] has X(z) = 1 / (1 - 0.5 z^{-1}) = z / (z - 0.5), ROC |z| > 0.5. The pole at 0.5 is inside the unit circle, so the sequence decays and the system is stable.
entries.fact: The Z-transform is the discrete-time twin of the Laplace transform: it turns difference equations into algebra and convolution into multiplication. The region of convergence (ROC) decides causality and stability: a causal sequence has an ROC outside the outermost pole, and a system is stable if the unit circle lies inside the ROC. Poles inside the unit circle give decaying responses; poles outside give growing ones.
entries.formula: X(z) = sum_{n=-inf}^{inf} x[n] z^{-n}; x[n] = a^n u[n] <-> X(z) = 1 / (1 - a z^{-1}), ROC |z| > |a|; delay: x[n-1] <-> z^{-1} X(z); convolution: x * h <-> X(z) H(z).
entries.subject: Signals & Systems

entries.example: A 220 V shunt motor draws Ia = 10 A with Ra = 1 ohm: back-EMF Eb = 220 - 10 x 1 = 210 V. Halving the flux (field weakening) roughly doubles the speed, at the cost of lower torque.
entries.fact: A DC machine converts between electrical and mechanical energy through the interaction of armature current and flux. As a generator the induced EMF is E = P Phi N Z / (60 A); as a motor the same EMF acts as back-EMF opposing the supply, and speed is roughly (V - Ia Ra) / (k Phi). A shunt motor holds speed nearly constant, a series motor gives very high starting torque but must never run unloaded, and speed is controlled by varying armature voltage or field flux (field weakening raises speed above base speed).
entries.formula: Generated EMF Eg = P Phi N Z / (60 A); motor: V = Eb + Ia Ra; Eb = k Phi omega; torque T = k Phi Ia; speed N proportional to (V - Ia Ra) / Phi.
entries.subject: Electrical Machines
entries.topic: DC machines: motoring, generating and speed control

entries.example: A 4-pole, 50 Hz motor has Ns = 1500 rpm. Running at Nr = 1440 rpm, slip s = (1500 - 1440) / 1500 = 0.04, and rotor frequency is 0.04 x 50 = 2 Hz.
entries.fact: The stator rotating field at synchronous speed Ns = 120 f / P induces currents in the rotor, and the rotor chases the field but never catches it: slip s = (Ns - Nr) / Ns. Rotor frequency is s f, torque is proportional to s R2 / (R2^2 + (s X2)^2), and maximum torque occurs at slip s_max = R2 / X2. Adding rotor resistance (slip-ring motor) raises starting torque and lowers starting current. No-load and blocked-rotor tests give the equivalent-circuit parameters.
entries.formula: Ns = 120 f / P; slip s = (Ns - Nr) / Ns; rotor frequency = s f; T proportional to s R2 / (R2^2 + (s X2)^2); maximum torque at s_max = R2 / X2.
entries.subject: Electrical Machines
entries.topic: Three-phase induction motor: slip and torque-speed characteristics

entries.example: A generator with no-load voltage E = 253 V and full-load terminal voltage V = 230 V has regulation (253 - 230) / 230 = 10 percent. Raising excitation raises E and supplies more reactive power to the grid.
entries.fact: A synchronous generator runs exactly at synchronous speed, with frequency fixed by speed and pole count, f = P N / 120. Its terminal voltage falls with load because of armature reaction and synchronous reactance Xs; voltage regulation is (E - V) / V at constant excitation, often found by the synchronous-impedance method. Generators in parallel must match voltage, frequency, phase sequence and phase angle before synchronising, after which real power is shared by the prime mover input and reactive power by excitation.
entries.formula: f = P N / 120; regulation = (E - V) / V x 100 percent; power output P = (E V / Xs) sin(delta), where delta is the load (power) angle; E = V + j Ia Xs (cylindrical rotor, ignoring resistance).
entries.subject: Electrical Machines
entries.topic: Synchronous machines: regulation and parallel operation

entries.example: A transformer delivers 8 kW with iron loss 200 W and copper loss 300 W: eta = 8000 / (8000 + 200 + 300) = 8000 / 8500 = 94.1 percent. If the load halves, copper loss falls to one quarter, 75 W.
entries.fact: The open-circuit test (rated voltage on one side, other side open) measures core (iron) loss and the magnetising branch, because copper loss is negligible at no-load current. The short-circuit test (rated current, low voltage) measures copper loss and the series impedance, because core loss is negligible at low voltage. Voltage regulation is the rise in secondary voltage from full load to no load at constant primary voltage; efficiency is output over output plus iron plus copper loss, and is maximum when iron loss equals copper loss.
entries.formula: OC test: iron loss Pi at rated V; SC test: copper loss Pcu at rated I; regulation = (V_no-load - V_full-load) / V_full-load x 100 percent; efficiency eta = output / (output + Pi + Pcu); maximum efficiency when Pi = Pcu.
entries.subject: Electrical Machines

entries.example: On a 10 MVA, 11 kV base, Z_base = 11^2 / 10 = 12.1 ohm. An impedance of 1.21 ohm is 1.21 / 12.1 = 0.1 pu.
entries.fact: Per-unit values express voltages, currents, impedances and powers as fractions of chosen base values, so transformers disappear from the numbers and equipment of very different ratings can be compared directly. Base impedance is V_base^2 / S_base, and a per-unit impedance changes with the square of the voltage-base ratio when the base changes. In load-flow work the network is described by the bus admittance matrix Ybus, where the diagonal element is the sum of admittances connected to that bus and an off-diagonal element is minus the admittance between the two buses.
entries.formula: pu value = actual value / base value; Z_base = V_base^2 / S_base; Z_pu(new) = Z_pu(old) x (S_base(new)/S_base(old)) x (V_base(old)/V_base(new))^2; Ybus_ii = sum of admittances at bus i; Ybus_ij = -y_ij.
entries.subject: Power Systems
entries.topic: Per-unit quantities and bus admittance matrix

entries.example: Va = 230 at 0 deg, Vb = 230 at -120 deg, Vc = 230 at 120 deg is balanced, so V1 = 230 V and V0 = V2 = 0. If Vc becomes 0 (a fault), zero and negative sequence components appear and the sequence networks must be solved together.
entries.fact: Any unbalanced three-phase set can be resolved into positive-, negative- and zero-sequence components using the operator a = e^{j120 deg}. A balanced system has only positive sequence; zero sequence needs a return path (neutral or earth) and is absent in a three-wire system. Fault currents are found by connecting the sequence networks: a single line-to-ground fault connects all three in series, a line-to-line fault connects positive and negative in parallel, and a three-phase fault uses positive sequence only.
entries.subject: Power Systems

entries.example: A machine with Pm = 1.0 pu and Pmax = 2.0 pu is initially at delta0 = 30 deg (sin delta0 = 0.5). If a fault drives the angle to delta_c = 60 deg, A1 = integral of (1 - 2 sin delta) from 30 to 60 deg; stability depends on whether the post-fault curve provides an equal A2 before delta reaches 150 deg, where Pe falls back to Pm.
entries.fact: The swing equation describes the rotor angle of a synchronous machine: accelerating power Pm - Pe drives the angle, with inertia constant H. During a fault Pe collapses and the rotor gains kinetic energy, shown as the accelerating area A1 on the power-angle curve. After clearing, Pe exceeds Pm and the rotor gives the energy back, shown as the decelerating area A2. The machine stays in synchronism on the first swing if a decelerating area equal to A1 is available before the angle reaches the unstable equilibrium point.
entries.formula: Swing equation: (2H / omega_s) d^2 delta / dt^2 = Pm - Pe; Pe = Pmax sin(delta); stability if A1 = integral_{delta0}^{delta_c} (Pm - Pe) d delta equals A2 = integral_{delta_c}^{delta_max} (Pe - Pm) d delta.
entries.subject: Power Systems
entries.topic: Equal area criterion for transient stability

entries.example: Two units have incremental costs 0.02 P1 + 10 and 0.04 P2 + 8 Rs/MWh. At lambda = 20, P1 = (20 - 10)/0.02 = 500 MW and P2 = (20 - 8)/0.04 = 300 MW, together meeting an 800 MW demand at equal incremental cost.
entries.fact: Economic load dispatch shares the total demand among generators so total fuel cost is minimum, subject to meeting the load. Without losses the optimum is equal incremental fuel cost for every unit on line: each unit is loaded until its dF/dP equals the system lambda. With transmission losses, each unit's incremental cost is multiplied by its penalty factor, 1 / (1 - dP_L/dP_i), so a unit whose output raises losses a lot is loaded less. Units are kept within their minimum and maximum limits.
entries.formula: Optimum (no losses): dF1/dP1 = dF2/dP2 = ... = lambda; with losses: (dF_i/dP_i) x [1 / (1 - dP_L/dP_i)] = lambda; sum of P_i = demand (+ losses).
entries.subject: Power Systems
entries.topic: Economic load dispatch with and without losses

entries.example: s^3 + 3 s^2 + 2 s + 5: Routh rows are s^3: 1, 2; s^2: 3, 5; s^1: (3x2 - 5)/3 = 1/3; s^0: 5. First column 1, 3, 1/3, 5 is all positive, so the system is stable.
entries.fact: Routh-Hurwitz decides stability from the characteristic polynomial alone, without finding the roots. Build the Routh array from the polynomial coefficients; the system is stable if and only if every element of the first column has the same sign (all positive for a polynomial with positive leading coefficient). Each sign change in the first column counts one root in the right half-plane. A zero in the first column is handled by replacing it with a small epsilon, and a whole zero row means symmetric roots on the imaginary axis, handled with an auxiliary polynomial.
entries.formula: For a(s) = a_n s^n + ... + a_0, form the Routh array; stable iff no sign changes in the first column. Number of right-half-plane poles = number of sign changes. Auxiliary polynomial from the row above a zero row.
entries.subject: Control Systems

entries.example: If at the gain-crossover frequency the phase of G(j omega) is -150 deg, the phase margin is 180 - 150 = 30 deg, so the closed loop is stable with moderate damping.
entries.fact: A Bode plot shows magnitude in dB and phase in degrees against log frequency, built by adding the contributions of poles, zeros and gain. Gain margin is how much the gain can rise before the phase reaches -180 deg at the phase-crossover frequency; phase margin is 180 deg plus the phase at the gain-crossover frequency (where magnitude is 0 dB). Positive gain and phase margins mean a stable closed loop, and larger phase margin (typically 30 to 60 deg) means a better-damped, less oscillatory response.
entries.formula: Magnitude in dB = 20 log10 |G(j omega)|; gain margin GM = -20 log10 |G(j omega_pc)| at phase -180 deg; phase margin PM = 180 deg + angle G(j omega_gc) at |G| = 1 (0 dB).
entries.subject: Control Systems
entries.topic: Bode plots and gain and phase margins

entries.example: For G(s) = K / [s (s+1) (s+2)] there are 3 poles and no finite zeros, so 3 branches go to infinity along asymptotes at 60, 180 and 300 deg, meeting at centroid (-1 - 2) / 3 = -1. A lead compensator adds a zero near the crossover to pull the locus left and raise the phase margin.
entries.fact: The root locus plots how the closed-loop poles move as the gain K goes from 0 to infinity, starting at the open-loop poles and ending at the open-loop zeros (or at infinity along asymptotes). A point is on the locus if the angle condition holds: the sum of angles from zeros minus the sum from poles is an odd multiple of 180 deg. Lag compensation improves steady-state accuracy, lead compensation adds phase near crossover and improves transient response and stability margins, and lag-lead combines both.
entries.formula: Angle condition: sum of angles from zeros - sum of angles from poles = (2k + 1) x 180 deg; asymptotes at angles (2k+1) x 180 deg / (n - m), centroid = (sum of poles - sum of zeros) / (n - m).
entries.subject: Control Systems

entries.example: A buck converter from 12 V with D = 0.5 gives 6 V. The same duty ratio in a boost converter gives 12 / 0.5 = 24 V, and in a buck-boost gives -12 V (inverted).
entries.fact: A buck converter steps voltage down, a boost steps it up, and a buck-boost can do either but inverts the polarity, all by switching an inductor with duty ratio D (fraction of the period the switch is on). In continuous conduction the output follows the duty ratio: buck Vout = D Vin, boost Vout = Vin / (1 - D), buck-boost Vout = -D Vin / (1 - D). Thyristors, MOSFETs and IGBTs are the switching devices; the inductor and output capacitor smooth the switched waveform.
entries.formula: Buck: Vout = D Vin; Boost: Vout = Vin / (1 - D); Buck-boost: Vout = -D Vin / (1 - D); D = Ton / T, 0 < D < 1.
entries.subject: Power Systems
entries.topic: Buck, boost and buck-boost DC-DC converters

entries.example: W1 = 2000 W and W2 = 1000 W give P = 3000 W and tan(phi) = sqrt(3) x 1000 / 3000 = 0.577, so phi = 30 deg and power factor = 0.866 lagging.
entries.fact: In a three-wire three-phase system, two wattmeters suffice to measure total power: the sum of their readings is the total active power, regardless of balance. The difference of the readings gives the reactive power, and the power factor follows from the ratio of the difference to the sum. If the power factor is below 0.5, one wattmeter reads negative (its coil connections must be reversed to read it, and the reading is taken as negative).
entries.formula: Total power P = W1 + W2; reactive power Q = sqrt(3) (W1 - W2); tan(phi) = sqrt(3) (W1 - W2) / (W1 + W2); power factor = cos(phi).
entries.subject: Power Systems

entries.example: A = [[1, 2], [2, 4]] has its second row twice the first, so rank = 1 and det = 0. The system A x = [3, 6] is consistent (infinitely many solutions), but A x = [3, 5] is inconsistent.
entries.fact: The rank of a matrix is the number of linearly independent rows or columns. A system A x = b has a solution if and only if rank(A) = rank([A|b]); it is unique if that rank also equals the number of unknowns, and has infinitely many solutions if the rank is smaller. Vectors are linearly independent if only the trivial combination gives zero, and a basis is an independent set that spans the space. Eigenvalues and eigenvectors come from det(A - lambda I) = 0, as in the EE entry on eigenvalues.
entries.formula: rank(A) = number of independent rows = number of independent columns; A x = b consistent iff rank(A) = rank([A | b]); unique solution iff rank = n (unknowns); det(A - lambda I) = 0 gives eigenvalues.
entries.subject: Engineering Mathematics
entries.topic: Linear algebra: rank, basis and solution of linear equations

entries.example: For F = (x, 0, 0), div F = 1 and curl F = 0. The flux of F out of the unit cube is integral of div F over the volume = 1 x 1 = 1, matching the surface integral.
entries.fact: The gradient of a scalar points in the direction of fastest increase; the divergence of a vector field measures net outflow per unit volume; the curl measures local rotation. A field with zero curl is conservative and can be written as a gradient, and a field with zero divergence is solenoidal. Gauss, Stokes and Green theorems convert volume integrals of divergence and surface integrals of curl into surface and line integrals, and are used throughout electromagnetics.
entries.formula: grad f = (df/dx, df/dy, df/dz); div F = dFx/dx + dFy/dy + dFz/dz; curl F = grad x F; Gauss: integral_V div F dV = integral_S F . dS; Stokes: integral_S curl F . dS = integral_C F . dr.
entries.subject: Engineering Mathematics
entries.topic: Vector analysis: gradient, divergence, curl and integral theorems

entries.example: f(z) = 1/(z^2 + 4) has a simple pole at z = 2i with residue 1/(4i). On a small circle around 2i only, the integral is 2 pi i x 1/(4i) = pi/2.
entries.fact: A function is analytic where it is differentiable in the complex sense (Cauchy-Riemann equations hold); analytic functions have power-series (Taylor) expansions, and functions with isolated singularities have Laurent expansions with negative powers. The residue theorem says the integral around a closed contour is 2 pi i times the sum of residues inside, which evaluates many real integrals. Convergence tests (ratio, root, comparison) decide whether a series converges.
entries.formula: Cauchy-Riemann: du/dx = dv/dy, du/dy = -dv/dx; integral_C f(z) dz = 2 pi i x sum of residues; simple pole residue = lim_{z->z0} (z - z0) f(z); ratio test: series converges if lim |a_{n+1}/a_n| < 1.
entries.subject: Engineering Mathematics
entries.topic: Complex analysis: analytic functions, Taylor and Laurent series, residue theorem

entries.example: A network with Vth = 6 V and Rth = 2 ohm feeding a 4 ohm load delivers V = 6 x 4/6 = 4 V. Its Norton form is a 3 A source in parallel with 2 ohm.
entries.fact: Any linear network seen from two terminals is equivalent to a voltage source Vth in series with Rth, or a current source IN = Vth/Rth in parallel with Rth. Vth is the open-circuit voltage and Rth the resistance looking back with independent sources turned off. The reciprocity theorem says that in a linear network with only one source, swapping the source and the measurement point leaves the measured response unchanged. Superposition lets each independent source be considered alone, with the others turned off.
entries.formula: Vth = open-circuit voltage; Rth = Vth / I_sc; IN = Vth / Rth; reciprocity: response at port 2 to a source at port 1 equals response at port 1 to the same source at port 2.
entries.subject: Networks

entries.example: V_rms = 230 V, I_rms = 10 A at power factor 0.8 lagging: P = 230 x 10 x 0.8 = 1840 W, Q = 230 x 10 x 0.6 = 1380 VAR, and apparent power is 2300 VA.
entries.fact: In sinusoidal steady state, voltages and currents are phasors and impedances are complex: Z = R + jX, with X = omega L for an inductor and -1/(omega C) for a capacitor. Complex power S = V_rms I_rms* = P + jQ, where P is average power in watts, Q is reactive power in VAR, and |S| is apparent power in VA. Maximum average power is delivered when the load impedance is the complex conjugate of the source impedance.
entries.formula: Z_L = j omega L; Z_C = 1/(j omega C); S = V_rms I_rms* = P + j Q; |S| = V_rms I_rms; power factor = cos(phi) = P/|S|; maximum power when Z_L = Zth*.
entries.subject: Networks
entries.topic: Phasor analysis, complex power and maximum power transfer

entries.example: Series RLC with R = 20 ohm, L = 10 mH, C = 100 nF: omega_0 = 1/sqrt(1e-9) = 31623 rad/s, zeta = 10 x sqrt(100e-9/10e-3) = 10 x 0.00316 = 0.0316, so the transient is a lightly damped oscillation near 5033 Hz.
entries.fact: Network equations in the time domain become algebraic in the s-domain: a resistor stays R, an inductor becomes sL (plus an initial-flux voltage source), and a capacitor becomes 1/(sC) (plus an initial-charge source). Solving for the s-domain current or voltage and inverting gives the transient, whose character is set by the poles: real distinct poles give overdamped decay, a repeated pole gives critically damped decay, and complex poles give damped oscillation. The damping ratio and natural frequency of a series RLC circuit are zeta = (R/2) sqrt(C/L) and omega_0 = 1/sqrt(LC).
entries.formula: s-domain: R -> R; L -> sL; C -> 1/(sC); series RLC: s^2 + (R/L) s + 1/(LC) = 0; omega_0 = 1/sqrt(LC); zeta = (R/2) sqrt(C/L); zeta < 1 underdamped, = 1 critically damped, > 1 overdamped.
entries.subject: Networks
entries.topic: Transient analysis of RL, RC and RLC circuits with Laplace transform

entries.fact: Fourier series handles periodic signals, the Fourier transform handles aperiodic ones, the DTFT handles discrete-time signals (periodic in frequency with period 2 pi), and the DFT is the sampled, finite-length version used in computation. The DFT of length N is X[k] = sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n] e^{-j 2 pi k n / N}, and the FFT computes it in O(N log N) instead of O(N^2). Sampling in one domain causes periodicity in the other, which is why aliasing appears when sampling is too slow.
entries.formula: Fourier series: periodic -> discrete spectrum; FT: X(omega) = integral x(t) e^{-j omega t} dt; DTFT: X(e^{j w}) = sum_n x[n] e^{-j w n}; DFT: X[k] = sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n] e^{-j 2 pi k n / N}.
entries.subject: Signals & Systems
entries.topic: Fourier series, Fourier transform, DTFT and DFT

entries.example: x = [1, 2] convolved with h = [1, 1] gives y = [1, 3, 2]. A system with H(z) = 1/(1 - 0.5 z^{-1}) has one pole at 0.5, inside the unit circle, so it is stable and causal.
entries.fact: An LTI system is fully described by its impulse response h[n]: the output is the convolution sum of the input with h. In the z-domain the transfer function H(z) = Y(z)/X(z) is a ratio of polynomials; its poles decide stability (all inside the unit circle) and causality, and its zeros shape the frequency response. The frequency response is H(e^{j w}), obtained by evaluating H(z) on the unit circle. Group delay is minus the derivative of phase with respect to frequency, and phase delay is minus phase divided by frequency.
entries.formula: y[n] = sum_k x[k] h[n-k]; H(z) = Y(z)/X(z); stable iff all poles satisfy |p| < 1; frequency response H(e^{j w}) = H(z) at z = e^{j w}; group delay tau_g = -d(angle H)/d w.
entries.subject: Signals & Systems
entries.topic: Z-transform, LTI systems, convolution, poles and zeros

entries.example: Silicon with n = 1e16 cm^-3 and electron mobility 1350 cm^2/Vs has resistivity rho = 1 / (1.6e-19 x 1e16 x 1350) = about 0.46 ohm-cm. At 300 K, D_n = mu_n x 0.02585 = about 34.9 cm^2/s.
entries.fact: In a semiconductor, electrons in the conduction band and holes in the valence band carry current. Intrinsic carrier concentration n_i grows with temperature; doping adds donors (n-type, electrons majority) or acceptors (p-type, holes majority), with n p = n_i^2 in equilibrium. Drift current follows the electric field with mobility mu; diffusion current follows the concentration gradient with diffusivity D, linked by the Einstein relation D/mu = kT/q (about 25.85 mV at 300 K). Poisson equation links charge to potential, and the continuity equation is conservation of carriers including generation and recombination.
entries.formula: Drift: J_n(drift) = q n mu_n E; diffusion: J_n(diff) = q D_n dn/dx; Einstein: D/mu = kT/q = about 25.85 mV at 300 K; n p = n_i^2; resistivity rho = 1 / [q (n mu_n + p mu_p)]; Poisson: d^2 V/dx^2 = -rho_charge / epsilon.
entries.subject: Electronic Devices
entries.topic: Semiconductors: energy bands, drift, diffusion and continuity

entries.example: With N_A = 1e17 cm^-3, N_D = 1e15 cm^-3 and n_i = 1e10 cm^-3, Vbi = 0.02585 x ln(1e32/1e20) = 0.02585 x 27.63 = about 0.71 V. A 5.1 V Zener in reverse breakdown holds about 5.1 V across a load despite supply changes.
entries.fact: A p-n junction has a built-in potential Vbi = Vt ln(N_A N_D / n_i^2) across its depletion region; forward bias shrinks the barrier and current grows exponentially, reverse bias widens it and only a small saturation current flows until breakdown. A Zener diode is designed to break down at a controlled reverse voltage and so holds a nearly constant voltage, used as a regulator. An LED emits light when carriers recombine, a photodiode generates current from absorbed light (reverse biased), and a solar cell is a large photodiode operated to deliver power to a load.
entries.formula: Diode: I = I_s (e^{V/(eta Vt)} - 1), Vt = kT/q = about 26 mV at 300 K; Vbi = Vt ln(N_A N_D / n_i^2); depletion width W proportional to sqrt(Vbi - V); Zener: reverse breakdown at a fixed Vz.
entries.subject: Electronic Devices
entries.topic: P-N junction, Zener diode, LED, photodiode and solar cell

entries.example: A BJT biased at Ic = 1 mA has gm = 1e-3 / 0.026 = about 38.5 mS, so with Rc = 2 k ohm the small-signal voltage gain is about -77. A MOSFET with mu C_ox (W/L) = 1 mA/V^2 and overdrive 1 V carries Id = 0.5 mA.
entries.fact: A BJT is a current-controlled device: collector current Ic = beta Ib in active mode, with transconductance gm = Ic/Vt. A MOSFET is voltage-controlled: in saturation Id = (1/2) mu C_ox (W/L) (Vgs - Vth)^2, with gm = sqrt(2 mu C_ox (W/L) Id). A MOS capacitor goes from accumulation through depletion to inversion as gate voltage rises, and inversion is what forms the MOSFET channel. Small-signal analysis replaces each device by its gm and output resistance to find voltage gain, input and output resistance; gain falls at high frequency because of device capacitances (Miller effect) and at low frequency because of coupling capacitors.
entries.formula: BJT: Ic = beta Ib; gm = Ic/Vt; MOSFET saturation: Id = (1/2) mu C_ox (W/L)(Vgs - Vth)^2; gm = 2 Id / (Vgs - Vth); common-emitter gain about -gm Rc (with load); common-source gain about -gm Rd.
entries.subject: Electronic Devices
entries.topic: BJT, MOSFET and MOS capacitor; small-signal amplifiers

entries.example: A full-wave rectifier with Vm = 10 V gives Vdc = 20/pi = 6.37 V before filtering. With a 100 uF capacitor, 50 Hz mains and 10 mA load, ripple is about 0.01 / (2 x 50 x 100e-6) = 1 V peak-to-peak.
entries.fact: A clipper uses a diode (and a reference voltage) to cut off the part of a waveform above or below a level; a clamper uses a diode plus a capacitor to shift the whole waveform up or down by a DC level without changing its shape. A half-wave rectifier passes only one half-cycle (average output Vm/pi), a full-wave rectifier uses both (average 2 Vm/pi), and a capacitor filter smooths the ripple, with ripple falling as capacitance and load resistance rise. Peak inverse voltage ratings decide diode choice: a bridge rectifier needs PIV of Vm, a centre-tapped full-wave needs 2 Vm.
entries.formula: Half-wave average: Vdc = Vm / pi; full-wave average: Vdc = 2 Vm / pi; ripple (capacitor filter, full-wave): Vr(pp) about I_load / (2 f C); bridge PIV = Vm; centre-tapped PIV = 2 Vm.
entries.subject: Analog Circuits
entries.topic: Diode circuits: clipping, clamping and rectifiers

entries.example: An integrator with R = 10 k ohm and C = 100 nF fed a constant 1 V gives a ramp of slope -1/(RC) = -1000 V/s, reaching -1 V in 1 ms. A Schmitt trigger with Vsat = 12 V, R1 = 1 k ohm and R2 = 9 k ohm has thresholds at +/- 1.2 V.
entries.fact: An ideal op-amp has infinite gain, infinite input resistance and zero output resistance, so with negative feedback the two inputs sit at the same voltage (virtual short) and draw no current. That gives the inverting gain -Rf/R1, the non-inverting gain 1 + Rf/R1, summers, differentiators and integrators (output -1/(RC) times the integral of the input). A Schmitt trigger uses positive feedback to give two thresholds and hysteresis, cleaning up noisy signals; an oscillator needs loop gain of at least 1 with zero total phase shift (Barkhausen criterion). Active filters use op-amps with RC networks: a Sallen-Key second-order low-pass has fc = 1/(2 pi sqrt(R1 R2 C1 C2)) and Q = 0.707 gives a Butterworth (maximally flat) response.
entries.formula: Inverting gain = -Rf/R1; non-inverting gain = 1 + Rf/R1; integrator: Vo = -(1/RC) integral Vi dt; differentiator: Vo = -RC dVi/dt; Schmitt thresholds = +/- [R1/(R1+R2)] Vsat; Sallen-Key fc = 1/(2 pi sqrt(R1 R2 C1 C2)); Barkhausen: loop gain = 1 at 0 deg (or 360 deg) phase.
entries.subject: Analog Circuits
entries.topic: Op-amp circuits: amplifiers, integrators, filters, Schmitt trigger and oscillators

entries.example: F(A,B,C) = sum m(1,3,5,7) is 1 exactly when C = 1, so the minimised form is F = C, one wire and no gates. The 4-bit binary number 1101 is 13 in decimal.
entries.fact: Digital numbers are binary; integers convert by repeated division by 2 and fractions by repeated multiplication by 2, and floating-point numbers store a sign, exponent and mantissa (IEEE 754). Combinational outputs depend only on present inputs: Boolean algebra and Karnaugh maps minimise the sum-of-products form, grouping 1s in powers of two (pairs, quads, octets), including wrap-around and don't-care cells. Standard blocks are adders, comparators, code converters, multiplexers (a 2^n-to-1 mux needs n select lines) and decoders. A static CMOS gate uses a PMOS pull-up network dual to the NMOS pull-down network.
entries.formula: Binary 1011 = 1x8 + 0x4 + 1x2 + 1 = 11 decimal; De Morgan: NOT(A B) = (NOT A) + (NOT B), NOT(A + B) = (NOT A)(NOT B); 2^n-to-1 multiplexer needs n select lines; K-map group size must be a power of 2.
entries.subject: Digital Circuits
entries.topic: Number systems, combinational logic and Karnaugh maps

entries.example: A 3-bit ripple counter with 10 ns clock-to-Q per flip-flop accumulates 30 ns of delay, so its reliable maximum clock is about 1/30 ns = 33 MHz. A mod-10 counter needs 4 flip-flops (2^3 = 8 is too few).
entries.fact: Sequential outputs depend on present inputs and past history, stored in latches (level-sensitive) and flip-flops (edge-triggered: D, JK, T). Counters and shift registers are built from flip-flops; an n-bit ripple counter divides by 2^n, and a finite state machine is described by a state diagram with states, inputs, outputs and transitions (Mealy outputs depend on input and state, Moore on state only). Timing must satisfy setup time (data stable before the clock edge) and hold time (data stable after it); the critical path is the longest combinational delay between flip-flops and sets the maximum clock frequency.
entries.formula: Mod-n counter needs ceil(log2 n) flip-flops; max clock frequency f_max = 1 / (t_clk-to-Q + t_comb(max) + t_setup); setup slack = T_clk - (t_clk-to-Q + t_comb + t_setup) must be >= 0.
entries.subject: Digital Circuits
entries.topic: Sequential circuits: latches, flip-flops, counters, FSMs and timing

entries.example: An 8-bit ADC with Vref = 5 V has LSB = 5/256 = 19.5 mV, so an input of 1.00 V reads about code 51. A 4-bit flash ADC needs 15 comparators.
entries.fact: An ADC converts an analog voltage to a digital code; an n-bit ADC with reference Vref has LSB step Vref / 2^n, and successive-approximation, flash (fastest, 2^n - 1 comparators) and integrating types trade speed against accuracy. A DAC does the reverse, for example with an R-2R ladder. ROM is non-volatile, SRAM is fast and uses 6 transistors per cell, DRAM is dense but needs refresh. In computer organisation, the ALU does arithmetic and logic, the control unit fetches and decodes instructions, addressing modes (immediate, direct, indirect, register) say where operands live, and pipelining overlaps instruction stages to raise throughput.
entries.formula: ADC resolution (LSB) = Vref / 2^n; quantisation error is at most +/- LSB/2; flash ADC needs 2^n - 1 comparators; R-2R DAC output steps by Vref / 2^n per LSB; pipeline throughput approaches one instruction per clock once filled.
entries.subject: Digital Circuits
entries.topic: ADCs, DACs, semiconductor memories and computer organisation

entries.example: For a system with P = 0 open-loop unstable poles, the Nyquist plot must not encircle -1 at all. If the plot crosses the negative real axis at -0.5, the gain margin is 1/0.5 = 2, or 6 dB.
entries.fact: Routh-Hurwitz tests stability from the characteristic polynomial: no sign changes in the first column of the Routh array means no right-half-plane poles. The Nyquist criterion tests stability from the open-loop frequency response: plot G(j omega) H(j omega) as omega goes from -inf to +inf and count encirclements N of the -1 point; with P open-loop right-half-plane poles, the closed loop has Z = N + P unstable poles, so Z = 0 means stable. Nyquist also gives gain and phase margins directly from the plot.
entries.formula: Routh: stable iff first column has no sign changes; Nyquist: Z = N + P, where N = clockwise encirclements of -1, P = open-loop right-half-plane poles; stable iff Z = 0; gain margin from the -180 deg crossing, phase margin from the |GH| = 1 crossing.
entries.subject: Control Systems

entries.example: For G(s) = K / [s (s+1) (s+2)], the three branches go to infinity along asymptotes at 60, 180 and 300 deg from centroid -1. If the phase at gain crossover is -150 deg, the phase margin is 30 deg.
entries.fact: The root locus shows closed-loop pole movement as gain K rises from 0 to infinity, starting at open-loop poles and ending at zeros or at infinity along asymptotes. Bode plots show magnitude (dB) and phase versus log frequency; phase margin is 180 deg plus the phase at the 0 dB crossover, and gain margin is measured at the -180 deg phase crossover. A lead compensator adds phase near crossover, improving phase margin and transient response; a lag compensator raises low-frequency gain and improves steady-state accuracy; lag-lead combines both.
entries.formula: Root-locus angle condition: sum of angles from zeros - sum from poles = (2k+1) x 180 deg; asymptotes at (2k+1) x 180 deg / (n - m); phase margin PM = 180 deg + angle G(j omega_gc); lead adds positive phase, lag adds negative phase at high frequency but gain at low frequency.
entries.subject: Control Systems
entries.topic: Root locus, Bode plots and lead-lag compensation

entries.example: White noise with two-sided PSD N0/2 = 1e-9 W/Hz through a low-pass filter of bandwidth 1 MHz passes total power 1e-9 x 2 x 1e6 = 2 mW (counting both sidebands) in the idealised flat-band calculation; in practice the one-sided PSD N0 is used with positive frequencies only.
entries.fact: A random process is described by its autocorrelation R_xx(tau), the average of x(t) x(t + tau), and its power spectral density (PSD) S_xx(f), which are a Fourier pair (Wiener-Khinchin theorem): the PSD shows how power is spread over frequency. White noise has a flat PSD (N0/2, two-sided) and an autocorrelation that is a delta function, so its samples are uncorrelated. Passing a random signal through an LTI system multiplies its PSD by |H(f)|^2, and the output autocorrelation is the inverse transform of that.
entries.formula: Wiener-Khinchin: S_xx(f) = integral R_xx(tau) e^{-j 2 pi f tau} d tau; white noise: S = N0/2 (two-sided), R(tau) = (N0/2) delta(tau); output PSD: S_yy(f) = |H(f)|^2 S_xx(f); total power = R_xx(0) = integral S_xx(f) df.
entries.subject: Communication
entries.topic: Random processes: autocorrelation, power spectral density and white noise

entries.example: Broadcast FM with peak deviation 75 kHz and audio up to 15 kHz has Carson bandwidth 2 x (75 + 15) = 180 kHz. A receiver tuned to 100 MHz with a 10.7 MHz IF has its image at 100 + 2 x 10.7 = 121.4 MHz (for low-side LO injection).
entries.fact: In amplitude modulation the carrier amplitude follows the message; in angle modulation (FM and PM) the frequency or phase follows it, giving FM a constant envelope and better noise immunity at the cost of more bandwidth. Carson rule estimates FM bandwidth as 2 (delta_f + f_m), where delta_f is the peak frequency deviation. A superheterodyne receiver mixes the incoming signal down to a fixed intermediate frequency (IF), so most gain and selectivity sit in fixed IF filters; the image frequency, spaced 2 f_IF away, is the main spurious response and must be rejected by the RF front end.
entries.formula: FM: instantaneous frequency f_i(t) = fc + k_f m(t); modulation index beta = delta_f / f_m; Carson bandwidth BW about 2 (delta_f + f_m); superheterodyne: f_IF = |f_RF - f_LO|; image frequency = f_RF +/- 2 f_IF.
entries.subject: Communication
entries.topic: Angle modulation, FM spectra and superheterodyne receivers

entries.example: BPSK at Eb/N0 = 10 dB (a ratio of 10) has BER = Q(sqrt(20)) = Q(4.47), about 3.9 x 10^-6, roughly 4 errors per million bits. 16-QAM carries 4 bits per symbol but needs considerably higher Eb/N0 for the same BER.
entries.fact: Digital modulation maps bits to symbols: ASK varies amplitude, FSK varies frequency, PSK varies phase and QAM varies both amplitude and phase, packing more bits per symbol at the cost of needing higher SNR. The matched filter maximises SNR at the sampling instant and is the optimal linear receiver in white Gaussian noise; MAP and ML detection then pick the most likely symbol, ML when all symbols are equally likely. Inter-symbol interference (ISI) is avoided when pulses satisfy the Nyquist criterion (zero crossings at other sampling instants, e.g. raised-cosine pulses). Bit error rate for BPSK in AWGN is Q(sqrt(2 Eb/N0)), falling steeply as Eb/N0 rises.
entries.formula: BPSK BER = Q(sqrt(2 Eb/N0)); QPSK carries 2 bits per symbol at the same BER as BPSK per bit; matched filter output SNR = 2 E / N0; Nyquist ISI-free criterion: pulse sampled at symbol spacing is zero at all non-zero multiples of T.
entries.subject: Communication
entries.topic: Digital modulation, matched filter, ISI, MAP and ML detection

entries.example: A binary symmetric source has entropy 1 bit per symbol. A 1 MHz channel with SNR = 15 has capacity 1e6 x log2(16) = 4 Mbps. Hamming (7,4) with data 1011 and parity bits placed at positions 1, 2, 4 can correct any single flipped bit in the 7-bit codeword.
entries.fact: Entropy H is the average information per symbol: H = -sum p_i log2 p_i bits, maximum log2 M for M equally likely symbols. Mutual information is the reduction in uncertainty about one variable from knowing another. Shannon channel capacity C = B log2(1 + SNR) is the maximum error-free rate over a bandlimited AWGN channel. Errors are corrected with redundancy: a Hamming (7,4) code adds 3 parity bits to 4 data bits and corrects any single-bit error, and a CRC appends a remainder computed by polynomial division that detects burst errors.
entries.formula: Entropy H = -sum_i p_i log2 p_i; capacity C = B log2(1 + SNR) bits/s; Hamming (n, k) with r parity bits needs 2^r >= n + 1 and corrects 1 error; CRC: append remainder of data polynomial divided by generator polynomial.
entries.subject: Communication
entries.topic: Information theory: entropy, channel capacity, Hamming codes and CRC

entries.example: In free space, a plane wave with E = 10 V/m peak has H = E / 377 = 26.5 mA/m, and its time-average power density is (1/2) x 10 x 0.0265 = 0.133 W/m^2.
entries.fact: Maxwell equations unify electricity and magnetism: Gauss law (electric flux from charge), Gauss law for magnetism (no magnetic monopoles, so magnetic flux through a closed surface is zero), Faraday law (changing magnetic flux induces an electric field) and Ampere-Maxwell law (currents and changing electric flux produce magnetic fields). In differential form they give the wave equation, so light is an electromagnetic wave with speed c = 1/sqrt(mu epsilon). The Poynting vector S = E cross H gives power flow per unit area, and boundary conditions say the tangential E and normal B are continuous across an interface (without surface current or charge).
entries.formula: Differential: div D = rho; div B = 0; curl E = -dB/dt; curl H = J + dD/dt; wave speed c = 1/sqrt(mu epsilon) = 3 x 10^8 m/s in free space; Poynting vector S = E x H (W/m^2); average power = (1/2) Re(E x H*).
entries.subject: Communication

entries.example: Copper (sigma = 5.8e7 S/m) at 1 MHz has skin depth about 65 micrometres (65.2/sqrt(f in Hz) mm = 65.2/1000 mm), so a 1 MHz current flows only in a thin surface layer and AC resistance is far above DC resistance.
entries.fact: A uniform plane wave in a lossless medium has E and H perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel, with ratio equal to the intrinsic impedance eta = sqrt(mu/epsilon) (377 ohm in free space). At an interface part of the wave reflects and part refracts (Snell law); polarisation describes the direction of the E-field, and at the Brewster angle the reflected wave is fully polarised. In a good conductor the wave decays exponentially with skin depth delta = sqrt(2/(omega mu sigma)) = 1/sqrt(pi f mu sigma), the depth at which the field falls to 1/e of its surface value.
entries.formula: Intrinsic impedance eta = sqrt(mu/epsilon); phase velocity v = 1/sqrt(mu epsilon); Snell: sin(theta_t)/sin(theta_i) = n1/n2; skin depth delta = sqrt(2/(omega mu sigma)) = 1/sqrt(pi f mu sigma); field decays as e^{-x/delta}.
entries.subject: Communication
entries.topic: Plane waves: reflection, refraction, polarisation and skin depth

entries.example: A 100 ohm load on a 50 ohm line gives Gamma = (100-50)/(100+50) = 1/3 and VSWR = (1+1/3)/(1-1/3) = 2. A quarter-wave transformer of impedance sqrt(50 x 100) = 70.7 ohm matches it.
entries.fact: A transmission line has distributed inductance and capacitance per unit length, giving characteristic impedance Z0 = sqrt(L/C) and propagation velocity v = 1/sqrt(LC). A load ZL reflects with coefficient Gamma = (ZL - Z0)/(ZL + Z0); the standing-wave ratio is VSWR = (1 + |Gamma|)/(1 - |Gamma|), and power is fully delivered only when ZL = Z0. Impedance matching (quarter-wave transformer, stub, or L-network) removes reflections. The Smith chart plots normalised impedance on the reflection-coefficient plane, so matching and line transformations are read off graphically; S-parameters describe multi-port networks in the same reflection/transmission language.
entries.formula: Z0 = sqrt(L/C); v = 1/sqrt(LC); reflection coefficient Gamma = (ZL - Z0)/(ZL + Z0); VSWR = (1 + |Gamma|)/(1 - |Gamma|); input impedance of a line of length l: Zin = Z0 (ZL + j Z0 tan(beta l)) / (Z0 + j ZL tan(beta l)); quarter-wave: Zin = Z0^2 / ZL.
entries.subject: Communication
entries.topic: Transmission lines: characteristic impedance, matching and Smith chart

entries.example: A rectangular waveguide with broad side a = 2 cm has TE10 cutoff fc = 3e8/(2 x 0.02) = 7.5 GHz; a 10 GHz signal propagates, a 5 GHz signal does not. A half-wave dipole at 100 MHz is 1.5 m long.
entries.fact: A rectangular waveguide guides waves only above its cutoff frequency: for the dominant TE10 mode, fc = c/(2a), where a is the broad dimension, and below cutoff the wave is evanescent. Light propagates in an optical fibre by total internal reflection, with single-mode fibre carrying one mode and multimode fibre many. A half-wave dipole is the reference antenna (about 73 ohm input resistance, gain 2.15 dBi); a monopole over a ground plane is half a dipole. A linear array of elements with controlled phase shifts steers its beam without moving the antenna.
entries.formula: Rectangular waveguide TE10 cutoff: fc = c/(2a); circular waveguide TE11 cutoff about 1.841 c/(2 pi r); dipole length = lambda/2; monopole length = lambda/4 over a ground plane; array factor for N elements spaced d: AF = sum exp(j n (beta d cos theta + alpha)).
entries.subject: Communication
entries.topic: Waveguides, optical fibres, dipole and monopole antennas and arrays

entries.example: A = [[1, 2], [2, 4]] has rank 1 (second row is twice the first) and determinant 0, so it is singular and has eigenvalue 0. Its other eigenvalue is the trace, 5.
entries.fact: The rank of a matrix is the number of independent rows or columns. A system A x = b is consistent if and only if rank(A) = rank([A|b]), with a unique solution when the rank equals the number of unknowns. Eigenvalues come from det(A - lambda I) = 0; their product is the determinant and their sum is the trace. Eigenvectors give the directions a matrix only scales, which is how vibration modes and system poles are understood.
entries.formula: Consistent iff rank(A) = rank([A | b]); unique iff rank = n; det(A - lambda I) = 0; det(A) = product of eigenvalues; trace(A) = sum of eigenvalues.
entries.subject: Engineering Mathematics
entries.topic: Linear algebra: matrix algebra, rank, eigenvalues

entries.example: A square wave of amplitude 1 is odd, so its Fourier series is (4/pi)[sin x + sin 3x/3 + sin 5x/5 + ...]. For F = (x, y, z), div F = 3, so flux out of the unit sphere is 3 x (4 pi/3) = 4 pi.
entries.fact: A periodic function expands into sines and cosines; even functions need only cosines, odd functions only sines, and the coefficients come from integrating over one period. The vector theorems convert between integrals: Gauss turns a volume integral of divergence into surface flux, Stokes turns a surface integral of curl into a line integral around the boundary, and Green is the planar form of Stokes. These are the integral forms behind Gauss law and Faraday law.
entries.formula: f(x) = a0/2 + sum [a_n cos(n pi x / L) + b_n sin(n pi x / L)]; Gauss: integral_V div F dV = integral_S F . dS; Stokes: integral_S curl F . dS = integral_C F . dr; Green: integral_C (P dx + Q dy) = integral_D (dQ/dx - dP/dy) dA.
entries.subject: Engineering Mathematics
entries.topic: Fourier series and vector integral theorems

entries.example: f(z) = 1/(z^2 + 1) has a simple pole at z = i with residue 1/(2i). On a small circle around i only, the integral is 2 pi i x 1/(2i) = pi.
entries.fact: A function is analytic where it satisfies the Cauchy-Riemann equations; such functions have Taylor expansions, and functions with isolated singularities have Laurent expansions including negative powers. The residue theorem says the integral around a closed contour equals 2 pi i times the sum of residues at singularities inside it, and the residue at a simple pole z0 is the limit of (z - z0) f(z). This evaluates real integrals of rational and trigonometric functions that are hard to do directly.
entries.formula: Cauchy-Riemann: du/dx = dv/dy, du/dy = -dv/dx; integral_C f(z) dz = 2 pi i x sum of residues; Res at simple pole z0 = lim_{z->z0} (z - z0) f(z); Cauchy integral formula: f(a) = (1/2 pi i) integral_C f(z)/(z - a) dz.
entries.subject: Engineering Mathematics
entries.topic: Complex variables: analytic functions and residue theorem

entries.example: Solving x^2 - 2 = 0 from x0 = 1.5: x1 = 1.5 - 0.25/3 = 1.4167, already close to sqrt(2) = 1.4142. Trapezoidal rule on x^2 from 0 to 1 with h = 0.5 gives (0.25)[0 + 2 x 0.25 + 1] = 0.375, against the exact 1/3.
entries.fact: Newton-Raphson solves f(x) = 0 by iterating x_{n+1} = x_n - f(x_n)/f'(x_n), converging fast near a simple root but needing a good start and a non-zero derivative. Matrix inversion (Gauss-Jordan) solves linear systems directly. Numerical integration uses the trapezoidal rule (error order h^2) or Simpson rule (error order h^4, needs an even number of intervals). Linear regression fits y = a + b x by least squares, minimising the sum of squared residuals, and correlation r in [-1, 1] measures linear association.
entries.formula: Newton-Raphson: x_{n+1} = x_n - f(x_n)/f'(x_n); trapezoidal: integral about (h/2)[f0 + 2 f1 + ... + 2 f_{n-1} + fn]; Simpson: integral about (h/3)[f0 + 4 f1 + 2 f2 + 4 f3 + ... + fn]; least squares slope b = sum (x - xbar)(y - ybar) / sum (x - xbar)^2.
entries.subject: Engineering Mathematics
entries.topic: Numerical methods: matrix inversion, nonlinear equations, integration and regression

entries.example: A 1 uC point charge gives E = 9000 V/m at 1 m. A coil of 100 turns carrying 2 A (MMF 200 A-turns) on a core of reluctance 1e6 A-turns/Wb carries flux 0.2 mWb.
entries.fact: Gauss law says the electric flux through a closed surface equals the enclosed charge over epsilon; by symmetry a point charge gives E = Q/(4 pi epsilon r^2), a line charge gives E falling as 1/r, and a plane sheet gives a constant field. A current element produces magnetic field by the Biot-Savart law, and Ampere law gives B = mu_0 I/(2 pi r) around a long straight wire. A magnetic circuit follows MMF = N I driving flux through reluctance R = l/(mu A), and self-inductance is L = N Phi/I with mutual inductance M = k sqrt(L1 L2) between coupled coils.
entries.formula: integral_S D . dS = Q_enclosed; E = Q/(4 pi epsilon r^2) point charge; B = mu_0 I/(2 pi r) long wire; MMF = N I; reluctance R = l/(mu A); Phi = MMF/R; L = N Phi/I; M = k sqrt(L1 L2).
entries.subject: Electrical Circuits
entries.topic: Electricity and magnetism: Gauss law, Biot-Savart law and magnetic circuits

entries.example: A network with Vth = 12 V and Rth = 4 ohm delivers maximum power 12^2/(4 x 4) = 9 W to a 4 ohm load, at 50 percent efficiency.
entries.fact: KCL says the currents entering a node sum to zero (charge conservation) and KVL says the voltages around a loop sum to zero (energy conservation); nodal and mesh analysis are systematic ways of writing these equations. Any linear network seen from two terminals is a Thevenin source Vth in series with Rth, or equivalently a Norton source IN = Vth/Rth in parallel with Rth. Superposition considers each independent source alone, and reciprocity says swapping a single source and the measurement point leaves the response unchanged. Maximum power is delivered when the load equals Rth (or the conjugate impedance for AC).
entries.formula: KCL: sum of currents at a node = 0; KVL: sum of voltages around a loop = 0; Vth = open-circuit voltage; Rth = Vth/I_sc; IN = Vth/Rth; maximum power when R_L = Rth, P_max = Vth^2/(4 Rth).
entries.subject: Electrical Circuits
entries.topic: Kirchhoff laws, Thevenin, Norton, superposition and reciprocity

entries.example: An RC low-pass with R = 1 k ohm and C = 0.16 uF has fc = 1/(2 pi x 1000 x 0.16e-6) = about 995 Hz. At 995 Hz a 10 V input gives about 7.07 V out; at 10 kHz it gives about 1 V.
entries.fact: In sinusoidal steady state, impedances are complex (j omega L, 1/(j omega C)) and voltages and currents are phasors. Apparent power S = P + jQ, with P the average power and Q the reactive power; series and parallel resonance both occur at f0 = 1/(2 pi sqrt(LC)), where the impedance is purely resistive. A locus diagram traces the tip of the current or voltage phasor as a parameter (such as frequency or resistance) varies. Simple RC and RL networks are first-order low-pass or high-pass filters with cutoff fc = 1/(2 pi RC) (or R/(2 pi L)), passing frequencies below (or above) the cutoff with -3 dB at fc.
entries.formula: Z_L = j omega L; Z_C = 1/(j omega C); S = V_rms I_rms* = P + jQ; f0 = 1/(2 pi sqrt(LC)); RC low-pass cutoff fc = 1/(2 pi RC); at fc the output is 1/sqrt(2) (about -3 dB) of the input.
entries.subject: Electrical Circuits
entries.topic: Phasor analysis, resonance, locus diagrams and RLC filters

entries.example: A 4-pole, 50 Hz motor has Ns = 1500 rpm; at Nr = 1440 rpm, slip is 0.04 and rotor frequency is 2 Hz. A transformer delivering 8 kW with 200 W iron and 300 W copper loss is 8000/8500 = 94.1 percent efficient.
entries.fact: A transformer transfers power by mutual induction: V2/V1 = N2/N1 = I1/I2 for an ideal transformer. The open-circuit test (rated voltage, secondary open) gives iron loss and the magnetising branch; the short-circuit test (rated current, low voltage) gives copper loss and series impedance. Voltage regulation is (V_no-load - V_full-load)/V_full-load, and efficiency is maximum when iron loss equals copper loss. A three-phase induction motor runs at slip s = (Ns - Nr)/Ns with Ns = 120 f/P; torque is proportional to s R2/(R2^2 + (s X2)^2), maximum at s = R2/X2, and the no-load and blocked-rotor tests give the equivalent circuit.
entries.formula: V2/V1 = N2/N1; regulation = (V_nl - V_fl)/V_fl x 100 percent; eta = output/(output + Pi + Pcu), maximum when Pi = Pcu; Ns = 120 f/P; s = (Ns - Nr)/Ns; rotor frequency = s f.
entries.subject: Electrical Circuits
entries.topic: Single-phase transformer and three-phase induction motor

entries.example: y' + 2y = 0 with y(0) = 3 gives Y(s) = 3/(s + 2), so y(t) = 3 e^{-2t}. The discrete sequence (0.5)^n u[n] has Z-transform z/(z - 0.5) with pole at 0.5, inside the unit circle, so it is stable.
entries.fact: The Laplace transform turns differential equations into algebra (differentiation becomes multiplication by s, minus initial values), the Fourier transform decomposes a signal into frequencies (convolution becomes multiplication), and the Z-transform does the same for discrete-time signals and difference equations. The transfer function H(s) = Y(s)/X(s) is the Laplace transform of the impulse response, and poles in the left half-plane mean stability for continuous systems, inside the unit circle for discrete ones. The region of convergence decides causality and stability of a Z-transform.
entries.formula: Laplace: X(s) = integral_0^inf x(t) e^{-s t} dt; L{dx/dt} = s X(s) - x(0); Fourier: X(omega) = integral x(t) e^{-j omega t} dt; Z: X(z) = sum x[n] z^{-n}; a^n u[n] <-> 1/(1 - a z^{-1}), ROC |z| > |a|.
entries.subject: Signals & Systems

entries.example: x = [1, 2] convolved with h = [1, 1] gives y = [1, 3, 2]. The autocorrelation of a signal at zero lag equals its energy; a delayed copy of a signal cross-correlates maximally at a lag equal to the delay.
entries.fact: The impulse response h(t) of an LTI system is its output for a unit impulse, and the output for any input is the convolution of the input with h. In the frequency domain convolution becomes multiplication by the transfer function H, whose magnitude and phase give the frequency response; first-order systems roll off at 20 dB/decade past their corner, second-order at 40 dB/decade. Correlation measures similarity between two signals as a function of lag: autocorrelation peaks at zero lag with the signal power, and cross-correlation peaks at the lag where the signals best align, which is how time delay is measured.
entries.formula: y(t) = integral x(tau) h(t - tau) d tau; y[n] = sum_k x[k] h[n-k]; H(s) = Y(s)/X(s); autocorrelation R_xx(tau) = integral x(t) x(t + tau) dt, R_xx(0) = signal power.
entries.subject: Signals & Systems

entries.example: x = [1, 0, 1, 0], N = 4: X[0] = 2, X[1] = 0, X[2] = 2, X[3] = 0. A 3-tap moving-average FIR y[n] = (x[n] + x[n-1] + x[n-2])/3 is a simple low-pass filter.
entries.fact: The DFT samples the DTFT at N equally spaced frequencies, X[k] = sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n] e^{-j 2 pi k n / N}, and the FFT computes it in O(N log N). FIR filters use only feedforward taps, so they are always stable and can have exactly linear phase, but need many taps for sharp cutoffs. IIR filters use feedback, so they achieve sharp cutoffs with few coefficients but can be unstable and have non-linear phase. Filter design starts from the required passband, stopband and transition width, then picks the order and the window (FIR) or prototype (IIR, e.g. Butterworth or Chebyshev).
entries.formula: DFT: X[k] = sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n] e^{-j 2 pi k n / N}; FIR: y[n] = sum_{k=0}^{M} b_k x[n-k]; IIR: y[n] = sum b_k x[n-k] - sum a_k y[n-k]; FIR always stable, linear phase possible; IIR stable iff poles inside the unit circle.
entries.subject: Signals & Systems
entries.topic: DFT, FFT, IIR and FIR digital filters

entries.example: A system with one forward path of gain 10 and one feedback loop of gain -2 has Delta = 1 - (-2) = 3 and T = 10/3 = 3.33. Adding a second loop that does not touch the first contributes its product to Delta.
entries.fact: A signal flow graph represents a system as nodes (signals) joined by directed branches (gains). Mason gain formula gives the overall transfer function from the forward paths and loops: sum over forward paths of (path gain x its cofactor) divided by the determinant Delta. Delta is 1 minus the sum of individual loop gains, plus the sum of products of pairs of non-touching loops, minus the sum of products of triples of non-touching loops, and so on; a path cofactor is Delta with all loops touching that path removed.
entries.formula: T = (sum_k M_k Delta_k) / Delta; Delta = 1 - sum L1 + sum L2 - sum L3 + ...; M_k = gain of k-th forward path; Delta_k = Delta with loops touching path k removed.
entries.subject: Control Systems
entries.topic: Signal flow graphs and Mason gain formula

entries.example: s^3 + 4 s^2 + 5 s + 2 has Routh rows 1, 5; 4, 2; 4.5; 2, all positive in the first column, so it is stable. A 0.1 s delay at 10 rad/s adds phase lag of 1 rad, about 57 deg, which can erase a phase margin.
entries.fact: Routh-Hurwitz tests stability from the characteristic polynomial (no sign changes in the first column means stable); Nyquist counts encirclements of -1 by the open-loop frequency response; root locus traces closed-loop poles as gain varies. Bode plots give gain and phase margins, the usual robustness measures. Lead compensation adds phase near crossover and speeds up the response, lag raises low-frequency gain and cuts steady-state error, and lag-lead does both. In state space, x-dot = A x + B u and y = C x + D u, and stability is decided by the eigenvalues of A. A pure time delay e^{-sT} adds phase lag proportional to frequency and hurts stability margins.
entries.formula: Routh: stable iff first column has no sign changes; Nyquist: Z = N + P, stable iff Z = 0; phase margin = 180 deg + angle G(j omega_gc); state space: x-dot = A x + B u, y = C x + D u; delay: e^{-sT} adds phase -omega T.
entries.subject: Control Systems
entries.topic: Stability criteria, compensators, state space and time-delay systems

entries.example: A BJT at Ic = 2 mA has gm = 2e-3/0.026 = about 77 mS, so with Rc = 1 k ohm the voltage gain is about -77. A 5.1 V Zener holds about 5.1 V across its load in reverse breakdown.
entries.fact: A diode conducts exponentially in forward bias, I = Is (e^{V/(eta Vt)} - 1) with Vt about 26 mV at 300 K, and blocks in reverse until breakdown; a Zener diode breaks down at a controlled reverse voltage and regulates it. A BJT in active mode has Ic = beta Ib and transconductance gm = Ic/Vt, so it is a current-controlled current source. A MOSFET in saturation has Id = (1/2) mu Cox (W/L) (Vgs - Vth)^2 and is voltage-controlled. Small-signal analysis replaces each device by its gm and output resistance to find gain and input/output resistance; feedback trades gain for bandwidth, linearity and stable resistance.
entries.formula: Diode: I = Is (e^{V/(eta Vt)} - 1); BJT: Ic = beta Ib, gm = Ic/Vt; MOSFET saturation: Id = (1/2) mu Cox (W/L)(Vgs - Vth)^2, gm = 2 Id/(Vgs - Vth); common-emitter gain about -gm Rc.
entries.subject: Instrumentation
entries.topic: Diode, Zener diode, BJT and MOSFET: characteristics and small-signal analysis

entries.example: An instrumentation amplifier with R = 10 k ohm and Rg = 1 k ohm and a unity second stage has gain 1 + 20 = 21, so a 10 mV bridge output becomes 210 mV. A PLL with f_ref = 1 MHz and N = 50 outputs 50 MHz.
entries.fact: An ideal op-amp with negative feedback keeps its inputs at equal voltage and draws no input current, giving adder, subtractor, integrator (Vo = -1/(RC) integral Vi dt), differentiator, difference amplifier and precision rectifier (a diode inside the loop removes the 0.7 V diode drop). An instrumentation amplifier uses two non-inverting stages plus a difference stage to give high input impedance, high CMRR and gain set by one resistor Rg. A phase-locked loop locks a VCO to a reference: with a divide-by-N counter in the loop, f_out = N f_ref. Noise in circuits comes from thermal noise (4 k T R per hertz), shot noise and 1/f noise, and shielding and grounding keep interference out of low-level measurements.
entries.formula: Inverting gain = -Rf/R1; non-inverting = 1 + Rf/R1; integrator Vo = -(1/RC) integral Vi dt; instrumentation amplifier gain = (1 + 2R/Rg) x (Rf/R1); PLL: f_out = N f_ref; thermal noise voltage density = sqrt(4 k T R) V/sqrt(Hz).
entries.subject: Instrumentation
entries.topic: Op-amp applications, instrumentation amplifier, PLL and noise

entries.example: A Sallen-Key low-pass with R1 = R2 = 15.9 k ohm and C1 = C2 = 10 nF has fc = 1/(2 pi x 15900 x 10e-9) = about 1000 Hz. A Wien-bridge oscillator with R = 16 k ohm and C = 10 nF oscillates near 995 Hz.
entries.fact: Active filters use op-amps with RC networks instead of inductors: a first-order stage rolls off at 20 dB/decade, a second-order Sallen-Key stage at 40 dB/decade, with fc = 1/(2 pi sqrt(R1 R2 C1 C2)) and Q = 0.707 for a Butterworth (maximally flat) response. An oscillator needs loop gain of at least 1 with zero total phase shift (Barkhausen criterion); RC phase-shift and Wien-bridge oscillators set frequency with RC networks, and LC oscillators with a tank circuit. A voltage-controlled oscillator tunes its frequency with a control voltage, and a function generator combines oscillators, integrators and comparators to produce sine, square and triangle waves.
entries.formula: Sallen-Key low-pass: fc = 1/(2 pi sqrt(R1 R2 C1 C2)); Butterworth Q = 0.707; Barkhausen: loop gain >= 1 at 0 deg (360 deg) total phase; Wien bridge: f0 = 1/(2 pi RC); first-order roll-off 20 dB/decade, second-order 40 dB/decade.
entries.subject: Instrumentation
entries.topic: Active filters, oscillators and signal generators

entries.example: F = sum m(1,3,5,7) over three variables is 1 exactly when C = 1, so the minimised form is F = C. A CMOS gate switching 10 pF at 5 V and 10 MHz dissipates about 10e-12 x 25 x 10e6 = 2.5 mW of dynamic power.
entries.fact: Boolean functions are minimised with algebra or Karnaugh maps, grouping 1s in powers of two (pairs, quads, octets) with wrap-around and don't-care cells, to get the smallest sum-of-products form. TTL logic uses bipolar transistors, runs on 5 V, and has fast switching but higher static power; CMOS uses complementary PMOS/NMOS pairs, draws almost no static power, has high noise margins and wide supply range, and dominates modern digital ICs. Key datasheet figures are propagation delay, fan-out (how many inputs one output can drive), noise margin and power dissipation.
entries.formula: De Morgan: NOT(A B) = (NOT A) + (NOT B); K-map groups must be powers of 2; CMOS static power about 0, dynamic power = C V^2 f; TTL supply 5 V, typical noise margin about 0.4 V.
entries.subject: Instrumentation
entries.topic: Boolean minimisation and IC families: TTL and CMOS

entries.example: A 555 astable with R1 = 1 k ohm, R2 = 10 k ohm and C = 10 uF gives T = 0.693 x (1000 + 20000) x 10e-6 = 0.146 s, so f = about 6.9 Hz. A mod-10 counter needs 4 flip-flops.
entries.fact: Flip-flops (D, JK, T) store one bit on a clock edge; latches are level-sensitive. Shift registers move bits along on each clock, counters divide the clock (a mod-n counter needs ceil(log2 n) flip-flops), and comparators and Schmitt triggers clean up and compare levels. An astable multivibrator free-runs as a clock; the 555 timer in astable mode gives frequency f = 1.44/((R1 + 2 R2) C) with duty cycle set by R1 and R2. Setup and hold times must be met, and the critical path sets the maximum clock frequency.
entries.formula: Mod-n counter needs ceil(log2 n) flip-flops; 555 astable: f = 1.44 / ((R1 + 2 R2) C); T = 0.693 (R1 + 2 R2) C; f_max = 1 / (t_clk-to-Q + t_comb(max) + t_setup).
entries.subject: Instrumentation
entries.topic: Sequential circuits, multivibrators, timers and counters

entries.example: A 10-bit ADC with Vref = 5 V has LSB = 5/1024 = 4.88 mV, so a 1.00 V input reads about code 205. A 4-bit flash ADC needs 15 comparators.
entries.fact: An ADC quantises an analog voltage into an n-bit code with step LSB = Vref/2^n: successive-approximation ADCs are the common middle ground, flash ADCs are fastest (2^n - 1 comparators), integrating (dual-slope) ADCs are slow but reject mains noise, and sigma-delta ADCs oversample for high resolution. DACs use weighted resistors or an R-2R ladder. Key ADC/DAC figures are resolution, quantisation error (+/- LSB/2), conversion/settling time and effective number of bits. A microprocessor/microcontroller runs the data-acquisition system: sensor, signal conditioning, ADC, processor, memory and I/O; a DCS distributes control across many controllers in a plant, and a PLC runs rugged ladder-logic control of machines and processes.
entries.formula: ADC LSB = Vref / 2^n; quantisation error <= LSB/2; flash comparators = 2^n - 1; DAC R-2R output steps by Vref/2^n per LSB; sample-and-hold freezes the input during conversion.
entries.subject: Instrumentation
entries.topic: ADCs, DACs, embedded systems, DCS and PLC

entries.example: A Maxwell bridge with R2 = 100 ohm, R3 = 200 ohm and C1 = 1 uF measures Lx = 100 x 200 x 1e-6 = 20 mH. A Wien bridge with R = 16 k ohm and C = 10 nF balances at f = 1/(2 pi x 16000 x 10e-9) = about 995 Hz.
entries.fact: AC bridges measure inductance, capacitance and frequency by balancing arms at null, like the Wheatstone bridge does for resistance. The Maxwell bridge measures inductance against a known capacitance (Lx = R2 R3 C1); the Anderson bridge is a modified Maxwell that suits low-Q coils; the Schering bridge measures capacitance and dissipation factor (tan delta); the Wien bridge measures frequency, f = 1/(2 pi RC), and is also the basis of the Wien-bridge oscillator. A Q-meter measures the quality factor of a coil directly by resonance: Q = Vc/V, the ratio of the capacitor voltage to the applied voltage at resonance.
entries.formula: Maxwell bridge: Lx = R2 R3 C1; Schering bridge: Cx = C1 (R3/R4), tan(delta) = omega C1 R1; Wien bridge: f = 1/(2 pi R C); Q-meter: Q = Vc / V at resonance; Q = omega L / R for a coil.
entries.subject: Measurements
entries.topic: AC bridges: Maxwell, Anderson, Schering, Wien and Q-meter

entries.example: A 100/5 A CT with 4 A in its secondary carries 4 x (100/5) = 80 A in the primary. A timer counting 50000 cycles in a 1 s gate reads 50 kHz.
entries.fact: Instrument transformers scale high voltages and currents down for meters: a potential transformer (PT) scales voltage by its turns ratio, a current transformer (CT) scales current, and its secondary must never be open-circuited while the primary carries current. A true-RMS meter reads the RMS value of any waveform, while an average-responding meter is calibrated for sine waves only and reads wrong on distorted waveforms. A timer/counter measures frequency, period and time interval by counting cycles against a reference clock. An oscilloscope shows voltage against time (or X-Y), with time base, volts/division, triggering and bandwidth setting what can be seen; shielding and grounding keep interference out of the measurement.
entries.formula: PT: V_secondary = V_primary x (N2/N1); CT: I_secondary = I_primary x (N1/N2); true RMS = sqrt(mean of v^2); frequency = counts / gate time; oscilloscope bandwidth should exceed the highest signal frequency of interest.
entries.subject: Measurements
entries.topic: Instrument transformers, true-RMS meters, timer/counter and oscilloscope

entries.example: A parallel-plate sensor with A = 1 cm^2, d = 1 mm in air has C = 8.85e-12 x 1e-4 / 1e-3 = 0.885 pF; halving the gap doubles the capacitance to 1.77 pF. A Hall sensor with a 10 mA current in a 0.1 T field gives a voltage proportional to B, used to measure current without breaking the circuit.
entries.fact: Resistive sensors change resistance with the measured quantity (strain gauge, RTD, thermistor, LDR); capacitive sensors change C = epsilon A/d with gap or overlap or dielectric; inductive sensors change inductance with a moving core (LVDT gives a linear AC output versus core position); piezoelectric sensors generate charge under force or vibration (high impedance, needs a charge amplifier); Hall sensors give a voltage proportional to magnetic field times current. Signal conditioning matches the sensor to the ADC: bridge completion, amplification (often an instrumentation amplifier), filtering, isolation and linearisation.
entries.formula: Capacitance C = epsilon A / d; Hall voltage V_H = I B / (n q t); piezoelectric charge Q = d x F (d = piezoelectric coefficient); LVDT output is linear in core displacement with a null at centre; strain gauge: delta R/R = G_f x strain.
entries.subject: Instrumentation
entries.topic: Sensors: resistive, capacitive, inductive, piezoelectric and Hall effect

entries.example: A Pt100 at 100 C reads R = 100 x (1 + 0.00385 x 100) = 138.5 ohm. A type-K thermocouple gives about 41 uV per deg C, so a 250 deg C difference gives about 10.3 mV.
entries.fact: A thermocouple joins two dissimilar metals; the Seebeck effect gives a voltage roughly proportional to the temperature difference between the hot junction and the cold (reference) junction, so the reference temperature must be known or compensated. An RTD (usually Pt100, 100 ohm at 0 C) has resistance rising almost linearly with temperature, R = R0 (1 + alpha T) with alpha = 0.00385 per deg C for platinum, and 3- or 4-wire connection cancels lead resistance. A thermistor is a semiconductor whose resistance falls steeply (NTC) with temperature, very sensitive over a narrow range. A pyrometer measures temperature from thermal radiation without contact, and a bolometer detects radiation by the heating it causes.
entries.formula: Thermocouple: V about S x (T_hot - T_ref), S = Seebeck coefficient; RTD: R = R0 (1 + alpha T), Pt100 alpha = 0.00385 /deg C; thermistor (NTC): R falls exponentially with T; radiation: emitted power proportional to T^4 (Stefan-Boltzmann).
entries.subject: Instrumentation
entries.topic: Temperature measurement: thermocouple, RTD, thermistor, pyrometer and bolometer

entries.example: A venturi whose differential pressure quadruples has its flow doubled, since Q is proportional to sqrt(delta p). A tank of water 2 m deep gives a differential pressure of 1000 x 9.81 x 2 = 19.6 kPa at the bottom.
entries.fact: Variable-head meters (orifice, venturi) infer flow from the pressure drop, Q proportional to sqrt(delta p); variable-area (rotameter) meters read flow from a float position; electromagnetic meters use the voltage induced in a conductive fluid moving in a magnetic field, E = B d v; turbine meters count rotor speed; ultrasonic meters use transit time or Doppler shift; open-channel meters use a weir or flume. Pressure is measured by Bourdon tubes, diaphragms and strain-gauge transducers, and very low pressure by a McLeod gauge. Liquid level uses floats, capacitance, ultrasonic or differential pressure. pH is measured with a glass electrode (about 59 mV per pH at 25 C), conductivity with a conductance cell, and viscosity with rotational or capillary viscometers.
entries.formula: Orifice/venturi: Q proportional to sqrt(delta p); electromagnetic: E = B d v; turbine: flow proportional to rotor frequency; pH electrode: about 59.16 mV per pH unit at 25 C (Nernst); differential-pressure level: delta p = rho g h.
entries.subject: Instrumentation
entries.topic: Flow, pressure, level, pH, conductivity and viscosity measurement

entries.example: Telephone PCM samples at 8 kHz with 8 bits per sample, giving a bit rate of 64 kbps. An AM signal carrying 5 kHz audio occupies 10 kHz of bandwidth.
entries.fact: Amplitude modulation varies the carrier amplitude with the message, frequency modulation varies its frequency; both shift the message to a carrier frequency for transmission, and Shannon sampling theorem says a bandlimited signal is recovered from samples taken faster than twice its highest frequency. Pulse code modulation samples, quantises and encodes the signal into bits, with bit rate = sampling frequency x bits per sample. Frequency-division multiplexing stacks channels in frequency, time-division multiplexing interleaves them in time. Digital modulation (ASK, PSK, FSK, QAM) maps bits to carrier amplitude, phase, frequency or combinations, with QAM packing the most bits per symbol.
entries.formula: Sampling theorem: fs > 2 f_max; PCM bit rate = fs x n bits; AM bandwidth = 2 f_m; FM Carson bandwidth about 2 (delta_f + f_m); FDM stacks in frequency, TDM interleaves in time.
entries.subject: Instrumentation
entries.topic: Modulation, PCM, multiplexing and digital modulation

entries.example: A solution with molar absorptivity 1000 L/mol/cm in a 1 cm cuvette at 0.001 mol/L has absorbance A = 1000 x 0.001 x 1 = 1, so it transmits 10 percent of the light. An interferometer with 600 nm light moves one fringe per 300 nm of mirror displacement.
entries.fact: Optical sources are LEDs (incoherent, broad spectrum) and lasers (coherent, narrow spectrum); detectors are photodiodes (current proportional to light), light-dependent resistors (resistance falls with light) and square-law detectors (output proportional to optical power). An interferometer splits light into two paths and recombines it; the fringe shift measures displacement or refractive-index change to a fraction of a wavelength, which is the basis of precision metrology and fibre-optic sensing (where the measurand changes the fibre phase, intensity or wavelength). A UV-VIS spectrophotometer measures absorbance (Beer-Lambert law, A = epsilon c l), and a mass spectrometer separates ions by mass-to-charge ratio m/z, giving composition from the mass spectrum.
entries.formula: Beer-Lambert: A = epsilon c l; interferometer fringe shift: one fringe per half-wavelength of path change (delta = lambda/2 per fringe); mass spectrometer: ions separated by m/z; photodiode current proportional to incident optical power.
entries.subject: Instrumentation
entries.topic: Optical instrumentation: sources, detectors, interferometry, fibre sensing and spectrometry

entries.example: A = [[2, 0], [0, 3]] has eigenvalues 2 and 3, determinant 6 and trace 5. A singular matrix has a zero eigenvalue and no inverse.
entries.fact: A system of linear equations has a solution exactly when rank(A) = rank([A|b]), and a unique solution when that rank equals the number of unknowns. Eigenvalues come from det(A - lambda I) = 0; their product is the determinant and their sum is the trace. Eigenvectors are the directions a matrix only scales, which is how principal components and vibration modes are found in biomedical data and mechanics.
entries.formula: Consistent iff rank(A) = rank([A | b]); unique iff rank = n; A v = lambda v; det(A - lambda I) = 0; det(A) = product of eigenvalues; trace(A) = sum of eigenvalues.
entries.subject: Engineering Mathematics
entries.topic: Linear algebra: matrix algebra, eigenvalues and eigenvectors

entries.example: A square wave of amplitude 1 has Fourier series (4/pi)[sin x + sin 3x/3 + sin 5x/5 + ...]. An ECG signal is analysed the same way: its harmonics describe the sharp QRS complex, and low-pass filtering removes high-frequency noise.
entries.fact: A periodic biomedical signal (such as an ECG waveform) expands into a Fourier series of sines and cosines; even functions need only cosines, odd functions only sines. The vector theorems convert between integrals: Gauss turns a volume integral of divergence into surface flux, Stokes turns a surface integral of curl into a line integral, and Green is the planar form of Stokes. Fourier analysis is also the basis of frequency-domain filtering of ECG and EEG signals.
entries.formula: f(x) = a0/2 + sum [a_n cos(n pi x / L) + b_n sin(n pi x / L)]; Gauss: integral_V div F dV = integral_S F . dS; Stokes: integral_S curl F . dS = integral_C F . dr.
entries.subject: Engineering Mathematics
entries.topic: Fourier series and vector integral theorems

entries.example: To estimate a mean with margin E = 2, sigma = 10 and 95 percent confidence (Z = 1.96), n = (1.96 x 10 / 2)^2 = 96.04, so 97 subjects are needed. A study with power 0.8 has a 20 percent chance of missing a real effect (type II error).
entries.fact: Newton-Raphson iterates x_{n+1} = x_n - f(x_n)/f'(x_n) to solve nonlinear equations, and matrix inversion (Gauss-Jordan) solves linear systems. Numerical integration uses the trapezoidal or Simpson rule. In statistics, a test of significance asks whether an observed difference could arise by chance: the p-value is the probability of data at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true, and p < 0.05 is the usual threshold.
