Power is 1 - beta, the probability of detecting a real effect; larger samples, larger effects and smaller variance all raise power, and sample size is chosen from the required power, effect size and significance level. Linear regression fits y = a + b x by least squares and correlation r measures linear association.
entries.formula: Newton-Raphson: x_{n+1} = x_n - f(x_n)/f'(x_n); Simpson: integral about (h/3)[f0 + 4 f1 + 2 f2 + ... + fn]; sample size for a mean: n = (Z_{alpha/2} sigma / E)^2; power = 1 - beta; regression slope b = sum (x - xbar)(y - ybar) / sum (x - xbar)^2.
entries.subject: Engineering Mathematics
entries.topic: Numerical methods, tests of significance, power and sample size

entries.example: An RC low-pass with R = 16 k ohm and C = 10 nF has fc = 1/(2 pi x 16000 x 10e-9) = about 995 Hz, suitable for removing mains-frequency noise above the ECG band. A network with Vth = 6 V and Rth = 2 ohm delivers maximum power 6^2/(4 x 2) = 4.5 W to a 2 ohm load.
entries.fact: Independent sources fix their voltage or current regardless of the circuit; dependent sources depend on another voltage or current in the circuit, and practical sources have internal resistance. KCL (currents at a node sum to zero) and KVL (voltages around a loop sum to zero) are the analysis laws, and any linear network seen from two terminals is a Thevenin source Vth in series with Rth (or a Norton source IN = Vth/Rth in parallel). In AC steady state, series and parallel resonance both occur at f0 = 1/(2 pi sqrt(LC)), and simple RC networks are first-order low-pass or high-pass filters with cutoff fc = 1/(2 pi RC), used as the front end of biopotential amplifiers.
entries.formula: KCL: sum of currents at a node = 0; KVL: sum of voltages around a loop = 0; Vth = open-circuit voltage, Rth = Vth/I_sc; f0 = 1/(2 pi sqrt(LC)); RC cutoff fc = 1/(2 pi RC); RMS of a sine = peak / sqrt(2).
entries.subject: Biomedical Signals
entries.topic: Electric circuits: sources, Kirchhoff laws, Thevenin and resonance

entries.example: An ECG with useful content up to 150 Hz must be sampled above 300 samples/s; clinical ECGs commonly use 500 samples/s. An EEG amplifier with tau = 0.16 s has a low-frequency corner of about 1 Hz.
entries.fact: The Laplace transform turns differential equations into algebra and gives the transfer function H(s) = Y(s)/X(s); the Fourier transform decomposes a signal into frequencies, turning convolution into multiplication. A first-order system has a corner at 1/tau and rolls off at 20 dB/decade; a second-order system has natural frequency omega_n and damping ratio zeta. Shannon sampling theorem says a signal bandlimited to f_max is recovered from samples taken faster than 2 f_max; sampling slower causes aliasing, where high frequencies fold onto low ones, so biomedical recorders use an anti-aliasing low-pass filter before the ADC.
entries.formula: Laplace: L{dx/dt} = s X(s) - x(0); Fourier: X(omega) = integral x(t) e^{-j omega t} dt; sampling: fs > 2 f_max (Nyquist rate = 2 f_max); first-order corner omega_c = 1/tau; second-order: s^2 + 2 zeta omega_n s + omega_n^2.
entries.subject: Biomedical Signals
entries.topic: Signals and systems: Laplace and Fourier transforms, sampling theorem

entries.example: x = [1, 0, 1, 0], N = 4: X[0] = 2, X[1] = 0, X[2] = 2, X[3] = 0. A 3-tap moving-average FIR y[n] = (x[n] + x[n-1] + x[n-2])/3 smooths an ECG trace but delays it by one sample.
entries.fact: Discrete signals are analysed with the Z-transform (the discrete twin of Laplace), the DFT, X[k] = sum x[n] e^{-j 2 pi k n / N}, and the FFT that computes it fast. A discrete LTI system is stable when all its poles lie inside the unit circle. FIR filters use feedforward only, are always stable and can have exactly linear phase; IIR filters use feedback, are sharper for the same order but can be unstable and have non-linear phase. Digital filtering is how ECG baseline wander and 50 Hz interference are removed in software.
entries.formula: Z: X(z) = sum x[n] z^{-n}; DFT: X[k] = sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n] e^{-j 2 pi k n / N}; stable iff all poles satisfy |p| < 1; FIR: y[n] = sum b_k x[n-k]; IIR: y[n] = sum b_k x[n-k] - sum a_k y[n-k].
entries.subject: Biomedical Signals
entries.topic: Discrete-time signals: Z-transform, DFT, IIR and FIR filters

entries.example: An ECG front end with an instrumentation amplifier gain of 1000 turns a 1 mV QRS complex into 1 V. A BJT biased at 1 mA has gm = 38.5 mS, so with Rc = 2 k ohm its stage gain is about -77.
entries.fact: A diode conducts exponentially in forward bias and blocks in reverse; a BJT has Ic = beta Ib with transconductance gm = Ic/Vt; a MOSFET in saturation has Id = (1/2) mu Cox (W/L)(Vgs - Vth)^2. An ideal op-amp with negative feedback keeps its inputs equal and draws no input current, giving inverting gain -Rf/R1, non-inverting gain 1 + Rf/R1, and adder, subtractor, integrator and differentiator circuits. The instrumentation amplifier (two non-inverting stages plus a difference stage) gives the high input impedance and high common-mode rejection needed to record millivolt biopotentials in the presence of large common-mode interference, and active filters use op-amps with RC networks instead of inductors.
entries.formula: Diode: I = Is (e^{V/(eta Vt)} - 1); BJT gm = Ic/Vt; MOSFET Id = (1/2) mu Cox (W/L)(Vgs - Vth)^2; inverting gain = -Rf/R1; non-inverting = 1 + Rf/R1; instrumentation amplifier gain = (1 + 2R/Rg) x (Rf/R1); integrator Vo = -(1/RC) integral Vi dt.
entries.subject: Biomedical Signals
entries.topic: Analog electronics: diode, BJT, MOSFET and op-amp circuits

entries.example: A 10-bit ADC with Vref = 3.3 V has LSB = 3.3/1024 = 3.22 mV, so a 1 mV ECG signal spans less than one LSB before amplification, which is why the front-end gain comes first. A mod-10 counter needs 4 flip-flops.
entries.fact: Binary numbers, Boolean algebra and Karnaugh maps describe combinational logic (adders, comparators, multiplexers, encoders/decoders), while flip-flops, shift registers and counters build sequential logic, described by state diagrams. A Schmitt trigger adds hysteresis to clean up noisy thresholds. An ADC converts an analog voltage to a digital code with step LSB = Vref/2^n (successive-approximation is the usual choice for biomedical recorders); a DAC does the reverse. A microprocessor system (CPU, memory, I/O) runs the data-acquisition and signal-processing software, interfacing to sensors through ADCs and to displays and networks through its I/O ports.
entries.formula: Binary 1011 = 11 decimal; De Morgan: NOT(A B) = (NOT A) + (NOT B); ADC LSB = Vref / 2^n; quantisation error <= LSB/2; mod-n counter needs ceil(log2 n) flip-flops.
entries.subject: Biomedical Signals
entries.topic: Digital electronics: number systems, logic, ADC/DAC and microprocessors

entries.example: Two measurements with standard uncertainties 0.1 and 0.2 combine to sqrt(0.01 + 0.04) = 0.224 for their sum. A Wheatstone bridge with R1 = 100, R2 = 200 and R3 = 150 ohm balances when R4 = 300 ohm.
entries.fact: SI units standardise measurement; systematic errors bias every reading the same way (calibration removes them) while random errors scatter readings and are reduced by averaging. Accuracy is closeness to the true value, precision is repeatability, and uncertainty propagates: for a sum, variances add, so the standard uncertainty is the root-sum-of-squares. Bridges measure resistance, inductance and capacitance by null balance (Wheatstone for R, Maxwell and Schering for L and C); a Q-meter measures coil quality factor by resonance. A control system is described by its transfer function, the Laplace ratio of output to input, and feedback (P, PI, PID) is used to hold a physiological variable or a device output at its set point.
entries.formula: Wheatstone balance: R1/R2 = R3/R4; for y = x1 + x2, sigma_y = sqrt(sigma_1^2 + sigma_2^2); relative error = absolute error / true value; transfer function H(s) = Y(s)/X(s); Q = omega L / R.
entries.subject: Biomedical Signals
entries.topic: Measurement errors, bridges and control-system basics

entries.example: A strain gauge with gauge factor 2 under 0.001 strain changes resistance by 0.2 percent, read by a Wheatstone bridge. A Hall sensor measures current in a wire without breaking the circuit, from the magnetic field the current produces.
entries.fact: Resistive sensors change resistance (strain gauge, RTD, thermistor); capacitive sensors change C = epsilon A/d with gap or dielectric; inductive sensors change inductance with a moving core; piezoelectric sensors generate charge under force or vibration; Hall sensors give a voltage proportional to magnetic field; electrochemical sensors generate a current or voltage from a chemical reaction (glucose, pH, oxygen); optical sensors use light absorption or scattering. Signal conditioning bridges, amplifies (often with an instrumentation amplifier), filters and isolates the sensor output before digitisation. LASERs are used in sensing (low-power, e.g. pulse oximetry and flow) and in therapy (high-power, e.g. surgery and phototherapy).
entries.formula: C = epsilon A / d; Hall voltage V_H = I B / (n q t); piezoelectric charge Q = d x F; strain gauge delta R/R = G_f x strain; pH electrode about 59 mV per pH at 25 C.
entries.subject: Biomedical Signals
entries.topic: Sensors and signal conditioning: resistive, capacitive, inductive, piezoelectric, Hall, electrochemical and optical

entries.example: Alpha waves (8-13 Hz) dominate the EEG of a relaxed person with eyes closed and are replaced by beta activity when the eyes open. An EMG electrode over a contracting biceps shows bursts of activity that grow with force.
entries.fact: Biopotentials arise from ion flows across cell membranes; the resting potential is about -70 mV inside a neuron, and an action potential is a brief depolarisation to about +30 mV. EEG records brain activity from the scalp: delta (< 4 Hz, deep sleep), theta (4-8 Hz), alpha (8-13 Hz, relaxed awake) and beta (13-30 Hz, active thinking). EMG records muscle activity, EOG records eye movements from the corneo-retinal potential, ERG records retinal response to light, GSR (skin conductance) tracks sweat-gland activity and arousal, and PCG records heart sounds (S1, S2) with a microphone. All are microvolt-to-millivolt signals recorded with differential amplifiers and heavy common-mode rejection.
entries.formula: Resting potential about -70 mV; action potential peak about +30 mV; EEG bands: delta < 4 Hz, theta 4-8 Hz, alpha 8-13 Hz, beta 13-30 Hz; EMG bandwidth roughly 20-500 Hz; GSR rises with sweat-gland activity.
entries.subject: Biomedical Signals
entries.topic: Biopotentials: EEG, EMG, EOG, ERG, GSR and PCG

entries.example: A blood pressure of 120/80 mmHg gives MAP = 80 + 40/3 = 93.3 mmHg. An ultrasonic Doppler probe with a 5 MHz beam at 60 deg to a vessel measures a shift proportional to blood velocity.
entries.fact: Blood pressure is measured with a sphygmomanometer: cuff pressure is raised above systolic, then lowered while listening for Korotkoff sounds (systolic at first sound, diastolic at disappearance), or oscillometrically from cuff-pressure oscillations. Mean arterial pressure is about DBP + (SBP - DBP)/3. Body temperature is measured with thermistors, RTDs or infrared sensors. Blood flow is measured by electromagnetic (voltage induced in the moving conductive blood), ultrasonic Doppler (frequency shift proportional to velocity) or indicator-dilution methods, and volume by plethysmography. Respiratory measurements use spirometry (volumes and flow rates) and capnography (end-tidal CO2); cardiac output is measured by the Fick principle or thermodilution.
entries.formula: MAP about DBP + (SBP - DBP)/3; Doppler shift delta f = 2 f0 v cos(theta) / c; electromagnetic flow voltage E = B d v; Fick cardiac output = oxygen consumption / (arterial - venous oxygen content).
entries.subject: Biomedical Signals
entries.topic: Blood pressure, body temperature, blood flow and respiratory measurement

entries.example: A defibrillator with C = 100 uF charged to 1000 V stores (1/2) x 100e-6 x 1e6 = 50 J. A pulse oximeter reading 98 percent means about 98 percent of haemoglobin is oxygenated.
entries.fact: A sphygmomanometer measures blood pressure with an inflatable cuff; a ventilator moves air in and out of the lungs at set rate, volume and pressure; a cardiac pacemaker delivers timed electrical pulses to trigger heartbeats; a defibrillator delivers a large shock to reset fibrillation, with stored energy E = (1/2) C V^2; a pulse oximeter estimates SpO2 from the ratio of red to infrared light absorption through a finger; a hemodialyzer passes blood across a semi-permeable membrane to remove waste. Electrical safety uses isolation (optical or transformer) so that leakage current through a patient stays tiny: microshock (current through the heart, e.g. via a catheter) is dangerous at tens of microamperes, so isolated, low-leakage design is mandatory.
entries.formula: Defibrillator energy E = (1/2) C V^2; pulse oximeter SpO2 from red/infrared absorption ratio; ventilator delivers set tidal volume at set rate; isolation (optical or transformer) limits patient leakage current.
entries.subject: Biomedical Signals
entries.topic: Medical equipment: sphygmomanometer, ventilator, pacemaker, defibrillator, pulse oximeter, hemodialyzer and electrical safety

entries.example: After a meal, rising blood glucose triggers insulin release, which drives glucose into cells and brings blood glucose back toward about 90 mg/dL; failure of this loop is diabetes.
entries.fact: The cell is the basic unit of life: the nucleus holds DNA, mitochondria make ATP, the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi process proteins, and the membrane controls what enters and leaves. The four tissue types are epithelial (covers surfaces), connective (supports, e.g. bone, blood, fat), muscle (contracts) and nervous (signals). Homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment (temperature, pH, glucose, ions) by negative-feedback loops: a sensor detects a deviation, a control centre compares it with a set point, and an effector corrects it, as in blood-glucose control by insulin.
entries.formula: Homeostasis by negative feedback: sensor -> control centre -> effector -> correction toward set point; four tissue types: epithelial, connective, muscle, nervous; cell organelles: nucleus, mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, cell membrane.
entries.subject: Physiology

entries.example: At rest, heart rate 72 beats/min and stroke volume 70 mL give cardiac output 72 x 0.07 = 5.04 L/min. During exercise both rise, and cardiac output can exceed 20 L/min.
entries.fact: The circulatory system pumps blood through two circuits: the pulmonary circuit (right heart to lungs and back) and the systemic circuit (left heart to the body). The cardiac cycle has systole (contraction, ejecting blood) and diastole (relaxation, filling); stroke volume times heart rate is cardiac output, about 5 L/min at rest. The respiratory system moves air through the trachea and bronchi to the alveoli, where oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange by diffusion across a thin membrane; breathing is driven mainly by the diaphragm, and gas exchange follows partial-pressure gradients.
entries.formula: Cardiac output = heart rate x stroke volume; blood pressure = cardiac output x total peripheral resistance; alveolar gas exchange by diffusion down partial-pressure gradients; tidal volume about 500 mL at rest.
entries.subject: Physiology

entries.example: The kidneys filter about 180 L of fluid per day and reabsorb almost all of it, excreting about 1.5 L of urine. Thyroxine from the thyroid sets the basal metabolic rate.
entries.fact: The musculoskeletal system (bones, joints, muscles) supports the body and produces movement; skeletal muscle contracts on signals from motor neurons. The excretory system (kidneys) filters blood, reabsorbs water and solutes, and excretes waste as urine, also regulating blood pressure and pH. The endocrine system releases hormones (e.g. insulin, thyroxine, adrenaline) into blood for slow, widespread control. The nervous system (brain, spinal cord, peripheral nerves) gives fast, targeted control by electrical signals. The gastrointestinal system digests food and absorbs nutrients, and the reproductive system produces gametes and sex hormones.
entries.formula: Kidney filtration: glomerular filtration rate about 125 mL/min in a healthy adult; endocrine control is hormonal and slow, nervous control is electrical and fast; skeletal muscle is voluntary and striated, smooth muscle lines organs, cardiac muscle is striated and involuntary.
entries.subject: Physiology
entries.topic: Other organ systems: musculoskeletal, excretory, endocrine, nervous, gastrointestinal and reproductive

entries.example: A tissue with mu 10 percent above water has HU = 1000 x 0.10 = 100. A 10 cm slab of tissue with mu = 0.2/cm transmits e^{-2} = 13.5 percent of the incident X-ray intensity.
entries.fact: X-rays are produced when fast electrons strike a metal target, and they are attenuated exponentially as they pass through tissue, I = I0 e^{-mu x}, with attenuation depending on tissue density and atomic number, so bone appears bright and soft tissue dark on a radiograph. CT rotates an X-ray source and detectors around the patient and reconstructs cross-sectional images from many projections (filtered back-projection or iterative reconstruction). CT numbers are expressed in Hounsfield units: air -1000, water 0, soft tissue about +40, bone +400 to +1000 and higher.
entries.formula: Attenuation: I = I0 e^{-mu x}; Hounsfield unit HU = 1000 x (mu - mu_water) / mu_water; CT reconstructs cross-sections from projections taken at many angles.
entries.subject: Medical Imaging

entries.example: In an FDG-PET scan, a tumour taking up more glucose than surrounding tissue appears as a bright spot. The 511 keV annihilation photons are detected in coincidence, which is what localises the source.
entries.fact: SPECT (single photon emission computed tomography) images a gamma-emitting radiotracer (commonly technetium-99m) with a gamma camera rotating around the patient, reconstructing 3D maps of tracer uptake, e.g. blood flow in the heart or brain. PET (positron emission tomography) uses a positron emitter (commonly fluorine-18 in FDG); each positron annihilates with an electron, producing two 511 keV gamma photons travelling in opposite directions, and coincidence detection of the pair locates the event along a line of response. PET shows metabolic activity (FDG uptake in tumours) with higher sensitivity and resolution than SPECT.
entries.formula: PET annihilation: positron + electron -> two 511 keV photons at 180 deg to each other; SPECT: single gamma photons imaged by a rotating gamma camera; tracer uptake maps function, not just anatomy.
entries.subject: Medical Imaging

entries.example: At 1.5 T, protons precess at 42.58 x 1.5 = 63.9 MHz. Fat has a short T1 and appears bright on T1-weighted images, while fluid has a long T2 and appears bright on T2-weighted images.
entries.fact: MRI images hydrogen nuclei (protons) in water and fat. A strong static field B0 aligns the protons, which precess at the Larmor frequency omega = gamma B0 (gamma/2 pi = 42.58 MHz/T for protons); a radiofrequency pulse at that frequency tips the magnetisation, and the signal it gives off as it relaxes is spatially encoded with gradient fields. T1 (spin-lattice) relaxation is the recovery of longitudinal magnetisation and T2 (spin-spin) is the decay of transverse magnetisation; different tissues have different T1 and T2, giving soft-tissue contrast without ionising radiation.
entries.formula: Larmor frequency: omega = gamma B0, f = (gamma/2 pi) B0 = 42.58 MHz/T x B0; T1 = longitudinal recovery time constant; T2 = transverse decay time constant; signal decays as e^{-t/T2} and recovers as (1 - e^{-t/T1}).
entries.subject: Medical Imaging

entries.example: A person of 70 kg (weight 686 N) has a hip joint force of about 3 x 686 = 2058 N during walking. A knee extensor muscle with a 4 cm moment arm must exert 250 N to produce a 10 N m knee moment.
entries.fact: Joint mechanics is analysed with free-body diagrams: forces and moments on a limb segment must satisfy equilibrium (sum of forces = 0, sum of moments = 0) for static analysis, and Newton second law for dynamics. Muscles pull across joints with a moment arm, so joint forces are often several times body weight; for example, the hip joint force in walking is about 3 times body weight. Gait analysis records the gait cycle (stance about 60 percent, swing about 40 percent), step length, cadence, joint angles and ground-reaction forces, and is used to assess walking disorders and prosthesis design.
entries.formula: Static equilibrium: sum F = 0, sum M = 0; joint moment = muscle force x moment arm; gait cycle: stance about 60 percent, swing about 40 percent; hip joint force in walking about 3 x body weight.
entries.subject: Biomechanics
entries.topic: Biomechanics of joints and gait analysis

entries.example: A femur shaft of cross-section 3 cm^2 carrying 3000 N has stress 3000 / 3e-4 = 10 MPa, well below cortical bone strength. With E = 18 GPa, the strain is 10e6 / 18e9 = 0.00056, or 0.056 percent.
entries.fact: Bone has two forms: dense cortical (compact) bone forming the outer shell of long bones, and porous cancellous (trabecular) bone inside, a lattice of struts that is light and strong. Cortical bone is anisotropic (stronger along the shaft than across it) with Young modulus about 17-20 GPa and compressive strength about 150-200 MPa; cancellous bone is much weaker and more compliant (modulus 0.1-2 GPa). Bone remodels in response to load (Wolff law): increased loading strengthens it, disuse weakens it. Stress is force per area, strain is fractional deformation, and the stress-strain curve gives modulus, yield and ultimate strength.
entries.formula: Stress sigma = F / A; strain epsilon = delta L / L; Young modulus E = sigma / epsilon (elastic region); cortical bone E about 17-20 GPa, cancellous bone E about 0.1-2 GPa; Wolff law: bone adapts to the loads placed on it.
entries.subject: Biomechanics
entries.topic: Hard tissues: structure and mechanical properties of bone

entries.example: A tissue with E = 1 MPa and eta = 10 MPa s has tau = 10 s: under a sudden fixed strain its stress falls to 37 percent of the initial value in 10 s. Under constant stress, a Voigt tissue reaches 63 percent of its final strain in one time constant.
entries.fact: Soft tissues are viscoelastic: they behave partly like an elastic solid (spring) and partly like a viscous fluid (dashpot), showing stress relaxation (stress falls under constant strain), creep (strain grows under constant stress) and hysteresis. The Maxwell model (spring and dashpot in series) describes stress relaxation well but creeps forever; the Kelvin-Voigt model (spring and dashpot in parallel) describes creep well but not relaxation. Their relaxation time is tau = eta / E, where eta is viscosity and E is modulus; real tissues need multi-element (generalised) models.
entries.formula: Maxwell: sigma + tau d(sigma)/dt = E d(epsilon)/dt, tau = eta / E; stress relaxation: sigma(t) = sigma_0 e^{-t/tau}; Kelvin-Voigt: sigma = E epsilon + eta d(epsilon)/dt; creep: epsilon(t) = (sigma_0 / E)(1 - e^{-t/tau}).
entries.subject: Biomechanics
entries.topic: Soft-tissue viscoelasticity: Maxwell and Voigt models

entries.example: Halving a vessel radius raises its resistance 16-fold, so the same flow needs 16 times the pressure drop. A 1 mm radius vessel 10 cm long with blood viscosity 0.0035 Pa s has resistance 8 x 0.0035 x 0.1 / (pi x (1e-3)^4) = about 8.9e8 Pa s/m^3.
entries.fact: Blood is a non-Newtonian fluid: its apparent viscosity (about 3-4 cP at high shear, higher at low shear) falls as shear rate rises because red cells deform and align, and it is slightly shear-thinning. Flow in a vessel follows Poiseuille law for steady laminar flow, Q = pi delta p r^4 / (8 eta L), so flow is extremely sensitive to radius: halving the radius cuts flow 16-fold, which is why small stenoses matter so much. Flow is usually laminar (Reynolds number below about 2000 in large vessels) but can become turbulent at stenoses or heart valves; pulsatile flow is described by the Womersley number.
entries.formula: Poiseuille: Q = pi delta p r^4 / (8 eta L); resistance R = 8 eta L / (pi r^4); Reynolds Re = rho v D / eta; blood viscosity about 3-4 cP (0.003-0.004 Pa s) at high shear; pressure drop proportional to flow x resistance.
entries.subject: Biomechanics
entries.topic: Biofluid mechanics: blood flow in the cardiovascular system

entries.example: A hip implant pairs a titanium stem (strong, biocompatible) with a ceramic femoral head on a UHMWPE liner (low wear): each material is chosen for the job it does best in the same device.
entries.fact: Metallic biomaterials (stainless steel 316L, cobalt-chromium, titanium and its alloys) are strong, tough and fatigue-resistant, used for load-bearing implants such as hip stems and bone plates; titanium forms a stable oxide layer and integrates well with bone. Ceramics (alumina, zirconia, hydroxyapatite) are hard, wear-resistant and bioactive or inert, used for joint bearing surfaces and bone fillers, but are brittle. Polymers (UHMWPE for joint liners, PMMA bone cement, silicone, biodegradable PLA/PGA) are versatile and light but weaker and prone to wear and degradation. Composites combine phases (e.g. carbon-fibre reinforced polymer) to tailor stiffness and strength.
entries.formula: Metals: high strength and toughness, e.g. Ti-6Al-4V; ceramics: hard and wear-resistant but brittle, e.g. alumina, hydroxyapatite; polymers: light and versatile, e.g. UHMWPE, PMMA; composites: combined phases for tailored properties.
entries.subject: Biomaterials
entries.topic: Biomaterials: metallic, ceramic, polymeric and composite

entries.example: A biodegradable PLA suture holds a wound together, then hydrolyses into lactic acid that the body metabolises, so no removal is needed. A drug-eluting stent releases drug at a near-constant rate to prevent the artery re-narrowing.
entries.fact: Biocompatibility is the ability of a material to perform with an appropriate host response: no toxicity, no harmful immune reaction, no excessive inflammation. Bioactivity is the ability to bond with tissue (e.g. hydroxyapatite bonding to bone); biodegradability is breakdown into harmless products that the body clears (e.g. PLA sutures). Drug delivery systems control where, when and how fast a drug is released: zero-order release gives a constant rate, first-order release falls with remaining drug, and release can be triggered by pH, temperature or enzymes. Tissue engineering combines cells, a scaffold and signalling molecules to regenerate tissue, with the scaffold providing temporary mechanical support and a template for new tissue.
entries.formula: Biocompatibility: appropriate host response, no toxicity; bioactivity: chemical bonding to tissue; biodegradability: breakdown to harmless products; zero-order release: constant rate; first-order release: rate proportional to remaining drug.
entries.subject: Biomaterials
entries.topic: Implants: biocompatibility, bioactivity, biodegradability, drug delivery and tissue engineering

entries.example: A hydrogel with G' much larger than G'' behaves as a solid gel; if G'' dominates it flows like a liquid. FTIR of a polymer shows a carbonyl peak near 1730 cm^-1, confirming the ester group is present.
entries.fact: Rheology measures flow and deformation: the storage modulus G' (elastic, solid-like) and loss modulus G'' (viscous, liquid-like) describe a hydrogel or polymer. Atomic force microscopy (AFM) images surfaces at nanometre resolution by feeling them with a sharp tip, and also measures forces and stiffness at the cell scale. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images surfaces with an electron beam at high magnification and depth of field; transmission electron microscopy (TEM) passes electrons through a thin sample for internal structure at even higher resolution. Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) identifies chemical groups from their infrared absorption peaks, e.g. carbonyl and hydroxyl bands in polymers.
entries.formula: Rheology: G' = storage (elastic) modulus, G'' = loss (viscous) modulus; AFM: nanometre topography and force measurement; SEM: surface imaging, TEM: internal structure at higher resolution; FTIR: chemical groups from infrared absorption peaks.
entries.subject: Biomaterials
entries.topic: Biomaterial characterisation: rheology, AFM, electron microscopy and FTIR

entries.fact: A non-zero vector v is an eigenvector of a square matrix A if Av = λv, where λ is the eigenvalue. Eigenvalues are the roots of the characteristic equation det(A − λI) = 0. The Cayley-Hamilton theorem states that every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation, which lets powers of A be reduced to lower-degree polynomials.
entries.formula: det(A − λI) = 0; for a 2x2 matrix, A^2 − tr(A)A + det(A)I = 0 (Cayley-Hamilton)
entries.example: For A = [[2, 0], [0, 3]], det(A − λI) = (2 − λ)(3 − λ) = 0, so the eigenvalues are λ = 2 and 3, with eigenvectors along the x and y axes.
entries.subject: Engineering Mathematics

entries.fact: The Laplace transform converts a differential equation into an algebraic equation in s, which is easier to solve. Key transforms are L{1} = 1/s, L{e^(at)} = 1/(s − a), L{sin at} = a/(s^2 + a^2), and L{f'(t)} = sF(s) − f(0). The inverse transform then recovers the time-domain solution.
entries.example: Solve y' + y = 0, y(0) = 1: sY − 1 + Y = 0 gives Y = 1/(s + 1), so y(t) = e^(−t).
entries.subject: Engineering Mathematics

entries.fact: Simpson's 1/3 rule approximates a definite integral by fitting parabolas through groups of three points, and is exact for polynomials up to degree 3. It needs an even number of intervals n with step h = (b − a)/n. It is generally more accurate than the trapezoidal rule for the same number of intervals.
entries.example: ∫ from 0 to 1 of x^2 dx with n = 2, h = 0.5: (0.5/3)[0 + 4(0.25) + 1] = 0.333, which equals the exact value 1/3.
entries.subject: Engineering Mathematics

entries.topic: Field Capacity and Efficiency of Farm Implements
entries.fact: Theoretical field capacity (TFC) is the area covered per hour if the machine worked continuously at full width and speed. Effective field capacity (EFC) is what is actually achieved, reduced by turning, loading and overlap losses. Field efficiency is the ratio EFC/TFC, typically 65-85% for tillage and sowing operations.
entries.formula: TFC (ha/h) = speed (km/h) × width (m) / 10; EFC = TFC × field efficiency; time per ha = 1/EFC
entries.example: A seed drill at 5 km/h with 2 m width has TFC = 5 × 2/10 = 1.0 ha/h. At 75% field efficiency, EFC = 0.75 ha/h, so one hectare takes about 1.33 h.
entries.subject: Farm Machinery

entries.topic: Tractor Traction, Slip and Drawbar Pull
entries.fact: Wheel slip is the loss of forward motion because the driving wheels spin faster than the tractor advances, and it rises with drawbar load and soft soil. Gross traction is the thrust developed at the soil-wheel interface; subtracting rolling resistance gives the net drawbar pull available for the implement. The traction coefficient is drawbar pull divided by the dynamic weight on the drive wheels.
entries.formula: Slip (%) = (V0 − Va)/V0 × 100; drawbar pull = gross traction − rolling resistance; traction coefficient = pull / dynamic weight
entries.example: A tractor whose wheels would theoretically advance at 6 km/h but actually moves at 5.4 km/h has slip = (6 − 5.4)/6 = 10%, which is near the 10-15% range considered acceptable for good traction.
entries.subject: Farm Machinery

entries.topic: IC Engine Cycles: Otto and Diesel Efficiency
entries.fact: The Otto cycle (constant-volume heat addition) models spark-ignition petrol engines, and its air-standard efficiency depends only on the compression ratio r and the specific-heat ratio γ. The Diesel cycle (constant-pressure heat addition) models compression-ignition engines and also depends on the cut-off ratio ρ. Higher compression ratio raises efficiency in both, which is why diesel engines run at much higher compression ratios.
entries.example: For an Otto engine with r = 8 and γ = 1.4, η = 1 − 8^(−0.4) ≈ 1 − 0.435 = 56.5% air-standard efficiency (real brake efficiency is far lower, around 25-30%).
entries.subject: Farm Machinery

entries.fact: The Darcy-Weisbach equation gives the friction head loss in a pipe as a function of the friction factor f, pipe length and diameter, and flow velocity. For laminar flow f = 64/Re, while for turbulent flow f is read from Moody's diagram using the Reynolds number and the relative roughness of the pipe.
entries.formula: h_f = f × (L/D) × (v^2/(2g)); laminar: f = 64/Re; Re = ρvD/μ
entries.example: Water at v = 1 m/s in a 100 m long, 0.2 m diameter pipe with f = 0.02: h_f = 0.02 × (100/0.2) × (1/(2 × 9.81)) = 0.51 m of head lost to friction.
entries.subject: Soil & Water

entries.fact: A unit hydrograph (UH) is the direct-runoff hydrograph resulting from 1 cm of effective rainfall uniformly distributed over a catchment in a specified duration D. Because a catchment is treated as a linear system, the hydrograph for any storm is obtained by scaling the UH ordinates by the effective rainfall depth and adding (convolving) the responses of successive rainfall blocks. The base period of the UH stays constant regardless of rainfall depth.
entries.formula: Q(t) = UH ordinate × effective rainfall depth (cm); for multiple blocks, Q = sum over blocks of (UH shifted by block time × block rainfall)
entries.example: If a 1-hour UH has a peak ordinate of 10 m3/s per cm of effective rain, a storm with 2 cm of effective rainfall in one hour gives a peak discharge of 20 m3/s at the same time to peak.
entries.subject: Soil & Water

entries.fact: The USLE is an empirical model that predicts the long-term average annual soil loss from sheet and rill erosion on a hillslope. It multiplies five factors: rainfall erosivity R, soil erodibility K, topographic factor LS, cover-management factor C, and support-practice factor P. It does not predict gully erosion or single-storm losses.
entries.formula: A = R × K × LS × C × P, where A is soil loss in t/ha/yr
entries.example: With R = 300, K = 0.3, LS = 1.2, C = 0.4 and P = 0.8, A = 300 × 0.3 × 1.2 × 0.4 × 0.8 = 34.6 t/ha/yr, far above the tolerable limit of about 11 t/ha/yr, so conservation practices are needed.
entries.subject: Soil & Water

entries.topic: Psychrometry: Properties of Air-Water Vapour Mixtures
entries.fact: Psychrometry describes moist air using the humidity ratio W (kg of water per kg of dry air), relative humidity, dew-point temperature and wet-bulb temperature. The humidity ratio follows from the partial pressure of water vapour in the air. These properties govern drying, storage and air-conditioning of agricultural produce.
entries.formula: W = 0.622 × pv/(p − pv); relative humidity = pv/pvs × 100%
entries.example: At 30 °C and 60% relative humidity, pv ≈ 0.6 × 4.25 = 2.55 kPa, so W = 0.622 × 2.55/(101.3 − 2.55) ≈ 0.016 kg water per kg dry air.
entries.subject: Food Processing

entries.topic: Kinetics of Microbial Death: D-value, z-value and F0
entries.fact: Microbial death by heat follows first-order kinetics: each D-value is the time at a given temperature needed to reduce a population by 90% (one log cycle). The z-value is the temperature rise needed to reduce the D-value tenfold. The F0 value is the equivalent time at 121.1 °C, and a 12D process (F0 = 12 min for C. botulinum) is the standard for low-acid canned foods.
entries.formula: D = time for 1-log reduction at temperature T; log(D1/D2) = (T2 − T1)/z; F0 = D × log(N0/N)
entries.example: If C. botulinum spores have D121 = 1 min, a 12D (botulinum cook) process needs F0 = 12 × 1 = 12 min at 121.1 °C to reduce the population by 12 log cycles.
entries.subject: Food Processing

entries.topic: Thiem Equation for Steady Flow to a Well
entries.fact: The Thiem equation describes steady-state radial flow to a fully penetrating well in a confined aquifer. It relates the pumping rate to the drawdowns measured in two observation wells, and is used to estimate aquifer transmissivity T from a pumping test. It assumes a homogeneous, isotropic, infinite aquifer and constant pumping rate.
entries.formula: T = Q × ln(r2/r1) / (2π × (s1 − s2)), where T = K × b (transmissivity)
entries.example: Pumping Q = 0.05 m3/s with drawdown difference s1 − s2 = 2 m between wells at r2/r1 = 10: T = 0.05 × ln(10)/(2π × 2) = 0.05 × 2.303/12.57 ≈ 0.0092 m2/s.
entries.subject: Soil & Water

entries.topic: Enzyme Inhibition: Competitive, Non-competitive and Uncompetitive
entries.fact: A competitive inhibitor binds the active site and raises the apparent Km without changing Vmax, so its effect can be overcome by adding more substrate. A non-competitive inhibitor binds elsewhere and lowers Vmax without changing Km. An uncompetitive inhibitor binds only the enzyme-substrate complex, lowering both Vmax and Km. The inhibitor constant Ki measures binding strength; smaller Ki means stronger inhibition.
entries.formula: Competitive: v = Vmax[S]/(Km(1 + [I]/Ki) + [S]); non-competitive: Vmax_app = Vmax/(1 + [I]/Ki)
entries.example: If [I] = Ki for a competitive inhibitor, the apparent Km doubles, so twice as much substrate is needed to reach half of Vmax, while Vmax itself is unchanged.
entries.subject: Biochemistry

entries.fact: Genes on the same chromosome are linked and tend to be inherited together, but crossing over during meiosis produces recombinant gametes. The recombination frequency between two genes estimates their distance: 1% recombination equals 1 centiMorgan (cM). Genes 50 cM or more apart behave as if unlinked because multiple crossovers randomise their assortment.
entries.formula: Recombination frequency (%) = (recombinant progeny / total progeny) × 100; 1% RF = 1 cM
entries.example: In a test cross of 200 progeny, 30 are recombinant for genes A and B, so the distance is 30/200 × 100 = 15 cM.
entries.subject: Genetics

entries.topic: The lac Operon: Regulation of Gene Expression
entries.fact: The lac operon of E. coli contains the genes lacZ, lacY and lacA for lactose metabolism, controlled by the lacI repressor and the CAP-cAMP activator. Lactose (as allolactose) inactivates the repressor, while glucose lowers cAMP so CAP cannot activate transcription. The operon is therefore switched on only when lactose is present and glucose is absent, a classic example of combined negative and positive control.
entries.formula: Rule: lac operon ON only when lactose present AND glucose absent (AND logic of repressor release + CAP activation)
entries.example: E. coli grown in glucose plus lactose keeps the lac operon off (catabolite repression); when glucose runs out, cAMP rises, CAP binds, and beta-galactosidase is produced to use lactose.
entries.subject: Molecular Biology

entries.fact: A chemostat is a continuous culture in which fresh medium flows in at rate F and culture flows out at the same rate, keeping the volume V constant. At steady state the specific growth rate μ equals the dilution rate D = F/V. If D exceeds the maximum growth rate μmax, cells are washed out faster than they divide and the culture collapses.
entries.formula: D = F/V; at steady state μ = D; washout when D > μmax; biomass X = Y(S0 − S)
entries.example: A 10 L chemostat fed at 2 L/h has D = 0.2 h−1, so the cells grow at μ = 0.2 h−1 at steady state; raising the feed above μmax × V would wash the culture out.
entries.subject: Bioprocess Engineering

entries.fact: Aerobic cultures are usually limited by oxygen transfer from gas bubbles into the liquid. The volumetric mass-transfer coefficient kLa combines the liquid-side coefficient kL and the interfacial area a. The oxygen transfer rate OTR = kLa(C* − CL), where C* is the saturation concentration and CL the actual dissolved oxygen. At steady state OTR equals the oxygen uptake rate of the cells, so kLa must be high enough to meet demand.
entries.formula: OTR = kLa(C* − CL); OUR = qO2 × X; at steady state OTR = OUR
entries.example: With kLa = 100 h−1, C* = 8 mg/L and CL = 2 mg/L, OTR = 100 × (8 − 2) = 600 mg/L/h; a culture consuming oxygen faster than this becomes oxygen-limited.
entries.subject: Bioprocess Engineering

entries.fact: When an enzyme is immobilised in a porous particle, substrate must diffuse in before it can react, so the observed rate is lower than the intrinsic rate. The Thiele modulus φ compares the reaction rate to the diffusion rate: small φ means reaction-limited (the whole particle is used), large φ means diffusion-limited (only the outer shell reacts). The effectiveness factor η is the ratio of the observed rate to the rate without diffusion resistance.
entries.formula: φ = R√(k/Deff) (first order); η = tanh(φ)/φ for a slab; η → 1 when φ is small
entries.example: For φ = 0.3, η = tanh(0.3)/0.3 ≈ 0.97, so the immobilised enzyme works at 97% of its intrinsic rate and diffusion is barely limiting.
entries.subject: Bioprocess Engineering

entries.topic: Ideal Reactors: Batch, CSTR and PFR Design Equations
entries.fact: A batch reactor holds the same material while reaction proceeds, so its time is found by integrating the rate over conversion. A CSTR is perfectly mixed, so the whole volume sits at the exit concentration and its volume is proportional to the rate at that concentration. A PFR has concentration changing along its length, so its volume is the integral of dX/(−rA). For a given conversion, a PFR is smaller than a CSTR when the rate falls with conversion.
entries.formula: Batch: t = ∫dX/(−rA); CSTR: V = FA0·X/(−rA); PFR: V = FA0·∫dX/(−rA)
entries.example: For a first-order reaction needing 90% conversion, the PFR volume is about half the CSTR volume, because the CSTR operates entirely at the low exit concentration where the rate is slowest.
entries.subject: Bioprocess Engineering

entries.fact: Restriction endonucleases cut DNA at specific, usually palindromic, recognition sequences, producing sticky ends (with single-stranded overhangs) or blunt ends. Sticky ends from the same enzyme ligate efficiently, which is the basis of recombinant DNA cloning. A cloning vector must carry an origin of replication, a selectable marker such as an antibiotic-resistance gene, and a cloning site; common vectors are plasmids, lambda phage, cosmids and bacterial artificial chromosomes.
entries.formula: Rule: a vector needs an origin of replication + a selectable marker + a cloning site; sticky ends from the same enzyme ligate efficiently
entries.example: EcoRI cuts G^AATTC, leaving a 5' AATT overhang; a DNA fragment cut with EcoRI can be ligated into a plasmid cut with the same enzyme.
entries.subject: Molecular Biology

entries.fact: CRISPR-Cas9 edits DNA using a single guide RNA (sgRNA) that directs the Cas9 nuclease to a target sequence next to a PAM site (NGG in the common Streptococcus pyogenes system). Cas9 makes a double-strand break about 3 bp upstream of the PAM. The cell repairs it by error-prone non-homologous end joining, which usually knocks the gene out, or by homology-directed repair with a supplied template, which makes a precise edit.
entries.formula: Rule: Cas9 cuts ~3 bp upstream of the NGG PAM; NHEJ gives knockouts, HDR gives precise edits
entries.example: To knock out a gene, a sgRNA is designed against its early coding region; NHEJ repair introduces an indel that shifts the reading frame and destroys the protein.
entries.subject: Molecular Biology

entries.fact: An antibody is made of two heavy and two light chains forming a Y shape: the Fab arms bind antigen and the Fc stem carries out effector functions. There are five classes: IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE and IgD. In a sandwich ELISA the target antigen is captured by one antibody and detected by a second enzyme-linked antibody; the enzyme produces a coloured product whose absorbance is proportional to the antigen concentration.
entries.formula: Rule: in ELISA, absorbance is proportional to antigen concentration; IgG = 2 heavy + 2 light chains (Fab binds antigen, Fc mediates effector functions)
entries.example: A sandwich ELISA for HIV p24 antigen uses a capture antibody on the plate and an enzyme-linked detection antibody, giving a colour signal that quantifies viral protein in the sample.
entries.subject: Biochemistry

entries.topic: Laplace Transforms for Growth and Reaction ODEs
entries.fact: The Laplace transform turns a linear ODE with constant coefficients into an algebraic equation in s, which is useful for first-order growth, decay and reactor balance equations. The transform of a derivative is L{f'} = sF(s) − f(0), and L{e^(at)} = 1/(s − a). Inverting the result returns the time-domain solution.
entries.example: For exponential cell growth dX/dt = μX with X(0) = X0, the transform gives sX̄ − X0 = μX̄, so X̄ = X0/(s − μ) and inverting gives X(t) = X0·e^(μt).
entries.subject: Engineering Mathematics

entries.fact: Chromatographic resolution Rs measures how well two adjacent peaks are separated; Rs ≥ 1.5 means baseline separation. It depends on the difference in retention times relative to peak widths. The plate number N measures column efficiency, and a taller column or smaller particles raise N. Ion-exchange, gel-filtration, hydrophobic-interaction and affinity chromatography separate proteins by charge, size, hydrophobicity and specific binding respectively.
entries.example: Two peaks at 5.0 and 5.5 min with widths of 0.2 min each give Rs = 2(0.5)/(0.4) = 2.5, so they are fully baseline-separated.
entries.subject: Bioprocess Engineering

entries.fact: A particle confined to a one-dimensional box of length L with infinitely high walls has quantised energy levels, because its wavefunction must vanish at the walls. Only standing waves fitting an integer number of half-wavelengths are allowed. The ground state (n = 1) still has non-zero energy, the zero-point energy, so a confined particle can never be at rest.
entries.subject: Physical Chemistry

entries.fact: The Clausius-Clapeyron equation relates the slope of a phase boundary on a P-T diagram to the enthalpy change and volume change of the transition. For vaporisation, where the vapour volume dominates, it gives the vapour pressure as a function of temperature. It explains why vapour pressure rises steeply with temperature and why water boils at lower temperatures at altitude.
entries.formula: dP/dT = ΔH/(T·ΔV); ln(P2/P1) = −ΔHvap/R × (1/T2 − 1/T1)
entries.example: For water, ΔHvap ≈ 40.7 kJ/mol; the vapour pressure at 90 °C is about 0.70 atm, which is why water boils below 100 °C on a mountain where atmospheric pressure is lower.
entries.subject: Physical Chemistry

entries.fact: In dilute electrolyte solutions, ions are surrounded by an oppositely charged ionic atmosphere that lowers their activity below their concentration. The Debye-Hückel limiting law gives the mean ionic activity coefficient from the ionic strength of the solution. It is valid only at low ionic strength (below about 0.01 M), where ion-ion interactions dominate and ion size can be ignored.
entries.formula: log10 γ± = −A|z+·z−|√I; I = (1/2)Σci·zi^2; A = 0.509 for water at 25 °C
entries.example: For 0.01 M NaCl, I = 0.01, so log γ± = −0.509 × 1 × 0.1 = −0.0509, giving γ± ≈ 0.89, meaning the ions behave as if only 89% as concentrated.
entries.subject: Physical Chemistry

entries.fact: The Langmuir isotherm models adsorption as a monolayer on identical surface sites with no interaction between adsorbed molecules. The fractional surface coverage θ rises with gas pressure and saturates at θ = 1 when all sites are filled. At low pressure coverage is proportional to pressure (Henry's-law region). The linearised form is used to find the monolayer capacity and the adsorption equilibrium constant from experimental data.
entries.formula: θ = KP/(1 + KP); linear form: P/V = 1/(Vm·K) + P/Vm
entries.example: When KP = 1, θ = 0.5, so the surface is half covered; doubling the pressure to KP = 9 raises coverage only to 0.9, showing the saturation behaviour.
entries.subject: Physical Chemistry

entries.fact: In an octahedral complex, the five d orbitals split into a lower t2g set and an upper eg set separated by Δo, because the eg orbitals point directly at the ligands and are destabilised more. The crystal field stabilisation energy is CFSE = (−0.4·n_t2g + 0.6·n_eg)Δo. If Δo is smaller than the pairing energy P the complex is high-spin; if larger, it is low-spin. This splitting also explains the colours of transition-metal complexes through d-d transitions.
entries.formula: CFSE = (−0.4·n_t2g + 0.6·n_eg)Δo; high-spin if Δo < P, low-spin if Δo > P
entries.example: Fe2+ (d6) in a weak field is high-spin t2g^4 eg^2 with CFSE = (−1.6 + 1.2)Δo = −0.4Δo, while in a strong field it is low-spin t2g^6 with CFSE = −2.4Δo + 2P.
entries.subject: Inorganic Chemistry

entries.fact: Stable organometallic complexes usually have 18 valence electrons around the metal, filling the nine valence orbitals (one s, three p, five d) like a noble-gas configuration. Count the metal's group number plus 2 electrons for each 2-electron donor ligand (CO, phosphine, alkene) and 1 electron per X-type ligand (halide, alkyl). Complexes with 16 electrons, such as square-planar d8 species, are common exceptions.
entries.formula: Total electron count = metal group number + 2 × (number of L-type ligands) + 1 × (number of X-type ligands); stable at 18
entries.example: Fe(CO)5: Fe is group 8 and each CO donates 2 electrons, so 8 + 5 × 2 = 18 electrons, a stable complex.
entries.subject: Inorganic Chemistry

entries.fact: SN2 is a concerted one-step reaction: the nucleophile attacks from the back side as the leaving group departs, giving inversion of configuration (Walden inversion), with rate = k[RX][Nu]. It is favoured by primary substrates and strong nucleophiles. SN1 is two-step: ionisation to a planar carbocation is rate-determining, so rate = k[RX] and attack from either face gives racemisation. It is favoured by tertiary substrates and polar protic solvents that stabilise the carbocation.
entries.formula: SN2: rate = k[RX][Nu], inversion, 1° > 2° > 3°; SN1: rate = k[RX], racemisation, 3° > 2° > 1°
entries.example: tert-Butyl bromide with OH− reacts by SN1 to give racemic tert-butanol if the carbon were chiral, while methyl bromide reacts by SN2 with complete inversion.
entries.subject: Organic Chemistry

entries.fact: Pericyclic reactions are concerted reactions through a cyclic transition state, and their feasibility depends on orbital symmetry. A thermal reaction is allowed when the total number of (4q + 2)s and (4r)a components is odd. In practice: a thermal [4+2] cycloaddition (Diels-Alder) is allowed suprafacial-suprafacial, while a thermal [2+2] is forbidden and needs light. Electrocyclic ring closure is disrotatory for 4n + 2 pi electrons thermally and conrotatory for 4n pi electrons thermally, reversing under light.
entries.formula: Thermal: (4n + 2)π suprafacial allowed, (4n)π photochemical; electrocyclic: 4n + 2 thermal disrotatory, 4n thermal conrotatory
entries.example: Butadiene + ethylene gives cyclohexene thermally by a [4+2] Diels-Alder reaction, but two ethylenes do not dimerise thermally because [2+2] cycloaddition is symmetry-forbidden in the ground state.
entries.subject: Organic Chemistry

entries.topic: NMR Spectroscopy: Chemical Shift and Spin-Spin Splitting
entries.fact: In proton NMR, the chemical shift δ measures how shielded a nucleus is relative to TMS (0 ppm): electron-withdrawing groups deshield and shift signals downfield. Equivalent neighbouring protons split a signal into n + 1 peaks, where n is the number of protons on adjacent carbons, with coupling constant J in Hz. Integration gives the relative number of protons, so NMR reveals both the environment and the connectivity of hydrogens.
entries.formula: δ (ppm) = (ν_sample − ν_TMS)/ν_spectrometer × 10^6; splitting: n + 1 rule
entries.example: Bromoethane CH3CH2Br shows a triplet near 1.7 ppm (3H, split by 2 neighbours) and a quartet near 3.4 ppm (2H, split by 3 neighbours), the CH2 being downfield because bromine deshields it.
entries.subject: Spectroscopy

entries.fact: A compound is aromatic if it is cyclic, planar, fully conjugated, and has (4n + 2) pi electrons, which gives extra stability from a closed shell of delocalised electrons. A planar cyclic conjugated system with 4n pi electrons is antiaromatic and especially unstable. Non-planar or non-conjugated rings are simply non-aromatic. The rule also applies to charged species such as the cyclopentadienyl anion (6 pi electrons, aromatic).
entries.formula: Aromatic: cyclic, planar, conjugated, (4n + 2) π electrons; antiaromatic: 4n π electrons
entries.example: Benzene has 6 π electrons (n = 1) and is aromatic; cyclobutadiene has 4 π electrons and is antiaromatic; cyclopentadienyl anion has 6 π electrons and is aromatic.
entries.subject: Organic Chemistry

entries.fact: In a first-order reaction the rate is proportional to the concentration of one reactant, so a plot of ln[A] against time is a straight line with slope −k. The half-life is independent of the initial concentration, which is the signature of first-order kinetics. Many processes, including radioactive decay and some drug eliminations, follow first-order kinetics.
entries.example: A reaction with k = 0.0693 min−1 has t1/2 = 0.693/0.0693 = 10 min, so after 20 min only one-quarter of the reactant remains.
entries.subject: Physical Chemistry

entries.fact: A diatomic molecule treated as a rigid rotor has quantised rotational energies E_J = BJ(J + 1), where B = h/(8π²I) is the rotational constant and I = μr² is the moment of inertia. Microwave absorption follows the selection rule ΔJ = ±1, so spectral lines appear spaced by 2B. Measuring the spacing gives B, hence the bond length.
entries.formula: E_J = B·J(J + 1); B = h/(8π^2·I); line spacing = 2B; selection rule ΔJ = ±1
entries.example: For CO, B ≈ 1.93 cm−1, so its pure rotational lines are spaced by about 3.86 cm−1 in the microwave region, from which the C-O bond length (~1.13 Å) is calculated.
entries.subject: Spectroscopy

entries.fact: MacArthur and Wilson's theory says the number of species on an island reaches an equilibrium where the immigration rate of new species equals the extinction rate of resident species. Larger islands support more species because extinction rates are lower, and islands nearer the mainland support more because immigration is higher. The theory also predicts species richness from island area through the species-area relationship, and it is widely applied to habitat fragments and nature reserves.
entries.formula: Equilibrium when immigration rate = extinction rate; species richness S = c·A^z
entries.example: An island ten times larger than another, with z = 0.3, holds about 10^0.3 ≈ 2 times as many species at equilibrium, all else being equal.
entries.subject: Ecology

entries.topic: r/K Selection and Life History Strategies
entries.fact: Life histories lie on a continuum between r-selection and K-selection. r-selected species live in unstable environments, mature early, produce many small offspring with little parental care, and show boom-bust population dynamics. K-selected species live near the carrying capacity in stable environments, mature late, produce few large offspring with heavy care, and are strong competitors. Most species fall between the extremes.
entries.formula: Rule: r-selected = high fecundity, low care, unstable habitat; K-selected = low fecundity, high care, stable habitat near carrying capacity
entries.example: Mice are r-selected (many pups, short lives, rapid breeding), while elephants are K-selected (one calf after a 22-month gestation, years of care).
entries.subject: Evolution

entries.fact: Genetic drift is the random change in allele frequencies from one generation to the next due to sampling of gametes, and it is strongest in small populations, where it can fix or lose alleles by chance alone. FST measures how much genetic variation is partitioned among populations rather than within them: FST near 0 means populations are freely interbreeding, while high FST means they are strongly differentiated. Gene flow opposes drift and lowers FST.
entries.formula: FST = (HT − HS)/HT, where HT is total heterozygosity and HS is mean within-population heterozygosity; fixation probability of a neutral allele = its initial frequency
entries.example: If FST = 0.2, about 20% of the total genetic variation lies between populations and 80% within them, indicating moderate differentiation, perhaps from restricted gene flow.
entries.subject: Evolution

entries.topic: Primary Productivity: GPP, NPP and Respiration
entries.fact: Gross primary productivity (GPP) is the total carbon fixed by photosynthesis, while net primary productivity (NPP) is what remains after the producers' own respiration is subtracted. NPP is the energy available to herbivores and the rest of the food web. It is highest in tropical rainforests, estuaries and coral reefs, and lowest in deserts and the open ocean per unit area.
entries.formula: NPP = GPP − respiration (R)
entries.example: If a grassland fixes 10 g C/m2/day (GPP) and respires 4 g C/m2/day, its NPP is 6 g C/m2/day, which is the production available to grazers and decomposers.
entries.subject: Ecology

entries.fact: A species' niche is its role and requirements: the range of conditions and resources it can use. The fundamental niche is the full range it could occupy without competitors, while the realised niche is the smaller range it actually occupies once competition and predation are considered. Gause's competitive exclusion principle states that two species competing for the same limiting resource cannot coexist indefinitely; one will exclude the other, or they will diverge in resource use (character displacement).
entries.formula: Rule (Gause): two species cannot stably coexist on the same limiting resource; realised niche ⊆ fundamental niche
entries.example: In Gause's classic experiment, Paramecium aurelia drove P. caudatum extinct in mixed culture because both competed for the same bacterial food, while P. bursaria coexisted by feeding at a different depth.
entries.subject: Ecology

entries.fact: Optimal foraging theory predicts that natural selection favours foraging behaviour that maximises net energy gain per unit time. A forager should take a prey item only if its profitability (energy gained divided by handling time) exceeds the average rate of energy gain from the environment. As rich prey becomes more common, low-profit prey should be dropped from the diet, even if they are still abundant.
entries.formula: Rule: accept prey if E/h (energy per handling time) > average foraging rate of the environment
entries.example: Great tits take large, profitable caterpillars when they are common and ignore small ones, but add the small prey back to the diet when large prey become scarce.
entries.subject: Ecology

entries.fact: Kin selection explains altruism: a gene for helping relatives can spread if the benefit to the recipient, weighted by genetic relatedness, exceeds the cost to the helper. This is Hamilton's rule, rb > c, where r is the coefficient of relatedness, b the benefit and c the cost, all in units of reproductive success. It explains sterile worker castes in social insects, alarm calls, and food sharing among relatives.
entries.formula: Hamilton's rule: r·b > c; relatedness r = 0.5 for full siblings and offspring, 0.25 for half-siblings and grandchildren
entries.example: An alarm call that costs the caller 1 offspring-equivalent is favoured if it saves more than 2 full siblings (r = 0.5, so r·b = 0.5 × 2 = 1, just breaking even; saving 3 siblings makes it favoured).
entries.subject: Evolution

entries.fact: The chi-square test compares observed counts with the counts expected under a null hypothesis, and is used widely in ecology for testing Mendelian ratios, habitat associations and goodness of fit. The test statistic sums the squared deviations divided by expected values, and is compared with a critical value from the chi-square distribution at the chosen significance level (usually α = 0.05) with degrees of freedom (rows − 1)(columns − 1) for a contingency table.
entries.formula: χ² = Σ(O − E)^2/E; df = (rows − 1)(columns − 1) for a contingency table
entries.example: In a cross expecting a 3:1 ratio among 120 offspring, observing 90 dominant and 30 recessive gives χ² = 0, a perfect fit; a value above 3.84 (df = 1, α = 0.05) would reject the 3:1 hypothesis.
entries.subject: Ecology

entries.fact: In-situ conservation protects species in their natural habitats through protected areas, biosphere reserves and biodiversity hotspots (regions with exceptional endemism under severe threat). Ex-situ conservation protects them outside their habitat, in seed banks, gene banks, zoos, botanical gardens and captive-breeding programmes. The two approaches are complementary: in-situ preserves ecological interactions and ongoing evolution, while ex-situ provides insurance against extinction.
entries.formula: Rule: in-situ = protect in natural habitat (protected areas, hotspots); ex-situ = protect outside habitat (seed banks, zoos, captive breeding)
entries.example: The Western Ghats, a biodiversity hotspot, is conserved in-situ through national parks, while its seeds are also stored ex-situ in gene banks as backup against habitat loss.
entries.subject: Conservation Biology

entries.fact: The neutral theory holds that most molecular evolution is driven by random drift of neutral mutations rather than selection. Because neutral substitutions accumulate at a roughly constant rate per lineage, the genetic distance between two species is proportional to the time since they shared a common ancestor. Calibrating this rate with fossils gives a molecular clock for dating divergences.
entries.formula: Divergence time ≈ genetic distance / (2 × substitution rate per lineage)
entries.example: If two species differ by 2% at a gene that evolves at 1% per million years per lineage, they diverged about 2/(2 × 1) = 1 million years ago.
entries.subject: Evolution

entries.fact: The Lincoln-Petersen method estimates the size of a closed population from two samples: animals are captured, marked and released, then a second sample is taken. If marked animals mix randomly with unmarked ones, the proportion marked in the second sample estimates the proportion marked in the whole population. The method assumes a closed population with no births, deaths or migration between samples, equal catchability, and marks that are not lost.
entries.formula: N = (M × C)/R, where M = marked and released, C = total caught in second sample, R = marked animals recaptured
entries.example: Mark and release 50 fish; later catch 40 fish of which 10 are marked. N = (50 × 40)/10 = 200 fish in the population.
entries.subject: Ecology

entries.fact: The Red Queen hypothesis says that species must constantly adapt just to maintain their fitness relative to co-evolving antagonists such as parasites, predators and competitors — like running to stay in the same place. It explains why sexual reproduction persists despite its twofold cost: recombination generates novel gene combinations that help hosts keep up with rapidly evolving parasites.
entries.formula: Rule: relative fitness only stays constant if a species keeps adapting; no absolute progress is needed, only keeping pace with antagonists
entries.example: In New Zealand snails, sexual populations resist trematode parasites better than asexual clones, because recombination continually produces rare resistant genotypes that the parasites have not yet adapted to.
entries.subject: Evolution

entries.topic: Carbonate System and Alkalinity of Water
entries.fact: Dissolved carbon dioxide forms carbonic acid, which dissociates into bicarbonate and carbonate, so the carbonate system buffers natural waters around pH 7-8.5. Alkalinity is the water's capacity to neutralise acid, contributed mainly by bicarbonate and carbonate (plus hydroxide, minus hydrogen ions). It is measured by titration and reported as mg/L as CaCO3, and it governs pH stability in treatment plants and rivers.
entries.formula: CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3− ⇌ 2H+ + CO3^2−; alkalinity ≈ [HCO3−] + 2[CO3^2−] + [OH−] − [H+]
entries.example: A water sample needing acid titration equivalent to 200 mg/L as CaCO3 has alkalinity 200 mg/L as CaCO3, typical of a moderately hard groundwater that resists pH change.
entries.subject: Environmental Chemistry

entries.fact: The Monod model describes how microbial growth rate depends on the concentration of a limiting substrate, in the same mathematical form as Michaelis-Menten enzyme kinetics. Growth is slow when substrate is scarce and approaches the maximum rate μmax when substrate is abundant. The half-saturation constant Ks is the substrate concentration at which the growth rate is half of μmax, and the doubling time follows from the growth rate.
entries.formula: μ = μmax × S/(Ks + S); doubling time td = ln 2/μ
entries.example: With μmax = 0.5 h−1 and Ks = 20 mg/L, at S = 20 mg/L the growth rate is μ = 0.25 h−1, giving a doubling time of ln 2/0.25 ≈ 2.8 h.
entries.subject: Water Treatment

entries.fact: When organic waste enters a river, bacteria consume oxygen to decompose it (deoxygenation, rate k1) while oxygen dissolves back from the air (reaeration, rate k2). The dissolved-oxygen deficit first grows, reaches a maximum (the critical deficit) at a point downstream, then recovers. The Streeter-Phelps equation gives the deficit at any travel time downstream, and is the classical model of river pollution and self-purification.
entries.formula: D(t) = [k1·L0/(k2 − k1)] × (e^(−k1·t) − e^(−k2·t)) + D0·e^(−k2·t); critical deficit Dc = (k1/k2)·L0·e^(−k1·tc)
entries.example: With k1 = 0.2/d and k2 = 0.4/d, reaeration outpaces deoxygenation downstream, so the oxygen sag is shallower and the river recovers faster than if k2 were smaller.
entries.subject: Water Treatment

entries.topic: Activated Sludge: F/M Ratio and Sludge Age
entries.fact: In activated sludge treatment, the food-to-microorganism (F/M) ratio is the daily BOD load divided by the mass of microbes (MLSS) in the aeration tank, typically kept at 0.2-0.5 kg BOD per kg MLSS per day. A high F/M grows fast-settling young sludge but risks poor treatment; a low F/M gives good treatment but old, poorly settling sludge. Sludge age (solids retention time, SRT) is the average time biomass stays in the system and is controlled by wasting sludge.
entries.formula: F/M = Q·S0/(V·X); SRT = V·X/(Qw·Xw + Qe·Xe)
entries.example: A plant with Q = 10,000 m3/d, S0 = 200 mg/L BOD, V = 2,000 m3 and MLSS X = 3,000 mg/L has F/M = (10,000 × 0.2)/(2,000 × 3) = 0.33 kg BOD/kg MLSS·d, in the normal range.
entries.subject: Water Treatment

entries.fact: An electrostatic precipitator charges dust particles with a corona discharge and collects them on earthed plates. The Deutsch-Anderson equation gives collection efficiency from the total collecting area A, the particle drift velocity w (migration velocity towards the plate) and the gas flow rate Q. Efficiency rises steeply with area, so ESPs are large, and they routinely achieve over 99% removal of fly ash from power plants.
entries.formula: η = 1 − exp(−A·w/Q), where A = collecting area, w = drift velocity, Q = gas flow rate
entries.example: With A = 5,000 m2, w = 0.1 m/s and Q = 100 m3/s, η = 1 − e^(−5) ≈ 99.3% of the particulate matter is collected.
entries.subject: Air Pollution

entries.topic: Noise Levels: Decibel Addition and Leq
entries.fact: Sound levels are logarithmic, so decibels cannot be added directly: the combined level of two sources comes from adding their acoustic energies. Two equal sources raise the level by 3 dB, and ten equal sources by 10 dB. Leq is the energy-equivalent continuous level over a time period and is the standard measure for environmental noise assessment, with day-night levels (Ldn) adding a 10 dB penalty for night-time noise.
entries.formula: L_total = 10·log10(Σ10^(Li/10)); doubling equal sources adds 3 dB
entries.example: Two machines each producing 80 dB together produce 10·log10(2 × 10^8) = 83 dB, not 160 dB.
entries.subject: Air Pollution

entries.topic: Municipal Solid Waste: Generation and Hierarchy
entries.fact: Indian cities generate roughly 0.5 kg of municipal solid waste per person per day, with biodegradable waste forming about half of it. The waste hierarchy ranks options as reduce, reuse, recycle, recover energy, and finally dispose in a sanitary landfill. Collection, segregation at source, composting of wet waste and material recovery are the core of integrated solid waste management under India's Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016.
entries.formula: Rule: waste hierarchy = reduce > reuse > recycle > recover energy > landfill; typical Indian urban generation ≈ 0.5 kg/capita/day
entries.example: A city of 1 million people generates about 500 tonnes of waste per day; segregating the ~50% biodegradable fraction for composting halves the load sent to landfill.
entries.subject: Waste Management

entries.topic: Greenhouse Gases and Global Warming Potential
entries.fact: Greenhouse gases absorb outgoing long-wave infrared radiation and re-emit it, warming the Earth; the main ones are CO2, methane, nitrous oxide and fluorinated gases. Global warming potential (GWP) compares a gas's warming effect to CO2 over a chosen horizon (usually 100 years), accounting for both its heat-trapping strength and its atmospheric lifetime. Methane is short-lived but potent, so its GWP100 is about 28, while nitrous oxide is about 265.
entries.formula: CO2-equivalent = mass × GWP; GWP100: CO2 = 1, CH4 ≈ 28, N2O ≈ 265
entries.example: Emitting 1 tonne of methane is equivalent to about 28 tonnes of CO2 over 100 years, so cutting methane gives a fast climate benefit.
entries.subject: Air Pollution

entries.fact: A non-zero vector v is an eigenvector of a square matrix A if Av = λv, where λ is the eigenvalue. Eigenvalues come from the characteristic equation det(A − λI) = 0. They determine the stability of linear systems of differential equations: a system is stable if all eigenvalues have negative real parts. Symmetric matrices have real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors.
entries.formula: det(A − λI) = 0; for stability of dx/dt = Ax, need Re(λ) < 0 for all eigenvalues
entries.example: For A = [[0, 1], [−2, −3]], det(A − λI) = λ² + 3λ + 2 = 0 gives λ = −1, −2, both negative, so the system is stable and decays to equilibrium.
entries.subject: Engineering Mathematics

entries.fact: Bayes' theorem updates the probability of a hypothesis after seeing evidence, combining the prior probability with the likelihood of the evidence. It is the foundation of risk assessment and of interpreting diagnostic tests: even a very accurate test gives many false positives when the condition being tested is rare. The denominator is the total probability of the evidence under all hypotheses.
entries.formula: P(A|B) = P(B|A)·P(A)/P(B)
entries.example: A test is 99% sensitive and 99% specific, but a disease has 1% prevalence. A positive result is truly diseased with probability (0.99 × 0.01)/(0.99 × 0.01 + 0.01 × 0.99) = 0.5, only 50%, because false positives are as common as true positives.
entries.subject: Engineering Mathematics

entries.topic: Hypothesis Testing: Type I and Type II Errors
entries.fact: In hypothesis testing, a Type I error is rejecting a true null hypothesis (a false positive), with probability α, usually set at 0.05. A Type II error is failing to reject a false null hypothesis (a false negative), with probability β. Power = 1 − β is the chance of correctly detecting a real effect, and it rises with sample size and effect size. The t-test compares means, the F-test compares variances, and the chi-square test compares counts.
entries.formula: Type I error probability = α; Type II error probability = β; power = 1 − β
entries.example: Declaring a river polluted when it is actually clean is a Type I error (α = 0.05 means a 5% chance); declaring it clean when it is polluted is a Type II error, which a larger sample size reduces.
entries.subject: Engineering Mathematics

entries.fact: Darcy's law states that groundwater discharge through a porous medium is proportional to the hydraulic conductivity K, the cross-sectional area A, and the hydraulic gradient (head loss per unit length). The specific discharge (Darcy velocity) is not the true pore-water velocity, which is higher because water flows only through pores. Transmissivity T = K × b, where b is the saturated thickness, measures an aquifer's ability to transmit water.
entries.formula: Q = K·A·(dh/dl); specific discharge v = K·i; transmissivity T = K·b
entries.example: An aquifer with K = 10 m/day, gradient i = 0.01 and cross-section A = 100 m2 carries Q = 10 × 100 × 0.01 = 10 m3/day of groundwater.
entries.subject: Water Treatment

entries.fact: In a large, randomly mating population with no selection, mutation, migration or drift, allele and genotype frequencies stay constant from generation to generation. With two alleles at frequencies p and q, genotype frequencies are p², 2pq and q². Deviations from these frequencies signal that one of the assumptions is violated, which is how the principle is used to detect selection or inbreeding.
entries.formula: p + q = 1; p² + 2pq + q² = 1
entries.example: If a recessive disease affects 1 in 2,500 births (q² = 0.0004), then q = 0.02 and carriers are 2pq ≈ 2 × 0.98 × 0.02 ≈ 0.039, about 1 person in 26.
entries.subject: Genetics

entries.fact: The trp operon of E. coli encodes the enzymes for tryptophan synthesis and is a repressible system: the trp repressor is inactive on its own and is switched on by binding tryptophan, the end product. When tryptophan is plentiful the repressor blocks transcription; when it is scarce the operon is expressed. Attenuation adds a second layer: the leader sequence causes early termination when tryptophan is abundant. This contrasts with the inducible lac operon.
entries.formula: Rule: trp operon ON when tryptophan is scarce, OFF when tryptophan is abundant (repressor activated by the end product + attenuation)
entries.example: E. coli grown without tryptophan expresses the trp genes to synthesise it; adding tryptophan to the medium shuts the operon off within minutes, saving energy.
entries.subject: Genetics

entries.fact: DNA replication is semi-conservative: each new double helix keeps one old strand and one new strand. Helicase unwinds the duplex, single-strand binding proteins keep it open, primase lays down RNA primers, DNA polymerase III extends them in the 5' to 3' direction, and ligase joins the Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand. DNA polymerase also proofreads, giving an error rate near one in a billion bases.
entries.formula: Rule: semi-conservative replication; leading strand continuous, lagging strand as Okazaki fragments; synthesis always 5' → 3'
entries.example: The E. coli replisome copies about 1,000 nucleotides per second, so its 4.6 million base-pair genome is replicated in roughly 40 minutes.
entries.subject: Life Sciences

entries.topic: Electron Transport Chain and Oxidative Phosphorylation
entries.fact: The electron transport chain in the inner mitochondrial membrane passes electrons from NADH and FADH2 through complexes I-IV to oxygen, pumping protons into the intermembrane space. The resulting proton gradient drives ATP synthase (chemiosmosis). Each NADH yields about 2.5 ATP and each FADH2 about 1.5 ATP, so one glucose yields roughly 30-32 ATP in total from glycolysis, the TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation combined.
entries.formula: P/O ratio: NADH ≈ 2.5 ATP, FADH2 ≈ 1.5 ATP; glucose → ~30-32 ATP total
entries.example: The 10 NADH and 2 FADH2 made from one glucose contribute about 25 + 3 = 28 ATP through oxidative phosphorylation, with the rest coming from substrate-level phosphorylation in glycolysis and the TCA cycle.
entries.subject: Biochemistry

entries.fact: The pentose phosphate pathway runs parallel to glycolysis in the cytosol and has two products: NADPH for reductive biosynthesis (fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis) and ribose-5-phosphate for nucleotide synthesis. Its oxidative phase converts glucose-6-phosphate to ribulose-5-phosphate, releasing CO2 and making 2 NADPH. The non-oxidative phase interconverts sugars and can return intermediates to glycolysis.
entries.formula: Glucose-6-P + 2 NADP+ + H2O → ribulose-5-P + 2 NADPH + 2H+ + CO2
entries.example: One glucose-6-phosphate through the oxidative phase yields 2 NADPH, which the cell uses to reduce glutathione and protect against oxidative damage, and one ribose-5-phosphate for making nucleotides.
entries.subject: Biochemistry

entries.fact: An antibody is a Y-shaped molecule of two identical heavy chains and two identical light chains, held by disulfide bonds. The Fab arms contain the variable regions that bind antigen, while the Fc stem mediates effector functions such as complement activation and binding to immune cells. The five classes are IgG (most abundant in blood), IgA (mucosal surfaces), IgM (pentamer, first in the primary response), IgE (allergy and parasites) and IgD.
entries.formula: Rule: IgG = 2 heavy + 2 light chains; Fab binds antigen, Fc carries out effector functions; classes IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE, IgD
entries.example: IgM appears first after infection because its pentameric form binds antigen with high avidity, while IgG dominates later and provides long-lasting immunity.
entries.subject: Life Sciences

entries.topic: Bacterial Growth Curve and Generation Time
entries.fact: A batch culture passes through four phases: lag (adaptation, no net growth), log or exponential (cells divide at a constant maximum rate), stationary (growth equals death as nutrients run out) and death (cells die faster than they divide). In the log phase the population grows exponentially, so the specific growth rate μ and the generation (doubling) time td are found from the slope of log cell number against time.
entries.formula: μ = ln 2/td; N(t) = N0 × 2^(t/td)
entries.example: E. coli with a 20-minute generation time undergoes 3 doublings per hour, so 10³ cells become 8 × 10³ cells in one hour of log-phase growth.
entries.subject: Microbiology

entries.fact: Water potential Ψ is the chemical potential of water relative to pure water, and water always moves from higher to lower water potential. In plant cells Ψ = Ψs + Ψp, where the solute potential Ψs is negative and lowers with dissolved solutes, and the pressure potential Ψp is positive in turgid cells. Transpiration pulls water up the xylem because evaporation from leaves creates a very negative water potential there.
entries.formula: Ψ = Ψs + Ψp; Ψs = −iCRT (van't Hoff); water moves from high Ψ to low Ψ
entries.example: A cell with Ψs = −0.8 MPa and Ψp = 0.5 MPa has Ψ = −0.3 MPa, so it absorbs water from a surrounding solution at Ψ = −0.1 MPa until its turgor rises and the potentials equalise.
entries.subject: Botany

entries.fact: C3 plants fix CO2 directly with Rubisco in the Calvin cycle in mesophyll cells, but Rubisco also binds oxygen, causing photorespiration that wastes energy, especially in hot, dry conditions. C4 plants first fix CO2 with PEP carboxylase into a four-carbon acid in mesophyll cells and release it around Rubisco in bundle-sheath cells (Kranz anatomy), concentrating CO2 and suppressing photorespiration. CAM plants open stomata at night to fix CO2 as malic acid and release it for the Calvin cycle during the day, saving water.
