entries.fact: The Gibbs phase rule counts the independent intensive variables of a system at equilibrium: F = C - P + 2, where C is the number of components, P the number of phases and F the degrees of freedom. In process calculations, a degree-of-freedom analysis on the material balance is the same idea applied to streams: unknowns minus independent equations minus knowns must be zero before a balance can be solved. Tie components, recycle, bypass and purge streams are handled by writing balances around the right subsystem.
entries.formula: Gibbs phase rule: F = C - P + 2; Degrees of freedom (balance) = unknowns - independent equations - known compositions - extra relations; F = 0 means the system is fully specified
entries.example: Pure water (C=1) with liquid and vapour in equilibrium (P=2) has F = 1 - 2 + 2 = 1, so fixing temperature fixes the pressure (the vapour-pressure curve).
entries.subject: Chemical Process Calculations

entries.topic: First law for open and closed systems
entries.fact: The first law is energy conservation. For a closed system, delta U = Q - W. For a steady-flow open system (turbine, compressor, heat exchanger), the steady-flow energy equation adds kinetic and potential energy and flow work: the enthalpy change plus kinetic and potential changes equals heat minus shaft work. This is the workhorse for energy balances in process calculations, including reacting and multiphase systems.
entries.formula: Closed system: delta U = Q - W; Steady-flow energy equation: m(h2 - h1) + m(V2^2 - V1^2)/2 + m g (z2 - z1) = Q - W_s; For a turbine with negligible KE/PE: W_s = m(h1 - h2)
entries.example: Steam enters a turbine at h1 = 3000 kJ/kg and leaves at h2 = 2400 kJ/kg, 1 kg/s: shaft work = 1 x (3000-2400) = 600 kW (adiabatic, negligible KE/PE change).
entries.subject: Thermodynamics

entries.topic: Fugacity, activity coefficients and excess properties
entries.fact: Real mixtures deviate from ideality, and fugacity is the corrected pressure that makes chemical potential behave like an ideal gas: mu_i = mu_i^0 + RT ln(f_i/f_i^0). For liquids, non-ideality is folded into the activity coefficient gamma_i, with activity a_i = gamma_i x_i; excess Gibbs energy G^E measures the deviation from an ideal mixture. Fugacity coefficients and gamma_i come from equations of state and models such as Wilson, NRTL and UNIQUAC, and they are what make VLE prediction possible for non-ideal systems.
entries.formula: Chemical potential: mu_i = mu_i^0 + RT ln(f_i/f_i^0); Liquid activity: a_i = gamma_i x_i; Excess Gibbs energy: G^E = RT sum x_i ln gamma_i; Modified Raoult's law: y_i P = gamma_i x_i P_i^sat
entries.example: A mixture with gamma = 1.3 at x = 0.5 shows positive deviation from Raoult's law: its partial pressure is 30% higher than the ideal value.
entries.subject: Thermodynamics

entries.fact: At equilibrium the Gibbs energy is at a minimum, so the equilibrium constant K is fixed by the standard Gibbs energy change: delta G^0 = -RT ln K. The van't Hoff equation gives how K moves with temperature: exothermic reactions lose equilibrium conversion as temperature rises. K is written from activities of products over reactants, each raised to its stoichiometric coefficient, and it predicts the equilibrium composition of reacting systems.
entries.formula: delta G^0 = -RT ln K; van't Hoff: d ln K/dT = delta H^0/(R T^2); For aA + bB <=> cC + dD: K = (a_C^c a_D^d)/(a_A^a a_B^b)
entries.example: A reaction with delta G^0 = -11.4 kJ/mol at 298 K has K = e^(11400/(8.314 x 298)) = e^4.6 = 100, strongly favouring products.
entries.subject: Thermodynamics

entries.fact: A Newtonian fluid has viscosity independent of shear rate: shear stress is proportional to shear rate, tau = mu (du/dy). Non-Newtonian fluids do not: pseudoplastic fluids (paints, polymer solutions) thin with shear, dilatant fluids (corn-starch suspensions) thicken, and Bingham plastics (toothpaste, slurries) need a yield stress before they flow at all. The power-law model tau = K (du/dy)^n captures the first two, with n < 1 shear-thinning and n > 1 shear-thickening.
entries.formula: Newtonian: tau = mu du/dy; Power law: tau = K (du/dy)^n, n < 1 pseudoplastic, n > 1 dilatant; Bingham plastic: tau = tau_0 + mu_p du/dy
entries.example: A polymer solution with n = 0.5 halves its apparent viscosity when the shear rate is quadrupled, which is why it pumps more easily at high shear.
entries.subject: Fluid Mechanics

entries.topic: Flow through pipeline systems and friction factors
entries.fact: Pipe flow is laminar below Re ~ 2100 and turbulent above ~4000. The Darcy-Weisbach equation gives head loss from the friction factor f: 64/Re for laminar flow, and for turbulent flow f comes from the Moody chart or Colebrook equation as a function of Re and relative roughness. Minor losses from valves, bends and fittings are K times the velocity head, and pumps and compressors add head to the system. The mechanical energy balance ties pressure, velocity, elevation, loss and shaft work together.
entries.formula: Darcy-Weisbach: h_f = f (L/D)(V^2/(2g)); Laminar f = 64/Re; Colebrook: 1/sqrt(f) = -2 log((epsilon/D)/3.7 + 2.51/(Re sqrt(f))); Minor loss: h_m = K V^2/(2g)
entries.subject: Fluid Mechanics

entries.topic: Flow past immersed bodies: packed and fluidized beds
entries.fact: Fluid flowing through a packed bed loses pressure by viscous drag at low velocity and by inertia at high velocity; the Ergun equation adds both terms, with coefficients 150 and 1.75. As gas velocity rises, the bed expands and at the minimum fluidization velocity the drag balances the bed weight and the particles become suspended — a fluidized bed, with excellent mixing and heat transfer. Beyond that, particles are entrained. The Ergun equation also gives the pressure drop at incipient fluidization.
entries.formula: Ergun: delta P/L = 150 mu (1-eps)^2 v/(eps^3 dp^2) + 1.75 rho (1-eps) v^2/(eps^3 dp); At minimum fluidization: delta P/L = (1-eps)(rho_p - rho) g
entries.example: A bed with voidage 0.4 and particle diameter 1 mm at low velocity is dominated by the viscous (150) term, so pressure drop grows roughly linearly with velocity.
entries.subject: Fluid Mechanics

entries.fact: Boiling begins at nucleation sites on a heated surface: nucleate boiling is efficient, but beyond the critical heat flux a vapour film blankets the surface (film boiling) and heat transfer collapses — the boiling curve's peak is a design limit. Condensation on a cold surface is filmwise (a liquid film, lower coefficient) or dropwise (much higher coefficient, but hard to sustain). Evaporators boil a solution to concentrate it, using steam economy (kg vapour evaporated per kg steam) as the key performance measure.
entries.formula: Boiling regimes: natural convection, nucleate, transition, film boiling; Critical heat flux is the peak of the boiling curve; Steam economy = kg vapour evaporated / kg steam used; Film condensation: h proportional to (k^3 rho^2 g lambda/(mu D delta T))^0.25
entries.example: A single-effect evaporator with steam economy 0.9 evaporates 900 kg of water per 1000 kg of steam supplied.
entries.subject: Heat Transfer

entries.fact: Evaporating in several effects in series reuses the vapour from one effect as the heating steam of the next, so steam economy rises roughly with the number of effects. In forward feed, the liquor and vapour flow in the same direction and the last effect is under vacuum, which lowers boiling temperatures; backward feed suits viscous liquors. Each effect still follows the same heat-transfer and material-balance equations as a single effect, with a boiling-point rise correction for concentrated solutions.
entries.formula: Steam economy approx equal to number of effects (ideal); Overall economy = total vapour evaporated / steam supplied to first effect; Capacity of an effect: Q = U A delta T
entries.example: A triple-effect evaporator with steam economy 2.7 evaporates 2700 kg of water per 1000 kg of live steam, about three times a single effect.
entries.subject: Heat Transfer

entries.topic: Mass transfer coefficients and film, penetration and surface-renewal theories
entries.fact: Mass transfer across an interface is written with a coefficient: N_A = k (concentration difference), in the same form as heat transfer. The film theory assumes a stagnant film of fixed thickness, giving k = D/delta. Penetration theory treats unsteady diffusion into a fluid element exposed for a short time, giving k proportional to sqrt(D/t). Surface-renewal theory averages over a distribution of exposure times, also giving k proportional to sqrt(D). The momentum, heat and mass transfer analogies (Reynolds, Chilton-Colburn) link the three coefficients.
entries.formula: Film theory: k = D/delta; Penetration theory: k = 2 sqrt(D/(pi t)); Chilton-Colburn analogy: j_H = j_D, i.e. St_H Pr^(2/3) = St_M Sc^(2/3) = f/2
entries.example: If exposure time is quartered, penetration theory predicts the mass transfer coefficient doubles, since k scales as 1/sqrt(t).
entries.subject: Mass Transfer

entries.fact: The McCabe-Thiele method designs a binary distillation column graphically on a y-x diagram. The equilibrium curve, the 45-degree line, the rectifying and stripping operating lines, and the q-line (feed condition) are drawn; stages are stepped off between the operating lines and the equilibrium curve, each step being one theoretical stage. The feed stage is where the operating line changes, the minimum reflux ratio is found from the pinch at the feed intersection, and total reflux gives the minimum number of stages (Fenske).
entries.formula: Rectifying line: y = (R/(R+1)) x + x_D/(R+1); q-line slope = q/(q-1); Fenske (total reflux): N_min = log[(x_D/(1-x_D))((1-x_B)/x_B)]/log(alpha)
entries.example: A column separating a 50-50 mixture to 95% distillate and 5% bottoms with relative volatility 2 needs N_min = log[(19)(19)]/log 2 = 8.5, i.e. about 9 stages at total reflux.
entries.subject: Mass Transfer

entries.fact: Gas absorption transfers a solute from gas to liquid in a packed or tray column. Stage-wise contacting uses equilibrium stages with a stage efficiency; continuous contacting uses the height of a transfer unit (HTU) and the number of transfer units (NTU): column height Z = HTU x NTU, where NTU integrates the concentration driving force over the column. The same HTU-NTU framework applies to distillation, extraction and humidification. The operating line comes from the material balance and the equilibrium curve from VLE data.
entries.formula: Column height Z = H_OG x N_OG; N_OG = integral from y2 to y1 of dy/(y - y*); H_OG = G/(K_G a P); Overall coefficient: 1/K_G = 1/k_G + m/k_L
entries.example: If HTU is 0.5 m and NTU is 8, the packed height needed is 0.5 x 8 = 4 m.
entries.subject: Mass Transfer

entries.topic: Membrane separations: micro-, ultra-, nano-filtration and reverse osmosis
entries.fact: Membranes separate by size and solubility: microfiltration removes suspended particles (0.1-10 microns), ultrafiltration removes colloids and macromolecules, nanofiltration removes divalent ions and small organics, and reverse osmosis removes essentially all dissolved salts by applying pressure above the osmotic pressure. Flux is driven by the transmembrane pressure difference and falls as fouling builds; selectivity is set by pore size and by the membrane material's affinity for the permeating species.
entries.formula: Flux J = (permeability) x (driving force), e.g. J = L_p (delta P - delta pi) for reverse osmosis; Rejection R = 1 - C_p/C_f; Osmotic pressure pi = C R T (van't Hoff, dilute)
entries.example: Seawater at about 35,000 ppm has an osmotic pressure near 25 bar, so reverse osmosis must operate above roughly 25 bar to produce fresh water.
entries.subject: Mass Transfer

entries.topic: Ideal reactors: CSTR and PFR design equations
entries.fact: The two ideal reactors bracket real behaviour. A CSTR is perfectly mixed, so composition is uniform and equal to the outlet, and its volume follows from the design equation V = F_A0 X/(-r_A). A PFR has no axial mixing, composition varies along its length, and V = F_A0 times the integral of dX/(-r_A) from 0 to X. For a first-order reaction, the PFR needs less volume than a CSTR for the same conversion; for an autocatalytic reaction the order reverses at low conversion.
entries.formula: CSTR: V = F_A0 X/(-r_A); PFR: V = F_A0 integral_0^X dX/(-r_A); First-order CSTR: X = k tau/(1 + k tau); First-order PFR: X = 1 - e^(-k tau), tau = V/v0
entries.example: For a first-order reaction with k tau = 2, a CSTR reaches X = 2/3 = 0.67 while a PFR reaches X = 1 - e^(-2) = 0.86.
entries.subject: Chemical Reaction Engineering

entries.topic: Non-ideal reactors and residence time distribution
entries.fact: Real reactors deviate from ideal CSTR and PFR behaviour because of channelling, bypassing and dead zones. The residence time distribution E(t) is measured by a tracer pulse: E(t) dt is the fraction of fluid leaving with age between t and t+dt, and its mean is the space time. The single-parameter models (dispersion model and tanks-in-series) fit E(t) with one parameter — the Peclet number or the number of tanks N — and predict conversion between the CSTR and PFR limits.
entries.formula: Mean residence time tbar = integral t E(t) dt = V/v0; Variance sigma^2 = integral (t - tbar)^2 E(t) dt; Tanks-in-series: N = tbar^2/sigma^2; Dispersion model: Peclet Pe = u L/D_ax
entries.example: A tracer test with mean 100 s and variance 5000 s^2 fits N = 100^2/5000 = 2 tanks in series, far from plug flow (N large) and far from a single CSTR (N = 1).
entries.subject: Chemical Reaction Engineering

entries.topic: Heterogeneous catalysis: diffusion effects and catalyst deactivation
entries.fact: In a porous catalyst pellet, reaction and pore diffusion compete: the Thiele modulus phi measures their ratio, and the effectiveness factor eta is the actual rate divided by the rate if the whole pellet saw surface conditions. Large phi means diffusion-limited, with eta approx 1/phi and the observed rate scaling with sqrt(k D_e). Catalysts also deactivate by sintering, poisoning and coking, and the rate equation is multiplied by an activity factor a(t) that decays with time on stream.
entries.formula: Thiele modulus (first-order, sphere): phi = R sqrt(k/D_e); Effectiveness factor eta = (3/phi)(1/tanh(phi) - 1/phi); Diffusion-limited: eta approx 1/phi; Deactivation: -r_A' = k a(t) f(C), a(t) falling from 1
entries.example: A pellet with phi = 5 has eta = (3/5)(1/tanh 5 - 1/5) = 0.48, so less than half the pellet volume is effectively used.
entries.subject: Chemical Reaction Engineering

entries.topic: Process control: P, PI and PID controller modes
entries.fact: A feedback controller compares the measured variable with its set point and moves the valve to remove the error. Proportional (P) action gives an output proportional to the error but leaves steady-state offset; integral (I) action removes offset by acting on the accumulated error, at the risk of oscillation; derivative (D) action anticipates the error's trend and damps oscillation but amplifies noise. PID combines all three. Controller tuning (Ziegler-Nichols, Cohen-Coon) sets the gains, and stability is judged from the closed-loop characteristic equation and frequency response.
entries.formula: PID output: u(t) = K_c e(t) + (K_c/tau_I) integral e dt + K_c tau_D de/dt; P-only offset for a first-order process: offset proportional to 1/(1 + K_c K_p); Ziegler-Nichols (ultimate): K_c = 0.6 K_u, tau_I = P_u/2, tau_D = P_u/8
entries.example: A P-only level controller with K_c K_p = 4 leaves an offset of 1/(1+4) = 20% of the load change; adding integral action drives the steady-state offset to zero.
entries.subject: Chemical Process Calculations

entries.topic: Plant design and economics: cost estimation and profitability
entries.fact: Process economics starts with capital cost estimation from equipment costs, scaled by cost indices and the six-tenths rule, then adds installation factors. Profitability is judged by rate of return, payback period and discounted cash flow (net present value, internal rate of return). Depreciation spreads capital cost over plant life, and the total annualised cost combines annualised capital with operating cost for optimisation of equipment size, such as heat exchangers and multistage contactors.
entries.formula: Six-tenths rule: C2 = C1 (S2/S1)^0.6; Payback period = total capital investment / annual cash flow; NPV = sum of discounted cash flows - capital investment; Total annualised cost = annualised capital cost + annual operating cost
entries.example: An exchanger costing Rs 10 lakh at 50 m^2 scales to 100 m^2 as 10 x (2)^0.6 = Rs 15.2 lakh by the six-tenths rule.
entries.subject: Chemical Process Calculations

entries.topic: Chemical technology: ammonia, urea and sulfuric acid industries
entries.fact: Ammonia is made by the Haber process: nitrogen and hydrogen react over an iron catalyst at about 450-500 deg C and 150-300 bar, N2 + 3H2 <=> 2NH3, with unreacted gas recycled after ammonia is condensed out. Urea is made from ammonia and CO2 via ammonium carbamate, and is the world's main nitrogen fertiliser. Sulfuric acid is made by the contact process: sulfur is burned to SO2, oxidised to SO3 over a vanadium catalyst, and absorbed into concentrated acid to form oleum.
entries.formula: Haber process: N2 + 3H2 <=> 2NH3 (iron catalyst, 450-500 deg C, 150-300 bar); Urea: 2NH3 + CO2 -> NH2CONH2 + H2O; Contact process: 2SO2 + O2 <=> 2SO3, then SO3 + H2SO4 -> H2S2O7 (oleum)
entries.example: Ammonia synthesis is exothermic, so high pressure and moderate temperature favour equilibrium conversion, but the rate needs the high temperature and catalyst — a classic equilibrium-versus-rate trade-off.
entries.subject: Chemical Process Calculations

entries.fact: For a square matrix A, a non-zero vector x is an eigenvector if A x = lambda x, where lambda is the eigenvalue. Eigenvalues are the roots of det(A - lambda I) = 0; their sum is the trace and their product is the determinant. In PI they appear in vibration analysis, principal stresses and the stability of linear systems.
entries.formula: det(A - lambda I) = 0; A x = lambda x; sum of eigenvalues = trace(A); product of eigenvalues = det(A)
entries.example: For A = [[5,0],[0,2]], det(A - lambda I) = (5-lambda)(2-lambda) = 0, so eigenvalues are 5 and 2.
entries.subject: Engineering Mathematics

entries.fact: The Laplace transform converts a differential equation in time into an algebraic equation in s. It is defined as L{f(t)} = integral from 0 to infinity of e^(-st) f(t) dt. It is the standard GATE tool for initial-value problems and for the dynamic response of mechanical and process systems.
entries.example: Solve y' + 3y = 0, y(0) = 2: sY - 2 + 3Y = 0 gives Y = 2/(s+3), so y(t) = 2 e^(-3t).
entries.subject: Engineering Mathematics

entries.topic: Probability distributions: binomial, Poisson, normal and exponential
entries.fact: A random variable is described by its distribution. Binomial counts successes in n fixed trials; Poisson counts rare events in a fixed interval with mean lambda; normal is the bell curve of mean mu and standard deviation sigma; exponential describes the time between Poisson events and is memoryless. Mean, median, mode and standard deviation summarise a data set, and linear regression fits a straight line by least squares.
entries.formula: Binomial mean np; Poisson: P(X=k) = e^(-lambda) lambda^k/k!; Normal: Z = (X - mu)/sigma; Exponential: f(t) = lambda e^(-lambda t), mean 1/lambda; Least-squares slope b = sum((x-xbar)(y-ybar))/sum((x-xbar)^2)
entries.example: Machine breakdowns average 2 per week (Poisson, lambda = 2): P(no breakdown in a week) = e^(-2) = 0.135.
entries.subject: Engineering Mathematics

entries.topic: Numerical integration: trapezoidal and Simpson's rules
entries.fact: When an integral has no closed form, it is approximated from sampled values. The trapezoidal rule joins points with straight lines; Simpson's 1/3 rule fits parabolas through triples of points and is exact for polynomials up to degree 3. Simpson's rule needs an even number of intervals, and both rules are used for numerical solution of differential equations by single- and multi-step methods.
entries.formula: Trapezoidal: integral approx (h/2)[f0 + 2(f1+...+f(n-1)) + fn]; Simpson 1/3: (h/3)[f0 + 4(f1+f3+...) + 2(f2+f4+...) + fn]
entries.example: Integrate f(x) = x^2 from 0 to 2 with h = 1: Simpson gives (1/3)[0 + 4(1) + 4] = 8/3 = 2.667, which is exact here.
entries.subject: Engineering Mathematics

entries.topic: Iron-carbon diagram and heat treatment of steels
entries.fact: The iron-carbon diagram maps the phases of steel against temperature and carbon content. The eutectoid point at 0.77% C and 727 deg C is where austenite transforms to pearlite, a lamellar mix of ferrite and cementite. Below 0.77% C steels are hypoeutectoid (ferrite + pearlite); above are hypereutectoid (pearlite + cementite). Heat treatment exploits this: annealing softens, normalising refines grain, quenching forms hard martensite, and tempering restores toughness.
entries.formula: Eutectoid: 0.77% C at 727 deg C, austenite -> pearlite; Eutectic: 4.3% C at 1147 deg C; Lever rule: fraction of a phase = opposite arm length / total tie-line length
entries.example: A 0.4% C steel cooled slowly contains proeutectoid ferrite fraction (0.77-0.4)/(0.77-0.022) = 0.49, the rest pearlite.
entries.subject: Manufacturing

entries.topic: Failure theories and Mohr's circle for stress
entries.fact: A part under combined loading fails when some equivalent stress reaches the material's limit. The maximum shear stress (Tresca) theory says yielding starts when the largest shear stress reaches half the yield strength; the distortion-energy (von Mises) theory uses the equivalent stress from all principal stresses and matches ductile metals better. For brittle materials the maximum principal stress theory applies. Mohr's circle gives the principal stresses and maximum shear from sigma_x, sigma_y and tau_xy.
entries.formula: von Mises: sigma_eq = sqrt(((sigma1-sigma2)^2 + (sigma2-sigma3)^2 + (sigma3-sigma1)^2)/2); Tresca: sigma1 - sigma3 = sigma_y at yield; Mohr: sigma_1,2 = sigma_avg +/- sqrt(((sigma_x-sigma_y)/2)^2 + tau_xy^2)
entries.example: For plane stress sigma_x = 100 MPa, sigma_y = 0, tau_xy = 0: von Mises sigma_eq = 100 MPa and Tresca equivalent is also 100 MPa, so both predict yielding at sigma_y = 100 MPa.
entries.subject: Manufacturing

entries.topic: Sand casting: patterns, gating and risers
entries.fact: Sand casting starts with a pattern, oversized by the shrinkage allowance and with draft so it withdraws cleanly from the mould. The gating system (pouring basin, sprue, runner, gates) fills the mould smoothly; the choke controls the filling rate. The casting solidifies from the walls inward and shrinks, so a riser — a reservoir of molten metal with a larger modulus (volume/surface area) than the casting — feeds the shrinkage and must solidify last, per Chvorinov's rule. Defects include porosity, cold shuts and misruns, checked by non-destructive testing.
entries.formula: Chvorinov's rule: solidification time t = C (V/A)^2; Riser modulus must exceed casting modulus: (V/A)_riser > (V/A)_casting; Pattern shrinkage allowance is about 1-2% for cast iron and steel
entries.example: A cube of side 100 mm has modulus V/A = 16.7 mm and solidifies in time proportional to 16.7^2; its riser needs a larger modulus so it freezes later.
entries.subject: Manufacturing

entries.topic: Bulk metal forming: forging, rolling, extrusion and drawing
entries.fact: Bulk forming shapes metal by plastic deformation above or below the recrystallisation temperature (hot, warm or cold working). Ideal work per volume is the area under the true stress-strain curve, and slab analysis adds friction to estimate the real load: forging load is roughly flow stress times projected area, with a friction factor. Rolling load depends on the contact length and mean flow stress; extrusion and wire drawing are analysed the same way, with redundant work raising the load. Common defects are laps, cracks, barrelling in forging and centre burst in drawing.
entries.formula: Ideal work per volume w = integral sigma d(epsilon); Forging load P approx sigma_f x A x (1 + mu factor); Rolling: contact length L = sqrt(R delta h); Flow stress sigma_f = K epsilon^n (strain hardening)
entries.example: Forging a disc of area 0.01 m^2 with flow stress 100 MPa needs an ideal load of about 100e6 x 0.01 = 1000 kN before friction is added.
entries.subject: Manufacturing

entries.fact: Welding joins metals by melting (fusion) or by pressure without melting (solid state). Arc processes dominate: SMAW (stick), GMAW/MIG, GTAW/TIG, plasma arc and submerged arc, each with its own heat source, shielding and deposition rate. Solid-state processes — friction, friction-stir and ultrasonic welding — join without melting the base metal. Weld defects include porosity, slag inclusion, undercut, lack of fusion and cracking, and heat-affected-zone cracking is checked by inspection. Brazing and soldering join with a filler metal that melts below the base metal.
entries.formula: Heat input per unit length H = (V I eta)/v, where eta is arc efficiency and v is travel speed; Higher heat input widens the heat-affected zone and slows cooling
entries.example: An arc at 25 V, 200 A, 70% efficiency and travel speed 5 mm/s gives heat input (25 x 200 x 0.7)/5 = 700 J/mm.
entries.subject: Manufacturing

entries.fact: In orthogonal cutting the tool edge is perpendicular to the cutting velocity and the chip forms by shear along a shear plane at angle phi. Merchant's circle relates the cutting force Fc, thrust force Ft, shear force and friction force on the rake face. The shear angle follows from the chip thickness ratio r = t1/t2, and specific cutting energy is cutting force per unit material removed. Machining parameters set the material removal rate, and tool materials, wear and cutting fluids decide tool life and surface quality.
entries.formula: tan phi = r cos(alpha)/(1 - r sin(alpha)); Shear force Fs = Fc cos phi - Ft sin phi; Material removal rate MRR = v f d; Specific cutting energy u = Fc/(f d)
entries.example: With rake angle 10 deg and chip thickness ratio r = 0.4: tan phi = 0.4 cos10/(1 - 0.4 sin10) = 0.423, so phi = 22.9 degrees.
entries.subject: Manufacturing

entries.topic: Non-traditional machining: EDM, ECM, USM, AJM, LBM and EBM
entries.fact: Non-traditional processes remove material without a conventional cutting edge, so they can machine very hard materials and complex shapes. EDM removes metal by electric sparks between tool and workpiece; wire EDM cuts profiles with a travelling wire. ECM dissolves metal anodically in an electrolyte, giving a stress-free surface. USM and AJM erode material with abrasive particles in a slurry or gas jet; LBM and EBM melt or vaporise material with a focused beam. Material removal rate, surface roughness and power consumption all depend on the process parameters, such as current in EDM or voltage in ECM.
entries.formula: ECM material removal: MRR = (A I)/(F rho z) in Faraday terms, i.e. mass removed proportional to current and time; EDM: MRR rises with discharge current and pulse on-time; USM: MRR rises with abrasive grain size and vibration amplitude
entries.example: ECM of iron (atomic weight 56, valency 2) at 1000 A removes mass at a rate proportional to 56 x 1000/(2 x 96485) = 0.29 g/s before efficiency losses.
entries.subject: Manufacturing

entries.topic: Computer integrated manufacturing: CAD/CAM, CNC and robots
entries.fact: CAD builds the geometric model of a part; CAM turns it into tool paths and CNC code (G-code) that drives the machine tool. A CNC machine positions the tool by programmed coordinates, giving repeatability that manual machines cannot match. Industrial robots — articulated, SCARA, Cartesian and cylindrical configurations — automate handling, welding and assembly, with drives and controls setting speed and accuracy. Group technology groups similar parts into families for cellular manufacturing, and flexible manufacturing systems link cells with automated material handling.
entries.formula: CNC positioning: absolute (G90) vs incremental (G91) coordinates; Robot degrees of freedom decide the reachable workspace; Group technology uses part-family coding to form manufacturing cells
entries.example: A CNC program line G01 X50 Y25 F100 moves the tool in a straight line to (50, 25) at a feed of 100 mm/min.
entries.subject: Manufacturing

entries.topic: Metrology: limits, fits, tolerances and gauge design
entries.fact: No part can be made exactly to size, so a tolerance band is specified around the nominal size. A fit describes how mating parts assemble: clearance fits always leave space, interference fits always overlap, and transition fits may do either. The hole-basis system is standard, with IT grades setting tolerance magnitude. Limit gauges check parts quickly: a GO gauge must enter and a NO-GO gauge must not, and Taylor's principle says the GO gauge checks the maximum-material condition over the full feature length while the NO-GO gauge checks a single cross-section.
entries.formula: Maximum clearance = max hole - min shaft; Maximum interference = max shaft - min hole; Tolerance = upper deviation - lower deviation; Gauge tolerance is about 10% of the work tolerance
entries.example: A 50 H7/g6 fit: the H7 hole is 50.000 to 50.025 mm and the g6 shaft is 49.975 to 49.991 mm, so clearance is always between 0.009 and 0.050 mm — a clearance fit.
entries.subject: Metrology

entries.fact: Surface finish is described by the roughness profile after form and waviness are filtered out. The common parameter Ra is the arithmetic average of absolute deviations from the mean line; Rz is the average of the five highest peaks and five deepest valleys. Roughness is measured by contact (stylus profilometer) or non-contact (optical interferometry) methods. Finish affects friction, wear, fatigue and sealing, and is specified with the lay and the sampling length.
entries.formula: Ra = (1/l) integral |y| dx over the sampling length; Rz = average of the five largest peak-to-valley heights; Rq = root mean square roughness
entries.example: A turned surface specified as Ra 1.6 microns is smoother than a rough-milled surface at Ra 6.3 microns; grinding is typically needed to reach Ra below 0.8 microns.
entries.subject: Metrology

entries.fact: Acceptance sampling inspects a sample from a lot and accepts or rejects the whole lot by a rule such as accept if defectives are at most c in a sample of n. The operating characteristic (OC) curve plots the probability of acceptance against the lot's fraction defective, summarised by the producer's risk (rejecting a good lot, at AQL) and the consumer's risk (accepting a bad lot, at LTPD). Single, double and multiple sampling plans trade inspection effort against discrimination.
entries.formula: OC curve: P(accept) = sum from d=0 to c of C(n,d) p^d (1-p)^(n-d) (binomial); Producer's risk alpha at AQL; Consumer's risk beta at LTPD
entries.example: A plan n = 50, c = 1 accepts a lot with 2% defectives with probability about (0.98)^50 + 50 x 0.02 x (0.98)^49 = 0.74.
entries.subject: Quality Control

entries.fact: Reliability R(t) is the probability that a system survives to time t. For a constant failure rate lambda (exponential life), R(t) = e^(-lambda t) and the mean time between failures MTBF = 1/lambda. Maintainability is captured by mean time to repair MTTR, and steady-state availability is MTBF/(MTBF + MTTR). System reliability follows from the configuration: series systems multiply reliabilities, parallel systems multiply unreliabilities. Preventive maintenance, predictive maintenance and total productive maintenance aim to raise availability and cut unplanned downtime.
entries.formula: Exponential reliability: R(t) = e^(-lambda t); MTBF = 1/lambda; Availability A = MTBF/(MTBF + MTTR); Series: R_sys = product of R_i; Parallel: R_sys = 1 - product of (1 - R_i)
entries.example: A machine with MTBF 500 h and MTTR 20 h has availability 500/520 = 0.962; two such machines in parallel have system reliability 1 - (1-0.9)^2 = 0.99 if each has R = 0.9.
entries.subject: Quality Control

entries.topic: Work study: method study and time study
entries.fact: Work study improves productivity by examining how work is done. Method study (Taylor, Gilbreth) records and questions the present method and designs a better one, using process charts and the principles of motion economy. Time study measures the work: observed time is rated for pace to give normal time, and allowances for fatigue, delays and personal needs give the standard time. Work sampling estimates the proportion of time spent on activities from random observations, and predetermined motion-time systems (PMTS) build times from basic motions.
entries.formula: Normal time = observed time x rating factor; Standard time = normal time x (1 + allowance fraction); Work sampling: proportion estimate p with standard error sqrt(p(1-p)/n)
entries.example: An operation observed at 2.0 min with a rating of 110% has normal time 2.2 min; with 15% allowances the standard time is 2.2 x 1.15 = 2.53 min.
entries.subject: Industrial Engineering

entries.topic: Facility design: plant layout and assembly line balancing
entries.fact: Plant layout arranges machines and workstations to minimise material movement: process layout groups similar machines, product layout follows the line, and cellular layout groups part families. Assembly line balancing assigns tasks to workstations so that each station's time is as close as possible to the cycle time, which is set by demand: cycle time = available time / required output. Balance efficiency is the total work content divided by the number of stations times the cycle time; the balance delay is what remains.
entries.formula: Cycle time C = available time per period / demand per period; Minimum stations = total work content / cycle time; Balance efficiency = total work content/(number of stations x cycle time); Balance delay = 1 - efficiency
entries.example: A line must make 480 units in an 8-hour shift: cycle time = 480/480 = 1 min/unit. With total work content 4.2 min, at least 5 stations are needed (4.2/1 = 4.2, rounded up).
entries.subject: Industrial Engineering

entries.topic: Production control: MRP, MRP-II and ERP
entries.fact: Material requirements planning explodes the master production schedule through the bill of materials, netting gross requirements against on-hand stock and scheduled receipts to time orders for components. MRP-II adds capacity planning and shop-floor control; ERP integrates the whole business — production, inventory, purchasing, finance and sales — in one system. Push systems (MRP) schedule from a plan, while pull systems (JIT/kanban) produce only on actual demand, and lean manufacturing targets the elimination of waste.
entries.formula: Net requirements = gross requirements - on-hand - scheduled receipts; Planned order release = net requirements offset backwards by lead time; MRP inputs: master production schedule, bill of materials, inventory records
entries.example: A product needing 2 units of part X per unit, with a schedule of 100 products and 50 X in stock, has gross requirement 200, net requirement 150, to be ordered one lead time ahead.
entries.subject: Industrial Engineering

entries.fact: The transportation problem ships from sources to destinations at minimum cost, subject to supply and demand. An initial basic feasible solution comes from the north-west corner, least-cost or Vogel's approximation method (VAM gives the best start); optimality is tested by the MODI (u-v) method, and degeneracy is handled when occupied cells are fewer than m+n-1. The assignment problem is the special case of one-to-one matching (one worker per job), solved in polynomial time by the Hungarian method.
entries.formula: Transportation: minimise sum c_ij x_ij subject to supply and demand constraints; Degeneracy when occupied cells < m + n - 1; Hungarian method: subtract row minima, then column minima, cover zeros with minimum lines, iterate to an assignment
entries.example: A 3-source, 4-destination problem needs 3+4-1 = 6 occupied cells for a non-degenerate basic feasible solution.
entries.subject: Operations Research

entries.fact: Queues are described by Kendall notation A/B/c: arrival process, service process and number of servers, with M for Markovian (Poisson arrivals, exponential service). The M/M/1 queue has utilisation rho = lambda/mu, average number in system L = rho/(1-rho) and average time in system W = 1/(mu - lambda), linked by Little's law L = lambda W. Stability needs rho < 1; multi-server M/M/c models follow the same logic with Erlang formulas.
entries.formula: M/M/1: utilisation rho = lambda/mu; L = rho/(1-rho); W = 1/(mu - lambda); Little's law: L = lambda W; Stability requires rho < 1
entries.example: A single-server counter with arrivals 10/hour and service 15/hour has rho = 0.67, average number in system L = 2, and average time in system W = 1/(15-10) = 0.2 h = 12 min.
entries.subject: Operations Research

entries.topic: Project management: PERT, CPM and Gantt charts
entries.fact: CPM schedules a project with known activity durations: the critical path is the longest chain through the network, it sets the project duration, and activities on it have zero float (slack). PERT handles uncertain durations with three estimates per activity — optimistic, most likely and pessimistic — and an expected time that weights the most likely estimate fourfold. The project variance is the sum of variances of critical activities, giving the probability of meeting a deadline from the normal distribution. Gantt charts show the same schedule as bars against time.
entries.formula: PERT expected time te = (to + 4 tm + tp)/6; Variance sigma^2 = ((tp - to)/6)^2; CPM: total float = latest start - earliest start; critical path has zero total float
entries.example: An activity with to = 4, tm = 7, tp = 16 days has te = (4+28+16)/6 = 8 days and standard deviation (16-4)/6 = 2 days.
entries.subject: Operations Research

entries.example: For a 2R planar arm with link lengths l1 = l2 = 1 m, det(J) = l1*l2*sin(theta2) = sin(theta2). At theta2 = 0 (arm fully stretched) or theta2 = 180 degrees (fully folded), det(J) = 0: the arm is singular and cannot move its tip in the radial direction, however large the joint torques.
entries.fact: A manipulator is at a singularity when its Jacobian loses rank, i.e. det(J) = 0 for a square Jacobian, so the end-effector loses the ability to move (or exert force) in some Cartesian direction. At a singularity, inverse kinematics has no unique solution and joint velocities needed for a given tip velocity blow up. Common types are wrist singularities (axes of joints 4 and 6 align), elbow singularities (arm fully stretched or folded) and shoulder singularities (wrist centre lies on the first joint axis).
entries.formula: Singularity when det(J(q)) = 0 (square J) or rank(J(q)) < min(6, n). For a 2R planar arm: det(J) = l1*l2*sin(theta2). Near a singularity, joint velocity qdot = J^(-1) * xdot grows without bound.
entries.subject: Kinematics

entries.example: A single pendulum link (point mass m = 2 kg at length l = 0.5 m): L = (1/2)*m*l^2*thetadot^2 + m*g*l*cos(theta). The equation of motion is m*l^2*thetaddot + m*g*l*sin(theta) = tau. At theta = 30 degrees the gravity torque to hold it still is m*g*l*sin(30) = 2*9.81*0.5*0.5 = 4.91 Nm.
entries.fact: Lagrangian dynamics derives a robot's equations of motion from energy, not from free-body diagrams. With generalised coordinates q, kinetic energy T and potential energy U, the Lagrangian is L = T - U, and each joint obeys the Euler-Lagrange equation. Collecting terms for all joints gives the manipulator equation, in which M(q) is the symmetric positive-definite inertia matrix, C(q, qdot) carries Coriolis and centrifugal effects, and g(q) is gravity. At rest only the gravity term remains, so tau = g(q) is the holding torque.
entries.formula: L = T - U; d/dt(dL/dqdot_i) - dL/dq_i = tau_i. Manipulator equation: M(q)*qddot + C(q, qdot)*qdot + g(q) = tau. Kinetic energy: T = (1/2)*qdot^T*M(q)*qdot.
entries.subject: Dynamics & Control
entries.topic: Lagrangian dynamics and the manipulator equation

entries.example: Holding a 5 kg link horizontally with its centre of mass 0.3 m from the joint: the static joint torque is m*g*r = 5*9.81*0.3 = 14.7 Nm. Newton-Euler computes this (and the dynamic torques) link by link instead of from one big energy expression, which is why it is the standard O(n) algorithm in robot controllers.
entries.fact: The Newton-Euler method derives the same equations of motion as Lagrange, but by applying Newton's law (F = m*a) and Euler's rotational law (N = I*alpha + omega x (I*omega)) to each link in turn. A forward recursion propagates velocities and accelerations from the base to the tip; a backward recursion propagates forces and moments from the tip to the base, giving the joint torques. It is computationally efficient (O(n) in the number of joints) and is the basis of the recursive Newton-Euler algorithm used for inverse dynamics in real controllers.
entries.formula: Newton: F = m*a_cm. Euler: N = I*alpha + omega x (I*omega). Inverse dynamics (RNEA): given q, qdot, qddot, the recursion returns tau; forward dynamics: qddot = M(q)^(-1)*(tau - C(q, qdot)*qdot - g(q)).
entries.subject: Dynamics & Control

entries.example: Choose Kp = 100, Kd = 20 for one joint. The error dynamics are eddot + 20*edot + 100*e = 0, i.e. natural frequency wn = sqrt(100) = 10 rad/s and damping ratio zeta = Kd/(2*sqrt(Kp)) = 20/20 = 1, so the tracking error decays critically damped, with no overshoot.
entries.fact: Computed-torque (inverse-dynamics) control cancels the robot's nonlinear dynamics by feeding back the model: the controller computes the torque that would make the arm behave like a set of independent double integrators, then adds PD terms on the tracking error. If the model is exact, each joint's error obeys a linear second-order equation, so Kp and Kd can be set from a desired natural frequency and damping ratio. Its weakness is model error: wrong masses or friction leave residual dynamics, so in practice it is combined with robust or adaptive terms.
entries.formula: tau = M(q)*(qddot_d + Kp*e + Kd*edot) + C(q, qdot)*qdot + g(q), where e = q_d - q. Ideal error dynamics: eddot + Kd*edot + Kp*e = 0. Damping ratio: zeta = Kd/(2*sqrt(Kp)); wn = sqrt(Kp).
entries.subject: Dynamics & Control

entries.example: For a PD-controlled joint with error e and error rate edot, take V = (1/2)*edot^2 + (1/2)*Kp*e^2 (kinetic-like plus potential-like energy). Then Vdot = -Kd*edot^2 <= 0, so the energy never grows and the equilibrium e = 0 is stable; with Kd > 0 the error decays.
entries.fact: Lyapunov stability proves a control system is stable without solving its differential equations: find a positive-definite energy-like function V (V = 0 only at the equilibrium, V > 0 elsewhere) and show its time derivative Vdot <= 0 along trajectories. If Vdot is strictly negative (except at the equilibrium), the equilibrium is asymptotically stable. The classical Routh-Hurwitz criterion is the complementary algebraic test: a linear system's characteristic polynomial has all roots in the left half-plane (stable) iff all entries in the first column of the Routh array are positive.
entries.formula: Lyapunov: V(x) > 0 for x != 0, V(0) = 0, and Vdot(x) <= 0 => stable; Vdot(x) < 0 for x != 0 => asymptotically stable. Routh-Hurwitz: stability iff the first column of the Routh array has no sign changes.
entries.subject: Dynamics & Control

entries.example: A DC servo motor with torque constant Kt = 0.1 Nm/A driven at 3 A produces tau = 0.1*3 = 0.3 Nm. A 200-step-per-revolution stepper motor moves 360/200 = 1.8 degrees per step, so 50 steps rotate it 90 degrees, with no position sensor needed if no steps are missed.
entries.fact: Robot joints are usually driven by DC servo motors (brushed or brushless) through a gearbox, because they give smooth, controllable torque proportional to current and are easily closed-loop controlled with an encoder. The back-EMF grows with speed, so at high speed less voltage is left to drive current and torque falls. Stepper motors move in fixed angular steps and hold position open-loop, which suits low-cost positioning, but they lose steps under overload and are noisier and less efficient than servos at high speed. Gear reduction multiplies torque by the gear ratio (and divides speed), at the cost of added friction and backlash.
entries.formula: DC motor: tau = Kt*I; back-EMF Eb = Ke*omega; V = I*R + Eb (steady state). Stepper step angle = 360 degrees / steps per revolution. Gearbox: tau_out = N*tau_motor, omega_out = omega_motor/N (ideal, N = gear ratio).
entries.subject: Sensors & Actuators

entries.example: A 1024-pulse-per-revolution incremental encoder with quadrature decoding gives 4*1024 = 4096 counts per revolution, so the angular resolution is 360/4096 = 0.088 degrees per count. An absolute encoder instead reports the exact angle at power-on, with no homing move needed.
entries.fact: An encoder measures joint angle: an optical or magnetic disc with slots interrupts a light beam (or changes a magnetic field) as it turns, producing pulses. Incremental encoders count pulses from a reference mark, so they lose absolute position at power-off and need homing; quadrature decoding (two channels A and B, 90 degrees apart) gives direction and four counts per pulse period. Absolute encoders output a unique code for each angle, so position is known immediately. A resolver is a rugged analogue alternative that outputs sine/cosine signals proportional to angle and survives harsh factory environments better than optical encoders.
entries.formula: Resolution (degrees) = 360 / counts per revolution. Quadrature counts per rev = 4 * pulses per rev (PPR). Angle = counts * (360 / counts per rev).
entries.subject: Sensors & Actuators
entries.topic: Encoders and resolvers for position sensing

entries.example: A wrist force sensor reads 10 N of contact force applied 0.2 m from the joint axis: the joint feels a torque of tau = r x F = 0.2*10 = 2 Nm. A controller can use that reading to cap contact force, e.g. to stop before damaging a part or hurting a person.
entries.fact: Force/torque sensors, usually strain-gauge based, measure the six components of force and moment at the wrist or in a joint, enabling force control, assembly (peg-in-hole), and safe human-robot contact. Tactile sensors measure distributed pressure over a gripper surface, proximity sensors (ultrasonic, infrared, capacitive) detect nearby objects without contact, and vision (cameras) gives the richest sensing but needs processing. Sensor choice trades accuracy, bandwidth, cost and robustness.
entries.formula: Torque from a force at a distance: tau = r x F (magnitude r*F*sin(theta)). Strain-gauge bridge output is proportional to applied strain, hence to force.
entries.subject: Sensors & Actuators

entries.example: A pneumatic cylinder at 6 bar (600,000 Pa) with a 50 mm bore (area pi*0.025^2 = 0.00196 m2) pushes with F = P*A = 600,000*0.00196 = 1,178 N, about 1.18 kN. The same force from a hydraulic cylinder needs far less area because hydraulic pressure is typically 100-200 bar.
entries.fact: Pneumatic actuators use compressed air (typically 5-7 bar): they are fast, clean, cheap and safe in explosive atmospheres, but air is compressible, so force and position control are soft and imprecise. Hydraulic actuators use pressurised oil (typically 100-200 bar): they deliver very large forces in a compact size and are stiff and precise, but need pumps, seals and maintenance and can leak. The choice is force and precision (hydraulic) versus speed, cleanliness and cost (pneumatic); electric servos beat both on controllability.
entries.formula: Actuator force: F = P*A, where P is pressure and A is piston area. Cylinder speed: v = Q/A, where Q is volume flow rate.
entries.subject: Sensors & Actuators

entries.example: A 2R planar arm has two joint angles, so its configuration space is a torus: each angle wraps around at 360 degrees, and the point (350 degrees, 10 degrees) is adjacent to (0 degrees, 10 degrees). An obstacle in the workspace becomes a forbidden region in this torus, and a valid motion is a continuous curve that stays in the free part.
entries.fact: The configuration space (C-space) is the space of all joint configurations q of a robot; for an n-joint arm it is n-dimensional. Obstacles in the workspace map to forbidden regions C_obs in C-space, and the free space C_free is everything else. Motion planning is then a geometric problem in C-space: find a continuous path from the start configuration to the goal that stays inside C_free. The workspace is where the task is described; the C-space is where the planning is done, because joint limits and self-collision are simple bounds there.
entries.formula: C-space: q in R^n (or a torus for revolute joints). C = C_free union C_obs. A valid path is a continuous curve q(t) with q(t) in C_free for all t, q(0) = q_start, q(1) = q_goal.
entries.subject: Motion Planning

entries.example: An RRT planning for a mobile robot samples a random point, finds the nearest tree node, and extends one step of size 0.1 m toward it. After a few thousand iterations the tree has spread through the free space and reached the goal region, even in a cluttered room where a grid search would be far too large.
entries.fact: Sampling-based planners avoid building the C-space explicitly. RRT (Rapidly-exploring Random Tree) grows a tree from the start by sampling random configurations, steering a small step from the nearest tree node toward each sample, and keeping the step if it is collision-free; it is fast and explores large spaces well, but the path is jagged and only probabilistically complete. PRM (Probabilistic Roadmap) instead samples many collision-free configurations, connects nearby ones into a roadmap graph, and then searches the graph with A*; the roadmap can be reused for many queries in the same environment. RRT* rewires the tree to converge toward the optimal path.
entries.formula: RRT step: q_new = q_near + eta*(q_rand - q_near)/||q_rand - q_near||, kept only if the segment q_near to q_new is collision-free. PRM: roadmap graph G = (V, E) of sampled free configurations; query = graph search (e.g. A*) from q_start to q_goal.
entries.subject: Motion Planning

entries.example: With attractive gain k_att = 1 and the robot 2 m from the goal, U_att = (1/2)*1*2^2 = 2 and the attractive force magnitude is k_att*2 = 2 (in force units), pulling it toward the goal. The classic failure is a U-shaped obstacle: the repulsive push balances the attraction and the robot stalls in a local minimum short of the goal.
entries.fact: Artificial potential fields plan by treating the goal as an attractor and obstacles as repellers: the robot follows the negative gradient of the total potential, i.e. it rolls downhill. The method is simple, fast and reactive, so it is popular for mobile-robot obstacle avoidance. Its main flaw is local minima, where attractive and repulsive forces cancel away from the goal and the robot gets stuck; narrow passages and oscillations near obstacles are other known problems. It is a local method, unlike RRT/PRM which plan globally.
entries.formula: U_att(q) = (1/2)*k_att*||q - q_goal||^2. U_rep(q) = (1/2)*k_rep*(1/d - 1/d0)^2 if d < d0, else 0, where d is distance to the nearest obstacle and d0 the influence range. U_total = U_att + U_rep; motion follows F = -grad(U_total).
entries.subject: Motion Planning

entries.example: Move one joint from 0 to 90 degrees (pi/2 = 1.571 rad) in tf = 2 s, at rest at both ends, with a cubic polynomial: a0 = 0, a1 = 0, a2 = 3*(1.571)/2^2 = 1.178, a3 = -2*(1.571)/2^3 = -0.393, so q(t) = 1.178*t^2 - 0.393*t^3. Peak velocity is 1.5*(1.571)/2 = 1.18 rad/s at t = 1 s. A trapezoidal profile would instead accelerate at constant amax, cruise at vmax, then decelerate, which respects velocity and acceleration limits directly.
entries.fact: A path is the geometry of the motion; a trajectory adds the timing law. In joint space, a cubic polynomial fits position and velocity at both ends (four conditions, four coefficients) and gives smooth position and velocity, but acceleration jumps at the ends. A quintic polynomial also fixes the end accelerations (six conditions). The trapezoidal velocity profile is the industrial workhorse: constant acceleration, constant velocity, constant deceleration, which makes it easy to respect vmax and amax, but acceleration is discontinuous at the phase switches. Via points are handled by joining polynomial segments with continuous velocity.
entries.formula: Cubic: q(t) = a0 + a1*t + a2*t^2 + a3*t^3, with q(0) = q0, q(tf) = qf, qdot(0) = v0, qdot(tf) = vf. Rest-to-rest: a0 = q0, a1 = 0, a2 = 3*(qf - q0)/tf^2, a3 = -2*(qf - q0)/tf^3; peak velocity = 1.5*(qf - q0)/tf. Trapezoidal: distance = (1/2)*vmax*(tf + t_cruise), where t_cruise is the constant-velocity time.
entries.subject: Trajectory Planning
entries.topic: Joint-space trajectory planning: cubic, quintic and trapezoidal profiles

entries.example: In a bottling plant, field sensors and actuators wire into PLCs that run the filling sequence in real time; the SCADA system in the control room shows tank levels and line speed on one screen, logs every batch, and raises an alarm if a tank runs low, while the plant MES above it schedules the day's orders.
entries.fact: Industrial automation is organised in layers: field devices (sensors, actuators) at the bottom, PLCs and controllers doing real-time control, SCADA (Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition) monitoring, logging and alarming from a control room, then MES for production scheduling and ERP for business planning. SCADA supervises but does not replace the PLC's real-time loop: if SCADA goes down, the PLCs keep running the process. Modern plants link these layers over industrial Ethernet and fieldbus networks.
entries.formula: Automation hierarchy (bottom to top): field devices -> PLC / DCS (real-time control) -> SCADA (supervision, logging, alarms) -> MES (production management) -> ERP (business planning). Rule: SCADA monitors and commands; the PLC controls.
entries.subject: Automation & PLC
entries.topic: SCADA and the industrial automation hierarchy

entries.example: Question: 'The author mentions X mainly to...' — the correct answer is the option that matches the paragraph's function, not the one that merely repeats a detail. Skim the passage first for structure (thesis, evidence, conclusion), read the question stem, then scan back for the exact lines that answer it; never pick an option that uses passage words but reverses the author's stance.
entries.fact: Reading comprehension in GATE GA is about function, not memory: most questions ask for the main idea, the author's purpose, an inference, or the meaning of a word in context. Read for structure first — what is the claim, what is the evidence, what is the conclusion — and treat each paragraph as doing one job. Eliminate options that are too extreme (always, never), out of scope, or true statements that do not answer the question asked. For vocabulary-in-context, substitute each option back into the sentence and keep the one that preserves the meaning.
entries.formula: RC method: skim for structure -> read the question stem -> locate the relevant lines -> eliminate extreme/out-of-scope options -> verify the chosen option against the text. Inference = what must be true from the passage, not what could be true.
entries.subject: Verbal Aptitude

entries.example: A price rises 20% then falls 20%: 100 -> 120 -> 96, a net change of -4%, not 0%. A ratio problem: if A:B = 3:4 and B:C = 5:7, then A:B:C = 15:20:28 (make B common: multiply the first ratio by 5 and the second by 4). If 40% of a class of 250 are girls, there are 0.4*250 = 100 girls.
entries.fact: Percentage change is always relative to the starting value, so successive changes do not cancel: a +x% change followed by -x% leaves a net loss of (x/100)^2 of the original. Ratio problems are solved by making the common term equal across ratios, and mixture/alligation problems by weighted averages. In GATE GA, convert percentages to fractions early (25% = 1/4, 12.5% = 1/8) to keep the arithmetic mental.
entries.formula: Percentage change = (new - old)/old * 100%. Successive +x% then -x%: net = -x^2/100 %. Ratio A:B = a:b means A = a/(a+b) of the total. Weighted average = (w1*x1 + w2*x2)/(w1 + w2).
entries.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

entries.example: Choose a 3-member team from 10 people: C(10,3) = 10!/(3!*7!) = 120 ways. Arrange 3 distinct books on a shelf: P(3,3) = 3! = 6 ways; arrange 3 out of 5 books: P(5,3) = 5*4*3 = 60. If a password uses 2 distinct letters from 26, there are P(26,2) = 26*25 = 650 possibilities.
entries.fact: Use permutations when order matters (arrangements, rankings, passwords) and combinations when it does not (teams, selections, committees). The key check is: swap two chosen items — if the result is a different outcome, it is a permutation; if it is the same outcome, it is a combination. Remember C(n,r) = C(n,n-r), which halves the work when r is large, and that arrangements with repeated items divide by the factorials of the repeat counts.
entries.formula: P(n,r) = n!/(n-r)! (order matters). C(n,r) = n!/(r!*(n-r)!) (order does not matter). C(n,r) = C(n,n-r). With repeats: arrangements of n items with repeats a, b = n!/(a!*b!).
entries.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

entries.example: Statements: All cats are animals. All animals need food. Conclusion 'All cats need food' follows (chain of All statements). Conclusion 'Some cats are animals' also follows, since All implies Some for a non-empty group. But from 'Some animals are black' alone, 'Some cats are black' does NOT follow — the black animals might all be dogs.
entries.fact: A syllogism tests whether a conclusion must follow from the given statements, assuming the statements are true even if they contradict real-world facts. Draw Venn diagrams: 'All A are B' puts circle A inside B; 'Some A are B' means the circles overlap; 'No A is B' means they are disjoint. A conclusion is valid only if it holds in every diagram consistent with the statements — test it by trying to draw a counterexample. 'All' implies 'Some' (for non-empty sets), but 'Some' never implies 'All'.
entries.formula: Validity rule: a conclusion is valid only if it is true in every Venn diagram consistent with the statements. All A are B + All B are C => All A are C. Some A are B does not imply Some A are not B, nor All A are B.
entries.subject: Logical Reasoning

entries.example: Blood relation: A is the brother of B, and B is the mother of C, so A is the maternal uncle of C. Coding-decoding: if CAT is coded as 3-1-20 (letter positions), then DOG is 4-15-7; if CAT is coded as DBU (each letter shifted +1), then DOG is coded as EPH.
entries.fact: Blood-relation questions are solved by drawing a family tree with one symbol per person and labelling each link (father, mother, brother, sister, son, daughter); 'maternal' means the mother's side, 'paternal' the father's side, and a person's spouse is an in-law, not a blood relative. Coding-decoding questions usually use letter positions (A=1 ... Z=26), a fixed shift (Caesar cipher), reversal, or a letter-to-number substitution — test the given example against each pattern before applying it to the target word.
entries.formula: Letter positions: A=1, B=2, ..., Z=26. Caesar shift: coded letter = plain letter shifted by k positions (wrap Z to A). Blood-relation rule: draw the tree first; never reason in words alone.
entries.subject: Logical Reasoning

entries.example: Quarterly sales: Q1 120, Q2 150, Q3 180, Q4 200 (total 650). Q4's share is 200/650 = 30.8%. Growth from Q3 to Q4 is (200-180)/180 = 11.1%. If a pie chart shows Q4 as 30.8% of a total of 650, the angle is 0.308*360 = 111 degrees.
entries.fact: Data interpretation questions give a table, bar chart, line graph or pie chart and ask for totals, shares, growth rates, averages or the maximum/minimum category. Always read the units and the base first — a percentage of what? — and estimate before calculating exactly, since GATE options are usually far apart. For pie charts, share and angle are the same information: angle = share * 360 degrees. For line graphs, the steepest segment is the fastest growth, not necessarily the largest value.
entries.formula: Share = part/total * 100%. Growth rate = (new - old)/old * 100%. Pie-chart angle = share * 360 degrees. Average = total/n. Read the units and the base before computing anything.
entries.subject: Data Interpretation

entries.example: A train at 60 km/h covers 60*2.5 = 150 km in 2.5 hours. Two trains 300 km apart approach each other at 60 and 90 km/h: relative speed 150 km/h, so they meet after 300/150 = 2 hours, 120 km from the first train's start. A boat's downstream speed is boat + stream; upstream is boat - stream.
entries.fact: Time-speed-distance is one equation with three quantities: knowing any two gives the third. Convert units first: km/h to m/s multiply by 5/18, m/s to km/h multiply by 18/5. When two objects move toward each other, add their speeds (relative speed); when one chases another, subtract them. Average speed over a journey is total distance divided by total time, not the average of the speeds, unless equal distances are covered at each speed.
entries.formula: Distance = speed * time. Relative speed: approaching = v1 + v2; chasing = |v1 - v2|. km/h to m/s: multiply by 5/18. Average speed = total distance / total time. For equal distances at speeds v1, v2: average speed = 2*v1*v2/(v1 + v2).
entries.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

entries.example: Two fair dice: P(sum = 7) = 6/36 = 1/6, since the favourable pairs are (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1). Drawing one card from a deck: P(ace) = 4/52 = 1/13; P(red card) = 26/52 = 1/2. P(at least one head in 2 tosses) = 1 - P(no heads) = 1 - 1/4 = 3/4.
entries.fact: For equally likely outcomes, probability is favourable outcomes divided by total outcomes. The complement rule is the fastest shortcut in aptitude: P(at least one) = 1 - P(none). For independent events, P(A and B) = P(A)*P(B); for mutually exclusive events, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B); in general P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B). 'With replacement' keeps probabilities constant across draws; 'without replacement' changes them after each draw.
entries.formula: P(E) = favourable outcomes / total outcomes. P(not E) = 1 - P(E). Independent: P(A and B) = P(A)*P(B). General: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B). Conditional: P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B).
entries.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

entries.fact: Simple interest (SI) is charged only on the principal, so it grows linearly. Compound interest (CI) is charged on principal plus accumulated interest, so it grows exponentially — the interest itself earns interest. For the same principal, rate and time (more than 1 year), CI is always greater than SI.
entries.formula: SI = P*R*T/100. Amount with SI: A = P(1 + R*T/100). CI amount: A = P*(1 + R/100)^T. CI = A - P. Difference (2 years): CI - SI = P*(R/100)^2.
entries.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
